As he pushes open the gate and passes up the wide white walk, he sees a flutter of female garments; his wife, looking fresh and cool and sweet, steps down from the veranda to meet him. At the bottom of the steps she stands waiting, with a smile of ineffable joy, an attitude of matchless grace and dignity. Ah, how beautiful she is! He springs forward with extended arms. As he is about to clasp her he feels a stunning blow upon the back of the neck; a blinding white light shines all about him with a sound like the shock of a cannon—then all is darkness and silence! Peyton Farquhar was dead; his body, with a broken neck, swung gently from side to side beneath the timbers of the Owl Creek bridge.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The story is told in three parts, and each does something different. In the first, we watch an execution in northern Alabama during the Civil War. A man stands on a railroad bridge with his hands tied behind him and a rope around his neck. Soldiers in Federal uniform go about the grim business with stiff formality. Bierce's narrator remarks that death is a dignitary who, when he comes announced, is to be received with formal manifestations of respect. The condemned man looks at the water below, thinks of his wife and children, and a plank is pulled away.

The second part steps back. The man is Peyton Farquhar, a well-to-do Alabama planter, a slave owner and an ardent supporter of the Southern cause, who could not serve in the army and has wished for a chance to help. One evening a gray-clad soldier stops at his gate and tells him that Union forces are repairing the railroad, and that anyone caught tampering with the Owl Creek bridge will be hanged. Farquhar eagerly asks what a man might do, and the soldier points out the pile of dry driftwood against the bridge before riding away. He was, we learn, a Federal scout, and Farquhar has been tricked into a trap.

In the third part the rope seems to break. Farquhar drops into the river, frees his hands, tears the noose from his neck, and swims under a hail of rifle fire. His senses are sharpened beyond belief. He sees each leaf and each insect, the dewdrops on the grass, even the gray eye of a marksman. He escapes into the forest, wanders for a day and a night, and at last reaches his own gate, where his wife comes down the steps to meet him with a smile of joy. As he reaches for her, he feels a blow on his neck, a white light, and then darkness. His body is swinging beneath the bridge.

The twist is that the whole escape, which seems to take hours, took place in the instant between the drop and the rope's end. It was a dream of survival, a last flash of hope in a dying mind. Bierce has planted clues: the strange metallic sound Farquhar hears as he falls, which turns out to be his watch ticking slowly in his stretched perception; the swollen neck and tongue, which are signs of a hanged man and not a swimmer; the road that seems unreal and the stars that seem to be in strange patterns.

What it means goes beyond the trick. Farquhar's fantasy is a romantic adventure story, a hero outwitting the enemy and returning to his family. That is exactly the type of war fantasy Bierce despised. The narrative lets the reader enjoy it, and then takes it away. The story says that the way people dream of war, as escape, glory and homecoming, is a lie told in the last seconds before the truth arrives.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
As a piece of craft, An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge is dazzling, though it is also a story whose fame rests heavily on one device, and that device deserves scrutiny.

The great achievement is the manipulation of time. Bierce stretches a single second into pages of vivid narration, and he does it so convincingly that most first-time readers believe in the escape completely. He does this by making the third section feel more real than the first. The details of the river, the sensation of being underwater, the pain, the sharpness of sight, are so specific that we do not stop to ask whether they are plausible. In a sense, he plays on the way our own minds work, accepting what is vividly described.

He also plays fair. The clues are there on a second reading, and this is what separates a great twist from a cheap one. The sound like a blacksmith's hammer, slowed to the pace of a death knell, is a lovely touch, since it is really his own watch, stretched out by his dying mind. The surreal clarity of the forest, the sense that the road is endless, and the physical wounds all stand as quiet signals. A twist that makes the reader want to go back and read again is the best kind.

The prose is also controlled. Bierce writes in a cool, almost clinical voice, which makes the horror sharper. The opening, with its careful physical description of the bridge, the planks, the sentinels, is like a stage direction. Only gradually does the narrator's irony appear, as in the remark that this was evidently no vulgar assassin, since the liberal military code makes provision for hanging gentlemen too.

Now the weaknesses. First, the story is partly a one-trick piece. Once you know the ending, some of its force fades, and it can feel like a clever mechanism more than a deep exploration of a human being. Farquhar himself is thinly drawn. We learn that he is a planter and that his wife and children are dear to him, and little else. The story is more interested in the structure of his experience than in who he is.

Second, the middle section is stiff. The scene in which the scout deceives Farquhar is functional and a bit contrived, and Farquhar's gullibility is hard to believe in a man so devoted to the cause.

Third, the language of the escape sometimes becomes overwrought. Bierce's flourishes of fantasy, his visions of an enchanted forest, can feel like a writer stretching to impress. Yet in the end these flaws are small. The story achieves what it sets out to do with almost frightening precision, and its best passages, the sound, the silence and the final blow, are among the finest in American short fiction.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
When Bierce published this story in the San Francisco Examiner in July 1890, he was already well known as a columnist. The next year he gathered it in a collection called Tales of Soldiers and Civilians, the book that later made his reputation as a fiction writer. Over time it became his most famous work, outshining even his satirical Devil's Dictionary, though the two share the same sardonic worldview.

In literary history, the story is often seen as an early example of realistic war writing in America. Before Bierce, much Civil War fiction was sentimental and patriotic. His tales, written by a man who had actually smelled the smoke, showed the war as chaotic, senseless and often ironic. This helped open a path for later war writers. Stephen Crane's The Red Badge of Courage, which appeared in 1895, belongs to the same new, unromantic spirit, and later writers about the First World War and beyond inherited the same suspicion of heroics.

The story's most obvious legacy is the structure it popularized. The idea that an apparently real sequence is actually the dream of a dying person has been used countless times. It is often called the Owl Creek device, or the Owl Creek twist. Films, television shows and novels have returned to it. The 1990 film Jacob's Ladder uses it in a way that is easily recognized, and other stories that reveal a protagonist to be dead or dreaming owe a debt to Bierce, whether directly or through intermediaries.

The most celebrated adaptation is the French short film La Riviere du hibou, directed by Robert Enrico in 1962. It won prizes at Cannes and then the Academy Award for best live-action short in 1964. It was also shown on American television in the Twilight Zone series that same year, introducing the story to a new audience. The film is remarkable for how it handles time, using sound, repetition and stretched time to turn the escape into a kind of dream.

In the classroom, the story is a staple of American literature courses, taught both as a model of irony and as a gateway to discussions of the Civil War and of point of view. It is also a favorite example in creative writing classes for teaching the unreliable perspective, since the reader's belief is deliberately manipulated.

Finally, the story contributed to the myth of Bierce himself. His disappearance in Mexico in 1913 or 1914, at the age of seventy-one, left a mystery that has fed novels, films and speculation, and his own vanishing has become part of how readers think about the story's fascination with unknowable ends.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers have loved this story, above all, for its ending. Few endings in the short story hit as hard. The sudden shift from a joyful reunion to a broken neck swinging under the bridge is a shock that people remember all their lives, and many describe the feeling of reading the last paragraph as like falling through a floor. It is rare for a twist to be both surprising and inevitable, and that combination is much of the story's charm.

They also admire the way it dramatizes consciousness. Anyone who has experienced a sudden accident, a fall, or a moment of danger knows that time seems to stretch and the senses seem to sharpen. Bierce captures this in a way that feels uncannily true. The passage in which Farquhar sees every leaf, every insect and every drop of dew resonates with readers because it matches something real about the mind in crisis, even if the story pushes it to an extreme.

Another source of admiration is Bierce's cool irony. Readers like the way he describes grim matters with dry wit. The formal ritual of the execution, the sentinels like statues, the comment on the dignity of death, all create a distinctive tone of sardonic gravity. For those who enjoy a writer with an edge, Bierce is a treat.

Many readers also love the story's economy. At only a few thousand words, it contains a whole structure of shock and reversal. It is a favorite of people who want to learn how stories work, since it shows how structure can be the meaning. The three-part design, the careful placing of clues, and the way the narrator withholds information are all highly instructive.

There is, too, an emotional pull that some may not expect from such a cold writer. Farquhar's longing for his wife and children is real, and the moment when he nearly reaches them is heartbreaking. Even readers who find his politics repugnant often feel pity for him as he dies in the grip of that hope. The story invites us to feel that pity without excusing him, and that is a delicate thing to achieve.

Finally, readers love to reread it. The same story reads differently the second time, when every detail becomes a clue. Few stories reward a second reading so thoroughly. It becomes a kind of puzzle box, and discovering how carefully it was built is a pleasure in itself.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
For a story so often anthologized, An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge has met a number of real objections, and some of them are worth taking seriously.

The first is the charge that the twist is a gimmick. Some critics and readers feel that the story is built entirely to deliver its surprise, and that once the surprise is known, little remains. Over the decades, the device has been used so often that it has become a cliche, and some people hold the original responsible for the copies. A related complaint is that the dream ending cheats, since the reader has been led to believe in events that never happened. Defenders respond that Bierce plants fair clues, but the sense of being tricked remains for some.

A second criticism concerns characterization. Farquhar is more a type than a person, and the story gives him little inner life beyond his hope of escape. His wife and children are barely sketched, appearing mostly as a vision. A reader who wants psychological depth may find the story shallow, a brilliant structure with little inside it.

A third complaint concerns the style. Bierce's prose can be stiff and ornate, with a nineteenth-century formality that some find dated. The long descriptive passages and the heavy irony can slow the story, and the language of the escape section has been called overwrought.

Then there is the question of moral perspective, which has grown more prominent. Farquhar is a slave owner and an ardent secessionist, and the story offers him as a figure of some sympathy, even as it mocks his illusions. Modern readers sometimes wonder how to take this. Is Bierce asking us to feel for a man who fought to preserve slavery? The story does not dwell on slavery, mentions it only in passing, and its main target is the romance of war itself, not the cause of either side. Some critics find that this narrow focus lets the reader avoid the larger moral questions. Others argue that the irony cuts both ways, since the Union scout wins by a trick that is itself hardly noble.

Finally, some have noted that the story is more a technical feat than an emotional or political statement, and that Bierce's cynicism, though bracing, can feel cold. In his stories, nobody is saved, and the universe offers no meaning. For readers who prefer consolation, this can be hard to bear. But that coldness is also what makes the story unforgettable, and few critics deny its power even when they quarrel with its method.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge sits at a crossing of several traditions. It is, first, part of the American short story as it developed in the nineteenth century, a form shaped by Edgar Allan Poe, who insisted that a story should aim at a single effect. Bierce admired Poe's tales of horror and obsession, and Owl Creek reads like a Poe story of the mind under pressure, but with the supernatural replaced by psychology. It also belongs to the realist and naturalist movements, which rejected sentimentality and saw human beings as small creatures caught in forces beyond their control.

In the story of war literature, it stands as a bridge between the romantic accounts that dominated after the Civil War and the bleaker work that followed. Crane's Red Badge of Courage, Hemingway's tales of the First World War, and later fiction by writers such as Tim O'Brien, in The Things They Carried, all inherit something from Bierce's suspicion that heroism is a story told after the fact, and that war leaves private, distorted memories. Bierce's other war stories, such as Chickamauga, with its child wandering among the dying, are equally dark, and together they form one of the most unsparing portraits of the Civil War.

In terms of technique, the story is a landmark in the use of subjective time. Later writers of stream of consciousness, like Virginia Woolf and James Joyce, would explore how the mind stretches and compresses moments, though in a very different mode. Closer in spirit are stories that dwell on a single instant of death or crisis. The Argentine writer Jorge Luis Borges, in The Secret Miracle, imagines a condemned man granted a year of thought in the instant before the firing squad, a story that is a clear cousin of Bierce's, and it shows how the idea traveled across cultures.

The film tradition also owes it a great deal. Beyond Jacob's Ladder, one can think of movies and episodes that hinge on the revelation that the protagonist's journey happens in the mind at the moment of death. Whether or not they acknowledge it, they work in Bierce's shadow.

Why does it matter today? Because it is a perfectly shaped story that you can read in twenty minutes, and because it asks questions that have not gone away. How do we narrate our own endings? What lies do we tell ourselves about violence and glory? The story invites us to enjoy a thrilling escape and then makes us feel the cost of enjoying it. It is a short, hard lesson in how stories deceive, and why that matters.

stories.keyContext: Ambrose Bierce published An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge in 1890, in a San Francisco newspaper. It is one of the most famous short stories ever written about the American Civil War, and one of the most famous surprise endings in all of fiction. Bierce knew his subject firsthand. He enlisted in the Union Army as a young man, fought at Shiloh and other bloody battles, and was badly wounded in the head. He came out of the war with a sharp tongue and little patience for the romantic way many Americans liked to talk about glory and sacrifice. Later he became a feared journalist, called Bitter Bierce, and in 1913 he vanished into Mexico for good. The story follows a condemned man on a railroad bridge in Alabama, and what happens in the seconds around his execution. Pay attention to time and to sound. It is a story about how the mind behaves at the edge of death, and about the gap between how war is imagined and what it does.

stories.title: A Haunted House
stories.author: Virginia Woolf
stories.epigraph: “Oh, is this your buried treasure? The light in the heart.”
paragraphs: Whatever hour you woke there was a door shutting. From room to room they went, hand in hand, lifting here, opening there, making sure—a ghostly couple.
“Here we left it,” she said. And he added, “Oh, but here too!” “It’s upstairs,” she murmured. “And in the garden,” he whispered. “Quietly,” they said, “or we shall wake them.”

But it wasn’t that you woke us. Oh, no. “They’re looking for it; they’re drawing the curtain,” one might say, and so read on a page or two. “Now they’ve found it,” one would be certain, stopping the pencil on the margin. And then, tired of reading, one might rise and see for oneself, the house all empty, the doors standing open, only the wood pigeons bubbling with content and the hum of the threshing machine sounding from the farm. “What did I come in here for? What did I want to find?” My hands were empty. “Perhaps it’s upstairs then?” The apples were in the loft. And so down again, the garden still as ever, only the book had slipped into the grass.

But they had found it in the drawing room. Not that one could ever see them. The window panes reflected apples, reflected roses; all the leaves were green in the glass. If they moved in the drawing room, the apple only turned its yellow side. Yet, the moment after, if the door was opened, spread about the floor, hung upon the walls, pendant from the ceiling—what? My hands were empty. The shadow of a thrush crossed the carpet; from the deepest wells of silence the wood pigeon drew its bubble of sound. “Safe, safe, safe,” the pulse of the house beat softly. “The treasure buried; the room . . .” the pulse stopped short. Oh, was that the buried treasure?

A moment later the light had faded. Out in the garden then? But the trees spun darkness for a wandering beam of sun. So fine, so rare, coolly sunk beneath the surface the beam I sought always burnt behind the glass. Death was the glass; death was between us; coming to the woman first, hundreds of years ago, leaving the house, sealing all the windows; the rooms were darkened. He left it, left her, went North, went East, saw the stars turned in the Southern sky; sought the house, found it dropped beneath the Downs. “Safe, safe, safe,” the pulse of the house beat gladly. “The Treasure yours.”

The wind roars up the avenue. Trees stoop and bend this way and that. Moonbeams splash and spill wildly in the rain. But the beam of the lamp falls straight from the window. The candle burns stiff and still. Wandering through the house, opening the windows, whispering not to wake us, the ghostly couple seek their joy.

“Here we slept,” she says. And he adds, “Kisses without number.” “Waking in the morning—” “Silver between the trees—” “Upstairs—” “In the garden—” “When summer came—” “In winter snowtime—” The doors go shutting far in the distance, gently knocking like the pulse of a heart.

Nearer they come, cease at the doorway. The wind falls, the rain slides silver down the glass. Our eyes darken, we hear no steps beside us; we see no lady spread her ghostly cloak. His hands shield the lantern. “Look,” he breathes. “Sound asleep. Love upon their lips.”

Stooping, holding their silver lamp above us, long they look and deeply. Long they pause. The wind drives straightly; the flame stoops slightly. Wild beams of moonlight cross both floor and wall, and, meeting, stain the faces bent; the faces pondering; the faces that search the sleepers and seek their hidden joy.

“Safe, safe, safe,” the heart of the house beats proudly. “Long years—” he sighs. “Again you found me.” “Here,” she murmurs, “sleeping; in the garden reading; laughing, rolling apples in the loft. Here we left our treasure—” Stooping, their light lifts the lids upon my eyes. “Safe! safe! safe!” the pulse of the house beats wildly. Waking, I cry “Oh, is this your buried treasure? The light in the heart.”

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
There is hardly a plot in A Haunted House, and that is the point. The story opens with a door shutting, whatever hour you wake. A ghostly couple move from room to room, hand in hand, lifting and opening things, saying to each other, here we left it, and here too, it is upstairs, and in the garden. They keep quiet so as not to wake the living people sleeping in the house. And the narrator, one of those living people, notices the sounds, imagines what the ghosts are doing, gets up to look, and finds nothing but empty rooms, open doors, wood pigeons, apples in the loft, and a book that has slipped into the grass.

The question the story circles is what the ghosts are looking for. They call it the treasure, and they say it is safe. The house's own pulse beats the word safe, safe, safe, like a heart. The narrator, too, seems to be searching, asking what did I come in here for, what did I want to find, with hands that are empty. That repeated image of empty hands is the story's ache. We all walk into rooms and forget why. We all seem to be reaching for something just out of sight.

Then comes the central, strangest passage. The narrator says that death was the glass, that death was between us. The woman died first, hundreds of years ago, and sealed the windows. The man left the house, wandered north and east, saw the stars turn in a southern sky, and at last found the house again, dropped beneath the Downs. So the ghosts are lovers separated by death and now reunited. Their long searching is a kind of mourning that turns into joy.

In the final movement the ghostly couple finds the sleeping living pair, a man and a woman, and looks down at them. They see love upon their lips. And the ghosts realize that the treasure they buried was exactly this: the life, warmth and tenderness that the living still have. Then, as their lamp lifts the lids of the narrator's eyes, the narrator wakes and asks, is this your buried treasure? The light in the heart.

So the story turns the usual ghost tale inside out. Nothing here is frightening. The dead are gentle, and they are drawn to the living not out of malice but out of love. The deeper suggestion is that love outlasts death, that what people leave behind in a house, a garden, a bed, is not a curse but a glow. A reader may also find the haunted house a picture of a mind, in which memories drift through the rooms, and the glass of the windows, reflecting apples and roses, is the thin barrier between the present and the past.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
A Haunted House is one of Woolf's most delicate pieces, and its best qualities are inseparable from its weaknesses, so it deserves a balanced look.

What is masterful first. The music of the prose is extraordinary. Woolf repeats words and rhythms like a refrain, the door shutting, the pulse of the house, safe, safe, safe, so that the story feels less like a narration than a chant. The sentences are short in the first half and begin to sweep and swell as the ghosts draw near the sleepers. The line about the wood pigeon drawing its bubble of sound from the deepest wells of silence is the kind of image that only a writer with perfect ear could produce. In a few paragraphs she creates a whole atmosphere of summer afternoon and haunted night.

The point of view is also clever. We are never sure who is speaking or who is dreaming. The voice is a you, then a one, then an us, and finally an I who seems to be asleep. The shifting perspective lets Woolf blur the line between living and dead, waking and dreaming, so that the haunting feels less like an event than a condition of consciousness.

And the ending is quietly overwhelming. After the cool, sensory images, the final line arrives like a sudden warmth. It is a risk to end a story on a phrase as bare as the light in the heart, and that it works is a mark of how carefully the groundwork was laid.

But there are real limitations. The story is extremely slight, and some readers find it more of an exercise than a finished work. Because so little happens, it can seem to float without grip. The repeated phrases, charming at first, can become mannered, and the heavy use of lyrical vocabulary can feel precious. A reader who wants a story with characters, conflict and consequence will probably be frustrated.

There is also a certain vagueness at the center. The central metaphor, that death is the glass between us, is evocative but not fully explained, and the logic of the ghosts' journey, the man traveling north and east and seeing the stars of a southern sky, is more suggestive than clear. At times the story seems to want credit for depth it has not entirely earned, using mystery as a shield.

Compared with Woolf's best later work, such as Mrs Dalloway and To the Lighthouse, this is a sketch. The experiments she carries out here are done better elsewhere, with more human substance. Still, as a small, shimmering piece, it is hard to fault in its own terms. It does what a lyric poem does, offering one mood with great purity. Judged as a story, it is uneven. Judged as a prose poem, it is nearly perfect.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The immediate impact of A Haunted House was modest, and it is important to say so plainly. Monday or Tuesday appeared in 1921 in a small printing from the Hogarth Press, the press Virginia and Leonard Woolf had started in 1917, initially as therapy and a hobby, setting type by hand on a small machine in their dining room. The collection was Woolf's only book of short fiction published in her lifetime, and it received a mixed response. Some reviewers were curious or admiring, others found the pieces puzzling and slight. It did not make her famous.

What it did was serve as a workshop. The stories in the collection, including The Mark on the Wall, Kew Gardens and this one, were laboratories where Woolf tested the techniques that would transform her novels. The fluid movement between minds, the focus on moments rather than events, the use of repeated images and rhythms, all feed into Jacob's Room in 1922, Mrs Dalloway in 1925, and To the Lighthouse in 1927. In that sense, A Haunted House matters as a seed. It shows Woolf finding a voice in which the inner life matters more than outward action.

The story also became a key text in the idea of modernism in English fiction. Woolf's essay on Modern Fiction, written in 1919, argued that the novelist should record the atoms as they fall upon the mind, and should not follow the old materialist habits of plot and description. A Haunted House is a small demonstration of that program. It is often cited in discussions of how modernists treated time, memory and consciousness.

After Woolf's death in 1941, her husband Leonard gathered her remaining stories into a posthumous collection in 1944, which took the title A Haunted House and Other Short Stories. That book made the piece famous as a title and brought it to a wide readership. Since then it has been regularly reprinted and is a favorite in anthologies of ghost stories and of modernist fiction.

In education, it is widely taught, because it is short enough to read aloud in class and rich enough to support long discussion. Teachers use it to introduce Woolf and to show how a ghost story can be subverted. Its imagery has also drawn visual artists and performers, perhaps fittingly given Woolf's close relationship with the painter Vanessa Bell and the woodcuts that first accompanied it.

Its quiet influence extends to later writers of gentle, melancholy hauntings, for whom the ghost is a figure of memory and longing, not terror.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers who love A Haunted House tend to love it for its beauty, and for the feeling it leaves behind. It is a story that is felt before it is understood.

First, many are drawn to the sheer sound of it. When the story is read aloud, as it often is, the repetitions and the pulse of the house make it hypnotic. The phrase safe, safe, safe takes on the rhythm of a heartbeat, or a lullaby. Listeners often say that it feels more like music than prose, and that they come away remembering the mood rather than the details. For people who enjoy being carried along by language, the story is a delight.

Second, readers cherish the tenderness of the ghosts. In most ghost stories, the dead are threatening. Here they are gentle, even shy, whispering to each other not to wake the sleepers. The idea of a dead couple who still love each other, and who return to the house to find their happiness again, is moving. Many readers connect it with their own experience of loss, of places where someone who is gone still seems to linger. The idea that the dead are not angry but fond is a comfort.

Third, readers admire the way the story captures ordinary sensations. The wood pigeons, the threshing machine, the apples in the loft, the shadow of a thrush crossing the carpet, are all so exact that the house feels real. This combination of the precise and the ethereal is typical of Woolf, and it gives the story its peculiar glow.

Fourth, readers value the ambiguity. The story does not tell you who the ghosts are, whether the narrator is awake, or what the treasure is. People enjoy finding their own meaning in it. For some it is about marriage, for others about grief, for others about the way a mind retains its past. A story that can bear so many readings tends to be loved for its generosity.

Finally, there is the ending. The last line, the light in the heart, has been quoted and treasured. It is a phrase that is simple, warm and open, and it leaves many readers with a sense of consolation. In an age that often prefers irony, a story that dares to end on such sincerity can feel like a gift.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
It would be a mistake to claim that A Haunted House has stirred great controversy. It is a small piece, and the critical conversation around it is mostly part of the larger conversation about Woolf's experimental fiction. Still, the objections are worth setting out.

The most common criticism, from the 1920s onward, has been about difficulty and vagueness. Some early readers of Monday or Tuesday found the pieces too elusive, more like impressions than stories. They asked what the point was, and whether the elaborate style disguised an absence of content. The same complaint has followed the story into the classroom, where students sometimes feel there is no clear meaning to grasp. Critics who prefer fiction with firm plots and fully drawn characters have judged it an exercise in mood and not a story.

A second criticism concerns preciousness. Woolf's lyrical style, with its drifting syntax and its poetic images, can seem self-regarding, a performance of sensitivity. Some readers have felt that the story luxuriates in its own beauty. Because the dead couple are so idealized, and the lovers so serene, others find it sentimental, a comforting vision of eternal love that avoids the harder truths of loss.

A third line of argument comes from critics who question the privileging of the interior, subjective experience that Woolf championed. Some in her own time, and some later, argued that this approach turned away from society, politics and the material world. Her fellow writers were divided. Some of her contemporaries admired her bravery, while others felt that experimental prose of this kind risked being a luxury for a leisured class. This complaint is less about this story in particular than about the movement it belongs to, but it has been applied.

There are also interpretive disputes. Readers disagree about whether the ghosts represent a living marriage, a dead one, or the narrator's own memories, and about whether the story is hopeful or sorrowful. The phrase death was the glass has been read as an affirmation that love survives and as a bleak note that death separates us permanently. The text allows both, and some critics find that the ambiguity is a weakness rather than a strength.

Finally, some feminist and biographical readings have noted undertones, such as childlessness and the longing for a life not lived, though these claims remain speculative. In the end, the real pushback has been less about flaws than about taste: this is a story that rewards readers who enjoy atmosphere, and may leave others cold.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
A Haunted House belongs to the great movement of early twentieth-century modernism, and within it to a particular strand that sought to capture consciousness itself. Alongside James Joyce, Dorothy Richardson and Marcel Proust, Woolf was among the writers who tried to follow the flow of thought and sensation, rather than outward events. Her story applies that approach to a classic form, the ghost story, and in doing so it quietly transforms it.

The ghost story has a long lineage. In the nineteenth century it flourished in the work of Charles Dickens, Sheridan Le Fanu and Henry James, whose The Turn of the Screw is perhaps the most famous haunting in English. These tales often used ghosts to explore guilt, repression and fear. M. R. James brought the form to a peak of antiquarian dread in the early twentieth century. Woolf deliberately turns away from that tradition of fear. Her ghosts are loving, and the true haunting is not horror but memory. In this she is closer to the Romantic poets, and to writers who treated the dead as presences of feeling.

What descends from it? The idea of the benevolent or melancholic ghost, a figure of longing and not terror, runs through later writing. Shirley Jackson's The Haunting of Hill House, though darker, shares Woolf's sense that a house can be a mind. Later writers of domestic and literary hauntings, from Toni Morrison's Beloved to the quiet, grieving ghosts in contemporary fiction and film, belong to a family in which the dead are intimate rather than monstrous. The film A Ghost Story, in which a sheet-draped figure watches time pass in a house, feels close to Woolf in mood, whether or not it was influenced directly.

A useful comparison is with Woolf's own The Mark on the Wall and Kew Gardens, from the same collection, which also treat small observations as gateways to larger meditations. Another is with her later novel To the Lighthouse, in which an empty house, passing through years and war, becomes a character in itself, a theme that A Haunted House anticipates in miniature.

Why does it still matter? Because it is a pocket-sized lesson in what fiction can do beyond telling a plot. It shows that a few paragraphs can hold an entire emotional world, and that a ghost story can be about love. For a first-time reader of Woolf, it is a gentle doorway into her way of seeing. And for anyone who has ever walked into a room and wondered what they came for, or felt the presence of someone no longer there, it offers an image of consolation: that what we have loved is kept safe, and that the light in the heart is real.

stories.keyContext: Virginia Woolf wrote A Haunted House around 1920 and published it in 1921 in Monday or Tuesday, her first collection of short experimental pieces. The book came from the Hogarth Press, the small publishing house she and her husband Leonard ran by hand in their home, and it carried woodcuts by her sister, the painter Vanessa Bell. Woolf was then in her late thirties, part of the Bloomsbury circle of writers and artists, and she was determined to break with the plain, orderly style of Victorian novels. She believed that real life was a luminous, shifting halo of impressions, not a neat chain of events. This story is barely two pages long. A ghostly couple wander through a house, searching for something they once left behind, while a living person lies reading or sleeping inside it. It is less a ghost story than a love poem in prose, about death, memory, and what lasts. Let the sounds and images wash over you.

stories.title: The Open Window
stories.author: Saki (H. H. Munro)
stories.epigraph: “Romance at short notice was her speciality.”
paragraphs: “My aunt will be down presently, Mr. Nuttel,” said a very self-possessed young lady of fifteen; “in the meantime you must try and put up with me.”

Framton Nuttel endeavoured to say the correct something which should duly flatter the niece of the moment without unduly discounting the aunt that was to come. Privately he doubted more than ever whether these formal visits on a succession of total strangers would do much towards helping the nerve cure which he was supposed to be undergoing.

“I know how it will be,” his sister had said when he was preparing to migrate to this rural retreat; “you will bury yourself down there and not speak to a living soul, and your nerves will be worse than ever from moping. I shall just give you letters of introduction to all the people I know there. Some of them, as far as I can remember, were quite nice.”

Framton wondered whether Mrs. Sappleton, the lady to whom he was presenting one of the letters of introduction, came into the nice division. “Do you know many of the people round here?” asked the niece, when she judged that they had had sufficient silent communion.

“Hardly a soul,” said Framton. “My sister was staying here, at the rectory, you know, some four years ago, and she gave me letters of introduction to some of the people here.” He made the last statement in a tone of distinct regret.

“Then you know practically nothing about my aunt?” pursued the self-possessed young lady. “Only her name and address,” admitted the caller. He was wondering whether Mrs. Sappleton was in the married or widowed state. An undefinable something about the room seemed to suggest masculine habitation.

“Her great tragedy happened just three years ago,” said the child; “that would be since your sister’s time.” “Her tragedy?” asked Framton; somehow in this restful country spot tragedies seemed out of place.

“You may wonder why we keep that window wide open on an October afternoon,” said the niece, indicating a large French window that opened on to a lawn. “It is quite warm for the time of the year,” said Framton; “but has that window got anything to do with the tragedy?”

“Out through that window, three years ago to a day, her husband and her two young brothers went off for their day’s shooting. They never came back. In crossing the moor to their favourite snipe-shooting ground they were all three engulfed in a treacherous piece of bog. It had been that dreadful wet summer, you know, and places that were safe in other years gave way suddenly without warning. Their bodies were never recovered. That was the dreadful part of it.” Here the child’s voice lost its self-possessed note and became falteringly human. “Poor aunt always thinks that they will come back someday, they and the little brown spaniel that was lost with them, and walk in at that window just as they used to do. That is why the window is kept open every evening till it is quite dusk. Poor dear aunt, she has often told me how they went out, her husband with his white waterproof coat over his arm, and Ronnie, her youngest brother, singing ‘Bertie, why do you bound?’ as he always did to tease her, because she said it got on her nerves. Do you know, sometimes on still, quiet evenings like this, I almost get a creepy feeling that they will all walk in through that window—”

She broke off with a little shudder. It was a relief to Framton when the aunt bustled into the room with a whirl of apologies for being late in making her appearance. “I hope Vera has been amusing you?” she said. “She has been very interesting,” said Framton. “I hope you don’t mind the open window,” said Mrs. Sappleton briskly; “my husband and brothers will be home directly from shooting, and they always come in this way. They’ve been out for snipe in the marshes today, so they’ll make a fine mess over my poor carpets. So like you menfolk, isn’t it?”

She rattled on cheerfully about the shooting and the scarcity of birds, and the prospects for duck in the winter. To Framton it was all purely horrible. He made a desperate but only partially successful effort to turn the talk on to a less ghastly topic; he was conscious that his hostess was giving him only a fragment of her attention, and her eyes were constantly straying past him to the open window and the lawn beyond. It was certainly an unfortunate coincidence that he should have paid his visit on this tragic anniversary.

“The doctors agree in ordering me complete rest, an absence of mental excitement, and avoidance of anything in the nature of violent physical exercise,” announced Framton, who laboured under the tolerably wide-spread delusion that total strangers and chance acquaintances are hungry for the least detail of one’s ailments and infirmities, their cause and cure. “On the matter of diet they are not so much in agreement,” he continued. “No?” said Mrs. Sappleton, in a voice which only replaced a yawn at the last moment. Then she suddenly brightened into alert attention—but not to what Framton was saying. “Here they are at last!” she cried. “Just in time for tea, and don’t they look as if they were muddy up to the eyes!”

Framton shivered slightly and turned towards the niece with a look intended to convey sympathetic comprehension. The child was staring out through the open window with a dazed horror in her eyes. In a chill shock of nameless fear Framton swung round in his seat and looked in the same direction. In the deepening twilight three figures were walking across the lawn towards the window; they all carried guns under their arms, and one of them was additionally burdened with a white coat hung over his shoulders. A tired brown spaniel kept close at their heels. Noiselessly they neared the house, and then a hoarse young voice chanted out of the dusk: “I said, Bertie, why do you bound?”

Framton grabbed wildly at his stick and hat; the hall door, the gravel drive, and the front gate were dimly noted stages in his headlong retreat. A cyclist coming along the road had to run into the hedge to avoid imminent collision. “Here we are, my dear,” said the bearer of the white mackintosh, coming in through the window, “fairly muddy, but most of it’s dry. Who was that who bolted out as we came up?” “A most extraordinary man, a Mr. Nuttel,” said Mrs. Sappleton; “could only talk about his illnesses, and dashed off without a word of goodbye or apology when you arrived. One would think he had seen a ghost.” “I expect it was the spaniel,” said the niece calmly; “he told me he had a horror of dogs. He was once hunted into a cemetery somewhere on the banks of the Ganges by a pack of pariah dogs, and had to spend the night in a newly dug grave with the creatures snarling and grinning and foaming just above him. Enough to make anyone lose their nerve.” Romance at short notice was her speciality.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
On its surface, The Open Window is a comic anecdote with a twist, and the plot can be told in a minute. A nervous young man named Framton Nuttel arrives at a country house in England carrying a letter of introduction from his sister. He has been sent to the countryside to rest his nerves, and he finds himself waiting in the drawing room for the lady of the house, a Mrs. Sappleton. Her fifteen-year-old niece, Vera, entertains him. Vera has a story. Three years ago, she says, her aunt's husband and her two young brothers went out through that very window to shoot, and they were swallowed by a bog and never seen again. Her aunt has kept the window open every evening since, in the belief that they will walk back in. When the aunt appears and says cheerfully that her husband and brothers will soon be home from shooting, Framton is horrified. The three men come striding across the lawn, one of them singing, and Framton flees in terror. Vera calmly explains to the family that he must have been frightened by the dog. The last line is the famous one: romance at short notice was her speciality.

What is the story really about? On one level, it is about the power of a good storyteller and the credulity of an audience. Vera does not lie clumsily. She builds her tale from small, convincing details: the white waterproof coat over the husband's arm, the youngest brother singing a teasing song to annoy his sister, the particular terrible summer when the bogs were treacherous. She even makes her voice falter at the right moment. Framton, who is already fragile, is helpless before such artistry.

The story is also about nerves, and about the way a mind prepared to find horror will find it. Framton has been sent away to cure his anxiety, and he talks only about his illnesses. He is a man who expects the worst, and Vera feeds that expectation. When the supposed ghosts appear, it is his own fear, as much as her story, that sends him running.

There is a third layer, subtler and more mischievous. The story shows how thin the surface of polite society is. In a quiet drawing room, over a pause in a conversation, a child can invent a tragedy and a ghost story, and nobody, including the narrator, objects. Saki delights in revealing the wildness beneath the good manners.

Finally, the closing joke does more than amuse. Having seen Vera deceive Framton, we watch her immediately deceive her aunt with a second fabrication, about the Ganges and the pariah dogs. The ending shows that for Vera, storytelling is a reflex, a pleasure in itself, and not a means to anything else.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
The Open Window is a nearly flawless miniature, and it is worth being specific about why, before looking at the few places where it is less impressive.

The first thing to admire is economy. In well under two thousand words, Saki establishes a setting, three characters, a mystery, a horror, and a reversal. Nothing is wasted. The opening line, in which the self-possessed young lady announces that her aunt will be down presently, instantly sets up the mismatch between Framton's anxiety and Vera's composure. Every detail does at least double duty: the open window is a stage prop for the false tragedy and then the doorway through which the apparent ghosts arrive.

The second is comic timing. The story depends on pace and on a kind of dramatic irony. We are not told right away that Vera is lying, but Saki drops tiny hints, such as the smoothness of her details, and a sharp reader may sense something. Then the aunt begins to chatter about her husband's shooting, and the dreadful logic of the situation unfolds with the neatness of a stage farce. The final reveal, with the second lie, is a masterstroke, because it recasts everything we just read as proof of her genius.

The third is the prose. Saki's sentences are urbane and dry. His descriptions of Framton, who endeavours to say the correct something that should flatter the niece without discounting the aunt, are packed with gentle mockery. The narration never raises its voice, and the contrast between the elegant tone and the absurd content gives the story its charm.

Now the limitations. The story is slight. It is a joke, beautifully built, but a joke all the same, and some readers feel that it has little emotional weight. Characters are types: the nervous invalid, the brisk hostess, the precocious girl. Framton is more a target than a person, and the reader is invited to laugh at him without much sympathy.

There is also the question of cruelty. The story's humor depends on a young girl terrorizing a fragile man for her own amusement. Saki keeps the tone light, but if you think about it for more than a moment, the prank is quite nasty, and no one is held accountable. Whether you find this delicious or distasteful depends on your temperament.

Finally, the twist, though skillful, can feel predictable to a modern reader who has met a hundred similar stories. It is perhaps unfair to hold that against it, since it helped create the template. In the end, the story is a gem, small and sharp, and what it lacks in depth it makes up for in precision.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The Open Window did a great deal for Saki's reputation, though that reputation was cut short. He published it in 1914, and within two years he was dead. When the First World War began, Saki, who was in his early forties and could have avoided service, chose to enlist as a private. He was killed by a sniper in France in November 1916. According to a story widely repeated, his last words were an order to a fellow soldier to put out a cigarette whose glow might draw fire. Whether or not the words are exact, they have the dry spirit of his writing. His sister, Ethel, later destroyed many of his papers, so the record of his life is thin, which makes his stories all the more central to how he is remembered.

Within his career, this story became the best known of a large body of short fiction. He had earlier published collections such as Reginald and The Chronicles of Clovis, filled with brilliant, malicious sketches of Edwardian society. Beasts and Super-Beasts, in which this appeared, was among his last books. The Open Window has since been reprinted more often than almost any of them.

Its influence on other writers is hard to measure precisely, but Saki is regularly named as a model for later humorists of the English tradition. P. G. Wodehouse, Evelyn Waugh and later writers of comic fiction, including Roald Dahl in his dark tales for adults, are often mentioned as heirs to his blend of elegance and cruelty. The idea of the cunning child who runs rings round the adults, and the polished, ironical short story ending on a sting, can be traced through a good deal of twentieth-century English humor.

In education, the story has had an enormous second life. It is probably one of the most taught short stories in the English-speaking world, especially in secondary schools. Teachers love it because it is short, funny, and a perfect example of an unreliable narrator, a twist ending, irony, and characterization through dialogue. Many people first met the idea of the surprise ending through this story.

It has also been adapted for radio, stage and film, and it is a favorite for school performances. Its basic idea, a fib so well told that it is believed, has entered popular culture as a model of the elaborate prank.

More broadly, the story helped define a particular tone: brittle, amused, and a little merciless, the tone of the Edwardian comedy of manners with a hint of the macabre. That tone remains a recognizable style in English writing today.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
People love The Open Window first of all because it is such a pleasure to read. It is a story with the satisfying click of a perfect joke: everything slots into place, and the ending delivers exactly the right amount of surprise. Readers often say they smiled or laughed out loud at the last line, and that they immediately wanted to read it again to catch the clues.

They love Vera. She is one of the great mischievous children in literature, a young person of dazzling poise who treats the adult world as a stage for her inventions. Readers delight in her audacity, her calm and her skill. There is something liberating about a character who exercises such power with such good humor. Many readers admit that they secretly side with her, and enjoy the way she runs rings around the grown-ups.

They also love the comic portrait of Framton Nuttel. His obsession with his own symptoms, his stumbling attempts at polite conversation and his headlong flight past the cyclist are drawn with affectionate mockery. The image of him grabbing his stick and hat and bolting down the gravel drive is one of the most vivid pieces of physical comedy in short fiction.

Writers admire the technique. Saki's handling of dialogue, in which the character of each speaker emerges through a few lines, is considered a model. The way the story seeds details, such as the window, the coat, the song, and the spaniel, and then pays them off, is widely studied. Readers who enjoy the craft of fiction see it as a lesson in how little is needed to create a complete world.

Another quality that readers prize is the wit of the sentences. Saki's gift for the dry aside, the phrase that is both elegant and savage, makes the story a pleasure at the level of the line. A reader might not remember the plot weeks later, but will remember the tone.

Finally, there is the sense of play. The story is a celebration of imagination for its own sake. Vera's tales have no purpose except the joy of inventing, and many readers find this infectious. In a world that often demands that stories mean something, it is refreshing to read one that simply enjoys itself. That playful, mischievous spirit is what has kept it alive for over a century.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Honesty requires admitting that The Open Window has not been the subject of heated critical debate. It is a short comic story, widely loved, and most of the commentary on it has been appreciative. Documentation of specific contemporary reviews is thin. But critics and readers over the years have raised several fair objections, which are worth considering.

The most common is that the story is slight. Compared with the richer, deeper fiction of near contemporaries such as Chekhov or Henry James, Saki's work can seem like clever trifles. Some critics have said that his stories are brilliant surfaces without much beneath them, witty without being wise. The Open Window, perfect as it is, has been held up as an example: a joke with no larger vision.

A second objection is about cruelty. Saki's humor is often mean-spirited, and the story's pleasure depends on a vulnerable man being frightened out of his wits. Some readers find this uncomfortable, and especially the fact that the narrative seems to take Vera's side. Her mischief has real consequences for Framton, who is, after all, a sick person, and the story offers no sympathy for him. Critics have occasionally noted a streak of misanthropy in Saki's work, a contempt for the dull, the weak and the earnest.

Related to this is the way the story treats nervous illness. Framton's condition is the engine of the joke, and a modern reader may feel uneasy about laughing at a man's anxiety. In 1914, rest cures for nervous complaints were common and often mocked. Today, many readers are more alert to the cruelty of ridiculing mental distress, and some find the story harder to enjoy as a result.

A fourth line of criticism concerns the social world of the story. It is a comfortable, upper-middle-class English country house, with servants unseen and a world of leisure. Saki was himself part of that world and satirized it, but his satire was gentle, and some critics have argued that it never really challenges the class assumptions it depicts. He is a satirist who enjoys the manners he mocks.

Finally, some have argued that the twist has been done to death since, and that the story now reads as a familiar mechanism. This is more a comment on its influence than on its quality, and most readers find that it still delights. The criticisms, then, are real but modest, and they mostly concern what the story does not attempt, not what it does.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
The Open Window sits in the tradition of the English comedy of manners, a form that stretches from Jane Austen to Oscar Wilde. In this tradition, the comedy arises from the gap between how people are supposed to behave and what they really do. Wilde is perhaps the nearest ancestor. His epigrams, his love of paradox and his sense of the absurdity beneath politeness all echo in Saki. But where Wilde's comedies tend to be warm and theatrical, Saki's are colder and more cruel, and often end with a sting.

It also belongs to the tradition of the short story with a twist, a form associated in America with O. Henry and in France with Guy de Maupassant. Saki shares their love of the surprise ending but uses it with a more cynical, aristocratic touch. His sketches of malicious children and fierce aunts reflect his own upbringing, and they carry a sense of the grotesque that connects him to the Victorian tradition of dark humor in writers like Lewis Carroll, whose Wonderland is also a place where manners are made absurd.

The story also touches the ghost story tradition, though as a parody. Edwardian readers loved tales of hauntings, and Saki takes the genre's machinery, the tragic backstory, the open window, the figures returning at dusk, and turns it into a prank. The effect is a kind of anti-ghost story, in which the supernatural is revealed as a fabrication. In this it is a useful companion to more serious hauntings, since it shows how a ghost story works by suggestion.

What descends from Saki is a line of British humor, dry, elegant and a little macabre. Wodehouse's brisk comedies, Waugh's satires and the dark tales of Roald Dahl, as well as the cunning children of contemporary comic fiction, share the family resemblance. The figure of the clever, amoral child who outwits grown-ups is a staple of comedy, from the stories of Richmal Crompton's William to modern television.

Saki's life adds a poignant frame. A writer who spent his career mocking the comfortable certainties of Edwardian England died in the war that ended that world, and his stories are now read as brilliant snapshots of a society just before it vanished.

Why does the story still matter? Because it is a perfect small machine, and because it contains a lasting truth about how easily we are led by a confident voice. In an age of persuasion and misinformation, Vera is a useful figure to keep in mind. Read it for the pleasure of the joke, and then notice how well it was built.

stories.keyContext: Saki was the pen name of Hector Hugh Munro, a British writer who published The Open Window in 1914 in his collection Beasts and Super-Beasts. He was born in Burma in 1870 and raised in Devon, in England, by strict aunts, a childhood that left him with a lasting talent for portraying formidable women and mischievous children. As an adult he worked as a journalist and became a master of the very short, very witty story, in which polite Edwardian society, with its tea tables and good manners, is quietly turned inside out. It is one of the most taught short stories in English, and it takes only a few minutes to read. A nervous visitor is left alone with a self-possessed young girl, and she tells him a remarkable tale. Saki would die in the First World War only two years later, shot by a sniper in France. Listen for the timing of the jokes, and for how easily a confident voice can make people believe almost anything.

stories.title: The Monkey's Paw
stories.author: W. W. Jacobs
stories.epigraph: “He wanted to show that fate ruled people’s lives, and that those who interfered with it did so to their sorrow.”
paragraphs: I. Without, the night was cold and wet, but in the small parlour of Laburnam Villa the blinds were drawn and the fire burned brightly. Father and son were at chess, the former, who possessed ideas about the game involving radical changes, putting his king into such sharp and unnecessary perils that it even provoked comment from the white-haired old lady knitting placidly by the fire.

“Hark at the wind,” said Mr. White, who, having seen a fatal mistake after it was too late, was amiably desirous of preventing his son from seeing it. “I’m listening,” said the latter, grimly surveying the board as he stretched out his hand. “Check.” “I should hardly think that he’d come to-night,” said his father, with his hand poised over the board. “Mate,” replied the son.

“That’s the worst of living so far out,” bawled Mr. White, with sudden and unlooked-for violence; “of all the beastly, slushy, out-of-the-way places to live in, this is the worst. Pathway’s a bog, and the road’s a torrent. I don’t know what people are thinking about. I suppose because only two houses in the road are let, they think it doesn’t matter.” “Never mind, dear,” said his wife, soothingly; “perhaps you’ll win the next one.” Mr. White looked up sharply, just in time to intercept a knowing glance between mother and son. The words died away on his lips, and he hid a guilty grin in his thin grey beard.

“There he is,” said Herbert White, as the gate banged to loudly and heavy footsteps came toward the door. The old man rose with hospitable haste, and opening the door, was heard condoling with the new arrival. The new arrival also condoled with himself, so that Mrs. White said, “Tut, tut!” and coughed gently as her husband entered the room, followed by a tall, burly man, beady of eye and rubicund of visage. “Sergeant-Major Morris,” he said, introducing him.

The sergeant-major shook hands, and taking the proffered seat by the fire, watched contentedly while his host got out whiskey and tumblers and stood a small copper kettle on the fire. At the third glass his eyes got brighter, and he began to talk, the little family circle regarding with eager interest this visitor from distant parts, as he squared his broad shoulders in the chair and spoke of wild scenes and doughty deeds; of wars and plagues and strange peoples.

“Twenty-one years of it,” said Mr. White, nodding at his wife and son. “When he went away he was a slip of a youth in the warehouse. Now look at him.” “He don’t look to have taken much harm,” said Mrs. White, politely. “I’d like to go to India myself,” said the old man, “just to look round a bit, you know.” “Better where you are,” said the sergeant-major, shaking his head. He put down the empty glass, and sighing softly, shook it again.

“I should like to see those old temples and fakirs and jugglers,” said the old man. “What was that you started telling me the other day about a monkey’s paw or something, Morris?” “Nothing,” said the soldier, hastily. “Leastways nothing worth hearing.” “Monkey’s paw?” said Mrs. White, curiously. “Well, it’s just a bit of what you might call magic, perhaps,” said the sergeant-major, offhandedly.

His three listeners leaned forward eagerly. The visitor absent-mindedly put his empty glass to his lips and then set it down again. His host filled it for him. “To look at,” said the sergeant-major, fumbling in his pocket, “it’s just an ordinary little paw, dried to a mummy.” He took something out of his pocket and proffered it. Mrs. White drew back with a grimace, but her son, taking it, examined it curiously. “And what is there special about it?” inquired Mr. White as he took it from his son, and having examined it, placed it upon the table.

“It had a spell put on it by an old fakir,” said the sergeant-major, “a very holy man. He wanted to show that fate ruled people’s lives, and that those who interfered with it did so to their sorrow. He put a spell on it so that three separate men could each have three wishes from it.” His manner was so impressive that his hearers were conscious that their light laughter jarred somewhat. “Well, why don’t you have three, sir?” said Herbert White, cleverly. The soldier regarded him in the way that middle age is wont to regard presumptuous youth. “I have,” he said, quietly, and his blotchy face whitened.

“And did you really have the three wishes granted?” asked Mrs. White. “I did,” said the sergeant-major, and his glass tapped against his strong teeth. “And has anybody else wished?” persisted the old lady. “The first man had his three wishes. Yes,” was the reply; “I don’t know what the first two were, but the third was for death. That’s how I got the paw.” His tones were so grave that a hush fell upon the group.

“If you’ve had your three wishes, it’s no good to you now, then, Morris,” said the old man at last. “What do you keep it for?” The soldier shook his head. “Fancy, I suppose,” he said, slowly. “I did have some idea of selling it, but I don’t think I will. It has caused enough mischief already. Besides, people won’t buy. They think it’s a fairy tale; some of them, and those who do think anything of it want to try it first and pay me afterward.” “If you could have another three wishes,” said the old man, eyeing him keenly, “would you have them?” “I don’t know,” said the other. “I don’t know.”

He took the paw, and dangling it between his forefinger and thumb, suddenly threw it upon the fire. White, with a slight cry, stooped down and snatched it off. “Better let it burn,” said the soldier, solemnly. “If you don’t want it, Morris,” said the other, “give it to me.” “I won’t,” said his friend, doggedly. “I threw it on the fire. If you keep it, don’t blame me for what happens. Pitch it on the fire again like a sensible man.” The other shook his head and examined his new possession closely. “How do you do it?” he inquired. “Hold it up in your right hand and wish aloud,” said the sergeant-major, “but I warn you of the consequences.”

“Sounds like the Arabian Nights,” said Mrs. White, as she rose and began to set the supper. “Don’t you think you might wish for four pairs of hands for me?” Her husband drew the talisman from pocket, and then all three burst into laughter as the sergeant-major, with a look of alarm on his face, caught him by the arm. “If you must wish,” he said, gruffly, “wish for something sensible.” Mr. White dropped it back in his pocket, and placing chairs, motioned his friend to the table. In the business of supper the talisman was partly forgotten, and afterward the three sat listening in an enthralled fashion to a second instalment of the soldier’s adventures in India.

“If the tale about the monkey’s paw is not more truthful than those he has been telling us,” said Herbert, as the door closed behind their guest, just in time for him to catch the last train, “we sha’nt make much out of it.” “Did you give him anything for it, father?” inquired Mrs. White, regarding her husband closely. “A trifle,” said he, colouring slightly. “He didn’t want it, but I made him take it. And he pressed me again to throw it away.” “Likely,” said Herbert, with pretended horror. “Why, we’re going to be rich, and famous and happy. Wish to be an emperor, father, to begin with; then you can’t be henpecked.” He darted round the table, pursued by the maligned Mrs. White armed with an antimacassar.

Mr. White took the paw from his pocket and eyed it dubiously. “I don’t know what to wish for, and that’s a fact,” he said, slowly. “It seems to me I’ve got all I want.” “If you only cleared the house, you’d be quite happy, wouldn’t you?” said Herbert, with his hand on his shoulder. “Well, wish for two hundred pounds, then; that ’ll just do it.” His father, smiling shamefacedly at his own credulity, held up the talisman, as his son, with a solemn face, somewhat marred by a wink at his mother, sat down at the piano and struck a few impressive chords. “I wish for two hundred pounds,” said the old man distinctly.

A fine crash from the piano greeted the words, interrupted by a shuddering cry from the old man. His wife and son ran toward him. “It moved,” he cried, with a glance of disgust at the object as it lay on the floor. “As I wished, it twisted in my hand like a snake.” “Well, I don’t see the money,” said his son as he picked it up and placed it on the table, “and I bet I never shall.” “It must have been your fancy, father,” said his wife, regarding him anxiously. He shook his head. “Never mind, though; there’s no harm done, but it gave me a shock all the same.”

They sat down by the fire again while the two men finished their pipes. Outside, the wind was higher than ever, and the old man started nervously at the sound of a door banging upstairs. A silence unusual and depressing settled upon all three, which lasted until the old couple rose to retire for the night. “I expect you’ll find the cash tied up in a big bag in the middle of your bed,” said Herbert, as he bade them good-night, “and something horrible squatting up on top of the wardrobe watching you as you pocket your ill-gotten gains.” He sat alone in the darkness, gazing at the dying fire, and seeing faces in it. The last face was so horrible and so simian that he gazed at it in amazement. It got so vivid that, with a little uneasy laugh, he felt on the table for a glass containing a little water to throw over it. His hand grasped the monkey’s paw, and with a little shiver he wiped his hand on his coat and went up to bed.

II. In the brightness of the wintry sun next morning as it streamed over the breakfast table he laughed at his fears. There was an air of prosaic wholesomeness about the room which it had lacked on the previous night, and the dirty, shrivelled little paw was pitched on the sideboard with a carelessness which betokened no great belief in its virtues. “I suppose all old soldiers are the same,” said Mrs. White. “The idea of our listening to such nonsense! How could wishes be granted in these days? And if they could, how could two hundred pounds hurt you, father?” “Might drop on his head from the sky,” said the frivolous Herbert.

“Morris said the things happened so naturally,” said his father, “that you might if you so wished attribute it to coincidence.” “Well, don’t break into the money before I come back,” said Herbert as he rose from the table. “I’m afraid it’ll turn you into a mean, avaricious man, and we shall have to disown you.” His mother laughed, and following him to the door, watched him down the road; and returning to the breakfast table, was very happy at the expense of her husband’s credulity. All of which did not prevent her from scurrying to the door at the postman’s knock, nor prevent her from referring somewhat shortly to retired sergeant-majors of bibulous habits when she found that the post brought a tailor’s bill.

“Herbert will have some more of his funny remarks, I expect, when he comes home,” she said, as they sat at dinner. “I dare say,” said Mr. White, pouring himself out some beer; “but for all that, the thing moved in my hand; that I’ll swear to.” “You thought it did,” said the old lady soothingly. “I say it did,” replied the other. “There was no thought about it; I had just—What’s the matter?”

His wife made no reply. She was watching the mysterious movements of a man outside, who, peering in an undecided fashion at the house, appeared to be trying to make up his mind to enter. In mental connection with the two hundred pounds, she noticed that the stranger was well dressed, and wore a silk hat of glossy newness. Three times he paused at the gate, and then walked on again. The fourth time he stood with his hand upon it, and then with sudden resolution flung it open and walked up the path. Mrs. White at the same moment placed her hands behind her, and hurriedly unfastening the strings of her apron, put that useful article of apparel beneath the cushion of her chair.

She brought the stranger, who seemed ill at ease, into the room. He gazed at her furtively, and listened in a preoccupied fashion as the old lady apologized for the appearance of the room, and her husband’s coat, a garment which he usually reserved for the garden. She then waited as patiently as her sex would permit, for him to broach his business, but he was at first strangely silent. “I—was asked to call,” he said at last, and stooped and picked a piece of cotton from his trousers. “I come from ‘Maw and Meggins.’”

The old lady started. “Is anything the matter?” she asked, breathlessly. “Has anything happened to Herbert? What is it? What is it?” Her husband interposed. “There, there, mother,” he said, hastily. “Sit down, and don’t jump to conclusions. You’ve not brought bad news, I’m sure, sir;” and he eyed the other wistfully. “I’m sorry—” began the visitor. “Is he hurt?” demanded the mother, wildly. The visitor bowed in assent. “Badly hurt,” he said, quietly, “but he is not in any pain.” “Oh, thank God!” said the old woman, clasping her hands. “Thank God for that! Thank—”

She broke off suddenly as the sinister meaning of the assurance dawned upon her and she saw the awful confirmation of her fears in the other’s averted face. She caught her breath, and turning to her slower-witted husband, laid her trembling old hand upon his. There was a long silence. “He was caught in the machinery,” said the visitor at length in a low voice. “Caught in the machinery,” repeated Mr. White, in a dazed fashion, “yes.” He sat staring blankly out at the window, and taking his wife’s hand between his own, pressed it as he had been wont to do in their old courting-days nearly forty years before. “He was the only one left to us,” he said, turning gently to the visitor. “It is hard.”

The other coughed, and rising, walked slowly to the window. “The firm wished me to convey their sincere sympathy with you in your great loss,” he said, without looking round. “I beg that you will understand I am only their servant and merely obeying orders.” There was no reply; the old woman’s face was white, her eyes staring, and her breath inaudible; on the husband’s face was a look such as his friend the sergeant might have carried into his first action. “I was to say that ‘Maw and Meggins’ disclaim all responsibility,” continued the other. “They admit no liability at all, but in consideration of your son’s services, they wish to present you with a certain sum as compensation.” Mr. White dropped his wife’s hand, and rising to his feet, gazed with a look of horror at his visitor. His dry lips shaped the words, “How much?” “Two hundred pounds,” was the answer. Unconscious of his wife’s shriek, the old man smiled faintly, put out his hands like a sightless man, and dropped, a senseless heap, to the floor.

III. In the huge new cemetery, some two miles distant, the old people buried their dead, and came back to a house steeped in shadow and silence. It was all over so quickly that at first they could hardly realize it, and remained in a state of expectation as though of something else to happen—something else which was to lighten this load, too heavy for old hearts to bear. But the days passed, and expectation gave place to resignation—the hopeless resignation of the old, sometimes miscalled, apathy. Sometimes they hardly exchanged a word, for now they had nothing to talk about, and their days were long to weariness.

It was about a week after that the old man, waking suddenly in the night, stretched out his hand and found himself alone. The room was in darkness, and the sound of subdued weeping came from the window. He raised himself in bed and listened. “Come back,” he said, tenderly. “You will be cold.” “It is colder for my son,” said the old woman, and wept afresh. The sound of her sobs died away on his ears. The bed was warm, and his eyes heavy with sleep. He dozed fitfully, and then slept until a sudden wild cry from his wife awoke him with a start.

“The paw!” she cried wildly. “The monkey’s paw!” He started up in alarm. “Where? Where is it? What’s the matter?” She came stumbling across the room toward him. “I want it,” she said, quietly. “You’ve not destroyed it?” “It’s in the parlour, on the bracket,” he replied, marvelling. “Why?” She cried and laughed together, and bending over, kissed his cheek. “I only just thought of it,” she said, hysterically. “Why didn’t I think of it before? Why didn’t you think of it?” “Think of what?” he questioned. “The other two wishes,” she replied, rapidly. “We’ve only had one.” “Was not that enough?” he demanded, fiercely. “No,” she cried, triumphantly; “we’ll have one more. Go down and get it quickly, and wish our boy alive again.”

The man sat up in bed and flung the bedclothes from his quaking limbs. “Good God, you are mad!” he cried, aghast. “Get it,” she panted; “get it quickly, and wish—Oh, my boy, my boy!” Her husband struck a match and lit the candle. “Get back to bed,” he said, unsteadily. “You don’t know what you are saying.” “We had the first wish granted,” said the old woman, feverishly; “why not the second?” “A coincidence,” stammered the old man. “Go and get it and wish,” cried his wife, quivering with excitement. The old man turned and regarded her, and his voice shook. “He has been dead ten days, and besides he—I would not tell you else, but—I could only recognize him by his clothing. If he was too terrible for you to see then, how now?” “Bring him back,” cried the old woman, and dragged him toward the door. “Do you think I fear the child I have nursed?”

He went down in the darkness, and felt his way to the parlour, and then to the mantelpiece. The talisman was in its place, and a horrible fear that the unspoken wish might bring his mutilated son before him ere he could escape from the room seized upon him, and he caught his breath as he found that he had lost the direction of the door. His brow cold with sweat, he felt his way round the table, and groped along the wall until he found himself in the small passage with the unwholesome thing in his hand. Even his wife’s face seemed changed as he entered the room. It was white and expectant, and to his fears seemed to have an unnatural look upon it. He was afraid of her.

“Wish!” she cried, in a strong voice. “It is foolish and wicked,” he faltered. “Wish!” repeated his wife. He raised his hand. “I wish my son alive again.” The talisman fell to the floor, and he regarded it fearfully. Then he sank trembling into a chair as the old woman, with burning eyes, walked to the window and raised the blind. He sat until he was chilled with the cold, glancing occasionally at the figure of the old woman peering through the window. The candle-end, which had burned below the rim of the china candlestick, was throwing pulsating shadows on the ceiling and walls, until, with a flicker larger than the rest, it expired. The old man, with an unspeakable sense of relief at the failure of the talisman, crept back to his bed, and a minute or two afterward the old woman came silently and apathetically beside him.

Neither spoke, but lay silently listening to the ticking of the clock. A stair creaked, and a squeaky mouse scurried noisily through the wall. The darkness was oppressive, and after lying for some time screwing up his courage, he took the box of matches, and striking one, went downstairs for a candle. At the foot of the stairs the match went out, and he paused to strike another; and at the same moment a knock, so quiet and stealthy as to be scarcely audible, sounded on the front door.
