The matches fell from his hand and spilled in the passage. He stood motionless, his breath suspended until the knock was repeated. Then he turned and fled swiftly back to his room, and closed the door behind him. A third knock sounded through the house. “What’s that?” cried the old woman, starting up. “A rat,” said the old man in shaking tones—“a rat. It passed me on the stairs.” His wife sat up in bed listening. A loud knock resounded through the house. “It’s Herbert!” she screamed. “It’s Herbert!”

She ran to the door, but her husband was before her, and catching her by the arm, held her tightly. “What are you going to do?” he whispered hoarsely. “It’s my boy; it’s Herbert!” she cried, struggling mechanically. “I forgot it was two miles away. What are you holding me for? Let go. I must open the door.” “For God’s sake don’t let it in,” cried the old man, trembling. “You’re afraid of your own son,” she cried, struggling. “Let me go. I’m coming, Herbert; I’m coming.”

There was another knock, and another. The old woman with a sudden wrench broke free and ran from the room. Her husband followed to the landing, and called after her appealingly as she hurried downstairs. He heard the chain rattle back and the bottom bolt drawn slowly and stiffly from the socket. Then the old woman’s voice, strained and panting. “The bolt,” she cried, loudly. “Come down. I can’t reach it.”

But her husband was on his hands and knees groping wildly on the floor in search of the paw. If he could only find it before the thing outside got in. A perfect fusillade of knocks reverberated through the house, and he heard the scraping of a chair as his wife put it down in the passage against the door. He heard the creaking of the bolt as it came slowly back, and at the same moment he found the monkey’s paw, and frantically breathed his third and last wish.

The knocking ceased suddenly, although the echoes of it were still in the house. He heard the chair drawn back, and the door opened. A cold wind rushed up the staircase, and a long loud wail of disappointment and misery from his wife gave him courage to run down to her side, and then to the gate beyond. The street lamp flickering opposite shone on a quiet and deserted road.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
On the surface, "The Monkey's Paw" is a simple chain of events. A retired working-class couple, Mr. and Mrs. White, and their grown son Herbert are spending a wet night in their isolated house. A family friend, Sergeant-Major Morris, shows them a withered monkey's paw that an Indian holy man enchanted so that three men could each have three wishes. Morris has used his own wishes, will not say what he wished for, and warns that the first owner's last wish was for death. He throws the paw on the fire, Mr. White pulls it out, and the family keeps it. Mr. White idly wishes for two hundred pounds, the exact sum he needs to pay off the house. The next day a representative from the firm of Maw and Meggins calls to say that Herbert has been killed in an accident at the factory, and that the company will pay compensation. The sum is two hundred pounds.

That is the heart of the story's cruelty. The paw does not break the rules of the world. It simply arranges for a wish to be granted through the one door that was open, and the door was a death. The old fakir wanted, in Morris's words, "to show that fate ruled people's lives, and that those who interfered with it did so to their sorrow." Notice that Mr. White's wish is nothing greedy. He wants a modest thing, and he makes the wish half in jest, with Herbert at the piano striking a mock-solemn chord. The story says that even small, harmless interference with fate has a price, and that price is not set by us.

The second wish carries the deeper horror. Ten days after the funeral, Mrs. White, mad with grief, makes her husband wish their son back. What follows is the most celebrated sequence in the story: a slow knocking at the door, a wife fumbling at a bolt she cannot reach, and a husband on his hands and knees searching for the paw in the dark. He already knows what a body that has been through the machinery must look like, and he is afraid of his own child. He makes the third and last wish, the knocking stops, and the open door shows only a quiet road under a flickering street lamp.

Jacobs never tells us what was on the step, and never says what the third wish was, though we can guess. Readers often miss that this restraint is the point. The reader supplies the horror, which is always worse than anything printed. A quieter layer is the difference between the two parents. Mrs. White cannot accept loss, while Mr. White finally does. His last wish is an act of mercy to everyone, including the thing that was once his son, and it is also an act of surrender. The story ends by teaching that sometimes the loving thing is to let the dead stay dead.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
As craft, "The Monkey's Paw" is close to flawless, and that is partly because it is so economical. It runs only a few thousand words, yet it has the structure of a three-act play. The first scene sets up the talisman, the second delivers the cruel payoff, and the third turns the screw. Each scene ends on a note that makes the reader hold their breath. Jacobs knew exactly where the story's energy was, and he never wastes a paragraph on explanation. The details he does choose are precise and memorable: the way the monkey's paw twists in Mr. White's hand like a living thing, the candle burning low in its china holder, the chair scraped across the passage floor.

The opening is a particularly clever piece of construction. A father and son play chess while the wind howls outside. Mr. White, who has "ideas about the game involving radical changes," puts his king in sharp and unnecessary perils, sees his blunder only after it is too late, and tries to distract his son so that he will not notice. It is funny, and it is also a miniature of the entire story: a man takes a needless risk, realizes the mistake too late, and hopes to escape without paying. Jacobs the humorist is doing real work here. The comedy of the early scenes makes the family so likeable that their ruin hurts.

There are weaknesses, and a fair reader should name them. Morris, the soldier with the dark secret, is a stock figure from adventure fiction, and his speech about the paw is a bit stagey. The exotic fakir is a vague, off-stage device, drawn from the thin Orientalism of the period, and it is fair to say the story does not take India or its culture seriously, treating it as a source of mysterious curses. Some of the dialogue is also dated, with its dutiful cries of "For God's sake" and its Victorian stiffness. Herbert, the doomed son, is a pleasant sketch rather than a person, so the grief we feel owes a good deal to the parents.

The story's other limitation is that its moral is almost too neat. Wishes bring ruin, fate is not to be tampered with, and the lesson arrives with the force of a fable. A modern reader may find it less psychologically complex than the best later horror. Yet the neatness is also its strength, because it lets the tale work like a perfectly cut piece of machinery. If it has a flaw, it is the same one as its virtue: it is so well engineered that it has little room for ambiguity beyond the final door.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
It is hard to overstate how far this short story traveled. Almost as soon as it appeared in 1902, in Harper's Monthly and then in Jacobs's collection The Lady of the Barge, it began to be reprinted, retold and performed. A stage version was made soon afterward, and the tale became a staple of the dramatic and radio repertory. For decades it was the story people meant when they said they wanted a good ghost story to read aloud. It has appeared in school anthologies on both sides of the Atlantic for more than a century, which has made it one of the first pieces of horror many readers ever meet.

Its biggest impact was the way it gave popular culture a durable idea: the wish that goes wrong in a way that follows the letter but ruins the spirit. The phrase "monkey's paw" has become shorthand for exactly this. People use it for a bargain with a hidden catch, a wish granted at a terrible price, or any situation in which getting what you asked for is the worst outcome. You will find it in films, television, comic books and everyday conversation. The long-running animated comedy The Simpsons gave it a famous parody in one of its Halloween episodes, which tells you how deeply the story has been absorbed.

The story also shaped the kind of horror that works by implication. Writers of ghost stories and weird fiction learned from it that the unseen is often more frightening than the shown, and that a modern, domestic setting can carry as much dread as any castle. Its descendants include stories about the dead returning in an unwelcome form, and the best known of those in later popular fiction is Stephen King's novel Pet Sematary, which plays on the same terrible logic of reviving a loved one. Several films have borrowed the premise directly or loosely.

For Jacobs himself, the effect was curious. He remained a humorist in the public mind, and most of his work, the comic stories of sailors and dockside swindlers, is now much less read. He is, in effect, a one-story author for most readers today. That is a bittersweet kind of fame, but it also shows that a single perfectly made story can outlast an entire career. Teachers use it today to show how suspense is built, how foreshadowing works, and how a story can say a great deal in a small number of words.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
The first thing readers love is the sheer pull of the suspense. The story is short, and nothing in it is padding. Many people remember reading it as a child, or hearing it read aloud, and recall the moment of the knocking on the door as one of the most chilling experiences of their early reading. Because the horror is withheld rather than displayed, it stays with you in a way that gorier stories do not. A great many readers have said that they could not stop imagining what stood on the doorstep, and that is exactly what Jacobs wanted.

They also admire how human it is. The Whites are not aristocrats or explorers. They are an ordinary older couple with a debt on the house, a good-natured son and a fireside, and the story gets its power from asking what they would do in the most ordinary kind of temptation. Everyone has idly wished for money. Everyone has lost, or fears losing, someone they love. The story takes those two common experiences and presses them together, so that a reader finishes the tale feeling that it could have happened to them. The grief is specific, too. Mrs. White's mad hope and Mr. White's dread are both understandable, and many readers have said they find the mother's desperate rush to the door the most moving part of the whole tale.

There is also pleasure in its craftsmanship, and writers have often said so. It is a model of how a story can be built around a single idea, with each scene pushing it a step further. The structure is as satisfying as a well-made joke, which perhaps is no accident for a comic writer. The three wishes are an ancient pattern in folktales, and readers enjoy feeling the old rhythm underneath a modern surface, waiting to see where the pattern will be broken.

Finally, readers love the ending's restraint. There is no explanation, no moral stated aloud, no monster revealed. The story closes on an empty road and a lamp. That quiet last image has been admired for more than a century as an example of how to stop at exactly the right moment, leaving the reader's imagination to finish the job. It is a lesson in trusting an audience that many later writers have taken to heart.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Because "The Monkey's Paw" has been so widely loved, it has drawn comparatively little hostile criticism, and it is fair to admit that the record of detailed reviews from its first appearance is thin. Jacobs was regarded in his own day as a popular humorist, and most commentary on his work concerned the comic stories, not this one. What objections exist have mostly come from later readers who look at it with a more skeptical eye.

The most common complaint is that the story is too tidy, a fable more than a piece of psychological fiction. The moral is clear, the three wishes land in a neat pattern, and little is left unresolved. Some critics have felt that this makes it more a clever mechanism than a deep exploration of grief. Others have noted that the characters are thinly drawn, especially Herbert and Morris, and that the story depends on conventions of the Victorian ghost tale that can feel predictable to a modern reader who has seen many imitations. The irony is that the story has been copied so often that its surprises can now seem familiar, though this is the fate of any influential work and not really a flaw in the original.

A more recent line of criticism concerns the colonial background. The curse comes from India, from an unnamed holy man whose reasons are reduced to a single sentence, and the story treats the East as a place of dark, unknowable power that can reach into an English living room. Readers today often point out that this reflects the habits of imperial adventure fiction, in which foreign religion and custom exist mainly to supply danger. It is also possible to read the story more charitably, as a tale in which the empire's loot, carried home by a soldier, brings consequences to ordinary people at home. Both readings are available, and the story does not push either one very hard.

Finally, some readers have pointed out a certain coldness in the machinery of the plot. Herbert's death is arranged with such neatness that it can feel more like a trick than a tragedy, and the compensation of exactly two hundred pounds is a joke the universe plays on the family. A reader who wants a tale about real mourning may find the story's coldly elegant design a little remote. Still, even critics who hold these reservations tend to agree that the story is among the best of its kind.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
"The Monkey's Paw" sits at the meeting point of two traditions. One is the folk tale about wishes, which stretches back through countless cultures, from the genie in the bottle to the fisherman's wife who asks for too much. The other is the late Victorian and Edwardian ghost story, the age of M. R. James and Arthur Machen, when writers were finding new ways to make readers afraid in rooms that looked perfectly safe. Jacobs fuses them. He takes the moral shape of a fairy tale and gives it the realistic surface, the nervous tension and the quiet understatement of a modern ghost story.

Its closest ancestors are tales of bargains that bite back. The monkey's paw is cousin to the cursed objects of Gothic fiction and to the stories of deals with the devil, in which the contract is always read too late. It also looks back to the old English tradition of the fireside tale, told on a stormy night to a gathered family, which is exactly the setting Jacobs places in the story's first scene. In a sense the Whites are listening to a ghost story and then living inside one.

Its descendants are numerous. Any later tale of a loved one returning wrong owes something to the third act of this one. Writers of horror and speculative fiction have reworked its core idea, and the phrase "careful what you wish for" has become one of the commonest morals in popular storytelling. Even science fiction has borrowed the pattern, with stories about machines or computers that fulfill a command with perverse literalness, which is the monkey's paw in modern clothing. Comparable works include the folk tale of the three wishes in which a couple wastes them on a sausage, and Poe's stories of dread built on a single image, though Jacobs is much more restrained than Poe.

Why does it still matter? Partly because it is among the purest demonstrations of how little a frightening story needs: a house, a family, an object and a rule. It is also because its emotional core has not aged. People still bargain with the universe when someone they love is in danger, and people still struggle to accept what cannot be undone. It rewards reading aloud, and it takes about twenty minutes. Few stories do so much in so little space, and it is worth reading at least once with the lights low.

stories.keyContext: W. W. Jacobs published "The Monkey's Paw" in 1902, and it has been frightening readers ever since. It is one of the most famous horror stories in English, and that is a little surprising, because Jacobs was best known as a humorist. He was a London clerk who made his name with gentle, funny tales about sailors and dockside characters. Here he took a very old folk idea, the wish that comes true in the worst possible way, and set it in a snug suburban house at the height of the British Empire. A soldier home from India carries the danger through the front door. Pay attention to how warm and ordinary everything feels at the start, with a fire, a game of chess and a family teasing each other. That comfort is the whole trick. The story is about the folly of trying to cheat fate, and about how grief can lead a person to ask for something no one should ask for.

stories.title: The Selfish Giant
stories.author: Oscar Wilde
stories.epigraph: “My own garden is my own garden; any one can understand that, and I will allow nobody to play in it but myself.”
paragraphs: Every afternoon, as they were coming from school, the children used to go and play in the Giant’s garden. It was a large lovely garden, with soft green grass. Here and there over the grass stood beautiful flowers like stars, and there were twelve peach-trees that in the spring-time broke out into delicate blossoms of pink and pearl, and in the autumn bore rich fruit. The birds sat on the trees and sang so sweetly that the children used to stop their games in order to listen to them. “How happy we are here!” they cried to each other.

One day the Giant came back. He had been to visit his friend the Cornish ogre, and had stayed with him for seven years. After the seven years were over he had said all that he had to say, for his conversation was limited, and he determined to return to his own castle. When he arrived he saw the children playing in the garden. “What are you doing here?” he cried in a very gruff voice, and the children ran away. “My own garden is my own garden,” said the Giant; “any one can understand that, and I will allow nobody to play in it but myself.” So he built a high wall all round it, and put up a notice-board: TRESPASSERS WILL BE PROSECUTED. He was a very selfish Giant.

The poor children had now nowhere to play. They tried to play on the road, but the road was very dusty and full of hard stones, and they did not like it. They used to wander round the high wall when their lessons were over, and talk about the beautiful garden inside. “How happy we were there,” they said to each other.

Then the Spring came, and all over the country there were little blossoms and little birds. Only in the garden of the Selfish Giant it was still winter. The birds did not care to sing in it as there were no children, and the trees forgot to blossom. Once a beautiful flower put its head out from the grass, but when it saw the notice-board it was so sorry for the children that it slipped back into the ground again, and went off to sleep. The only people who were pleased were the Snow and the Frost. “Spring has forgotten this garden,” they cried, “so we will live here all the year round.” The Snow covered up the grass with her great white cloak, and the Frost painted all the trees silver. Then they invited the North Wind to stay with them, and he came. He was wrapped in furs, and he roared all day about the garden, and blew the chimney-pots down. “This is a delightful spot,” he said, “we must ask the Hail on a visit.” So the Hail came. Every day for three hours he rattled on the roof of the castle till he broke most of the slates, and then he ran round and round the garden as fast as he could go. He was dressed in grey, and his breath was like ice.

“I cannot understand why the Spring is so late in coming,” said the Selfish Giant, as he sat at the window and looked out at his cold white garden; “I hope there will be a change in the weather.” But the Spring never came, nor the Summer. The Autumn gave golden fruit to every garden, but to the Giant’s garden she gave none. “He is too selfish,” she said. So it was always Winter there, and the North Wind, and the Hail, and the Frost, and the Snow danced about through the trees.

One morning the Giant was lying awake in bed when he heard some lovely music. It sounded so sweet to his ears that he thought it must be the King’s musicians passing by. It was really only a little linnet singing outside his window, but it was so long since he had heard a bird sing in his garden that it seemed to him to be the most beautiful music in the world. Then the Hail stopped dancing over his head, and the North Wind ceased roaring, and a delicious perfume came to him through the open casement. “I believe the Spring has come at last,” said the Giant; and he jumped out of bed and looked out.

What did he see? He saw a most wonderful sight. Through a little hole in the wall the children had crept in, and they were sitting in the branches of the trees. In every tree that he could see there was a little child. And the trees were so glad to have the children back again that they had covered themselves with blossoms, and were waving their arms gently above the children’s heads. The birds were flying about and twittering with delight, and the flowers were looking up through the green grass and laughing. It was a lovely scene, only in one corner it was still winter. It was the farthest corner of the garden, and in it was standing a little boy. He was so small that he could not reach up to the branches of the tree, and he was wandering all round it, crying bitterly. The poor tree was still quite covered with frost and snow, and the North Wind was blowing and roaring above it. “Climb up! little boy,” said the Tree, and it bent its branches down as low as it could; but the boy was too tiny.

And the Giant’s heart melted as he looked out. “How selfish I have been!” he said; “now I know why the Spring would not come here. I will put that poor little boy on the top of the tree, and then I will knock down the wall, and my garden shall be the children’s playground for ever and ever.” He was really very sorry for what he had done. So he crept downstairs and opened the front door quite softly, and went out into the garden. But when the children saw him they were so frightened that they all ran away, and the garden became winter again. Only the little boy did not run, for his eyes were so full of tears that he did not see the Giant coming. And the Giant stole up behind him and took him gently in his hand, and put him up into the tree. And the tree broke at once into blossom, and the birds came and sang on it, and the little boy stretched out his two arms and flung them round the Giant’s neck, and kissed him. And the other children, when they saw that the Giant was not wicked any longer, came running back, and with them came the Spring.

“It is your garden now, little children,” said the Giant, and he took a great axe and knocked down the wall. And when the people were going to market at twelve o’clock they found the Giant playing with the children in the most beautiful garden they had ever seen. All day long they played, and in the evening they came to the Giant to bid him good-bye.

“But where is your little companion?” he said: “the boy I put into the tree.” The Giant loved him the best because he had kissed him. “We don’t know,” answered the children; “he has gone away.” “You must tell him to be sure and come here to-morrow,” said the Giant. But the children said that they did not know where he lived, and had never seen him before; and the Giant felt very sad.

Every afternoon, when school was over, the children came and played with the Giant. But the little boy whom the Giant loved was never seen again. The Giant was very kind to all the children, yet he longed for his first little friend, and often spoke of him. “How I would like to see him!” he used to say. Years went over, and the Giant grew very old and feeble. He could not play about any more, so he sat in a huge armchair, and watched the children at their games, and admired his garden. “I have many beautiful flowers,” he said; “but the children are the most beautiful flowers of all.”

One winter morning he looked out of his window as he was dressing. He did not hate the Winter now, for he knew that it was merely the Spring asleep, and that the flowers were resting. Suddenly he rubbed his eyes in wonder, and looked and looked. It certainly was a marvellous sight. In the farthest corner of the garden was a tree quite covered with lovely white blossoms. Its branches were all golden, and silver fruit hung down from them, and underneath it stood the little boy he had loved. Downstairs ran the Giant in great joy, and out into the garden. He hastened across the grass, and came near to the child. And when he came quite close his face grew red with anger, and he said, “Who hath dared to wound thee?” For on the palms of the child’s hands were the prints of two nails, and the prints of two nails were on the little feet. “Who hath dared to wound thee?” cried the Giant; “tell me, that I may take my big sword and slay him.” “Nay!” answered the child; “but these are the wounds of Love.” “Who art thou?” said the Giant, and a strange awe fell on him, and he knelt before the little child. And the child smiled on the Giant, and said to him, “You let me play once in your garden, to-day you shall come with me to my garden, which is Paradise.” And when the children ran in that afternoon, they found the Giant lying dead under the tree, all covered with white blossoms.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
On its face, "The Selfish Giant" is a small fable about a garden. Children are in the habit of playing every afternoon in the Giant's lovely garden, with its soft grass, its flowers like stars and its twelve peach trees. The Giant has been away for seven years visiting a friend, the Cornish ogre, and when he returns he finds the children there, drives them out and builds a high wall. He puts up a notice board, and its message is blunt: "TRESPASSERS WILL BE PROSECUTED." His justification is a tidy bit of circular logic: "My own garden is my own garden." It sounds like common sense, and that is exactly why it is so chilling. The Giant thinks of ownership as a closed door, and the story answers that a closed door is also a closed life.

What follows is the story's central image. When spring comes everywhere else, it refuses to come to the Giant's garden. Snow and Frost move in, joined by the North Wind and the Hail, and the place stays in winter all year. The Giant, puzzled, sits at his window and says he hopes the weather will change. This is the moral cleverly turned into weather: because he has shut out the children, he has shut out the whole cycle of growth and joy. The garden's coldness is simply the outward form of the Giant's own cold heart. Notice that the Giant does not know why he is suffering. Selfishness, the story suggests, is often a blindness before it is a vice.

The thaw begins when a linnet sings at his window, and he sees the children have crept back through a hole in the wall. In every tree sits a child, and the trees are blooming. Only one corner is still in winter, where a small boy is too little to climb a tree. The Giant's heart melts, and he lifts the boy into the branches, knocks down the wall with an axe and tells the children the garden is theirs. The act of giving the garden away is what finally makes it his, and makes it alive.

The last section turns the fable into something else. Years later the Giant is old and feeble, and the little boy returns. The Giant sees marks of two nails on the boy's palms and feet and asks who has dared to wound him. The child answers, "these are the wounds of Love," and tells him he will come to the child's own garden, "which is Paradise." The child is Christ, and the story quietly becomes a parable about grace: the Giant's kindness to a child has been kindness to God. When the children find the Giant dead beneath the tree, covered in white blossoms, the story closes on a note of peace, not sorrow. The winter inside him has finally ended.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
The story's greatest strength is its economy and its sound. Wilde writes in short, clear sentences with the rhythm of something told aloud, and the story reads beautifully when spoken. The opening paragraph paints the garden in a few bright strokes, and the repetition of phrases such as "How happy we were there" gives the tale the quality of a song with a refrain. The personification of the seasons is delightful. Snow covers the grass "with her great white cloak," Frost paints the trees silver, and the Hail is "dressed in grey" with breath "like ice." Wilde gives the cruel weather the manners of unwelcome house guests who decide to stay on and break the roof slates, and that touch of humor keeps the story from heaviness.

The structure is also excellent. It moves in a clean cycle from happiness to loss to winter to renewal, and then onto the larger cycle of a life from youth through old age to death. The little boy who cannot climb the tree is a perfect emotional hinge, because he is both the smallest figure in the story and the one who turns it. The image of winter at the end, which the old Giant no longer hates because "it was merely the Spring asleep," is one of the most graceful lines in the tale, and it shows that the Giant has learned a patient kind of wisdom.

But an honest critic has to admit that the story is also sentimental, and that its sentiment can be sticky. The children are mostly an undifferentiated mass of innocence, and the Giant's conversion is quick and total. A reader may feel that the moral machinery is a little too visible, and that the Giant is more of a symbol than a person. The Christian ending, in particular, is the most debated part. For some readers it is a luminous and moving surprise. For others it is a sudden shift from storybook to sermon, in which the child's grand revelation arrives too neatly and too sweetly. Even readers who admire the ending sometimes feel that Wilde reaches for religious feeling more readily here than elsewhere in his work.

There is another quiet tension. Wilde was a skeptical, witty man who delighted in paradox, and this story is utterly earnest. That earnestness can feel at odds with what we know of his temperament, though it may be that he was simply good at changing voices. Taken as a whole, the story works because it is short, sincere and shapely. Its weaknesses are the weaknesses of its genre, in which simple good and simple evil are the rule, and it handles them with more grace than most.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
"The Selfish Giant" became one of the most beloved children's stories in English, and it has stayed in print and in school curricula for well over a century. Together with "The Happy Prince" and the other tales in the same book, it established Wilde as a writer who could do more than epigrams. It showed a gentle and humane side of him that surprised readers who knew him only as the witty aesthete. When his name later became associated with scandal after his trial and imprisonment in the 1890s, these tales were among the works that kept a warmer picture of him alive.

The story has been retold in picture books, read on radio, staged as plays and school pageants, and adapted into musical and operatic form and into animation. It remains a favorite of primary school teachers because its message of sharing is easy to grasp, and its language is a model of clear, musical English. It is also frequently read at funerals and in church services, because its last scene offers comfort about death.

The tale's reach also extends into surprising places. The idea of a hard-hearted owner whose selfishness blights his own land echoes in later writing about property and community. Wilde's essay "The Soul of Man Under Socialism," published a few years later in 1891, argues in much more abstract language that private property can warp the people who hold it as well as the people shut out by it. Many readers see the Giant's wall as a first, childlike version of that idea. In recent decades the title was borrowed for a British film, directed by Clio Barnard and released in 2013, which is a gritty drama about two boys in a northern English town. It is not an adaptation of the fairy tale in any strict way, but it borrows the title and the theme of selfishness and kindness set against social hardship.

For literary history, the tale helped confirm a late Victorian shift in children's literature. Where earlier moral tales were often heavy and bossy, writers such as Wilde and, before him, Hans Christian Andersen showed that a fairy tale could be poetic, sad and deeply felt without lecturing. Later writers of literary fairy tales owe something to that example, and the story remains a touchstone for anyone who wants to write a modern fable.

A last point is worth noting. Wilde's story is quietly modern in refusing to punish the Giant forever. Mercy is allowed to win, and the winter is understood as a pause rather than a sentence, which has made it a comfort to generations.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
The most obvious thing readers love is the garden itself. Wilde makes it so vivid, with its pink and pearl blossoms and its singing birds, that its loss feels like a real bereavement. Children respond to the simple justice of the plot, in which a bully is shut out of happiness by his own behavior. Adults respond to something deeper, a feeling that they know this Giant, and that they have sometimes been him in small ways. Readers often say that the story made them think about their own walls, whether of pride, of property or of fear.

They also love its tenderness. The Giant is not a monster. He is gruff, self-absorbed and lonely, with a limited conversation, as Wilde says drily, but he is capable of changing. His transformation, when he sees the weeping boy and says "How selfish I have been!", is one of the most satisfying turns in children's literature, because it is so unforced. The detail that the other children run away when they see him, frightened, and that only the boy with tear-filled eyes does not notice him, is the kind of true psychological touch that makes a fable feel alive.

Many readers cherish the last scene most of all. The reappearance of the little boy after years, with the marks of the nails, produces a shiver that even non-religious readers feel. The sentence "You let me play once in your garden, to-day you shall come with me to my garden, which is Paradise" has been quoted at funerals and in sermons precisely because it holds out a promise of reward for simple kindness. The Giant dies in peace under a tree covered in blossoms, and the story says that death can be gentle.

Finally, readers admire the music of the prose. People who read the story aloud to children often remark on how well the sentences carry. It is a story designed for the ear, with repetitions and refrains, and with a flow that makes the whole thing feel like a song. That is also why it works so well as audio. It asks very little of a reader and gives a great deal back, and for many people it is the first literary work that ever made them cry.

Many readers also mention how much the story matters to them as parents or teachers, and how often they have found themselves reaching for it when a child asks why sharing matters.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Little in the way of hostile criticism greeted "The Happy Prince and Other Tales" when it appeared, and in general the book was received warmly, though specific reviews of this one story are not especially well documented. Most of the pushback has been indirect and has come from later readers weighing the story against Wilde's reputation and its own sweetness.

The most frequent objection is sentimentality. Critics who prize toughness and irony have found the story too sugary, with its angelic children, its quick conversion and its heavenly ending. For these readers the story is lovely but easy, and it solves the problem of selfishness by having a magical child appear and everything turn out well. In real life, walls do not come down because a child cries in a tree.

A second objection concerns the Christian ending. Some readers feel that the revelation that the boy is Christ turns a humane and universal fable into a narrowly religious one, and that it was an odd move for a writer who was so often at odds with conventional religion. Others note that Wilde had a lifelong fascination with Christ as a figure of suffering and individual feeling, and that his interest was aesthetic and emotional more than doctrinal. This has led to debate about whether the ending is sincere devotion, a poet's fascination with a symbol, or a bit of both. A few readers have also found the idea that the Giant is rewarded with heaven for a late-life change of heart a little too easy, since the children he shut out spent years without a place to play.

A third line of criticism is political, and it points in an unexpected direction. Some readers see in the story an endorsement of generosity as a private virtue and wonder whether it lets structural questions off the hook. The Giant's conversion is personal, not systemic. He is moved to open the garden by feeling, not by law or justice, and the story offers no sense of what should happen if the owner stays hard-hearted. Others say that this misreads a fairy tale, which is not a political pamphlet.

Finally, a few have asked whether the story is quite as suitable for children as it appears, since it ends with a death and a vision of wounds. Most readers feel that Wilde handles this delicately, but the point has been raised.

The tale is also admired for how little it explains. It trusts the child listener to feel the sadness of the missing boy, and trusts the adult listener to understand who he is.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
"The Selfish Giant" belongs to the tradition of the literary fairy tale, a form in which a known author, rather than anonymous folk tradition, makes up a story with the feel of an old one. Its closest ancestor is Hans Christian Andersen, whose tales mix charm with sorrow and whose stories often end in death and a hint of heaven. Wilde's own "The Happy Prince" and "The Nightingale and the Rose" belong to the same family, with their gentle melancholy and their emphasis on sacrifice. Behind Andersen lies the older tradition of the moral parable and the Christian allegory, in which a simple story carries a spiritual truth.

The tale also belongs to a Victorian conversation about childhood. In the nineteenth century, writers were increasingly interested in the idea of children as innocents who could redeem the adult world, an idea you can find in Dickens, in the poetry of Wordsworth before him, and in the later boom in children's literature around the time of Lewis Carroll. The Giant's garden, a paradise from which children are shut out and to which they return, fits that strain of thought, and the story's emotional logic is that adults are saved by the children they would shut out.

Among later works, it can be set beside other stories about walls and gardens. The secret garden as a place of healing is a major theme in children's books, as is the idea of a hoarder or miser who is melted by kindness, a theme familiar from Dickens's A Christmas Carol. In the Giant we can see a cousin of Scrooge, with the difference that Wilde's tale is gentler and shorter, and ends in a far more mystical register. Comparisons might also be drawn with stories of gift and sacrifice such as Shel Silverstein's The Giving Tree, though that is a very different book with a different attitude toward giving.

It still matters because its central question has not gone away. Who gets to use the green spaces of the world, and what do we lose when we wall them off? It is also an unusually gentle gateway to Wilde. A reader who knows him only from The Importance of Being Earnest may be surprised to find that the same hand wrote this, and that it is full of warmth and conviction. It takes five minutes to read, and it leaves something behind.

stories.keyContext: Oscar Wilde is remembered for dazzling stage comedies and razor-sharp one-liners, which makes "The Selfish Giant" a surprise. It is a tender, simple fairy tale, and it appeared in 1888 in a little book called The Happy Prince and Other Tales. Wilde wrote these stories partly with his two young sons, Cyril and Vyvyan, in mind, and he was a loving father who enjoyed telling them stories. The tale draws on the fairy tales of Hans Christian Andersen, on Christian imagery, and on a typical Victorian concern with how the rich treat the poor and the young. It is short enough to read in five minutes, and it works on children and adults at once. Its subject is what happens to a person, and to a place, when everything is fenced off and kept for oneself. Listen for the seasons, because the weather in this story is a kind of moral barometer, and for the quiet surprise near the very end.

stories.title: Dr. Heidegger's Experiment
stories.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
stories.epigraph: “Think what a sin and shame it would be, if, with your peculiar advantages, you should not become patterns of virtue and wisdom to all the young people of the age!”
paragraphs: That very singular man, old Dr. Heidegger, once invited four venerable friends to meet him in his study. There were three white-bearded gentlemen, Mr. Medbourne, Colonel Killigrew, and Mr. Gascoigne, and a withered gentlewoman, whose name was the Widow Wycherly. They were all melancholy old creatures, who had been unfortunate in life, and whose greatest misfortune it was that they were not long ago in their graves. Mr. Medbourne, in the vigor of his age, had been a prosperous merchant, but had lost his all by a frantic speculation, and was now little better than a mendicant. Colonel Killigrew had wasted his best years, and his health and substance, in the pursuit of sinful pleasures, which had given birth to a brood of pains, such as the gout, and divers other torments of soul and body. Mr. Gascoigne was a ruined politician, a man of evil fame, or at least had been so till time had buried him from the knowledge of the present generation, and made him obscure instead of infamous. As for the Widow Wycherly, tradition tells us that she was a great beauty in her day; but, for a long while past, she had lived in deep seclusion, on account of certain scandalous stories which had prejudiced the gentry of the town against her. It is a circumstance worth mentioning that each of these three old gentlemen, Mr. Medbourne, Colonel Killigrew, and Mr. Gascoigne, were early lovers of the Widow Wycherly, and had once been on the point of cutting each other’s throats for her sake. And, before proceeding further, I will merely hint that Dr. Heidegger and all his four guests were sometimes thought to be a little beside themselves—as is not unfrequently the case with old people, when worried either by present troubles or woful recollections.
“My dear old friends,” said Dr. Heidegger, motioning them to be seated, “I am desirous of your assistance in one of those little experiments with which I amuse myself here in my study.”

If all stories were true, Dr. Heidegger’s study must have been a very curious place. It was a dim, old-fashioned chamber, festooned with cobwebs, and besprinkled with antique dust. Around the walls stood several oaken bookcases, the lower shelves of which were filled with rows of gigantic folios and black-letter quartos, and the upper with little parchment-covered duodecimos. Over the central bookcase was a bronze bust of Hippocrates, with which, according to some authorities, Dr. Heidegger was accustomed to hold consultations in all difficult cases of his practice. In the obscurest corner of the room stood a tall and narrow oaken closet, with its door ajar, within which doubtfully appeared a skeleton. Between two of the bookcases hung a looking-glass, presenting its high and dusty plate within a tarnished gilt frame. Among many wonderful stories related of this mirror, it was fabled that the spirits of all the doctor’s deceased patients dwelt within its verge, and would stare him in the face whenever he looked thitherward. The opposite side of the chamber was ornamented with the full-length portrait of a young lady, arrayed in the faded magnificence of silk, satin, and brocade, and with a visage as faded as her dress. Above half a century ago, Dr. Heidegger had been on the point of marriage with this young lady; but, being affected with some slight disorder, she had swallowed one of her lover’s prescriptions, and died on the bridal evening. The greatest curiosity of the study remains to be mentioned; it was a ponderous folio volume, bound in black leather, with massive silver clasps. There were no letters on the back, and nobody could tell the title of the book. But it was well known to be a book of magic; and once, when a chambermaid had lifted it, merely to brush away the dust, the skeleton had rattled in its closet, the picture of the young lady had stepped one foot upon the floor, and several ghastly faces had peeped forth from the mirror; while the brazen head of Hippocrates frowned, and said—“Forbear!”

Such was Dr. Heidegger’s study. On the summer afternoon of our tale a small round table, as black as ebony, stood in the centre of the room, sustaining a cut-glass vase of beautiful form and elaborate workmanship. The sunshine came through the window, between the heavy festoons of two faded damask curtains, and fell directly across this vase; so that a mild splendor was reflected from it on the ashen visages of the five old people who sat around. Four champagne glasses were also on the table. “My dear old friends,” repeated Dr. Heidegger, “may I reckon on your aid in performing an exceedingly curious experiment?”

Now Dr. Heidegger was a very strange old gentleman, whose eccentricity had become the nucleus for a thousand fantastic stories. Some of these fables, to my shame be it spoken, might possibly be traced back to my own veracious self; and if any passages of the present tale should startle the reader’s faith, I must be content to bear the stigma of a fiction monger. When the doctor’s four guests heard him talk of his proposed experiment, they anticipated nothing more wonderful than the murder of a mouse in an air pump, or the examination of a cobweb by the microscope, or some similar nonsense, with which he was constantly in the habit of pestering his intimates. But without waiting for a reply, Dr. Heidegger hobbled across the chamber, and returned with the same ponderous folio, bound in black leather, which common report affirmed to be a book of magic. Undoing the silver clasps, he opened the volume, and took from among its black-letter pages a rose, or what was once a rose, though now the green leaves and crimson petals had assumed one brownish hue, and the ancient flower seemed ready to crumble to dust in the doctor’s hands.

“This rose,” said Dr. Heidegger, with a sigh, “this same withered and crumbling flower, blossomed five and fifty years ago. It was given me by Sylvia Ward, whose portrait hangs yonder; and I meant to wear it in my bosom at our wedding. Five and fifty years it has been treasured between the leaves of this old volume. Now, would you deem it possible that this rose of half a century could ever bloom again?” “Nonsense!” said the Widow Wycherly, with a peevish toss of her head. “You might as well ask whether an old woman’s wrinkled face could ever bloom again.” “See!” answered Dr. Heidegger.

He uncovered the vase, and threw the faded rose into the water which it contained. At first, it lay lightly on the surface of the fluid, appearing to imbibe none of its moisture. Soon, however, a singular change began to be visible. The crushed and dried petals stirred, and assumed a deepening tinge of crimson, as if the flower were reviving from a deathlike slumber; the slender stalk and twigs of foliage became green; and there was the rose of half a century, looking as fresh as when Sylvia Ward had first given it to her lover. It was scarcely full blown; for some of its delicate red leaves curled modestly around its moist bosom, within which two or three dewdrops were sparkling.

“That is certainly a very pretty deception,” said the doctor’s friends; carelessly, however, for they had witnessed greater miracles at a conjurer’s show; “pray how was it effected?” “Did you never hear of the ‘Fountain of Youth’?” asked Dr. Heidegger, “which Ponce de Leon, the Spanish adventurer, went in search of two or three centuries ago?” “But did Ponce de Leon ever find it?” said the Widow Wycherly. “No,” answered Dr. Heidegger, “for he never sought it in the right place. The famous Fountain of Youth, if I am rightly informed, is situated in the southern part of the Floridian peninsula, not far from Lake Macaco. Its source is overshadowed by several gigantic magnolias, which, though numberless centuries old, have been kept as fresh as violets by the virtues of this wonderful water. An acquaintance of mine, knowing my curiosity in such matters, has sent me what you see in the vase.”

“Ahem!” said Colonel Killigrew, who believed not a word of the doctor’s story: “and what may be the effect of this fluid on the human frame?” “You shall judge for yourself, my dear colonel,” replied Dr. Heidegger; “and all of you, my respected friends, are welcome to so much of this admirable fluid as may restore to you the bloom of youth. For my own part, having had much trouble in growing old, I am in no hurry to grow young again. With your permission, therefore, I will merely watch the progress of the experiment.”

While he spoke, Dr. Heidegger had been filling the four champagne glasses with the water of the Fountain of Youth. It was apparently impregnated with an effervescent gas, for little bubbles were continually ascending from the depths of the glasses, and bursting in silvery spray at the surface. As the liquor diffused a pleasant perfume, the old people doubted not that it possessed cordial and comfortable properties; and though utter sceptics as to its rejuvenescent power, they were inclined to swallow it at once. But Dr. Heidegger besought them to stay a moment. “Before you drink, my respectable old friends,” said he, “it would be well that, with the experience of a lifetime to direct you, you should draw up a few general rules for your guidance, in passing a second time through the perils of youth. Think what a sin and shame it would be, if, with your peculiar advantages, you should not become patterns of virtue and wisdom to all the young people of the age!” The doctor’s four venerable friends made him no answer, except by a feeble and tremulous laugh; so very ridiculous was the idea that, knowing how closely repentance treads behind the steps of error, they should ever go astray again. “Drink, then,” said the doctor, bowing: “I rejoice that I have so well selected the subjects of my experiment.”

With palsied hands, they raised the glasses to their lips. The liquor, if it really possessed such virtues as Dr. Heidegger imputed to it, could not have been bestowed on four human beings who needed it more wofully. They looked as if they had never known what youth or pleasure was, but had been the offspring of Nature’s dotage, and always the gray, decrepit, sapless, miserable creatures, who now sat stooping round the doctor’s table, without life enough in their souls or bodies to be animated even by the prospect of growing young again. They drank off the water, and replaced their glasses on the table. Assuredly there was an almost immediate improvement in the aspect of the party, not unlike what might have been produced by a glass of generous wine, together with a sudden glow of cheerful sunshine brightening over all their visages at once. There was a healthful suffusion on their cheeks, instead of the ashen hue that had made them look so corpse-like. They gazed at one another, and fancied that some magic power had really begun to smooth away the deep and sad inscriptions which Father Time had been so long engraving on their brows. The Widow Wycherly adjusted her cap, for she felt almost like a woman again.

“Give us more of this wondrous water!” cried they, eagerly. “We are younger—but we are still too old! Quick—give us more!” “Patience, patience!” quoth Dr. Heidegger, who sat watching the experiment with philosophic coolness. “You have been a long time growing old. Surely, you might be content to grow young in half an hour! But the water is at your service.” Again he filled their glasses with the liquor of youth, enough of which still remained in the vase to turn half the old people in the city to the age of their own grandchildren. While the bubbles were yet sparkling on the brim, the doctor’s four guests snatched their glasses from the table, and swallowed the contents at a single gulp. Was it delusion? even while the draught was passing down their throats, it seemed to have wrought a change on their whole systems. Their eyes grew clear and bright; a dark shade deepened among their silvery locks, they sat around the table, three gentlemen of middle age, and a woman, hardly beyond her buxom prime.

“My dear widow, you are charming!” cried Colonel Killigrew, whose eyes had been fixed upon her face, while the shadows of age were flitting from it like darkness from the crimson daybreak. The fair widow knew, of old, that Colonel Killigrew’s compliments were not always measured by sober truth; so she started up and ran to the mirror, still dreading that the ugly visage of an old woman would meet her gaze. Meanwhile, the three gentlemen behaved in such a manner as proved that the water of the Fountain of Youth possessed some intoxicating qualities; unless, indeed, their exhilaration of spirits were merely a lightsome dizziness caused by the sudden removal of the weight of years. Mr. Gascoigne’s mind seemed to run on political topics, but whether relating to the past, present, or future could not easily be determined, since the same ideas and phrases have been in vogue these fifty years. Now he rattled forth full-throated sentences about patriotism, national glory, and the people’s right; now he muttered some perilous stuff or other, in a sly and doubtful whisper, so cautiously that even his own conscience could scarcely catch the secret; and now, again, he spoke in measured accents, and a deeply deferential tone, as if a royal ear were listening to his well-turned periods. Colonel Killigrew all this time had been trolling forth a jolly bottle song, and ringing his glass in symphony with the chorus, while his eyes wandered toward the buxom figure of the Widow Wycherly. On the other side of the table, Mr. Medbourne was involved in a calculation of dollars and cents, with which was strangely intermingled a project for supplying the East Indies with ice, by harnessing a team of whales to the polar icebergs.

As for the Widow Wycherly, she stood before the mirror courtesying and simpering to her own image, and greeting it as the friend whom she loved better than all the world beside. She thrust her face close to the glass, to see whether some long-remembered wrinkle or crow’s foot had indeed vanished. She examined whether the snow had so entirely melted from her hair that the venerable cap could be safely thrown aside. At last, turning briskly away, she came with a sort of dancing step to the table. “My dear old doctor,” cried she, “pray favor me with another glass!” “Certainly, my dear madam, certainly!” replied the complaisant doctor; “see! I have already filled the glasses.”

There, in fact, stood the four glasses, brimful of this wonderful water, the delicate spray of which, as it effervesced from the surface, resembled the tremulous glitter of diamonds. It was now so nearly sunset that the chamber had grown duskier than ever; but a mild and moonlike splendor gleamed from within the vase, and rested alike on the four guests and on the doctor’s venerable figure. He sat in a high-backed, elaborately-carved, oaken arm-chair, with a gray dignity of aspect that might have well befitted that very Father Time, whose power had never been disputed, save by this fortunate company. Even while quaffing the third draught of the Fountain of Youth, they were almost awed by the expression of his mysterious visage.

But, the next moment, the exhilarating gush of young life shot through their veins. They were now in the happy prime of youth. Age, with its miserable train of cares and sorrows and diseases, was remembered only as the trouble of a dream, from which they had joyously awoke. The fresh gloss of the soul, so early lost, and without which the world’s successive scenes had been but a gallery of faded pictures, again threw its enchantment over all their prospects. They felt like new-created beings in a new-created universe. “We are young! We are young!” they cried exultingly.

Youth, like the extremity of age, had effaced the strongly-marked characteristics of middle life, and mutually assimilated them all. They were a group of merry youngsters, almost maddened with the exuberant frolicsomeness of their years. The most singular effect of their gayety was an impulse to mock the infirmity and decrepitude of which they had so lately been the victims. They laughed loudly at their old-fashioned attire, the wide-skirted coats and flapped waist-coats of the young men, and the ancient cap and gown of the blooming girl. One limped across the floor like a gouty grandfather; one set a pair of spectacles astride of his nose, and pretended to pore over the black-letter pages of the book of magic; a third seated himself in an arm-chair, and strove to imitate the venerable dignity of Dr. Heidegger. Then all shouted mirthfully, and leaped about the room. The Widow Wycherly—if so fresh a damsel could be called a widow—tripped up to the doctor’s chair, with a mischievous merriment in her rosy face.

“Doctor, you dear old soul,” cried she, “get up and dance with me!” And then the four young people laughed louder than ever, to think what a queer figure the poor old doctor would cut. “Pray excuse me,” answered the doctor quietly. “I am old and rheumatic, and my dancing days were over long ago. But either of these gay young gentlemen will be glad of so pretty a partner.” “Dance with me, Clara!” cried Colonel Killigrew. “No, no, I will be her partner!” shouted Mr. Gascoigne. “She promised me her hand, fifty years ago!” exclaimed Mr. Medbourne. They all gathered round her. One caught both her hands in his passionate grasp—another threw his arm about her waist—the third buried his hand among the glossy curls that clustered beneath the widow’s cap. Blushing, panting, struggling, chiding, laughing, her warm breath fanning each of their faces by turns, she strove to disengage herself, yet still remained in their triple embrace. Never was there a livelier picture of youthful rivalship, with bewitching beauty for the prize. Yet, by a strange deception, owing to the duskiness of the chamber, and the antique dresses which they still wore, the tall mirror is said to have reflected the figures of the three old, gray, withered grandsires, ridiculously contending for the skinny ugliness of a shrivelled grandam.

But they were young: their burning passions proved them so. Inflamed to madness by the coquetry of the girl-widow, who neither granted nor quite withheld her favors, the three rivals began to interchange threatening glances. Still keeping hold of the fair prize, they grappled fiercely at one another’s throats. As they struggled to and fro, the table was overturned, and the vase dashed into a thousand fragments. The precious Water of Youth flowed in a bright stream across the floor, moistening the wings of a butterfly, which, grown old in the decline of summer, had alighted there to die. The insect fluttered lightly through the chamber, and settled on the snowy head of Dr. Heidegger.

“Come, come, gentlemen! come, Madam Wycherly,” exclaimed the doctor, “I really must protest against this riot.” They stood still and shivered; for it seemed as if gray Time were calling them back from their sunny youth, far down into the chill and darksome vale of years. They looked at old Dr. Heidegger, who sat in his carved arm-chair, holding the rose of half a century, which he had rescued from among the fragments of the shattered vase. At the motion of his hand, the four rioters resumed their seats; the more readily, because their violent exertions had wearied them, youthful though they were. “My poor Sylvia’s rose!” ejaculated Dr. Heidegger, holding it in the light of the sunset clouds; “it appears to be fading again.” And so it was. Even while the party were looking at it, the flower continued to shrivel up, till it became as dry and fragile as when the doctor had first thrown it into the vase. He shook off the few drops of moisture which clung to its petals. “I love it as well thus as in its dewy freshness,” observed he, pressing the withered rose to his withered lips. While he spoke, the butterfly fluttered down from the doctor’s snowy head, and fell upon the floor.

His guests shivered again. A strange chillness, whether of the body or spirit they could not tell, was creeping gradually over them all. They gazed at one another, and fancied that each fleeting moment snatched away a charm, and left a deepening furrow where none had been before. Was it an illusion? Had the changes of a lifetime been crowded into so brief a space, and were they now four aged people, sitting with their old friend, Dr. Heidegger? “Are we grown old again, so soon?” cried they, dolefully. In truth they had. The Water of Youth possessed merely a virtue more transient than that of wine. The delirium which it created had effervesced away. Yes! they were old again. With a shuddering impulse, that showed her a woman still, the widow clasped her skinny hands before her face, and wished that the coffin lid were over it, since it could be no longer beautiful.

“Yes, friends, ye are old again,” said Dr. Heidegger, “and lo! the Water of Youth is all lavished on the ground. Well—I bemoan it not; for if the fountain gushed at my very doorstep, I would not stoop to bathe my lips in it—no, though its delirium were for years instead of moments. Such is the lesson ye have taught me!” But the doctor’s four friends had taught no such lesson to themselves. They resolved forthwith to make a pilgrimage to Florida, and quaff at morning, noon, and night, from the Fountain of Youth.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The story opens like a tall tale told by a slightly mischievous uncle. Dr. Heidegger, "that very singular man," invites four old friends to his study. Three are men, Mr. Medbourne, Colonel Killigrew and Mr. Gascoigne, and one is a woman, the Widow Wycherly. Each is a ruin of a particular kind. Medbourne was a merchant who lost everything in a reckless gamble. Killigrew wasted his health and fortune on pleasure and is now crippled with gout. Gascoigne is a disgraced politician whose name is blurred by time. The widow was once a famous beauty who has lived in seclusion since scandal. Hawthorne adds a sly detail: all three men were once her lovers and had nearly killed each other over her.

The doctor's study is full of cobwebs, a skeleton in a closet, a mirror said to hold the spirits of the doctor's dead patients, and a book of magic. He shows his guests a rose, preserved for fifty-five years from the courtship of his lost fiancée, Sylvia Ward, who died on the eve of their wedding. He pours water from a vase, said to have come from the Fountain of Youth in Florida, over the withered flower, and it blooms again. The guests, skeptical but greedy, drink. As they do, they grow younger by decades. Their cheeks flush, their backs straighten and their voices turn lively and loud.

Here is what the story is really about. The newly young people do not become wiser. They repeat their old errors almost at once. Medbourne dreams of new money schemes, Killigrew drinks and carouses, Gascoigne talks politics with a sense of grand self-importance, and the Widow flirts at the mirror. Soon the three men are fighting over her again, and in the struggle the vase is smashed and the water spills. The magic is brief, the rose fades, and the guests find that they have aged all over again.

The decisive moment comes when Heidegger, still calm, says that if the fountain "gushed at my very doorstep," he would not stoop to drink from it. He has learned from watching how little experience changes a person who lacks the will to change. The ending is a bitter joke. The four guests have learned nothing at all, and they resolve to set off for Florida to find the fountain and drink from it morning, noon and night. The meaning, then, is not that youth is a curse or old age a blessing. It is that character, not years, decides how we live, and that folly is not a disease of age but a habit of the heart. It carries a sharper edge, too: that human beings are remarkably resistant to learning from their own lives.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
"Dr. Heidegger's Experiment" is one of those stories that is better as an idea than as a drama, and Hawthorne knows it. As a piece of design, however, it is superb. The setting is eerie and economical, a cluttered Gothic study full of strange objects that suggest a world beyond ordinary science. The four guests are drawn as types, with just enough comic detail to make them vivid, and their transformation is staged as a lively sequence of small scenes. The widow admiring herself in the mirror, the colonel singing a drinking song, and the politician imagining himself in grand debate are all quick, amusing and revealing. Hawthorne's ironic narrator, wry and detached, keeps the whole thing from becoming heavy.

The most admirable thing is how well it manages its ambiguity. Hawthorne never tells us whether the water is truly magical, whether the guests have really become young, or whether the effect is a kind of shared delirium. The narrator repeatedly reports the doctor's claims as hearsay and the study as the setting of "wonderful stories," leaving the reader to decide how much to believe. The mirror, the butterfly that revives and then dies, and the rose that blooms and fades all carry symbolic weight without ever being nailed down. That ability to hold the line between the fantastic and the psychological, so that the tale can be read either way, is Hawthorne's signature skill, and it is on early display here.

Nonetheless, there are limits. The story is quite schematic, and its characters are less people than allegorical figures, each standing for a single vice. The moral is clear almost from the first page, and the reader is waiting to watch the guests prove it. Some of the humor is a bit mannered, and the narrator's coyness, always hinting that the study's wonders are only rumor, can feel arch. The widow, in particular, is handled in a way that now reads as condescending, since the story's mockery falls most sharply on a vain woman, while the three men's follies are treated with more indulgence.

The story is also very short and does not develop its ideas at length. Compared with Hawthorne's later masterpieces such as "Young Goodman Brown" or "The Minister's Black Veil," it is lighter and more fable-like, with less psychological depth. It is a clever and elegant piece, not a profound one. But its elegance is real, and the final image of four foolish old people hurrying toward the fountain has the dark comic bite that makes the whole thing memorable.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The story was an early success for Hawthorne, and it appeared at an important moment. After years of writing in relative obscurity, he gathered his magazine pieces into Twice-Told Tales in 1837, and that book helped establish his reputation as a serious American writer. Reviewers noticed him, and the book introduced the world to his characteristic mixture of historical imagination, moral seriousness and cool irony. A later and more famous review of the collection by Edgar Allan Poe, published in the early 1840s, praised Hawthorne's originality even as it complained that he relied too much on allegory. Poe's remarks became part of the long conversation about what a short story should be.

The tale also helped to shape the genre of speculative fiction. It is an early American example of a story in which a scientist or experimenter tests an extraordinary substance on human subjects and observes the results. Hawthorne would return to this scenario in other works, including "Rappaccini's Daughter" and "The Birth-Mark," in which scientists meddle with nature and pay for it. These tales form an important line in the literature of the cautious or skeptical response to scientific ambition, and they are often cited as forerunners of stories about mad scientists and moral experiments.

Its central question has had a very long afterlife. The idea of a fountain or elixir of youth, and of the human response to being given it, has been revisited again and again. Later writers have asked what would happen if people could live forever, or be young again, and many of them have reached conclusions not far from Hawthorne's. Stories of immortality that turns sour, of the rejuvenated who repeat their mistakes and of the elderly who long for lost years all have this story somewhere in their family tree. In popular culture, its mood can be felt in countless tales about the cost of eternal youth.

For readers and teachers, the story has become a standard in American literature courses. It is short, it is accessible and it introduces the key habits of Hawthorne's art: allegory, symbol, ambiguity and moral irony. Students are often asked to debate whether the transformation is real, what the mirror signifies and whether Heidegger is wise or merely cold. The story also stays in memory because of its tone, which is at once amusing and unsettling. Even people who have never read the story may know its premise, because it has become one of those fables that circulate as part of the general culture.

One further point is that the story never lectures. Heidegger's closing remark is brief, and the final line about the pilgrimage to Florida is delivered with a straight face. Hawthorne trusts the irony to do the teaching, and that restraint is a mark of real craft.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers have long responded to the story's dry, mischievous charm. Hawthorne is often thought of as a gloomy writer, but this tale shows him in a playful mood. The narrator relishes the oddity of the doctor and his study, and the reader enjoys being let in on the joke. The cobwebbed library, the skeleton that is said to stand in the closet, and the black-bound book of magic whose title no one knows all contribute to a delicious Gothic atmosphere, and the sly commentary keeps it from tipping into melodrama.

They also admire its psychological truth. It is easy to believe that the four friends would act as they do. Anyone who has watched a person fall back into an old habit, or who has felt the pull of nostalgia and the wish to do it all again, recognizes the scene in which the rejuvenated guests rush to their old passions. The story gives a satisfying, slightly rueful sense of recognition. It suggests that we are less free than we like to think, and that our character is a kind of destiny. Many readers find this both amusing and a little frightening.

Another source of pleasure is the story's unexpected tenderness. Amid the satire, there is Heidegger's love for his lost Sylvia, and the moment when he presses the withered rose to his lips and says he loves it as well in its dryness as in its dewy freshness. That moment lifts the story out of simple mockery. It suggests that the doctor, alone among the characters, has made peace with time, and that love can survive loss and decay. Readers often single out that image as the emotional center of the tale.

Finally, people appreciate its brevity and its open ending. It can be read in twenty minutes, and it leaves a great deal to discuss. Writers and teachers like how much meaning Hawthorne packs into a handful of symbols. The ending, in which the four set off on their pilgrimage to Florida, is particularly relished for its comic sting. It is the perfect final touch, a reminder that human beings are almost endlessly capable of repeating themselves, and it sends the reader away smiling and a little chastened.

The story's staying power also owes something to its title character. Heidegger, calm, odd and a little sad, is a memorable figure, and readers often say they would like to know more about him.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Hawthorne's contemporaries generally received Twice-Told Tales with respect, but even admirers had reservations about the way he worked. The most famous is that of Edgar Allan Poe, who reviewed the collection in 1842. Poe admired Hawthorne's originality but argued that a heavy reliance on allegory weakened a story, and that a tale built on a moral meaning could lose the unity of effect he thought essential. That complaint has followed Hawthorne's more schematic pieces ever since, and "Dr. Heidegger's Experiment," with its four characters who each stand for a vice, is one of the clearest targets.

Another criticism has been that the story is thin. Because the moral is plain and the characters are types, some readers find it more of an anecdote than a fully realized tale. The magical premise is never developed, the transformation is described in a sequence of rapid, somewhat comic vignettes, and the ending follows predictably from the setup. When read beside Hawthorne's richer, darker work, it can seem a slight piece, more charming than deep. Some critics have also pointed out that Heidegger himself is oddly remote. He stands apart as a cool observer who tests his friends without apparent sympathy, and there is something faintly cruel about a man who invites old, broken people to be rejuvenated simply to prove a point. Readers have sometimes wondered whether the story endorses his detachment or quietly criticizes it.

More modern readers have raised objections of tone. The treatment of the Widow Wycherly, in particular, strikes many as dated, since the story is harder on her vanity than on the men's equally destructive habits, and it uses her desirability as the spark of the final quarrel. Questions have also been raised about the story's attitude toward age. Does it mock old people for wanting more life, or does it sympathize with them? Hawthorne's tone is ironic enough that both readings are possible, and some readers find that it comes close to treating the elderly as figures of fun.

Finally, a few critics have asked whether the story's pessimism is too easy. By suggesting that people cannot learn from experience, it settles a hard question with a joke. Others reply that Hawthorne is too much of a moralist to be so flippant, and that the bleakness is his point. The disagreement is part of the story's continuing life.

There is a final point that is easy to overlook. The tale offers no villain, only people, and that evenhandedness is a kind of compassion beneath the irony.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
"Dr. Heidegger's Experiment" belongs to American Romanticism, and more precisely to the strain that is often called Dark Romanticism. While writers like Ralph Waldo Emerson, a neighbor and contemporary, expressed trust in human nature and the unity of mind and universe, Hawthorne, Poe and later Herman Melville looked at guilt, error and the shadows within the self. Hawthorne's Puritan inheritance gave him a lifelong sense that people are flawed in ways that progress cannot fix. This story is a good example. The Enlightenment dream of improving life through science, and the optimistic dream of renewing oneself through a fresh start, are both gently tested and found wanting.

The story also stands in a long tradition of tales about the quest for eternal youth and the folly of wanting it. The legend of Ponce de Leon and the fountain in Florida, which Hawthorne cites, is only one piece of the tradition. Older versions include the Greek myth of Tithonus, who was granted eternal life but not eternal youth, and Jonathan Swift's immortal Struldbrugs in Gulliver's Travels, who live forever and wither horribly. Later descendants include Oscar Wilde's The Picture of Dorian Gray, in which youth is purchased at a moral price, and Karel Capek's play The Makropulos Affair, which imagines a woman wearied by centuries of life. Hawthorne's version is lighter than these, but it shares the idea that the wish to escape time is a trap.

It also forms part of a body of Hawthorne's work in which experimental science meets human limitation. Alongside "Rappaccini's Daughter," "The Birth-Mark" and "Ethan Brand," it expresses a recurring suspicion of those who treat other people as subjects for tests. In this sense it is a forerunner of the modern science fiction tale of the experiment that goes wrong, and of the cautionary story about the cost of conquering nature.

Why read it now? Partly because its question feels newly pressing in an age of longevity research and cosmetic reinvention. Partly because it is a model of the short allegory, in which every object means something and the meaning is never quite settled. And partly because it is short, witty and strange. It may not be Hawthorne's deepest work, but it shows his skill and his humor at their liveliest, and it leaves you thinking about what you would do with a second chance.

stories.keyContext: Nathaniel Hawthorne published "Dr. Heidegger's Experiment" in 1837, early in his career, and it appeared that year in his first major collection, Twice-Told Tales. Hawthorne came from Salem, Massachusetts, a town haunted by its Puritan past, and one of his own ancestors had been a judge at the Salem witch trials. He grew up to be a writer fascinated by guilt, pride and the stubborn flaws of human nature, and he had little patience for the sunny belief of his day that people could simply be improved. In this story, an odd old doctor invites four aged friends to his study and offers them a drink from the legendary Fountain of Youth.
