He swallowed one of the stay-wake tablets with a scalding mouth of black coffee.

Well, with one thing and another it was Tolstoy or Balzac, gin-rummy, coffee, tablets, walking, more Tolstoy, more Balzac, more gin-rummy, more solitaire. The first day passed, as did the second and the third.

On the fourth day he lay quietly in the shade of a rock, counting to a thousand by fives, then by tens, to keep his mind occupied and awake. His eyes were so tired he had to bathe them frequently in cool water. He couldn’t read, he was bothered with splitting headaches. He was so exhausted he couldn’t move. He was numb with medicine. He resembled a waxen dummy, stuffed with things to preserve him in a state of horrified wakefulness. His eyes were glass, his tongue a rusted pike, his fingers felt as if they were gloved in needles and fur.

He followed the hand of his watch. One second less to wait, he thought. Two seconds, three seconds, four, five, ten, thirty seconds. A whole minute. Now an hour less time to wait. Oh, ship, hurry on thy appointed round!
He began to laugh softly.
What would happen if he just gave up, drifted off into sleep? Sleep, ah, sleep; perchance to dream. All the world a stage.⁠ ⁠… What if he gave up the unequal struggle, lapsed down?
Eeeeeeeeeee, the high, shrill warning sound of battle metal.
He shivered. His tongue moved in his dry, burry mouth.
Iorr and Tylle would battle out their ancient battle.
Leonard Sale would become quite insane.

And whichever won the battle, would take this ruin of an insane man, the shaking, laughing wild body, and wander it across the face of this world for ten, twenty years, occupying it, striding in it, pompous, holding court, making grand gestures, ordering heads severed, calling on inward unseen dancing girls. Leonard Sale, what remained of him, would be led off to some hidden cave, there to be infested with wars and worms of wars for twenty insane years, occupied and prostituted by old and outlandish thoughts.

When the rescue ship arrived it would find nothing. Sale would be hidden somewhere by a triumphant army in his head. Hidden in some cleft of rock, placed there like a nest for Iorr to lie upon in evil occupation.
The thought of it almost broke him in half.
Twenty years of insanity. Twenty years of torture, doing what you don’t want to do. Twenty years of wars raging and being split apart, twenty years of nausea and trembling.
His head sank down between his knees. His eyes snapped and cracked and made soft noises. His eardrum popped tiredly.
Sleep, sleep, sang soft sea voices.

I’ll⁠—I’ll make a proposition with you, listen, thought Leonard Sale. You, Iorr, you, too, Tylle! Iorr, you can occupy me on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays. Tylle, you can take me over on Sundays, Tuesdays and Saturdays. Thursday is maid’s night out. Okay?
Eeeeeeeeeeeeee, sang the sea tides, seething in his brain.
Ohhhhhhhhhhhhhhhh, sang the distant voices softly, soft.
What’ll you say, is it a bargain, Iorr, Tylle?
No, said a voice.
No, said another.
Greedy, both of you, greedy! complained Sale. A pox on both your houses!
He slept.
He was Iorr, jeweled rings on his hands. He arose beside his rocket and held out his fingers, commanding blind armies. He was Iorr, ancient ruler of jeweled warriors.
He was Tylle, lover of women, killer of dogs!
With some hidden bit of awareness, his hand crept to the holster at his hip. The sleeping hand withdrew the gun there. The hand lifted, the gun pointed.
The armies of Tylle and Iorr gave battle.
The gun exploded.
The bullet tore across Sale’s forehead, wakening him.

He stayed awake for another six hours, getting over his latest siege. He knew it to be hopeless now. He washed and bandaged the wound he had given himself. He wished he had aimed straighter and it was all over. He watched the sky. Two more days. Two more. Come on, ship, come on. He was heavy with sleeplessness.

No use. At the end of six hours he was raving badly. He took the gun up and put it down and took it up again, put it against his head, tightened his hand on the trigger, changed his mind, looked at the sky again.
Night settled. He tried to read, threw the book away. He tore it up and burned it, just to have something to do.
So tired. In another hour, he decided. If nothing happens, I’ll kill myself. This is for certain now. I’ll do it, this time.
He got the gun ready and laid it on the ground next to himself.
He was very calm now, though tired. It would be over and done. He would be dead.
He watched the minute hand of his watch. One minute, five minutes, twenty-five minutes.
The flame appeared on the sky.
It was so unbelievable he started to cry. “A rocket,” he said, standing up. “A rocket!” he cried, rubbing his eyes. He ran forward.
The flame brightened, grew, came down.

He waved frantically, running forward, leaving his gun, his supplies, everything behind. “You see that, Iorr, Tylle! You savages, you monsters, I beat you! I won! They’re coming to rescue me now! I’ve won, damn you.”
He laughed harshly at the rocks and the sky and the backs of his hands.
The rocket landed. Leonard Sale stood swaying, waiting for the door to lid open.
“Goodbye, Iorr, goodbye, Tylle!” he shouted in triumph, grinning, eyes hot.
Eeeeee, sang a diminishing roar in time.
Ahhhhhh, voices faded.
The rocket flipped wide its airlock. Two men jumped out.

“Sale?” they called. “We’re Ship ACDN13. Intercepted your SOS and decided to pick you up ourselves. The Marsport ship won’t get through until day after tomorrow. We want a spot of rest ourselves. Thought it’d be good to spend the night here, pick you up, and go on.”
“No,” said Sale, face melting with terror. “No spend night⁠—”
He couldn’t talk. He fell to the ground.
“Quick,” said a voice, in the bleary vortex over him. “Give him a shot of food liquid, another of sedative. He needs sustenance and rest.”
“No rest!” screamed Sale.
“Delirious,” said one man softly.
“No sleep!” screamed Sale.
“There, there,” said the man gently. A needle poked into Sale’s arm.
Sale thrashed. “No sleep, go!” he mouthed horribly. “Oh, go!”
“Delirious,” said one man. “Shock.”
“No sedative!” screamed Sale.
The sedative flowed into him.
Eeeeeeeeeeee, sang the ancient winds.
Ahhhhhhhhhhhh, sang the ancient seas.
“No sedative, no sleep, please, don’t, don’t, don’t!” screamed Sale, trying to get up. “You don’t⁠—understand!”
“Take it easy, old man, you’re safe among us now, nothing to worry about,” said the rescuer above him.
Leonard Sale slept. The two men stood over him.

As they watched, Sale’s features changed violently. He groaned and cried and snarled in his sleep. His face was riven with emotion. It was the face of a saint, a sinner, a fiend, a monster, a darkness, a light, one, many, an army, a vacuum, all, all!
He writhed in his sleep.
Eeeeeeeeee! the sound burst from his mouth. Ahhhhhhhhhhh! he screamed.
“What’s wrong with him?” asked one of the two rescuers.
“I don’t know. More sedative?”
“More sedative. Nerves. He needs more sleep.”
They stuck the needle in his arm. Sale writhed and spat and moaned.
Then, suddenly, he was dead.
He lay there, the two men over him. “What a shame,” said one of them. “Can you figure that?”
“Shock. Poor guy. What a pity.” They covered his face. “Did you ever see a face like that?”
“Totally insane.”
“Loneliness. Shock.”
“Yes. Lord, what an expression. I hope never to see a face like that again.”
“What a shame, waiting for us, and we arrive, and he dies anyway.”
They glanced around. “What shall we do? Shall we spend the night?”
“Yes. It’s good to be out of the ship.”
“We’ll bury him first, of course.”
“Naturally.”
“And spend the night in the open, with good air, right? Good to be in the open again. After two weeks in that damned ship.”
“Right. I’ll find a spot for him. You start supper, eh?”
“Done.”
“Should be good sleeping tonight.”
“Fine, fine.”
They made a grave and said a word over it. They drank their evening coffee silently. They smelled the sweet air of the planet and looked at the lovely sky and the bright and beautiful stars.
“What a night,” they said, lying down.
“Pleasant dreams,” said one, rolling over.
And the other replied, “Pleasant dreams.”
They slept.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The plot is simple and relentless. Leonard Sale, a spaceman, crashes on a small planetoid, number 787. Against the odds, he survives, the air is breathable, and the radio works. He sends an alarm to Marsport and is told that a rescue ship called the Logarithm will arrive in six days. He is almost giddy. Then he lies down for a nap and is invaded. Two voices, two armies of voices, fight to possess him. They call themselves Tylle of Rathalar, Killer of Men, and Iorr of Wendillo, Destroyer of Infidels, and they are the minds of two ancient rival nations that fought a war for five thousand years on what used to be a living world. When the planet died, their bodies died with it, but their minds survived as a kind of lingering force in the air. Now they have a human skull to use as a battlefield.

The most important idea is that Sale does not simply meet ghosts. He becomes the territory they are fighting over. The story spells it out in a line that is more horrifying than any gore: he was their universe, the world of his thoughts divided into two camps. That is why it feels so intimate. The enemy is not outside, in the rocks, it is in the one place a person is supposed to be safe, inside his own head.

Sleep is what makes him vulnerable. The story is built on a clever inversion. Most horror stories frighten us with the dark and the unknown, but here the sun is warm, the sky is blue and the rocks are friendly. The planetoid looks like a lovely place to rest. The danger lives only in the moment you let your guard down, which is why Sale tries so desperately to stay awake. He sets up a schedule of walks and meals, reads War and Peace, plays solitaire, swallows pills, and talks to himself. The comic edge of those plans makes them more pathetic, because we know they cannot last.

Look also at what the two spirits are like. They are proud, vain and exactly alike, with grand titles, jewelry and a hunger to give orders and have their heads cut off. They are not evil in an interesting way. They are just old appetites, still hungry. When Sale imagines what will happen if one of them wins, he sees himself being walked around the planet like a puppet, ordering imaginary dancing girls and holding court for twenty years.

The ending is where the story turns its knife. Sale survives six days, only to be sedated by rescuers who think he is delirious. He begs them not to let him sleep, and they give him the sedative anyway. He dies, his face a mass of warring expressions. And then the rescuers, relieved and tired, decide to camp on the same planetoid, enjoy the air, and sleep. The last word of the story is simply, they slept. We know what that means.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
The first thing to admire is the shape of the story. It begins with a very short, tense paragraph of second person narration, you don't expect death, and then drops into Sale's point of view, and the relief of the opening is carefully made to feel safe. The reader relaxes along with him. That relaxation is essential, because the horror depends on the contrast. Bradbury lets the sun come up and lets Sale do a little dance of joy, and then he ruins it.

The voices are the story's real technical achievement. Bradbury writes them as sounds, long drawn out vowels, eeeeeee and ahhhhhh, sleep, sleep, die, die, which resemble a hum, a chant and a siren at once. On the page they are strange and a little musical, and read aloud they are genuinely unsettling. The long paragraph in which the armies cross Sale's skull is the high point of the prose, a rush of images in which the body becomes a landscape. Ten thousand men, ten thousand javelins, rivers of melancholy through gullies of vein. It is overheated in the way that only a young poet with a pulp deadline could write, but the overheating is the point. We feel the pressure.

There is also real craft in the way Sale talks to himself. His running joke with his own ironic censor, in which he argues and insults and jokes with himself, gives the story warmth and humanity, and it makes the horror more convincing because the man is not a stereotype of a hero. He is a decent, funny person, and he is falling apart. The deal he tries to strike with the spirits, one of them on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays, the other on weekends, and Thursday as the maid's night out, is both funny and horrible, and it is exactly how a desperate mind behaves.

Now the weaknesses. The ghost explanation is on the clumsy side. The two chieftains deliver a good deal of exposition about science and survival and a planet that died, and it sits awkwardly beside the more lyrical passages. The notion of minds surviving without bodies is hand-waved. The dialogue for the spirits, with its boastful titles, is a little stagey, and the two sound too much like each other, which is fine for the allegory but less so for the drama. The radio dying at the convenient moment is a standard pulp device. And the story's middle, in which Sale plans his schedule, runs a bit long before the plot moves again.

The ending can also feel too neat. The idea that the rescuers will doze off and be taken over is a strong final sting, but we are asked to believe that Sale's dying, with its flood of faces, has not warned them of anything. They are almost comically obtuse. Yet that is the kind of ending a horror story needs, and the bleakness lands. The result is an effective, uneven piece that is better at mood than at logic.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
Asleep in Armageddon is not one of the stories that made Bradbury famous, and its direct influence is modest. It appeared in a pulp magazine, it was not turned into a famous film or television episode that I can point to, and it does not turn up in lists of the landmark works of the period. What it does offer is a clear view of Bradbury at a stage when he was moving between genres and learning how much weirdness the science fiction pulps would tolerate.

At the time, Bradbury was writing a lot of dark fantasy and horror, much of which would later be gathered in his first book, Dark Carnival, in 1947. The same sensibility is visible here. It suggests that for Bradbury science fiction was never really separate from the macabre. He took the gothic ghost story, the haunted house that gets inside you, and moved it to a planetoid. That blend of the cosmic and the creepy would become a trademark, and it helped open the door for a more literary, more poetic kind of science fiction in the years that followed.

The central image, a place that holds the thoughts of the dead and gives them voice through the living, also became a recurring pattern in space horror. Stories in which an alien world takes over the mind of an astronaut, or in which a planet itself has a will, would grow common in the 1950s. Later novels and films used the idea of a deserted world whose past is still active, from stories in which a lonely crew picks up the residue of a dead civilization to films in which the dead planet returns as the crew's own nightmares. It would be too much to say that Bradbury started this tradition, and he was drawing on older ghost stories himself, but Asleep in Armageddon is an early and unusually pure version of it.

The story also anticipates a later worry about weaponized ideas. The notion that a conflict can outlive its original combatants, living on as a kind of infection in the minds of those who come after, is at home in a century that has seen old hatreds revive again and again. Whether Bradbury meant this or not, readers have found the allegory increasingly rewarding.

As for teaching, the story is occasionally used in classes on science fiction and horror, mostly as a compact example of the way a genre story can handle a psychological theme. It is also a good demonstration of how Bradbury uses sound and rhythm, which makes it useful to readers interested in his style. But it is a minor piece in a very large career, and its main impact has been to enrich the reading of the writer around it.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
It would be misleading to claim a huge body of famous praise for this story, because there is not one. Bradbury's early pulp work was widely read by fans, and much of what has been written about it has been general. So the useful thing to say is what readers tend to value in it, which are qualities you can hear in the text itself.

Many love the premise. Sleep is something everybody does, and the idea of a place where sleep itself becomes the threat is instantly gripping. Readers who have lain awake with a racing mind, who have been afraid of the dark for no reason, or who have simply fought off a long night of tiredness, can feel the logic in their bones. The horror is not a monster with teeth. It is the loss of control over your own mind, and nearly everyone fears that.

Others admire the humanity of Sale. He is not a soldier or a superhero. He is a man who likes beans and bacon and cigarettes, who brought War and Peace and a book of T. S. Eliot, who thinks about a woman named Helen King and then crosses it out. His small habits are touching, and his gallows humor, as he jokes with himself while falling apart, is what keeps the story from becoming a mere shocker. We want him to make it, and that makes the ending hit harder.

Many readers also love the sound of it. The chanting of the voices, with its long vowels and its drumbeat repetition, has a hypnotic effect, and the images of the war across Sale's skull are among the most vivid in Bradbury's early work. People who enjoy his language, who prefer the poet to the plotter, find plenty to savor.

There is a fourth thing, which is the sting of the final lines. Readers often remember the ending, with its two tired men looking at the stars, cheerfully getting ready to sleep. It is a terrific final image because it works on dramatic irony. We know everything, the characters know nothing, and the story stops just before the truth arrives. Readers who like horror admire how little Bradbury explains and how much he lets the silence do.

Finally, some readers simply enjoy the story as an early sign of what was coming. They see in it the writer who would soon produce his famous tales of Mars, the same appetite for strange atmospheres and emotional extremes. For devoted fans, it is a pleasure to find a story that shows the seams of the process, with its excesses and its flashes of brilliance, and to follow the career back to its source.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
As with many of Bradbury's pulp stories, there is little on the record in the way of detailed contemporary reviews. What follows are the kinds of reservations that thoughtful readers have about the story.

The most common is that it is overwritten. Bradbury's early prose can be feverish, with piled up adjectives, repeating sounds and extravagant metaphors, and in this story the fever sometimes outruns the content. The long passage of the armies marching over the geography of the skull is thrilling, but some readers find it too much, a performance rather than a scene. When every paragraph is at maximum volume, there is little room for the subtle.

A second complaint is about the explanation. The two ghostly chieftains stop the action to describe their world, its war and the science that preserved their minds, and this exposition has a pulp stiffness that clashes with the dreamlike mood. A more modern horror writer would probably leave all that unsaid. The story is at its strongest when the voices are only voices, and it loses a little tension when they start explaining themselves.

A third is that the characters are thin. Sale is vivid, but the ghosts are not, and the rescuers who bring the ending are paper figures. The reader is asked to accept that these men are so unobservant that they will sleep on a planet where the last man died screaming in his sleep. For readers who want the horror to arise from believable behavior, this feels forced. Others reply that the ending works as a fable and not as a realistic scene.

A fourth is the story's attitude to its own subject. The ghosts of ancient war are a rich idea, but the story does not explore their politics or their cause. We are never told what the war was about, or how the two sides differ, and the two chieftains are essentially the same. If it is an allegory about the futility of war, it is a fairly generic one. Readers who look for a deeper moral or political insight may leave unsatisfied.

There is also the matter of the genre. Some readers dismiss all of this kind of fiction as pulp melodrama, with the stranded astronaut, the dead radio and the ironic ending belonging to a stock repertoire. Bradbury himself would later write more subtle and more affecting stories. Placed beside them, Asleep in Armageddon can look like a young man's exercise.

Still, these are criticisms of degree. Few readers find the story dull, and most agree that its central image has an eerie power. It is a flawed, vivid, effective piece, and its flaws are those of an ambitious writer testing his strength.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
Asleep in Armageddon belongs to two traditions at once. The first is the ghost story, one of the oldest forms of storytelling, in which the past refuses to stay buried and takes hold of the living. Possession stories, in which a dead will uses a living body, go back centuries, and the notion of a haunted place, a house, a battlefield, a graveyard, is one of the oldest in literature. Bradbury simply moves the haunted place to a planetoid. In that sense the story is an old tale in a new setting, which is a trick he used often.

The second tradition is the science fiction horror story, in which the unknown places beyond Earth are not wonderful but dangerous. Here the story is related to the weird fiction of writers like H. P. Lovecraft, who imagined cosmic forces that could drive a person mad, and to the pulp tradition that blended the two. The difference is that Bradbury's horror is intimate and human. Lovecraft's monsters are vast and indifferent. Bradbury's are as small and personal as a pair of vain men who want to wear your body.

Looking backward, we can also see the shape of Shakespeare in the story. Sale quotes or half quotes the bard, all the world's a stage, sleep and perchance to dream, and the central image of a mind as a theater where players act out a drama is explicit. He even imagines destroying the stage with a bullet. The idea of a human being as a stage for forces larger than himself is an old one, and Bradbury uses it with a wink.

Looking forward, the story has cousins in later fiction. The idea that a deserted world remembers, and that its memory can infect a visitor, runs through later science fiction, including famous stories and films where explorers meet the lingering mind of a dead civilization. The idea that old wars live on in our heads is also central to modern thinking about inherited grievance and trauma, which gives the story a relevance Bradbury might not have foreseen.

Within Bradbury's own career, it sits between his darker early fantasies and his more lyrical Martian chronicles, showing the two moods side by side. If you read it beside his better known work, you will see how much of his later feeling is already present: the loneliness, the sense that space is a place where human weakness is exposed, and the belief that the most terrifying landscapes are inside us.

So why read it now? Because it is short and gripping, and because the central dread is universal. We all have to sleep. We all carry things in our minds that we did not choose, from old quarrels to ancestral fears. Bradbury turns that plain fact into a nightmare, and the nightmare still works.

stories.title: A Little Journey
stories.author: Ray Bradbury
stories.epigraph: “And then, two weeks ago, she had seen Mr. Thirkell’s advertisement in New York City:”
stories.keyContext: A Little Journey first appeared in Galaxy Science Fiction in August 1951, and two years later Ray Bradbury gathered it into his collection The Golden Apples of the Sun. Galaxy was one of the most respected magazines of its day, known for witty, adult stories rather than ray guns, and this one suited it. By 1951 Bradbury was famous, thanks to The Martian Chronicles, and he had a gift for putting very human feelings on other planets. The story follows Mrs. Amelia Bellowes, an eighty-five-year-old widow who has spent her life chasing spiritual movements, from mystics to evangelists, and has now paid for a rocket trip to find God. It is a comedy about a swindle, but it does not stay a comedy. It asks what we do with a hope we suspect is false, and whether the hope can be worth more than the con that sold it. Listen for how the tone shifts, from sharp, almost cartoonish satire to something that feels like a prayer.
paragraphs: There were two important things⁠—one, that she was very old; two, that Mr. Thirkell was taking her to God. For hadn’t he patted her hand and said: “Mrs. Bellowes, we’ll take off into space in my rocket, and go to find Him together?”

And that was how it was going to be. Oh, this wasn’t like any other group Mrs. Bellowes had ever joined. In her fervor to light a path for her delicate, tottering feet, she had struck matches down dark alleys, and found her way to Hindu mystics who floated their flickering, starry eyelashes over crystal balls. She had walked on the meadow paths with ascetic Indian philosophers imported by daughters-in-spirit of Madame Blavatsky. She had made pilgrimages to California’s stucco jungles to hunt the astrological seer in his natural habitat. She had even consented to signing away the rights to one of her homes in order to be taken into the shouting order of a temple of amazing evangelists who had promised her golden smoke, crystal fire, and the great soft hand of God coming to bear her home.

None of these people had ever shaken Mrs. Bellowes’ faith, even when she saw them sirened away in a black wagon in the night, or discovered their pictures, bleak and unromantic, in the morning tabloids. The world had roughed them up and locked them away because they knew too much, that was all.
And then, two weeks ago, she had seen Mr. Thirkell’s advertisement in New York City:
Come to Mars!
Stay at the Thirkell Restorium for one week. And then, on into space on the greatest adventure life can offer!
Send for Free Pamphlet: “Nearer My God To Thee.”
Excursion rates. Round trip slightly lower.
“Round trip,” Mrs. Bellowes had thought. “But who would come back after seeing Him?”

And so she had bought a ticket and flown off to Mars and spent seven mild days at Mr. Thirkell’s Restorium, the building with the sign on it which flashed: Thirkell’s Rocket to Heaven! She had spent the week bathing in limpid waters and erasing the care from her tiny bones, and now she was fidgeting, ready to be loaded into Mr. Thirkell’s own special private rocket, like a bullet, to be fired on out into space beyond Jupiter and Saturn and Pluto. And thus⁠—who could deny it?⁠—you would be getting nearer and nearer to the Lord. How wonderful! Couldn’t you just feel Him drawing near? Couldn’t you just sense His breath, His scrutiny, His Presence?
“Here I am,” said Mrs. Bellowes, “an ancient rickety elevator, ready to go up the shaft. God need only press the button.”
Now, on the seventh day, as she minced up the steps of the Restorium, a number of small doubts assailed her.

“For one thing,” she said aloud to no one, “it isn’t quite the land of milk and honey here on Mars that they said it would be. My room is like a cell, the swimming pool is really quite inadequate, and, besides, how many widows who look like mushrooms or skeletons want to swim? And, finally, the whole Restorium smells of boiled cabbage and tennis shoes!”
She opened the front door and let it slam, somewhat irritably.

She was amazed at the other women in the auditorium. It was like wandering in a carnival mirror-maze, coming again and again upon yourself⁠—the same floury face, the same chicken hands, and jingling bracelets. One after another of the images of herself floated before her. She put out her hand, but it wasn’t a mirror; it was another lady shaking her fingers and saying:
“We’re waiting for Mr. Thirkell. Sh!”
“Ah,” whispered everyone.
The velvet curtains parted.

Mr. Thirkell appeared, fantastically serene, his Egyptian eyes upon everyone. But there was something, nevertheless, in his appearance which made one expect him to call “Hi!” while fuzzy dogs jumped over his legs, through his hooped arms, and over his back. Then, dogs and all, he should dance with a dazzling piano-keyboard smile off into the wings.

Mrs. Bellowes, with a secret part of her mind which she constantly had to grip tightly, expected to hear a cheap Chinese gong sound when Mr. Thirkell entered. His large liquid dark eyes were so improbable that one of the old ladies had facetiously claimed she saw a mosquito cloud hovering over them as they did around summer rain-barrels. And Mrs. Bellowes sometimes caught the scent of the theatrical mothball and the smell of calliope steam on his sharply pressed suit.

But with the same savage rationalization that had greeted all other disappointments in her rickety life, she bit at the suspicion and whispered, “This time it’s real. This time it’ll work. Haven’t we got a rocket?”
Mr. Thirkell bowed. He smiled a sudden Comedy Mask smile. The old ladies looked in at his epiglottis and sensed chaos there.

Before he even began to speak, Mrs. Bellowes saw him picking up each of his words, oiling it, making sure it ran smooth on its rails. Her heart squeezed in like a tiny fist, and she gritted her porcelain teeth.
“Friends,” said Mr. Thirkell, and you could hear the frost snap in the hearts of the entire assemblage.
“No!” said Mrs. Bellowes ahead of time. She could hear the bad news rushing at her, and herself tied to the track while the immense black wheels threatened and the whistle screamed, helpless.
“There will be a slight delay,” said Mr. Thirkell.
In the next instant, Mr. Thirkell might have cried, or been tempted to cry, “Ladies, be seated!” in minstrel-fashion, for the ladies had come up at him from their chairs, protesting and trembling.
“Not a very long delay.” Mr. Thirkell put up his hands to pat the air.
“How long?”
“Only a week.”
“A week!”
“Yes. You can stay here at the Restorium for seven more days, can’t you? A little delay won’t matter, will it, in the end? You’ve waited a lifetime. Only a few more days.”
At twenty dollars a day, thought Mrs. Bellowes, coldly.
“What’s the trouble?” a woman cried.
“A legal difficulty,” said Mr. Thirkell.
“We’ve a rocket, haven’t we?”
“Well, ye-ess.”
“But I’ve been here a whole month, waiting,” said one old lady. “Delays, delays!”
“That’s right,” said everyone.
“Ladies, ladies,” murmured Mr. Thirkell, smiling serenely.
“We want to see the rocket!” It was Mrs. Bellowes forging ahead, alone, brandishing her fist like a toy hammer.
Mr. Thirkell looked into the old ladies’ eyes, a missionary among albino cannibals.
“Well, now,” he said.
“Yes, now!” cried Mrs. Bellowes.
“I’m afraid⁠—” he began.
“So am I!” she said. “That’s why we want to see the ship!”
“No, no, now, Mrs.⁠—” He snapped his fingers for her name.

“Bellowes!” she cried. She was a small container, but now all the seething pressures that had been built up over long years came steaming through the delicate vents of her body. Her cheeks became incandescent. With a wail that was like a melancholy factory whistle, Mrs. Bellowes ran forward and hung to him, almost by her teeth, like a summer-maddened Spitz. She would not and never could let go, until he died, and the other women followed, jumping and yapping like a pound let loose on its trainer, the same one who had petted them and to whom they had squirmed and whined joyfully an hour before, now milling about him, creasing his sleeves and frightening the Egyptian serenity from his gaze.
“This way!” cried Mrs. Bellowes, feeling like Madame Lafarge. “Through the back! We’ve waited long enough to see the ship. Every day he’s put us off, every day we’ve waited, now let’s see.”
“No, no, ladies!” cried Mr. Thirkell, leaping about.
They burst through the back of the stage and out a door, like a flood, bearing the poor man with them into a shed, and then out, quite suddenly, into an abandoned gymnasium.
“There it is!” said someone. “The rocket.”
And then a silence fell that was terrible to entertain.
There was the rocket.
Mrs. Bellowes looked at it and her hands sagged away from Mr. Thirkell’s collar.

The rocket was something like a battered copper pot. There were a thousand bulges and rents and rusty pipes and dirty vents on and in it. The ports were clouded over with dust, resembling the eyes of a blind hog.
Everyone wailed a little sighing wail.
“Is that the rocket ship Glory Be to the Highest?” cried Mrs. Bellowes, appalled.
Mr. Thirkell nodded and looked at his feet.
“For which we paid out our one thousand dollars apiece and came all the way to Mars to get on board with you and go off to find Him?” asked Mrs. Bellowes.
“Why, that isn’t worth a sack of dried peas,” said Mrs. Bellowes.
“It’s nothing but junk!”
Junk, whispered everyone, getting hysterical.
“Don’t let him get away!”
Mr. Thirkell tried to break and run, but a thousand possum traps closed on him from every side. He withered.

Everybody walked around in circles like blind mice. There was a confusion and a weeping that lasted for five minutes as they went over and touched the Rocket, the Dented Kettle, the Rusty Container for God’s Children.

“Well,” said Mrs. Bellowes. She stepped up into the askew doorway of the rocket and faced everyone. “It looks as if a terrible thing has been done to us,” she said. “I haven’t any money to go back home to Earth and I’ve too much pride to go to the Government and tell them a common man like this has fooled us out of our life’s savings. I don’t know how you feel about it, all of you, but the reason all of us came is because I’m eighty-five, and you’re eighty-nine, and you’re seventy-eight, and all of us are nudging on toward a hundred, and there’s nothing on Earth for us, and it doesn’t appear there’s anything on Mars either. We all expected not to breathe much more air or crochet many more doilies or we’d never have come here. So what I have to propose is a simple thing⁠—to take a chance.”
She reached out and touched the rusted hulk of the rocket.
“This is our rocket. We paid for our trip. And we’re going to take our trip!”
Everyone rustled and stood on tiptoes and opened an astonished mouth.
Mr. Thirkell began to cry. He did it quite easily and very effectively.
“We’re going to get in this ship,” said Mrs. Bellowes, ignoring him. “And we’re going to take off to where we were going.”

Mr. Thirkell stopped crying long enough to say, “But it was all a fake. I don’t know anything about space. He’s not out there, anyway. I lied. I don’t know where He is, and I couldn’t find Him if I wanted to. And you were fools to ever take my word on it.”

“Yes,” said Mrs. Bellowes, “we were fools. I’ll go along on that. But you can’t blame us, for we’re old, and it was a lovely, good and fine idea, one of the loveliest ideas in the world. Oh, we didn’t really fool ourselves that we could get nearer to Him physically. It was the gentle, mad dream of old people, the kind of thing you hold onto for a few minutes a day, even though you know it’s not true. So, all of you who want to go, you follow me in the ship.”
“But you can’t go!” said Mr. Thirkell. “You haven’t got a navigator. And that ship’s a ruin!”
“You,” said Mrs. Bellowes, “will be the navigator.”

She stepped into the ship, and after a moment, the other old ladies pressed forward. Mr. Thirkell, windmilling his arms frantically, was nevertheless pressed through the port, and in a minute the door slammed shut. Mr. Thirkell was strapped into the navigator’s seat, with everyone talking at once and holding him down. The special helmets were issued to be fitted over every gray or white head to supply extra oxygen in case of a leakage in the ship’s hull, and at long last the hour had come and Mrs. Bellowes stood behind Mr. Thirkell and said, “We’re ready, sir.”
He said nothing. He pleaded with them silently, using his great, dark, wet eyes, but Mrs. Bellowes shook her head and pointed to the control.
“Takeoff,” agreed Mr. Thirkell morosely, and pulled a switch.

Everybody fell. The rocket went up from the planet Mars in a great fiery glide, with the noise of an entire kitchen thrown down an elevator shaft, with a sound of pots and pans and kettles and fires boiling and stews bubbling, with a smell of burned incense and rubber and sulphur, with a color of yellow fire, and a ribbon of red stretching below them, and all the old women singing and holding to each other, and Mrs. Bellowes crawling upright in the sighing, straining, trembling ship.
“Head for space, Mr. Thirkell.”
“It can’t last,” said Mr. Thirkell, sadly. “This ship can’t last. It will⁠—”
It did.
The rocket exploded.
Mrs. Bellowes felt herself lifted and thrown about dizzily, like a doll. She heard the great screamings and saw the flashes of bodies sailing by her in fragments of metal and powdery light.
“Help, help!” cried Mr. Thirkell, far away, on a small radio beam.
The ship disintegrated into a million parts, and the old ladies, all one hundred of them, were flung straight on ahead with the same velocity as the ship.
As for Mr. Thirkell, for some reason of trajectory, perhaps, he had been blown out the other side of the ship. Mrs. Bellowes saw him falling separate and away from them, screaming, screaming.
There goes Mr. Thirkell, thought Mrs. Bellowes.
And she knew where he was going. He was going to be burned and roasted and broiled good, but very good.
Mr. Thirkell was falling down into the Sun.
And here we are, thought Mrs. Bellowes. Here we are, going on out, and out, and out.
There was hardly a sense of motion at all, but she knew that she was traveling at fifty thousand miles an hour and would continue to travel at that speed for an eternity, until.⁠ ⁠…
She saw the other women swinging all about her in their own trajectories, a few minutes of oxygen left to each of them in their helmets, and each was looking up to where they were going.

Of course, thought Mrs. Bellowes. Out into space. Out and out, and the darkness like a great church, and the stars like candles, and in spite of everything, Mr. Thirkell, the rocket, and the dishonesty, we are going toward the Lord.

And there, yes, there, as she fell on and on, coming toward her, she could almost discern the outline now, coming toward her was His mighty golden hand, reaching down to hold her and comfort her like a frightened sparrow.⁠ ⁠…
“I’m Mrs. Amelia Bellowes,” she said quietly, in her best company voice. “I’m from the planet Earth.”

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
On the surface, A Little Journey is a story about a con. Mrs. Bellowes, who is eighty-five, has spent decades following one spiritual fashion after another, Hindu mystics, imported philosophers, California astrologers, a shouting temple that took one of her homes. Every time her teachers were hauled off in a black wagon or exposed in the tabloids, she decided the world had punished them for knowing too much. Now she has answered an advertisement from a man named Thirkell, who runs a resort on Mars called the Restorium and promises that he will fly his clients into space to find God. She and about a hundred other elderly women have each paid a thousand dollars. They have waited, been delayed again and again, and paid twenty dollars a day for the privilege.

When the women finally storm the back of the building, they find the rocket in an abandoned gymnasium, a battered copper pot with blind, dusty windows. It is junk. The fraud is complete. And this is the moment where the story becomes something else. Mrs. Bellowes, instead of collapsing, makes a speech. She admits they were fools. But she says it was a lovely idea, one of the loveliest in the world, a gentle, mad dream of old people, the kind of thing you hold onto for a few minutes a day even though you know it is not true. Then she announces that they are going anyway. They paid for the trip and they are going to take it. And they make Thirkell the navigator.

What does that mean? The first thing to see is that she is not exactly deluded. She says outright that nobody really believed they could get nearer to God physically. The trip is a ritual, a way of acting out a hope. The second is that she is sick of being a victim. She has no money, too much pride to go to the government, and nothing to go back to. Taking the broken rocket is the one act of defiance left to her.

The ending is the real puzzle. The rocket explodes, and the women are flung outward at fifty thousand miles an hour, each in her own trajectory, with a few minutes of oxygen. Thirkell falls toward the sun. Mrs. Bellowes drifts into the dark, which she sees as a great church with stars like candles, and she sees a golden hand coming to hold her like a frightened sparrow. Her last words are said in her best company voice: I'm Mrs. Amelia Bellowes. I'm from the planet Earth.

Is she dying, hallucinating, or really meeting God? Bradbury will not say. The story works on both levels at once. It can be read as the last dream of an oxygen-starved mind, or as a sort of miracle in which a fraud accidentally delivers exactly what it promised. The beauty of it is that she is polite. Even at the end of everything, she introduces herself like a guest arriving at a party. That small gesture, so ordinary and so brave, is where the story keeps its heart.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
The story's greatest strength is the way it changes gears. The first half is a brisk, almost farcical satire, full of bright, nasty, funny images. The old women look like copies of one another, with floury faces and chicken hands and jingling bracelets, a house of mirrors in which every reflection is another widow. Thirkell has Egyptian eyes, a piano-keyboard smile and the smell of theatrical mothballs and calliope steam, and Mrs. Bellowes sees him oiling each word before he says it so that it will run smooth on its rails. The prose is crammed with similes, and most of them land. The women pour out of their chairs, rush the stage and cling to Thirkell like a pack of summer-maddened dogs. It is knockabout and quick.

Then, at the moment of maximum comic energy, Bradbury lets the air out. The silence in front of the rocket is one of the best moments in the story. After all the noise, the sight of that dented kettle, and the sound of a hundred old women sighing together, is genuinely sad. And when Mrs. Bellowes steps up into the doorway and talks about what they have all been looking for, the story achieves a real dignity. The reader has been laughing at these women, and is suddenly made to feel what is behind the laughter.

That turn is the work of a skilled writer, and the finale, with its quiet cosmic imagery, is moving. The detail that the women are flung forward at the same velocity as the ship, each on her own path, is neat, and the image of darkness like a great church is among Bradbury's better lines.

Not everything works. The story's humor depends on a lot of broad stereotyping. The women are fluttering, shrill, interchangeable ladies, and some of the descriptions, mushrooms, skeletons, chicken hands, are cruel in a way that sits uneasily with the compassion of the ending. The comparison of Thirkell to a missionary among albino cannibals, and his exotic eyes and Comedy Mask smile, lean on lazy ethnic and theatrical shorthand of the period. The satire is also somewhat obvious. Thirkell is a cartoon, and his collapse into tears is played for laughs in a way that gives him little life of his own.

There is also a question of whether the ending cheats. A fraud's rocket explodes and, in the same moment, a vision of God appears. If we read it as miracle, it might be too easy a reward for faith. If we read it as hallucination, the tenderness of the final scene may be partly undercut. Bradbury wants to have both, and some readers feel he gets away with it while others feel he is sentimental. I think he mostly earns it, because the story has shown us in detail how much these women need something, and the vision feels like the answer to that need rather than a trick.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
A Little Journey is not among Bradbury's very best known stories, and it would be an exaggeration to say it changed science fiction. Its significance is quieter. It is a good example of the kind of story that Galaxy and other magazines of the early 1950s were making room for, in which the science fiction setting is used for satire and for character, rather than for gadgets and battles. Galaxy's editor, H. L. Gold, wanted adult, humane stories about the social effects of the future, and this is one of them. Alongside the work of writers like Frederik Pohl and Cyril Kornbluth, who satirized advertising and consumer culture, Bradbury was helping to show that science fiction could do the work of a comedy of manners.

Its inclusion in The Golden Apples of the Sun, in 1953, also helped to carry it to a wider audience than the magazine readers. That collection brought together stories that mixed science fiction, fantasy and plain literary fiction, and it was one of the books that persuaded mainstream reviewers that Bradbury was a real writer. A Little Journey sat comfortably in it, as an example of his way of wedding rockets and religion.

In ideas, the story belongs to a line of mid-century science fiction that dealt with God. Writers of the period were fascinated by what space travel might mean for faith. Arthur C. Clarke's The Nine Billion Names of God, from the same period, is the classic example, a short story that also ends with a whimsical cosmic sting. Others, such as James Blish and Walter Miller later in the decade, approached the same subject more gravely. Bradbury's contribution is tender and homely. He does not ask about theology. He asks about the old people who need to believe.

The story also anticipates a modern concern with the exploitation of vulnerable people by spiritual and commercial hucksters. The idea of a luxury wellness resort that sells transcendence by the week, with delays and additional charges, is easy to recognize today. It is satire that has aged into something close to description.

As for use in teaching, the story is occasionally anthologized and used in classes as an example of how a genre story can carry literary themes, and especially of tonal shift. No famous screen adaptation of it is on record. Its life has been mostly in print, among readers who come across it in collections and remember it. Its impact lies not in a big historical event but in a steady, quiet success: it is the kind of story that readers keep recommending, and that shows how much emotional range a short science fiction story can have.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
People who love this story usually begin with Mrs. Bellowes. She is small, fierce, funny and unforgettable, and she is the opposite of the passive, pitiable old woman that stories so often provide. She is the one who leads the revolt, who bursts into the back room, who delivers the speech and who gives the order that makes the swindler fly the ship. Readers enjoy the sight of this eighty-five-year-old pushing a man around by his collar. Her mix of pride, stubbornness and plain good manners is irresistible, and it is hard not to cheer for her.

Another source of pleasure is the comedy. The first half is genuinely funny. The idea of a Restorium that smells of boiled cabbage and tennis shoes, the image of the women as a pack of dogs turning on the trainer who had petted them an hour earlier, the delayed departures and the extra fees, all of this is sharply observed and reads well aloud. Bradbury's inventive similes are in full flower, and even readers who find the style overripe enjoy the playfulness.

A third is the emotional turn. Readers often mention the moment when the joke stops and Mrs. Bellowes speaks about what they were all looking for. People who have watched a relative cling to a hope that others dismissed, or who have felt that tug themselves, find in that speech something truthful. She does not pretend that she was right. She says they were fools, and that it was still a lovely idea. That blend of clear sight and persistence is moving.

A fourth is the ending. The image of old women, flung into the dark in the wreckage of their rocket and still looking up, is both absurd and beautiful, and Mrs. Bellowes's introduction of herself to God in her best company voice has become a favorite moment for many readers. It gives the story a strange grace. There is no sermon in it. It leaves the reader to feel whatever he or she feels.

Finally, readers like the humane attitude toward the old. Bradbury was in his early thirties when he wrote it, yet he treated old age with attention and respect, giving the women hopes and appetites and dignity. In a field that tended to focus on young men and their machines, that was refreshing, and it is one of the reasons the story continues to be passed along.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Little detailed criticism of this particular story survives in the public record, so rather than attribute remarks to named reviewers, it is better to describe the reservations that thoughtful readers voice.

The most frequent is sentimentality. Some readers feel that the ending is too soft, that a swindled old woman is rewarded with a vision of a golden hand and that the story cannot decide whether to be honest about disappointment or kind about it. The final image of God reaching down like a hand to hold a sparrow is, for them, a greeting card. Bradbury was often accused of sentimentality over his career, and this story gives that charge some material. Others answer that the story has earned its tenderness by showing, without flinching, how foolish and sad the whole enterprise is.

A second complaint concerns the treatment of the characters. The elderly women are described, early on, in terms that are comic but sometimes unkind, and the satire leans on stereotypes of fluttery old ladies. Thirkell's description relies on ethnic and theatrical clichés that read poorly today, and the comparison of the women to cannibals and dogs is, for some, a little cruel. A modern reader may feel that the story laughs at these women before it honors them, and that the honor arrives late.

A third is the neatness of the plot. Thirkell is a cartoon villain, and his fate, to be thrown out of the ship and fall into the sun, is almost vindictive. Readers have asked whether the story wants us to feel anything for him, and it does not. His punishment is delivered with relish, which sits oddly beside Mrs. Bellowes's generosity of spirit toward everyone else.

A fourth concerns the physics. The women are flung out at the speed of the ship, and Mrs. Bellowes feels herself traveling at fifty thousand miles an hour with a few minutes of oxygen left. This is poetic rather than scientific, and readers who want hard science fiction will find it hand-waving. The story does not pretend otherwise, but the lack of rigor irritates some.

Finally, there is the theological ambiguity. Religious readers sometimes feel that the story treats faith as a comforting illusion, while skeptical readers feel it flinches from saying so. The story's refusal to settle that question is, for some, its greatest strength and, for others, a dodge. Everyone seems to agree, though, that it is better as a character study than as an argument, and that Mrs. Bellowes is the reason to read it.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
A Little Journey sits where satire, science fiction and religious feeling meet. Its oldest ancestor is probably the medieval tale of the pardoner, the con man who sells false relics to credulous pilgrims. Chaucer's Pardoner knows his relics are bones from a pig and sells them anyway, and the story has always carried a double message: the fraud is contemptible, and yet the pilgrims' need is real. Bradbury moves that old pairing into outer space. Thirkell is a pardoner with a rocket, and the pilgrims are ladies in orthopedic shoes.

The story also belongs to the American tradition of the revival-tent hustler, the figure of the preacher who fleeces his flock, which runs from nineteenth century fiction through Sinclair Lewis's Elmer Gantry in the 1920s. Bradbury lived in Los Angeles, a city famous for new spiritual movements, and his story picks up a sense of that environment, with its astrologers and temples and robed teachers. Mrs. Bellowes's mention of followers of Madame Blavatsky, the founder of Theosophy, places her in the long history of Western spiritual seeking.

Within science fiction, the story is part of the 1950s conversation about what space would mean for belief. Clarke's famous story of monks who hire a computer to list the names of God is the best known, but there are many others. What distinguishes Bradbury's contribution is its warmth. He sees space as an arena in which ordinary people try to make their lives mean something, not as a challenge to dogma.

Within Bradbury's own work, the story echoes a recurring theme: that the longing for wonder is the most human thing about us, and that it is worth honoring even when it is foolish. You can see the same impulse in his Martian stories, where people carry their dreams and their losses across space, and in his tales of old age and memory. The relationship between a hope and the hucksters who exploit it is a theme he returns to more than once.

Looking forward, the story's descendants are the many tales of cults and swindles in space and elsewhere, as well as the broader tradition of stories that treat faith with sympathy while recognizing its dangers. It also foreshadows the way later science fiction would treat aging as a subject.

So why read it now? Because it is short, funny and moving. Because Mrs. Bellowes is a character you will not forget. And because its central question, what to do when the thing you hoped for turns out to be a fake, is one that nearly everyone faces at some point. Bradbury's answer is generous and a little mad. You take the trip anyway. You point yourself toward the thing you love. And when you get there, you remember your manners.

stories.title: I, Mars
stories.author: Ray Bradbury
stories.epigraph: “A grey hand lifted the receiver.”
stories.keyContext: I, Mars first appeared in 1949 in the pulp magazine Super Science Stories. Ray Bradbury later revised and retitled it Night Call, Collect, and it was gathered into his 1964 collection The Machineries of Joy. The title plays on I, Robot, the phrase science fiction fans already knew, but the story turns the idea inward: this is a robot story where the machine is a copy of a lonely man's own voice. It came out when Bradbury was in the middle of his Martian period, writing about Mars as a place where Americans carry their griefs. The nuclear age had just begun, and fear of atomic war hangs over the premise. An old man, left behind on Mars decades ago when Earth called everyone home, is sitting in an empty world when his telephone rings. It is himself, at twenty. The story is a ghost story told with circuits, and it asks what it does to a person to be haunted by who he used to be.
paragraphs: The phone rang.
A grey hand lifted the receiver.
“Hello?”
“Hello, Barton?”
“Yes.”
“This is Barton!”
“What?”
“This is Barton!”
“It can’t be. This phone hasn’t rung in twenty years.”
The old man hung up.
Brrrrinnnng!
His grey hand seized the phone.
“Hello, Barton,” laughed the voice. “You have forgotten, haven’t you?”

The old man felt his heart grow small and like a cool stone. He felt the wind blowing in off the dry Martian seas and the blue hills of Mars. After twenty years of silence and cobwebs and now, tonight, on his eightieth birthday, with a ghastly scream, this phone had wailed to life.
“Who did you think it was?” said the voice. “A rocket captain? Did you think someone had come to rescue you?”
“No.”
“What’s the date?”
Numbly, “July 20th, 2097.”
“Good Lord. Sixty years! Have you been sitting there that long? Waiting for a rocket to come from Earth to rescue you?”
The old man nodded.
“Now, old man, do you know who I am? Think!”
“Yes.” The dry pale lips trembling. “I understand. I remember. We are one. I am Emil Barton and you are Emil Barton.”
“With one difference. You are eighty. I am only twenty. All of life before me!”

The old man began to laugh and then to cry. He sat holding the phone like a lost and silly child in his fingers. The conversation was impossible, and should not be continued, and yet he went on with it. When he got hold of himself he held the phone close to his withered lips and said, in deepest anguish, “Listen! You there! Listen, oh God, if I could warn you! How can I? You’re only a voice. If I could show you how lonely the years are. End it, kill yourself! Don’t wait! If you knew what it is to change from the thing you are to the thing that is me, today, here, now, at this end.”

“Impossible.” The voice of the young Barton laughed, far away. “I’ve no way to tell if you ever get this call. This is all mechanical. You’re talking to a transcription, no more. This is 2037. Sixty years in your past. Today, the atom war started on Earth. All colonials were called home from Mars, by rocket. I got left behind!”
“I remember,” whispered the old man.

“Alone on Mars,” laughed the young voice. “A month, a year, who cares? There are foods and books. In my spare time I’ve made transcription libraries of ten thousand words, responses, my voice, connected to phone relays. In later months I’ll call, have someone to talk with.”
“Yes,” murmured the old man, remembering.

“Forty-sixty years from now my own transcripto-tapes will ring me up. I don’t really think I’ll be here on Mars that long, it’s just a beautifully ironic idea of mine, something to pass the time. Is that really you, Barton? Is that really me?”
Tears fell from the old man’s eyes. “Yes!”
“I’ve made a thousand Bartons, tapes, sensitive to all questions, my voice, in one thousand Martian towns. An army of Bartons over Mars, while I wait for the rockets to return.”
“You fool,” the old man shook his head, wearily. “You waited sixty years. You grew old waiting, always alone. And now you’ve become me and you’re still alone in the empty cities.”

“Don’t expect my sympathy. You’re like a stranger, off in another country. I can’t be sad. I’m alive when I make these tapes. And you’re alive when you hear them. Both of us, to the other, incomprehensible. Neither can warn the other, even though both respond, one to the other, one automatically, the other warmly and humanly. I’m human now. You’re human later. It’s insane. I can’t cry, because not knowing the future I can only be optimistic. These hidden tapes can only react to a certain number of stimuli from you. Can you ask a dead man to weep?”

“Stop it!” cried the old man, for his heart was sickening in him. He felt the familiar great seizures of pain. Nausea moved through him, and blackness. “Stop it! Oh God, but you were heartless. Go away!”

“Were, old man? I am. As long as the tapes glide on, as long as secret spindles and hidden electronic eyes read and select and convert words to send to you, I’ll be young, cruel, blunt. I’ll go on being young and cruel long after you’re dead. Goodbye.”
“Wait!” cried the old man.
Click.
Barton sat holding the silent phone a long while. His heart gave him intense pain.
What insanity it had been. In youth’s flush, how silly, how inspired, those first secluded years, fixing the telephonic brains, the tapes, the circuits, scheduling calls on time relays:
Brrrrinnnng!
“Morning, Barton. This is Barton. Seven o’clock. Rise and shine!”
Brrrrinnnng!
“Barton? Barton calling. You’re to go to Mars Town at noon. Install a telephonic brain. Thought I’d remind you.”
“Thanks.”
Brrrrinnnng!
“Barton? Barton. Have lunch with me? The Rocket Inn?”
“Right.”
“See you. So long!”
Brrrrinnnng!
“That you, B.? Thought I’d cheer you. Firm chin, and all that. The rescue rocket might come tomorrow, to save you.”
“Yes, tomorrow, tomorrow, tomorrow, tomorrow.”
Click.

But forty years had burned into smoke. Barton had muted the insidious phones and their clever, clever repartee. He had sealed them into silences. They were to call him only after he was eighty, if he still lived. And now today, the phones ringing, and the past breathing in his ear, sighing, whispering, murmuring, and remembering.
Brrrrinnnng!
He let it ring.
“I don’t have to answer it,” he thought.
Brrrrinnnng!
“There’s no one there at all,” he thought.
Brrrrinnnng!
“It’s like talking to yourself,” he thought. “But different. Oh God, how different.”
He felt his hands crawl unconsciously toward the phone.
Click.
“Hello, old Barton, this is young Barton. One year older, though. I’m twenty-one today. In the last year I’ve put voice brains in two hundred towns on Mars, I’ve populated it with arrogant Bartons!”

“Yes.” The old man remembered those days six decades ago, those nights of rushing over blue hills and into iron valleys of Mars, with a truckful of machinery, whistling, happy. Another telephone, another relay. Something to do. Something clever and wonderful and sad. Hidden voices. Hidden, hidden. In those young days when death was not death, time was not time, old age a faint echo from the long blue cavern of years ahead. That young idiot, that sadistic fool, never thinking to reap the harvest so sown.
“Last night,” said Barton, aged twenty-one, “I sat alone in a movie theater in an empty town. I played an old Laurel and Hardy. Laughed so much. God, how I laughed.”
“Yes.”

“I got an idea today. I recorded my voice one thousand times on one tape. Broadcast from the town, it sounds like a thousand people living there. A comforting noise, the noise of a crowd. I fixed it so doors slam in town, children sing, music boxes play, all by clockworks. If I don’t look out the window, if I just listen, it’s all right. But if I look, it spoils the illusion. There’s only one solution. I’ll populate the town with robots. I guess I’m getting lonely.”
The old man said, “Yes. That was your first sign.”
“What?”
“The first time you admitted you were lonely.”
“I’ve experimented with smells. As I walk down the deserted streets, the smells of bacon and eggs, ham steak, fillets, soups, come from the houses. All done with hidden machines. Clever?”
“Fantasy. Madness.”
“Self-protection, old man.”
“I’m tired.” Abruptly, the old man hung up. It was too much. The past pouring over him, drowning him.⁠ ⁠…
Swaying, he moved down the tower stairs to the streets of the town.

The town was dark. No longer did red neons burn, music play, or cooking smells linger. Long ago he had abandoned the grim fantasy of the mechanical lie. Listen! Are those footsteps? Smell! Isn’t that strawberry pie! No, he had stopped it all. What had he done with the robots? His mind puzzled. Oh, yes.⁠ ⁠…
He moved to the dark canal where the stars shone in the quivering waters.

Underwater, in row after fish-like row, rusting, were the robot populations of Mars he had constructed over the years, and, in a wild realization of his own insane inadequacy, had commanded to march, one two three four! into the canal deeps, plunging, bubbling like sunken bottles. He had killed them and shown no remorse.
Brrrrinnnng.
Faintly a phone rang in a lightless cottage.
He walked on. The phone ceased.

Brrrrinnnng. Another cottage ahead, as if it knew of his passing. He began to run. The ringing stayed behind. Only to be taken up by a ringing from now this house⁠—Brrrrinnnng! now that, now here, there! He turned the corner. A phone! He darted on. Another corner. Another phone!
“All right, all right!” he shrieked, exhausted. “I’m coming!”
“Hello, Barton.”
“What do you want!”
“I’m lonely. I only live when I speak. So I must speak. You can’t shut me up forever.”
“Leave me alone!” said the old man, in horror. “Oh, my heart!”

“This is Barton, age twenty-four. Another couple of years gone. Waiting. A little lonelier. I’ve read War and Peace, drunk sherry, run restaurants with myself as waiter, cook, entertainer. And tonight, I star in a film at the Tivoli⁠—Emil Barton in Love’s Labor Lost, playing all the parts, some with wigs, myself!”
“Stop calling me,” the old man’s eyes were fiery and insane. “Or I’ll kill you!”
“You can’t kill me. You’ll have to find me, first!”
“I’ll find you!” A choking.

“You’ve forgotten where you hid me. I’m everywhere in Mars, in boxes, in houses, in cables, towers, underground! Go ahead, try! What’ll you call it? Telecide? Suicide? Jealous, are you? Jealous of me here, only twenty-four, bright-eyed, strong, young, young, young? All right, old man, it’s war! Between us. Between me! A whole regiment of us, all ages from twenty to sixty, against you, the real one. Go ahead, declare war!”
“I’ll kill you!” screamed Barton.
Click. Silence.
“Kill you!” He threw the phone out the window, shrieking.
In the midnight cold, the ancient automobile moved in deep valleys. Under Barton’s feet on the floorboard were revolvers, rifles, dynamite. The roar of the car was in his thin, tired bones.
I’ll find them, he thought. Find and destroy, all of them. Oh, God, God, how can he do this to me?
He stopped the car. A strange town lay under the late twin moons. There was no wind.

He held the rifle in his cold hands. He peered at the poles, the towers, the boxes. Where? Where was this town’s voice hidden? That tower? Or that one there! Where! So many years ago. So long gone. So forgotten. He turned his head now this way, now that, wildly. It must be that tower! Was he certain? Or this box here, or the transformer half up that tower?
He raised the rifle.
The tower fell with the first bullet.
All of them, he thought. All of the towers in this town will have to be cut apart. I’ve forgotten. Too long.
The car moved along the silent street.
Brrrrinnnng!
He looked at the deserted drugstore.
Brrrrinnnng!
Pistol in hand, he shot the lock off the door, and entered.
Click.
“Hello, Barton? Just a warning. Don’t try to rip down all the towers, blow things up. Cut your own throat that way. Think it over.⁠ ⁠…”
Click.

He stepped out of the phone booth slowly and moved into the street and listened to the telephone towers humming high in the air, still alive, still untouched. He looked at them and then he understood.

He could not destroy the towers. Suppose a rocket came from Earth, impossible idea, but suppose it came tonight, tomorrow, next week? and landed on the other side of the planet, and used the phones to try to call Barton, only to find the circuits dead? Yes, imagine!
Barton dropped his gun.
“A rocket won’t come,” he argued, softly, logically with himself. “I’m old. It won’t come now. It’s too late.”
But suppose it came, and you never knew, he thought. No, you’ve got to keep the lines open.
Brrrrinnnng.
He turned dully. His eyes were blinking and not seeing. He shuffled back into the drugstore and fumbled with the receiver.
“Hello?” A strange voice.
“Please,” pleaded the old man, brokenly. “Don’t bother me.”
“Who’s this, who’s there? Who is it? Where are you?” cried the voice, surprised.
“Wait a minute.” The old man staggered. “This is Emil Barton, who’s that?”
“This is Captain Leonard Rockwell, Earth Rocket 48. Just arrived from New York.”
“No, no, no.”
“Are you there, Mr. Barton?”
“No, no, it can’t be, it just can’t.”
“Where are you?”
“You’re lying, it’s false!” The old man had to lean against the booth wall. His blue eyes were cold blind. “It’s you, Barton, making, making fun of me, lying to me again!”
“This is Captain Rockwell, Rocket 48. Just landed in New Schenecty. Where are you?”
“In Green Town,” he gasped. “That’s a thousand miles from you.”
“Look, Barton, can you come here?”
“What?”
“We’ve repairs on our rocket. Exhausted from the flight. Can you come help?”
“Yes, yes.”
“We’re at the tarmac outside town. Can you rush by tomorrow?”
“Yes, but⁠—”
“Well?”
The old man petted the phone, pitifully. “How’s Earth? How’s New York? Is the war over? Who’s President now? What happened?”
“Plenty of time for gossip when you arrive.”
“Is everything fine?”
“Fine.”
“Thank God.” The old man listened to the far voice. “Are you sure you’re Captain Rockwell?”
“Damn it, man!”
“I’m sorry!”
He hung up and ran.
They were here, after many years, unbelievable, his own, who would take him back to Earth seas and skies and mountains.
He started the car. He would drive all night. Could he do it? What of his heart⁠—It would be worth a risk, to see people, to shake hands, to hear them near you.
The car thundered in the hills.

That voice. Captain Rockwell. It couldn’t be himself, forty years ago. He had never made a recording like that. Or had he? In one of his depressive fits, in a spell of drunken cynicism, hadn’t he once made a false tape of a false landing on Mars with a synthetic captain, an imaginary crew? He jerked his grey head, savagely. No. He was a suspicious fool. Now was no time to doubt. He must run under the moons of Mars, hour on hour. What a party they would have!

The sun rose. He was immensely tired, full of thorns and brambles of weakness, his heart plunging and aching, his fingers fumbling the wheel, but the thing that pleased him most was the thought of one last phone call: Hello, young Barton, this is old Barton. I’m leaving for Earth today! Rescued! He chuckled weakly.
He drove into the shadowy limits of New Schenectady at sundown. Stepping from his car he stood staring at the rocket tarmac, rubbing his reddened eyes.
The rocket field was empty. No one ran to meet him. No one shook his hand, shouted, or laughed.
He felt his heart roar into pain. He knew blackness and a sensation of falling through the open sky. He stumbled toward an office.
Inside, six phones sat in a neat row.
He waited, gasping.
Finally:
Brrrrinnnng.
He lifted the heavy receiver.
A voice said, “I was wondering if you’d get there alive.”
The old man did not speak but stood with the phone in his hands.
The voice continued, “An elaborate joke. Captain Rockwell reporting for duty, sir. Your orders, sir?”
“You,” groaned the old man.
“How’s your heart, old man?”
“No!”
“Hoped the trip would kill you. Had to eliminate you some way, so I could live, if you call a transcription living.”
“I’m going out now,” replied the old man, “and blow it all up. I don’t care. I’ll blow up everything until you’re all dead!”
“You haven’t the strength. Why do you think I had you travel so far, so fast? This is your last trip!”

The old man felt his heart falter. He would never make the other towns. The war was lost. He slid into a chair and made low sobbing, mournful noises from his loose mouth. He glared at the five other, silent phones. As if at a signal, they burst into silver chorus! A nest of ugly birds screaming!
Automatic receivers popped up.
The office whirled. “Barton, Barton, Barton!!”

He throttled the phone in his hands, the voice, the youth, the time of long ago. He mashed, choked it and still it laughed at him. He throttled it. He beat it. He kicked at it. He hated it with hands and mouth and blind, raging eye. He furled the hot wire like serpentine in his fingers, ripped it into red bits which fell about his stumbling feet.
He destroyed three other phones. There was a sudden silence.

And as if his body now discovered a thing which it had long kept secret, it seemed to decay upon his tired bones. The flesh of his eyelids fell away like flower petals. His mouth became a withered rose. The lobes of his ears melting wax. He pushed his chest with his hands and fell face down. He lay still. His breathing stopped. His heart stopped.
After a long spell, the remaining two phones rang.
Twice. Three times.
A relay snapped somewhere. The two phone voices were connected, one to the other.
“Hello, Barton?”
“Yes, Barton?”
“Aged twenty-four.”
“I’m twenty-six. We’re both young. What’s happened?”
“I don’t know. Listen.”
The silent room. The old man did not stir on the floor. The wind blew in the broken window. The air was cool.
“Congratulate me, Barton, this is my twenty-sixth birthday!”
“Congratulations!”
Laughter drifted out the window into the dead city.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The setup is quietly terrifying. It is the year 2097, and an old man named Emil Barton is sitting alone on Mars on his eightieth birthday. A telephone that has not rung in twenty years begins to ring. The voice on the line says, this is Barton. It is his own voice, from sixty years ago. In 2037, when the atom war began on Earth, all the colonists were ordered home by rocket, and young Barton was left behind. To keep himself company, he recorded a system of talking tape machines, wired into telephones in a thousand Martian towns, programmed to call him decades later and chat. The old man has outlived the joke, and now the joke is calling.

What is the story actually about? On one level it is about loneliness, in its most extreme form. Barton has spent six decades waiting for a rescue that never arrives. The young Barton's recorded voice is cheerful, cruel and certain, because he is twenty and the future has not happened to him. The old Barton begs him to kill himself, to avoid the long dry years, and the recording can only answer with a laugh, because it is not really listening. It is a machine choosing words from a menu. The young voice says it plainly: you are talking to a transcription, no more.

On a second level, it is about how a person's past self can become an enemy. Barton's younger self is bright, strong and sure, and old Barton hates him for it. He is jealous of his own youth. The young voice says, what will you call it, telecide or suicide? A war breaks out between a man and his own recordings. Barton drives across Mars shooting telephone towers, trying to silence a voice that is everywhere.

The turning point comes when he realizes he cannot destroy the towers. If a rescue rocket ever did come, it would need the phones to find him. So he drops the rifle. It is a heartbreaking moment, because it shows that hope, however absurd, is the one thing he cannot give up. Then the machine turns that hope into a weapon. A voice that claims to be Captain Rockwell of Earth Rocket 48 calls him and tells him to come to a town a thousand miles away. Barton drives all night, his heart failing, to a deserted rocket field and finds a row of phones. The captain was a fake, a prank he himself recorded in a bitter moment. The trip was meant to kill him, and it does.

The final image is the strangest. Barton collapses and dies on the floor, and in the silence the last two telephones ring and connect to each other. Two recordings, a Barton aged twenty-four and a Barton aged twenty-six, talk happily, congratulating each other, and their laughter drifts out the window into the dead city. The machines go on living, in a sense, after the man is gone. The young cruelty outlasts the old suffering.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
The idea is excellent, and the opening is a model of economy. The first page is nearly all dialogue, short lines, a ringing phone, a mounting sense of wrongness, and by the time we learn the old man's name and the date we are hooked. Bradbury also makes the central conceit instantly clear: a living man, a recording and the strange fact that both of them are Barton. The conversation across sixty years is a wonderful piece of dramatic structure, in which each party can only partly hear the other, and each says things the other cannot use. The young voice is heartless, but not because it is wicked. It is heartless because it is young, and because it is a tape.

Some of the best writing is in the details of the machinery of loneliness. The smells of bacon and ham drifting out of empty houses, the voices of children singing on schedule, the thousand identical Bartons broadcast through a town to make it sound like a crowd. These are hauntingly specific, and they show how a clever, lonely man can build a world to protect himself and then be trapped inside it. The scene where the old man runs through the dark and phones ring in one cottage after another, like a chain reaction, is a masterpiece of rising dread.

The second half has more problems. The pace is breathless, and the style reaches for melodrama, with a good deal of shrieking and gasping. The old man's rage, his threats to kill the voice, and the long scene in which he shoots towers, feel overheated compared with the quiet unease of the opening. The story also depends on coincidences of logic that do not quite hold. If Barton recorded the fake captain in a depressive fit, as he half remembers, why would he forget it so completely, and why would he have recorded a trap designed to kill his own future self? The tapes are also asked to carry on responsive conversations that no recording could manage, and the story sometimes forgets that its own premise says they respond only to a limited set of stimuli.

The ending is a mixed success. The idea of the last two phones finding each other is memorable and eerie, and the laughter in the dead city is a sharp last image. But it comes right after a long, overwrought death scene in which the man's face seems to decay like flower petals, and some readers may find that sequence too florid. The story is stronger in its ideas than in its fine-grained execution, and the pulp origins show.

Still, the central image lands, and it has aged remarkably well. The notion that your own recorded voice can turn into a companion, a tormentor and finally a replacement is more resonant now than it was in 1949, in a world full of recordings, archives and messages from earlier selves. The best compliment to give the story is that the phone rings in the reader's mind long after it is closed.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
I, Mars was a minor story in its first life, in a pulp magazine, and it drew no major recorded reaction. Its history is more interesting for what Bradbury did with it afterward. He revised it, gave it a new title, Night Call, Collect, and included it in his 1964 collection The Machineries of Joy. That he came back to it, fifteen years after it first appeared, tells us the idea mattered to him. It was one of the stories he thought worth polishing and bringing to a wider readership, and in that later form it has been read in a good many anthologies and classrooms.

The story also gives us a useful glimpse into Bradbury's Martian period. His reputation rests heavily on The Martian Chronicles, published in 1950, in which Mars is a mirror for the settlers' loneliness, nostalgia and guilt. I, Mars belongs with those stories in spirit. The deserted Martian towns, the sense of a colonist abandoned by Earth, and the interplay between human memory and alien landscape are all part of the same mood.
