“I tied them pink elephants of Gunther’s in neat alphabetical bundles and stacked them up to dry, ya louse!” Marnagan said. “But, damn you, they killed my partner before he had a chance!”
The guard laughed.

The airlock door was still wide open when Click reached it, his head swimming darkly, his lungs crammed with pain-fire and hell-rockets. He let himself down in, quiet and soft. He didn’t have a weapon. He didn’t have a weapon. Oh, damn, damn!

A tunnel curved, ending in light, and two men silhouetted in that yellow glare. Marnagan, backed against a wall, his helmet cracked, air hissing slowly out of it, his face turning blue. And the guard, a proton gun extended stiffly before him, also in a vac-suit. The guard had his profile toward Hathaway, his lips twisting: “I think I’ll let you stand right there and die,” he said quietly. “That what Gunther wanted, anyway. A nice sordid death.”
Hathaway took three strides, his hands out in front of him.
“Don’t move!” he snapped. “I’ve got a weapon stronger than yours. One twitch and I’ll blast you and the whole damned wall out from behind you! Freeze!”
The guard whirled. He widened his sharp eyes, and reluctantly, dropped his gun to the floor.
“Get his gun, Irish.”
Marnagan made as if to move, crumpled clumsily forward.
Hathaway ran in, snatched up the gun, smirked at the guard. “Thanks for posing,” he said. “That shot will go down in film history for candid acting.”
“What!”
“Ah: ah! Keep your place. I’ve got a real gun now. Where’s the door leading into the Base?”
The guard moved his head sullenly over his left shoulder.
Click was afraid he would show his weak dizziness. He needed air. “Okay. Drag Marnagan with you, open the door and we’ll have air. Double time! Double!”

Ten minutes later, Marnagan and Hathaway, fresh tanks of oxygen on their backs, Marnagan in a fresh bulger and helmet, trussed the guard, hid him in a huge trash receptacle. “Where he belongs,” observed Irish tersely.

They found themselves in a complete inner world; an asteroid nothing more than a honeycomb fortress sliding through the void unchallenged. Perfect front for a raider who had little equipment and was short-handed of men. Gunther simply waited for specific cargo ships to rocket by, pulled them or knocked them down and swarmed over them for cargo. The animals served simply to insure against suspicion and the swarms of tourists that filled the void these days. Small fry weren’t wanted. They were scared off.

The telepathic sending station for the animals was a great bank of intricate, glittering machine, through which strips of colored film with images slid into slots and machine mouths that translated them into thought-emanations. A damned neat piece of genius.

“So here we are, still not much better off than we were,” growled Irish. “We haven’t a ship or a space-radio, and more guards’ll turn up any moment. You think we could refocus this doohingey, project the monsters inside the asteroid to fool the pirates themselves?”
“What good would that do?” Hathaway gnawed his lip. “They wouldn’t fool the engineers who created them, you nut.”
Marnagan exhaled disgustedly. “Ah, if only the U.S. Cavalry would come riding over the hill⁠—”

“Irish!” Hathaway snapped that, his face lighting up. “Irish. The U.S. Cavalry it is!” His eyes darted over the machines. “Here. Help me. We’ll stage everything on the most colossal raid of the century.”
Marnagan winced. “You breathing oxygen or whiskey?”

“There’s only one stipulation I make, Irish. I want a complete picture of Marnagan capturing Raider’s Base. I want a picture of Gunther’s face when you do it. Snap it, now, we’ve got rush work to do. How good an actor are you?”
“That’s a silly question.”

“You only have to do three things. Walk with your gun out in front of you, firing. That’s number one. Number two is to clutch at your heart and fall down dead. Number three is to clutch at your side, fall down and twitch on the ground. Is that clear?”
“Clear as the Coal Sack Nebula.⁠ ⁠…”

An hour later Hathaway trudged down a passageway that led out into a sort of city street inside the asteroid. There were about six streets, lined with cube houses in yellow metal, ending near Hathaway in a wide, green-lawned Plaza.
Hathaway, weaponless, idly carrying his camera in one hand, walked across the Plaza as if he owned it. He was heading for a building that was pretentious enough to be Gunther’s quarters.
He got halfway there when he felt a gun in his back.
He didn’t resist. They took him straight ahead to his destination and pushed him into a room where Gunther sat.

Hathaway looked at him. “So you’re Gunther?” he said, calmly. The pirate was incredibly old, his bulging forehead stood out over sunken, questioningly dark eyes, and his scrawny body was lost in folds of metal-link cloth. He glanced up from a paper-file, surprised. Before he could speak, Hathaway said:
“Everything’s over with, Mr. Gunther. The Patrol is in the city now and we’re capturing your Base. Don’t try to fight. We’ve a thousand men against your eighty-five.”

Gunther sat there, blinking at Hathaway, not moving. His thin hands twitched in his lap. “You are bluffing,” he said, finally, with a firm directness. “A ship hasn’t landed here for an hour. Your ship was the last. Two people were on it. The last I saw of them they were being pursued to the death by the Beasts. One of you escaped, it seemed.”
“Both. The other guy went after the Patrol.”
“Impossible!”
“I can’t respect your opinion, Mr. Gunther.”

A shouting rose from the Plaza. About fifty of Gunther’s men, lounging on carved benches during their time-off, stirred to their feet and started yelling. Gunther turned slowly to the huge window in one side of his office. He stared, hard.
The Patrol was coming!
Across the Plaza, marching quietly and decisively, came the Patrol. Five hundred Patrolmen in one long, incredible line, carrying paralysis guns with them in their tight hands.
Gunther babbled like a child, his voice a shrill dagger in the air. “Get out there, you men! Throw them back! We’re outnumbered!”
Guns flared. But the Patrol came on. Gunther’s men didn’t run, Hathaway had to credit them on that. They took it, standing.

Hathaway chuckled inside, deep. What a sweet, sweet shot this was. His camera whirred, clicked and whirred again. Nobody stopped him from filming it. Everything was too wild, hot and angry. Gunther was throwing a fit, still seated at his desk, unable to move because of his fragile, bony legs and their atrophied state.
Some of the Patrol were killed. Hathaway chuckled again as he saw three of the Patrolmen clutch at their hearts, crumple, lie on the ground and twitch. God, what photography!

Gunther raged, and swept a small pistol from his linked corselet. He fired wildly until Hathaway hit him over the head with a paperweight. Then Hathaway took a picture of Gunther slumped at his desk, the chaos taking place immediately outside his window.
The pirates broke and fled, those that were left. A mere handful. And out of the chaos came Marnagan’s voice, “Here!”
One of the Patrolmen stopped firing, and ran toward Click and the Building. He got inside. “Did you see them run, Click boy? What an idea. How did we do?”
“Fine, Irish. Fine!”

“So here’s Gunther, the spalpeen! Gunther, the little dried up pirate, eh?” Marnagan whacked Hathaway on the back. “I’ll have to hand it to you, this is the best plan o’ battle ever laid out. And proud I was to fight with such splendid men as these⁠—” He gestured toward the Plaza.

Click laughed with him. “You should be proud. Five hundred Patrolmen with hair like red banners flying, with thick Irish brogues and broad shoulders and freckles and blue eyes and a body as tall as your stories!”
Marnagan roared. “I always said, I said⁠—if ever there could be an army of Marnagans, we could lick the whole damn uneeverse! Did you photograph it, Click?”
“I did.” Hathaway tapped his camera happily.

“Ah, then, won’t that be a scoop for you, boy? Money from the Patrol so they can use the film as instruction in Classes and money from Cosmic Films for the newsreel headlines! And what a scene, and what acting! Five hundred duplicates of Steve Marnagan, broadcast telepathically into the minds of the pirates, walking across a Plaza, capturing the whole shebang! How did you like my death-scenes?”
“You’re a ham. And anyway⁠—five hundred duplicates, nothing!” said Click. He ripped the film-spool from the camera, spread it in the air to develop, inserted it in the micro-viewer. “Have a look⁠—”

Marnagan looked. “Ah, now. Ah, now,” he said over and over. “There’s the Plaza, and there’s Gunther’s men fighting and then they’re turning and running. And what are they running from? One man! Me. Irish Marnagan! Walking all by myself across the lawn, paralyzing them. One against a hundred, and the cowards running from me!

“Sure, Click, this is better than I thought. I forgot that the film wouldn’t register telepathic emanations, them other Marnagans. It makes it look like I’m a mighty brave man, does it not? It does. Ah, look⁠—look at me, Hathaway, I’m enjoying every minute of it, I am.”

Hathaway swatted him on his backside. “Look here, you egocentric son of Erin, there’s more work to be done. More pirates to be captured. The Patrol is still marching around and someone might be suspicious if they looked too close and saw all that red hair.”

“All right, Click, we’ll clean up the rest of them now. We’re a combination, we two, we are. I take it all back about your pictures, Click, if you hadn’t thought of taking pictures of me and inserting it into those telepath machines we’d be dead ducks now. Well⁠—here I go.⁠ ⁠…”
Hathaway stopped him. “Hold it. Until I load my camera again.”
Irish grinned. “Hurry it up. Here come three guards. They’re unarmed. I think I’ll handle them with me fists for a change. The gentle art of uppercuts. Are you ready, Hathaway?”
“Ready.”
Marnagan lifted his big ham-fists.
The camera whirred. Hathaway chuckled, to himself.
What a sweet fade-out this was!

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
On the surface this is a rescue story with a gimmick. Two men crash on an asteroid, the oxygen is running out, and a pack of horrifying monsters pins them in a cave. Marnagan, the big patrolman, fires his proton gun and it does nothing. Hathaway, who cannot stop filming even when he is terrified, notices something odd when he develops his self-developing film: the pictures show Marnagan chatting and aiming his gun at empty air. The monsters never made it onto the film. Hathaway's conclusion is the heart of the story. If the camera cannot see them, they are not there. They are thoughts pushed into the mind by a telepathic machine, and a thing that lives only in your head can be walked through.

That is a neat trick, but the story is smarter than its trick. Look at what Hathaway says next. As long as the men believed in the creatures, they could have been frightened to death, or driven to suicide. The monsters cannot touch the body, but they can still kill, because fear is a real force. When Marnagan stumbles in the crowd of imaginary beasts and cries out that one of them is real, he is hit hard enough to be knocked down, and Hathaway has to throw himself over him and shout that it is not real until Marnagan says it back. Belief is the weapon, and disbelief is the armor. The story even has the two men deliberately believe in the monsters again, just enough to see them coming, so they can follow them back to their source. That is a surprisingly subtle idea for a pulp adventure: you have to control how much you believe.

The second layer is the camera itself. In the opening pages Hathaway is almost comically attached to his camera, filming a meteor hit, filming Marnagan swearing, filming a crash. Marnagan scolds him for caring more about film than about the death they nearly suffered. Yet the camera turns out to be the one witness that is never fooled. It records what is physically in front of it and nothing else. Hathaway's sudden grief at the thought of Marnagan dying shows that the man behind the lens is not as detached as he pretends.

The ending turns that idea inside out. Hathaway now uses film, the honest recorder, to make a lie. He photographs Marnagan acting out a heroic raid, feeds those images into the telepathic machine, and the pirates are overwhelmed by five hundred imaginary Marnagans. But when the real film is developed, only one man appears, walking alone across a lawn while grown pirates flee from him. The reader is left with two truths at once: the camera does not lie, and a camera in the right hands can still manufacture a legend. Marnagan, delighted with how brave the footage makes him look, understands this perfectly. The Irishman's final line about enjoying every minute is the story's joke and its gentle warning about image-making.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
The best thing about The Monster Maker is its energy. The opening is a small masterpiece of pulp momentum: a camera whirring, a meteor striking, a ship spinning like a cosmic merry-go-round, and then a quiet that is so complete you can almost hear the asteroids rushing up. Bradbury's habit of reaching for a startling comparison is already there. Hathaway and Marnagan are human dice in a croupier's cup. The sun overhead looks sick. These are the sentences of a young writer who cannot help turning every plain description into a picture, and in the best moments they lift a stock plot above its genre.

The central device, the film that refuses to register the monsters, is also genuinely clever. It is a fair-play puzzle: the clue is planted early when Hathaway notices the meteor was glowing hot, the gravity shifts at the ridge, and the self-developing film is introduced almost as a throwaway boast about his invention. When the solution arrives, the reader feels it was always sitting there. The final sequence, in which a camera that records only what is real and a machine that broadcasts only what is imagined produce two contradictory versions of the same battle, is the sort of loop that science fiction readers love.

The weaknesses are just as visible, and an honest reading has to admit them. The science is hand-waving even by 1944 standards. Super-gravity that drags ships out of space, meteors that are tossed like baseballs, and a telepathic projector that is fed by strips of colored film are all asserted rather than explained, and the story needs the reader not to ask how an asteroid fortress with eighty-five pirates has been hiding from the Patrol. Gunther himself is a cardboard villain, a shrunken old man in a metal cloak who shows up only to be defeated. The plot also lets Hathaway be right about everything the moment he opens his mouth, which drains some of the suspense.

The dialogue is the most uneven element. Marnagan's stage-Irish speech, with its endless references to his mother's sayings and Irish luck, was a stock comic type in the pulps and now reads as a caricature, and the wisecracks sometimes keep the tension from building. Still, the banter is also how the story shows courage. These men joke because they are scared, and Hathaway says so himself when he catches himself laughing in the face of death. The final scene, where Marnagan preens over footage that makes him look like a one-man army, is the best joke in the story and also the best bit of character work. The ending's repeated phrase about a sweet fade-out neatly echoes the opening's fade-out line, and the story, though slight, is well built.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
It is only fair to say at the start that The Monster Maker is a minor Bradbury story, and its direct influence is hard to trace. It appeared in a pulp magazine, not a prestige publication, and it has never been counted among the pieces that made his reputation. What can be said is that it shows the writer at a stage when he was learning his trade, and a few of its habits would stay with him for the rest of his career.

By 1944 Bradbury had been publishing in the pulps for several years and was selling steadily to magazines like Weird Tales and Planet Stories. He had sold newspapers on a Los Angeles street corner to get by, and he was still a couple of years from the breakthrough of the stories that would make up Dark Carnival and then The Martian Chronicles. A story like this one is a kind of workshop. It is fast, it follows the rules of the adventure magazines, and it contains moments, like the haunting silence after the crash, that point toward what he would do when he stopped imitating the formula.

The theme of perception is the part that echoes forward. In story after story Bradbury would come back to the idea that what we see depends on what we believe, and that fear can be a made thing. The nursery that produces its own lions in The Veldt, the Martians who create illusions in The Martian Chronicles, and the frightened people of his small-town horror all belong to the same family as these asteroid monsters. The Monster Maker is an early, cheerful, adventure-story version of the same instinct.

The other lasting thread is the writer's attention to media. Hathaway's camera is a sort of cousin to the wall-sized television screens of Fahrenheit 451, which Bradbury wrote years later. In 1944 the newsreel was the way ordinary people saw the war, and the idea that the picture you see may be shaped by the person who made it was very much in the air. The story did not change the world, and little is recorded about how readers reacted at the time, but it deserves its small place in the long story of how Bradbury turned pulp machinery into personal themes.

As for how it is taught or read now, it mostly survives for Bradbury completists and readers of Planet Stories era science fiction. That is not a failure. Plenty of important writers have early work that serves mainly to show how they got where they were going.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
It would be dishonest to claim a big body of documented reader response to a story this obscure. Planet Stories was a pulp whose readers wrote letters to the magazine, and Bradbury's work there was generally welcomed, though no specific reviews of this particular story are on record. What can be said is what a reader today, or an old pulp fan, would likely enjoy, and why the story has held up as a pleasant read.

The first pleasure is the partnership. Hathaway and Marnagan are an odd couple of the old-fashioned kind: the small, nervous man with brains and a camera, and the enormous red-haired patrolman with a bellow and a heart. Their affection is expressed entirely through insults. Marnagan calls Hathaway a film-developing flea; Hathaway calls him a ham and an egocentric son of Erin. But when the cave scene arrives and Marnagan says that if Hathaway tells him the animals are not there, that is good enough for him, the joking falls away and the friendship becomes real. That moment of trust, a big man deciding to walk into a monster pack because a small man said so, is the emotional high point of the story.

The second pleasure is the idea. Readers who like puzzle stories enjoy a solution that turns on a single odd detail, and the film that ignores the monsters is a satisfying one. It also taps something people understand from experience. Most of us have been frightened by something that turned out to be nothing, and the story gives that feeling a physical shape. The line about thinking it hard, keeping the thought alive while you walk into the creatures, rings true to anyone who has ever talked themselves through a panic.

The third is the sheer fun of the final reversal. Five hundred Marnagans marching across a plaza, an army that exists only inside the pirates' minds, and then a strip of film showing one lonely man. It is the kind of ending a reader finishes with a grin. The self-developing film, which Hathaway describes as one of his best inventions, adds a nice period gadget flavor, and the Hollywood language, with its fades, montages and profile shots, gives the story its own jokes.

Finally, there is Bradbury's prose, which even in a pulp setting carries a warmth the genre rarely had. Readers who come to this story after the later, more famous work often say they can hear the same voice in it, already inclined to wonder and to humor.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Because The Monster Maker is little discussed, there is no famous body of criticism to summarize. What follows are the objections a thoughtful reader would reasonably raise, which are also the common complaints about much of the pulp adventure of its period.

The first is that it is thin. The characters are types, and the plot is a chain of stock moves: a crash, a mysterious enemy, a time limit, a captured hero, a daring bluff. Readers who come to Bradbury for the aching small-town memories of Dandelion Wine or the sorrowful poetry of The Martian Chronicles may find the story frankly slight. It does not have the emotional depth that his best work reaches, and it ends on a joke rather than on a feeling that lingers.

The second is the dialogue. Marnagan's Irish speech is an ethnic caricature of a kind that was common in popular fiction of the time, built from exaggerated brogue, a love of fighting and an endless supply of Irish sayings. Modern readers may find it grating or tired, and the constant wisecracking can feel like a tic. Hathaway's Anglo-Swede gag, delivered while they are sitting in a death trap, shows how often the story prefers a quip to a pause.

The third is the plausibility problem. The story asks us to accept a lot without question. The monsters are said to be telepathic projections, but they push people over, and Marnagan is struck down by one that looks like it has weight. The story explains this as the force of belief, but a skeptical reader could say that it wants the monsters to be unreal when that helps the heroes and real when that raises the stakes. The villain's whole scheme, which is to drag ships down and let monsters scare away tourists, is also a clumsy way to run a pirate base, as the story half admits by having Hathaway describe it as saving men and ships.

A last complaint is about the premise of the finale. If the Patrol is imaginary, then the pirates are defeated by being tricked into surrender, yet the story also shows several of them dying, and the two heroes cheerfully knock out the rest. It sits uneasily between a trick story and a battle story. These are small faults, and they hardly prevent enjoyment, but they explain why the story is remembered as a lively minor work and not a major one.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
The Monster Maker belongs to the golden age of the science fiction pulps, the era when magazines like Planet Stories, Astounding and Thrilling Wonder offered readers bright covers and quick adventures across the solar system. Planet Stories in particular specialized in swashbuckling interplanetary action, and its pages were home to writers like Leigh Brackett, whose Mars was a dusty romantic frontier. Bradbury wrote for that market and often bent it. His Mars was already a place of memory and dreams. In this story he stays closer to the house style, with patrolmen, pirates, proton guns and an asteroid base, but he slips in his own preoccupations.

The plot is part of an old tradition, too. Stories of illusions that vanish when someone refuses to believe in them go back a long way, from fairy tales about spells broken by a clear head to the sort of ghost story in which the haunting is explained as a trick. Science fiction gave the idea a technological coat: the telepathic projector stands in for the sorcerer's curse. Later writers, including Bradbury himself, would use the same notion with more depth. Philip K. Dick built a career on the instability of what we perceive as real, and films about manufactured realities carry the same question forward. Placed beside those, The Monster Maker is a sprightly forerunner, not an equal.

It also belongs to the long conversation about film and truth. In 1944 the newsreel was the primary visual record of the war, and the idea that a photograph could be a witness, a weapon, or a forgery was becoming part of public life. Hathaway's camera is an early image of that tension. It is a recorder that cannot lie, held by a man who is happy to help create a legend. When people today worry about faked images and staged footage, they are asking the question this story asks lightly.

Why read it now? Not because it is great, but because it is lively, short, and revealing. It lets you watch a young writer exercise ideas he would later handle with more weight: fear as a made thing, the power of the picture, and friendship between mismatched men. It is also simply entertaining, and its central trick, the camera that sees only what is real, has a durable charm. Read it as a good-humored workshop piece from a writer who was still a few years from his masterworks and was already thinking in images.

stories.title: Don’t Get Technatal
stories.author: Ray Bradbury
stories.epigraph: “For several moments Stern had eyed his typewriter ominously, contemplating whether he should utter the unutterable. Finally:”
stories.keyContext: Don't Get Technatal is a very short, very early piece of Ray Bradbury's writing. He published it in the summer of 1939 in Futuria Fantasia, a homemade science fiction fan magazine that he edited and typed himself when he was eighteen, with money from his friend and fellow fan Forrest Ackerman. It is not a polished story, and it was never meant to be one. It was a young fan's joke, written for other fans. The background is the Great Depression, when a movement called Technocracy argued that engineers, not politicians, should run society, handing out equal shares of energy credit to everyone. Newspapers talked about it constantly. Bradbury imagines that world in the year 1975 and drops into the apartment of a pulp writer who is miserable because a perfect society has taken away all his plots. It takes about three minutes to read, and its main interest today is as a window onto a teenage writer already thinking about how happiness, control and storytelling collide.
paragraphs: For several moments Stern had eyed his typewriter ominously, contemplating whether he should utter the unutterable. Finally:

“Damn!” he roared. “I can’t write any more! Look, look at that!” He tore the sheet out of the rollers and crumpled it in his fist. “If I’d known it would be this way,” he said, “I wouldn’t have voted for it! Technocracy is ruining everything!”

Bella Stern, preoccupied with her knitting, glanced up in horror. “What a temper,” she exclaimed. “Can’t you keep your voice down?” She fussed with her work. “There now,” she cried, “you made me drop a stitch!”
“I want to be a writer!” Samuel Stern lamented, turning with grim eyes to his wife. “And the Technate has spoiled my fun.”
“The way you talk, Samuel,” said his wife, “I actually believe you want to go back to that barbarism prevalent in the dark thirties!”
“It sounds like one damned good idea!” he said. “At least I’d have something decent, or indecent, to write about!”
“What can you mean?” she asked, tilting her head back and thinking. “Why can’t you write? There are just oodles of things I can think of that are readable.”

Something like a tear rolled down Samuel’s cheek. “No more gangsters, no more bank robberies, no more holdups, no more good, old-fashioned burglaries, no more vice gangs!” His voice grew lachrymose as he proceeded down an infinite line of “no mores.” “No more sadness,” he almost sobbed. “Everybody’s happy, contented. No more strife and hard work. Oh, for the days when a gangland massacre was headline scoop for me!”
“Tush!” sniffed Bella. “Have you been drinking again, Samuel?”
He hiccuped gently.
“I thought so,” she said.
“I had to do something,” he declared. “I’m going nuts for want of a plot.”

Bella Stern laid her knitting aside and walked to the balcony, looked meditatively down into the yawning canyon of the New York street fifty stories below. She turned back to Sam with a reminiscent smile.
“Why not write a love story?”
“What!” Stern shot out of his chair like a hooked eel.
“Why, yes,” she concluded. “A nice love story would be very enjoyable.”

“Love!” Stern’s voice was thick with sarcasm. “Why, we don’t even have decent love these days. A man can’t marry a woman for her money, and vice-versa. Everyone under Technocracy gets the same amount of credit. No more Reno, no more alimony, no more breach of promise, or lawsuits! Everything is cut and dried. The days of society weddings and coming out parties are gone⁠—cause everyone is equal. I can’t write political criticisms about graft in the government, about slums and terrible living conditions, about poor starving mothers and their babies. Everything is okay⁠—okay⁠—okay⁠—” his voice sobbed off into silence.
“Which should make you very happy,” countered his wife.

“Which makes me very sick,” growled Samuel Stern. “Look, Bell, all my life I wanted to be a writer. Okay. I’m writing for the pulp magazines for a coupla years. Right? Okay. Then I’m writing sea stories, gangsters, political views, first class-bump-offs. I’m happy.⁠ ⁠… I’m in my element. Then⁠—bingo!⁠—in comes Technocracy, makes everyone happy⁠—bump! out goes me! I just can’t stand writing the stuff the people read today. Everything is science and education.” He ruffled his thick black hair with his fingers and glared.
“You should be joyful that the population is at work doing what they want to do,” Bella beamed.

Sam continued muttering to himself. “They took all the sex magazines off the market first thing, all of the gangster, murder and detective publications. They been educating the children and making model citizens out of them.”
“Which is as it should be,” finished Bella.
“Do you realize,” he blazed, whipping his finger at her, “that for two years there hasn’t been more than a dozen murders in the city? Not one suicide or gang war⁠—or⁠—”

“Heavens!” sighed Bella. “Don’t be prehistoric, Sam. There hasn’t been anything really criminal for twenty years now. This is 1975 you know.” She came over and patted him gently on the shoulder. “Why don’t you write something science-fictional?”
“I don’t like science,” he spat.
“Then your only alternative is love,” she declared firmly.

He formed the despicable word with his lips, then: “No, I want something new and different.” He got up and strode to the window. In the penthouse below he saw half a dozen robots moving about speedily, working. His face lit up suddenly, like that of a tiger spying his prey. “Jumping Jigwheels!” he cried. “Why didn’t I think of it before! Robots! I’ll write a love story about two robots.”
Bella squelched him. “Be sensible,” she said.

“It might happen some day,” he argued. “Just think. Love oiled, welded, built of metal, wired for sound!” He laughed triumphantly, but it was a low laugh, a strange little sound. Bella expected him to beat his chest next. “Robots fall in love at first sight,” he announced, “and blow an audio tube!”
Bella smiled tolerantly. “You’re such a child, Sam. I sometimes wonder why I married you.”

Stern sank down, burning slowly, a crimson flush rising in his face. Only half a dozen murders in two years, he thought. No more politics, no more to write about. He had to have a story, just had to have one. He’d go crazy if something didn’t happen soon. His brain was clicking furiously. A calliope of thought was tooting in his subconscious. He had to have a story. He turned and looked at his wife, Bella, who stood watching the air traffic go by the window, bending over the sill, looking down into the street fifty floors below.⁠ ⁠…
… and then he reached slowly and quietly for his atomic gun.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The story is a single conversation in a single room, and almost everything that matters is hidden in the jokes. Samuel Stern, a pulp magazine writer, sits at his typewriter in a fifty-story apartment in the New York of 1975. He is furious. He cannot write. His wife, Bella, who knits and cheerfully approves of everything, cannot understand why. The reason is that the Technate, the government of this future, has made life so smooth that there is nothing left for a writer of crime and adventure to write about. No gangsters, no holdups, no bank robberies, no scandals about graft, no starving mothers, no society weddings. Everyone gets the same credit, so no one marries for money. Only a dozen murders in two years. As Stern puts it, everything is okay, okay, okay.

The humor depends on the reversal. We are used to dystopias in which the horror is obvious: soldiers, prisons, suffering. Here the complaint is that the world is too good, and the person complaining is a hack who misses his raw material. Bella is the voice of the system, answering each of his grievances with a bright line about how this is as it should be and how he should be joyful that people are doing what they want. The comedy is that she is not wrong in any simple way, and Stern is not right in any noble way. He is not defending liberty. He is missing his job.

Underneath the gag there is a serious question that Bradbury would return to for the rest of his career: what happens to art, and to people, when conflict and pain are removed? Stern says everything is science and education now, and that he cannot stand writing the stuff people read today. The story hints that stories need trouble, and that a society that has banned trouble has also banned the thing that makes stories worth telling. Fahrenheit 451 would make a much more serious version of this argument, about a world that burns books to stay happy.

Then comes the last line, which is the real joke. Stern is desperate for a plot. His brain is clicking like a calliope. He looks at his wife, who is leaning out over the sill of a window fifty floors above the street. And then he reaches slowly and quietly for his atomic gun. The reader is left to supply the rest. He may be about to shoot her, or to shoot something else, or simply to stage a crime. The point is the leap: a man who cannot find a murder to write about is about to commit one. It is a dark punchline, in the manner of the pulp magazines Bradbury read, and it turns the whole tidy utopia into a place where the first murder in years might be committed by a bored author.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
It would be unfair to judge a teenager's fanzine sketch by the standards of a finished story, but it would also be dishonest to pretend it is better than it is. It is, frankly, a slight and uneven piece, and its main virtues are the ones you would expect from a clever eighteen-year-old: a good premise, a lively ear for patter, and a sharp final beat.

The premise is genuinely good. The idea of a writer made miserable by a perfect world is a witty inversion that gets the reader's attention in a couple of lines. It is also timely for its moment. Technocracy was a real movement of the early thirties, and the story's world, with its equal credits for everyone, comes straight out of the arguments people were having in newspapers. Bradbury uses it with a light touch, not trying to refute the movement, just imagining its consequences for one person. The pacing is well judged for a gag. The back-and-forth between Stern and Bella has the rhythm of a vaudeville routine, with Stern complaining and Bella supplying the straight lines, and the escalation, from crime to love to robots, builds toward the ending.

The ending itself is the best-crafted thing here. The last two paragraphs set the scene, with the balcony, the fifty floors and the wife bending over the sill, and then the final sentence arrives with a click. It is effective because it is abrupt. There is no explanation and no aftermath, just the reach for the gun. In a very short space Bradbury shows he understands how to end a story on an image that sticks.

The weaknesses are real, though. The characters are cartoons. Bella is an ideal housewife of the sitcom type, and Stern is a stage grouch. Much of the dialogue is broad slang of the period, with phrases like Jumping Jigwheels that will make a modern reader wince, and the humor sometimes gets in its own way. The setup is also rather talkative: Stern announces the rules of his world in speeches, explaining things the characters would both already know, which is the oldest trick for getting background across. The idea of a love story about two robots, with its joke about a blown audio tube, is also the weakest joke in the piece.

More importantly, the satire has no real bite. It lets the system off the hook because it never shows what the Technate costs anyone other than a hack writer, and Bradbury himself would do far better at that sort of thing later. As a piece of apprentice work, it shows promise. As a standalone story, it is a sketch.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The honest answer is that Don't Get Technatal had almost no impact outside the small world in which it appeared. It was published in Futuria Fantasia, a fan magazine produced in very small numbers, and it was not a story that critics reviewed or anthologies reprinted. Its significance is almost entirely biographical, and it is worth being clear about that and not inflating it.

What the story does reveal is how Bradbury got started. In the late thirties he was a teenager in Los Angeles, a member of the Los Angeles Science Fantasy Society, surrounded by other young fans who wrote letters, traded magazines and produced their own fanzines. Forrest Ackerman, an energetic fan and collector, was one of the people who encouraged him, and Futuria Fantasia, which Bradbury edited, was financed by Ackerman. The magazine ran only a handful of issues, and much of its content was written by Bradbury himself, sometimes under other names. It was a way to practice writing in public, to see his stories in print, and to find out what made readers laugh or shiver. Stories like this one are the early exercises of a writer who would go on to sell to professional magazines within a few years.

It also shows themes that would echo later. The worry about a society that has made itself too comfortable and too regulated would grow up into some of Bradbury's best-known work. The most obvious descendant is Fahrenheit 451, in which a government keeps its citizens content by banning books, and a minor but suggestive relative is the 1948 story Pillar of Fire, in which a future society has burned its ghost stories and horror writers. Here, in miniature and played for laughs, is the same fear: that a world without trouble is a world without stories, and that someone will pay for it.

In terms of culture at large, the story is a small footnote to the broader satire of technocratic planning that ran through twentieth-century fiction. It did not shape the conversation, and it is hard to find evidence that anyone cited it before Bradbury became famous. Today it is mostly read by completists and by those curious about how a major writer's voice formed. As teaching material, it is occasionally useful as an example of how early work can contain a writer's lifelong preoccupations in rough form, and as a reminder that every famous author began by sending something out into the void.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
For a story this obscure, there are no published reviews or documented fan letters to cite. Futuria Fantasia was a labor of love circulated among fans, and the surviving record of how it was received is thin. What can be said is what a reader might find appealing in the story, then and now.

The first appeal is the cleverness of the central reversal. Fans of science fiction in the thirties were used to stories that imagined the future as either a paradise or a nightmare. A story in which a paradise is a nightmare for one specific person, a hack who cannot sell his pulp stories anymore, would have made a pulp-reading audience laugh at itself. These readers knew exactly what a writer for the gangster and detective magazines did, and they knew how silly the dependence of those magazines on crime could look. The in-joke quality, a pulp writer complaining about running out of plots, is part of the charm.

The second is the sheer speed. The story takes only a few minutes to read, and nothing in it is padded. Stern's rant moves from crime to politics to love to robots with the tempo of a comedy routine, and there is real pleasure in the way each suggestion from Bella is shot down by an ever more ridiculous counterproposal. The robot love story, with its image of love oiled, welded and wired for sound, gives the reader a laugh and also a glimpse of a writer's mind grabbing at any idea in desperation.

The third is the snap ending, which readers of short fiction almost always enjoy. The last line, with Stern reaching for his atomic gun, turns the entire preceding conversation into a setup. A reader who has been smiling at a domestic squabble suddenly finds a murder in the air. The shock is cheerful, in the way pulp horror often is, and it leaves the reader with a grin and a small shiver.

Finally, readers today often value the story as a chance to see the beginning. People who love Bradbury's later work enjoy finding the earliest signs of the writer: the playfulness with language, the interest in what happens to imagination under pressure, the instinct for an image that lands. There is something touching about a young man at a typewriter writing a story about a man who cannot write. It is a small, funny self-portrait of the fan-writer as an anxious professional, composed by a teenager who had not yet sold a story to a paying magazine.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
There is no body of professional criticism on Don't Get Technatal that I can point to, so the objections here are the ones a careful reader would raise, not the record of a famous controversy.

The most obvious complaint is that it is minor. It runs to under a thousand words, its characters are thin, and its satire is a single joke stretched to a punchline. Readers who come to Bradbury through his mature work may be disappointed to find no trace of the lyricism, the sorrow or the small-town warmth that make his reputation. This is a fan magazine piece, and it reads like one.

A second complaint concerns the humor. The slang, the exaggerated reactions and the wisecracks belong to a particular kind of thirties comic writing, and they have aged poorly. Bella's cheerful obedience and her role as an endlessly patient wife make her a type, and the story's jokes at her expense, culminating in the implied threat to her, have a casual quality that modern readers may find uncomfortable. The ending can be read as a bit of black comedy, but it is also a joke in which a woman exists mainly to be a victim. Some readers will take it as a harmless gag in the pulp tradition, while others will see it as an example of how casually the genre treated women's lives.

A third point is intellectual. The story treats Technocracy as a convenient butt of satire and does not engage with what the movement actually argued. A reader who knows the history may feel that it flattens a complicated and short-lived political phenomenon into a cartoon of bland contentment. Similarly, the central assumption that a society without crime would have nothing to write about is itself questionable: a world of equal credits might have plenty of stories about envy, grief, love and ambition. Stern's lack of imagination is partly the point, but it also exposes how narrow his imagination is, and the story does not quite decide whether we are meant to sympathize with him or laugh at him.

Finally, a reader might fairly object to the way the story uses its ending to avoid resolving anything. The final line is clever, but it is also a way of stopping rather than concluding. These objections do not make the story bad. They make it a minor piece of juvenilia, which is exactly what it is.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
Don't Get Technatal sits at the edge of two traditions. One is the fan-written story, the playful, in-group fiction that grew up around the science fiction magazines of the thirties, when readers wrote letters, started clubs and then began publishing their own fiction. The other is the dystopian satire, the story that imagines a future society organized around one idea and shows the human cost.

The fan tradition explains the tone. Science fiction in the 1930s was a small, tightly knit community. Fans wrote to the magazines, met in local clubs like the Los Angeles Science Fantasy Society, and swapped homemade publications. Many of the professionals of the next generation, writers and editors alike, came out of that world, and Bradbury was one of them. The jokes in this story, about pulp writers, about plot shortages and about robot romances, are the jokes of insiders who knew the genre's habits.

The dystopian tradition explains the subject. Stories about planned, regulated societies go back at least to Edward Bellamy's Looking Backward, and they include Yevgeny Zamyatin's We, Aldous Huxley's Brave New World and, later, George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four. Huxley's novel, from 1932, is the closest relative: a world engineered for happiness in which conflict and art have been removed, and in which people are conditioned from birth. Bradbury's Technate belongs in the same family, though Bradbury's treatment is comic where Huxley's is chilly. The story also looks forward. Fahrenheit 451, with its fireman who burns books and its society that uses entertainment to keep people from thinking, is the grown-up version of the same worry. Even the idea of a writer finding the future's contentment unbearable is a thread in Bradbury's later fiction.

It is worth being clear about what this piece is not. It is not a work of literature that stands beside those novels. It is, as far as the record shows, an obscure piece of juvenilia whose main importance is that Bradbury wrote it. Why read it now? Because it takes three minutes, because it is funny in an old-fashioned way, and because it lets you see where a great storyteller began. It shows a teenager testing out a favorite theme, the fear that comfort can kill imagination, and learning how to end a story with a snap. Good writers do not arrive fully formed, and this little story is a reminder that even the greatest begin with a joke told to friends.

stories.title: The Fight of the Good Ship Clarissa
stories.author: Ray Bradbury
stories.epigraph: “The field was silent. The ship lay gleaming in the pink light of dawn that was just blooming over the mountains like a pale flower.”
stories.keyContext: The Fight of the Good Ship Clarissa is one of the earliest things Ray Bradbury ever published. It appeared in June 1938 in Imagination!, the fan magazine of the Los Angeles Science Fantasy Society, when he was seventeen and still a student at Los Angeles High School. It is not a story in the usual sense. It is a burlesque, a piece of deliberate nonsense that makes fun of the heroic space adventures filling the pulp magazines of the day, the ones with fearless rocket crews, hostile aliens and last-ditch battles. Bradbury had grown up devouring those magazines, and in the late thirties he and a circle of young fans in Los Angeles wrote, traded and teased each other about them. So this is a joke told by a fan to other fans, full of puns, wild similes and in-jokes about magazine editors. Read it as a teenager's playful goodbye to the clichés he loved, and listen for the sound of a future master testing out his voice.
paragraphs: The space rocket Clarissa was nine days out from Venus. The members of the crew were also out for nine days. They were hunters, fearless expeditionists who bagged game in Venusian jungles. At the start of our story they are busy bagging their pants, not to forget their eyes. A sort of lull has fallen over the ship (Note: a lull is a time warp that frequently attacks rockets and seduces its members into a siesta). It was during this lull that Anthony Quelch sat sprawled at his typewriter looking as baggy as a bag of unripe grapefruit. Anthony Quelch, the Cosmic Clamor Boy, with a face like turned linoleum on the third term, busy writing a book: Fascism Is Communism with a Shave for which he would receive 367 rubles, 10 pazinkas and incarceration in a cinema showing Gone with the Wind.

The boys upstairs were throwing a party in the control room. They had been throwing the same party so long the party looked like a worn out first edition of a trapeze artist. There is doubt in our mind as to whether they were trying to break the party up or just do the morning mopping and break the lease simultaneously. Arms, legs and heads littered the deck. The boys, it seems, threw a party at the drop of a chin. Sort of a space cataclysm with rules and little regulation⁠—kind of an atomic convulsion in the front parlor. The neighbors never complained. The neighbors were 450 million miles away. And the boys were tighter than a catsup bottle at lunchtime. The last time the captain had looked up the hatch and called to his kiddies in a gentle voice, “Hell!” the kiddies had thrown snowballs at him. The captain had vanished. Clever way they make these space bombs nowadays. A few minutes previous the boys had been tearing up old Amazings and throwing them at one another, but now they contented themselves with tearing up just the editors. Palmer was torn in half and he sat in a corner arguing with himself about rejecting a story for an hour before someone put him through an orange juice machine killing him. (Orange juice sorry, now?)

And then they landed on Venus. How in heck they got back there so quick is a wonder of science, but there they were. “Come on, girls!” cried Quelch, “put on your shin guards, get out there and dig ditches for good old W.P.A. and the Rover Boys Academy, earth branch 27!”

Out into the staggering rain they dashed. Five minutes later they came back in, gasping, reeling. They had forgotten their corsets! The Venusians closed in like a million landlords. “Charge, men!” cried Quelch, running the other way. And then⁠—battle! “What a fight, folks,” cried Quelch. “Twenty thousand earth men against two Venusians! We’re outnumbered, but we’ll fight!” Bloosh! “Correction⁠—ten thousand men fighting!” Kerblom! “One hundred men from earth left!” Boom! “This is the last man speaking, folks! What a fight. I ain’t had so much fun since⁠—Help, someone just clipped my corset strings!” Bwom! “Someone just clipped me!”
The field was silent. The ship lay gleaming in the pink light of dawn that was just blooming over the mountains like a pale flower.

The two Venusians stood weeping over the bodies of the Earthlings like onion peelers or two women in a bargain basement. One Venusian looked at the other Venusian, and in a high-pitched, hoarse, sad voice said: “Aye, aye, aye⁠—this⁠—hit shooden heppen to a dog⁠—not a doidy leedle dog!” And dawn came peacefully, like beer barrels, rolling.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
There is almost no plot to decipher, and that is the point. The rocket Clarissa is nine days out from Venus, and the crew, who are supposed to be fearless big-game hunters, are busy getting drunk at a party in the control room. The narrator keeps interrupting himself with fake explanations, such as the note that a lull is a time warp that attacks rockets and seduces the crew into a siesta. A man named Anthony Quelch, called the Cosmic Clamor Boy, sprawls at a typewriter writing a book called Fascism Is Communism with a Shave. Then, with no real transition, the ship has landed on Venus, the crew rushes out into the rain, rushes back in because they forgot their corsets, and a battle begins that is narrated by Quelch as a sports broadcaster would call it, with the number of surviving earthmen dropping from twenty thousand to ten thousand to one hundred to one. When the dust settles, two Venusians stand weeping over the bodies.

The best way to read this is as a parody of a type of story, not of any single story. The pulp space adventure of the thirties had a familiar set of moves: the brave crew, the strange planet, the monstrous natives, the desperate fight, the grim aftermath. Bradbury runs all of these through a blender. The brave crew is drunk and ridiculous. The monstrous natives are two small figures who speak in a Brooklyn-style dialect and cry. The desperate fight is a series of sound effects and shouted announcements. The grim aftermath, which a serious pulp would play for pathos, is played for laughs with a Venusian saying that this should not happen to a dog, not a dirty little dog. It is a story that deflates its own genre.

The details are also a map of what a teenager in 1938 had on his mind. The mention of Gone with the Wind and the W.P.A. and the Rover Boys places the joke in the popular culture of the time, and the references to old copies of Amazing and an editor named Palmer who is torn in half and then put through an orange juice machine are shots at the real editorial world of the science fiction magazines. Palmer is almost certainly Raymond Palmer, who had taken over Amazing Stories in 1938. The joke is that the fans who adore these magazines also love to imagine tearing up the people who reject their stories.

Beneath all this nonsense there is a serious insight: a genre can only be parodied by someone who loves it. The jokes are affectionate. The final image, the dawn blooming over the mountains like a pale flower, followed instantly by a comic cry and a simile about beer barrels rolling, shows a young writer who cannot resist beautiful language even when he is mocking it.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
Judged as a finished story, The Fight of the Good Ship Clarissa is a mess, and its author would probably have agreed. Judged as a stunt, it is surprisingly lively, and an honest assessment has to hold both of those truths at once.

What works is the sheer inventiveness of the sentences. Bradbury throws out comparisons at a reckless rate, and a fair number of them land. A man looks as baggy as a bag of unripe grapefruit. A face is like turned linoleum on the third term. The boys were tighter than a catsup bottle at lunchtime. The Venusians close in like a million landlords. Some of these are wonderful in the way absurd comparisons can be, because they are specific and unexpected. The parenthetical asides, like the claim that a lull is a time warp that seduces a crew into a siesta, mimic the pompous scientific explanations of the pulps and then undercut them. The cheerful violence toward language is exactly what a young writer with a gift for metaphor would do when given permission to be silly.

The sound-effects battle is also a well-judged piece of comic timing. Quelch announcing the shrinking numbers, with explosions in between, is a compact little routine that captures the way pulp action turns into noise. The final twist, with the victors being two crying Venusians, is a good reversal because it is delivered so quickly that the reader barely has time to see it coming.

But the weaknesses are everywhere. The humor is relentlessly scattershot, and the jokes come so fast that many of them miss. There are puns that are mostly noise, topical references that are impossible to follow without a footnote, and long runs where the metaphors seem to be there for their own sake. The story has no characters beyond the barest sketches and no narrative drive; the leap from the party to the landing on Venus is acknowledged as nonsense in the text itself, with the narrator wondering aloud how they got back so quickly. The political joke in the book title is cryptic and the story does nothing with it. A great deal of the humor depends on knowing the world of 1930s fandom, which makes it opaque to most modern readers.

There is also a sense in which the whole thing is a one-note performance. A parody works best when it has something to say about its target, and this one mostly shouts that the target is silly. Still, the energy is real, and the experiment is a revealing one. Many young writers copy their heroes, but fewer have the nerve to wreck them, and the wreckage here is full of life.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
It is important to be straightforward: this story had essentially no public impact. It appeared in a fan magazine with a tiny circulation, and no review, adaptation or major critical discussion of it is on record. Its importance is in what it tells us about a famous writer's beginnings.

In 1938, Bradbury was seventeen and part of a lively circle of science fiction fans in Los Angeles. The Los Angeles Science Fantasy Society, whose magazine Imagination! printed this story, was one of the places where young enthusiasts met, argued and published each other. Bradbury was a regular at its gatherings, where he mingled with other fans and with established writers who came through town. The society's fanzines were a kind of training ground, offering a place to see your name in print, to receive immediate feedback and to try out styles without the pressure of selling to a professional editor. Bradbury would graduate from high school in 1938 and go on to sell newspapers on the street while writing in the evenings, and these fanzine pieces were part of the long apprenticeship that preceded his professional sales.

In that light, this story is a document of a particular stage. It shows a young writer playing with voice, using exaggeration and wordplay to find what he could do. Bradbury himself later talked often about the importance of writing many bad stories to get to the good ones, and a piece like this is an example of the early, unpolished output that made that process possible. The habits it displays, the love of vivid comparisons, the willingness to turn a sentence on its head for the sake of a picture, and the instinct to take a familiar scenario and twist it, never left him. They would be harnessed to much more serious purposes in the stories of the forties and fifties.

It also reflects the culture of fandom that nurtured him. The science fiction community of the thirties was a small, gossipy world, and in-jokes about editors and writers were a form of belonging. Bradbury's later fame did not erase that: he remained a lifelong champion of fans and libraries.

As for how it is read today, it is mostly of interest to collectors and Bradbury scholars. It occasionally turns up in discussions of his juvenilia, and it is useful for teaching because it shows the raw material from which a style grows. It is not a story that anyone has argued changed literature, but it is a small piece of evidence that a seventeen-year-old with a typewriter and a strong sense of humor can begin to find a voice.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Reactions to this story are not well documented. A fanzine piece from 1938 would have been read by a few dozen or a few hundred people who knew one another, and their responses, if recorded at all, are not part of any easily accessible record. What I can offer is an account of what a reader might find enjoyable in it, particularly a reader who comes to it now as a Bradbury fan.

The first pleasure is the language. Bradbury's gift for metaphor shows even in this absurd setting, and some of the lines are plainly delightful. The comparison of a face to turned linoleum, the party that looks like a worn-out first edition of a trapeze artist, the neighbors who never complained because they were four hundred and fifty million miles away: these are lines that make a reader smile because they are surprising and compressed. Readers who love Bradbury for his prose will find in this story a rough, comic version of the same pleasure.

The second is the fearless silliness. The story does not apologize for itself. It dives into its own nonsense with a straight face, which is a quality that readers of comedy appreciate. The fake scientific note about the lull, the narrator who wonders how they got to Venus so quickly, and the battle that is announced like a sports event all show a writer who is having fun, and the fun is catching.

The third is the in-joke warmth. For people who knew the pulp magazines, a story that threw a party in which the crew tears up old issues of Amazing and then the editors themselves is a way of laughing at something they loved. The affection comes through even in the violence. Fans have always enjoyed poking at the things they care most about, and this story is an early example of that tradition.

The fourth is the final image. After all the noise, the story closes on a quiet picture of dawn over the mountains and two weeping figures, and then ruins it with a joke about beer barrels. It is a nice small demonstration of how a writer can hold beauty and comedy in the same hand. Many readers find that moment charming precisely because it is so brief.

Above all, readers who care about the history of a great writer value the story as a rare glimpse of the beginning. There is something endearing about a seventeen-year-old who already cannot stop making metaphors, and the story gives a sense of how much joy he took in words from the start.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Because the story is so obscure, there is no recorded body of criticism to describe. What follows are the objections that a fair-minded reader today might make, which are also the ordinary complaints about juvenile burlesque.

The first is the obvious one: it is not really a story. There is no plot to speak of, no character with any depth, and no emotional stake. The reader cannot care about the crew, because the crew is a joke, and cannot care about the Venusians, because they are punchlines. A story that is only a string of gags will always feel slight, and this one lasts only a few hundred words before it runs out of steam.

The second is the density of the jokes. In a short space the story crams puns, parodies, topical references and wild similes, and a good number of them do not work. Many references, such as the allusions to long-forgotten magazines and the offhand jokes about rubles and pazinkas and corsets, are hard to understand without knowing the context. Even a reader who appreciates the humor may find the noise exhausting, and the strain of trying to be funny in every sentence can make the piece feel forced.

The third is the matter of taste. Some of the humor depends on jokes about women's clothing, about foreigners and about accents. The Venusian speaks in a thick comic dialect, which was a common device in the humor of the day but is not likely to delight everyone now. A reader sensitive to such things may find the story dated, though it is hardly more offensive than much popular comedy of the period. It is more fair to say that it is bound to its time than to condemn it.

A fourth objection is about the political joke. The title of Quelch's book, which equates fascism and communism, is thrown in without any follow-through, and it is unclear whether Bradbury intends it as a real opinion, as a parody of the kind of glib political slogans that were in the air, or simply as a joke. The story does not help us decide.

None of these complaints should be pressed too hard. A seventeen-year-old's comic sketch for a fan club cannot be held to the same standard as a published novel. The criticisms are really observations about why it remains a curiosity and not a classic.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
The Fight of the Good Ship Clarissa belongs to two overlapping traditions: the fan culture of 1930s science fiction, and the long history of literary burlesque. The first explains why it exists. The second explains how it works.

Science fiction fandom began in the late twenties and thirties, when readers of the pulp magazines started writing to the letter columns, found each other, and began forming clubs. By the time Bradbury joined the Los Angeles group, there was an established tradition of fan magazines, little publications typed or mimeographed by enthusiasts, where members could publish stories, articles, jokes and gossip. Much of this material was, frankly, amateur, but some of it was a training ground for professionals. Many of the writers and editors who shaped the genre over the next decades got their start in this world, and the habit of teasing the magazines they loved was part of it. A parody like this one is a fan's way of showing how well he knows the formulas.

Burlesque is an old art. The idea of mocking a heroic genre by exaggerating its conventions goes back to Cervantes and Don Quixote, and it includes works like Henry Fielding's Shamela, Jane Austen's Northanger Abbey, which gently mocks the Gothic novel, and many later parodies of adventure and romance. In America, the humorists of the early twentieth century, with their love of absurd metaphors and mock-learned digressions, were a likely influence on a young writer with an ear for comic patter. The pulp space opera was an especially tempting target, because it was so earnest. Later science fiction would parody the field with more sophistication, as in the comic work of writers such as Douglas Adams, whose spaceships and aliens deflate the grand conventions in the same spirit, though with far more polish.

Bradbury's later career took him away from this kind of joke. Within a few years he was writing the weird and moving stories that became Dark Carnival and then The Martian Chronicles, where Mars is a place of nostalgia and loss and not a battlefield. But you can see in this early burlesque some of the qualities that remained: the fascination with metaphor, the sense of play, and the love of the genre he was mocking.

Why read it now? Not because it is a lost masterpiece, but because it is short, odd and revealing. It is one of the few places you can watch a great writer in his first public attempts, throwing words around with delight, long before he learned how to make them hurt. For anyone who loves Bradbury, it is a small and cheerful piece of the foundation.

stories.title: Pillar of Fire
stories.author: Ray Bradbury
stories.epigraph: “He came out of the earth, hating. Hate was his father; hate was his mother.”
stories.keyContext: Pillar of Fire is one of Ray Bradbury's most important early stories, though it ran in a pulp magazine, Planet Stories, in the summer of 1948. Bradbury later said it was a forerunner of Fahrenheit 451, and you can see why. It imagines the year 2349, when a clean, rational, cheerful society has burned its graveyards, along with its ghost stories and horror writers, because it considers fear unhealthy. In the middle of that world a dead man, William Lantry, climbs out of the last grave. He is furious, and he is utterly alone. The story came out of the post-war world, when people were hopeful about science and uneasy about what a perfect, sensible future might cost. Bradbury loved Edgar Allan Poe and Halloween, and this story is his love letter to the dark side of imagination, delivered from the point of view of a monster. Listen for what the story asks you to feel about him. It is not simple.
paragraphs: He came out of the earth, hating. Hate was his father; hate was his mother.
It was good to walk again. It was good to leap up out of the earth, off of your back, and stretch your cramped arms violently and try to take a deep breath!
He tried. He cried out.

He couldn’t breathe. He flung his arms over his face and tried to breathe. It was impossible. He walked on the earth, he came out of the earth. But he was dead. He couldn’t breathe. He could take air into his mouth and force it half down his throat, with withered moves of long-dormant muscles, wildly, wildly! And with this little air he could shout and cry! He wanted to have tears, but he couldn’t make them come, either. All he knew was that he was standing upright, he was dead, he shouldn’t be walking! He couldn’t breathe and yet he stood.

The smells of the world were all about him. Frustratedly, he tried to smell the smells of autumn. Autumn was burning the land down into ruin. All across the country the ruins of summer lay; vast forests bloomed with flame, tumbled down timber on empty, unleafed timber. The smoke of the burning was rich, blue, and invisible.

He stood in the graveyard, hating. He walked through the world and yet could not taste nor smell of it. He heard, yes. The wind roared on his newly opened ears. But he was dead. Even though he walked he knew he was dead and should expect not too much of himself or this hateful living world.
He touched the tombstone over his own empty grave. He knew his own name again. It was a good job of carving.
William Lantry
That’s what the grave stone said.
His fingers trembled on the cool stone surface.
Born 1898⁠—Died 1933
Born again⁠ ⁠… ?

What year? He glared at the sky and the midnight autumnal stars moving in slow illuminations across the windy black. He read the tiltings of centuries in those stars. Orion thus and so, Aurega here! and where Taurus? There!
His eyes narrowed. His lips spelled out the year:

An odd number. Like a school sum. They used to say a man couldn’t encompass any number over a hundred. After that it was all so damned abstract there was no use counting. This was the year 2349! A numeral, a sum. And here he was, a man who had lain in his hateful dark coffin, hating to be buried, hating the living people above who lived and lived and lived, hating them for all the centuries, until today, now, born out of hatred, he stood by his own freshly excavated grave, the smell of raw earth in the air, perhaps, but he could not smell it!
“I,” he said, addressing a poplar tree that was shaken by the wind, “am an anachronism.” He smiled faintly.

He looked at the graveyard. It was cold and empty. All of the stones had been ripped up and piled like so many flat bricks, one atop another, in the far corner by the wrought iron fence. This had been going on for two endless weeks. In his deep secret coffin he had heard the heartless, wild stirring as the men jabbed the earth with cold spades and tore out the coffins and carried away the withered ancient bodies to be burned. Twisting with fear in his coffin, he had waited for them to come to him.

Today they had arrived at his coffin. But⁠—late. They had dug down to within an inch of the lid. Five o’clock bell, time for quitting. Home to supper. The workers had gone off. Tomorrow they would finish the job, they said, shrugging into their coats.
Silence had come to the emptied tombyard.
Carefully, quietly, with a soft rattling of sod, the coffin lid had lifted.
William Lantry stood trembling now, in the last cemetery on Earth.

“Remember?” he asked himself, looking at the raw earth. “Remember those stories of the last man on earth? Those stories of men wandering in ruins, alone? Well, you, William Lantry, are a switch on the old story. Do you know that? You are the last dead man in the whole damned world!”

There were no more dead people. Nowhere in any land was there a dead person. Impossible? Lantry did not smile at this. No, not impossible at all in this foolish sterile, unimaginative, antiseptic age of cleansings and scientific methods! People died, oh my god, yes. But⁠—dead people? Corpses? They didn’t exist!
What happened to dead people?

The graveyard was on a hill. William Lantry walked through the dark burning night until he reached the edge of the graveyard and looked down upon the new town of Salem. It was all illumination, all color. Rocket ships cut fire above it, crossing the sky to all the far ports of earth.

In his grave the new violence of this future world had driven down and seeped into William Lantry. He had been bathed in it for years. He knew all about it, with a hating dead man’s knowledge of such things.
Most important of all, he knew what these fools did with dead men.
He lifted his eyes. In the center of the town a massive stone finger pointed at the stars. It was three hundred feet high and fifty feet across. There was a wide entrance and a drive in front of it.

In the town, theoretically, thought William Lantry, say you have a dying man. In a moment he will be dead. What happens? No sooner is his pulse cold when a certificate is flourished, made out, his relatives pack him into a car-beetle and drive him swiftly to⁠—
The Incinerator!
That functional finger, that Pillar of Fire pointing at the stars. Incinerator. A functional, terrible name. But truth is truth in this future world.
Like a stick of kindling your Mr. Dead Man is shot into the furnace.
Flume!
William Lantry looked at the top of the gigantic pistol shoving at the stars. A small pennant of smoke issued from the top.
There’s where your dead people go.

“Take care of yourself, William Lantry,” he murmured. “You’re the last one, the rare item, the last dead man. All the other graveyards of earth have been blasted up. This is the last graveyard and you’re the last dead man from the centuries. These people don’t believe in having dead people about, much less walking dead people. Everything that can’t be used goes up like a matchstick. Superstitions right along with it!”

He looked at the town. All right, he thought, quietly. I hate you. You hate me, or you would if you knew I existed. You don’t believe in such things as vampires or ghosts. Labels without referents, you cry! You snort. All right, snort! Frankly, I don’t believe in you, either! I don’t like you! You and your Incinerators.

He trembled. How very close it had been. Day after day they had hauled out the other dead ones, burned them like so much kindling. An edict had been broadcast around the world. He had heard the digging men talk as they worked!
“I guess it’s a good idea, this cleaning up the graveyards,” said one of the men.
“Guess so,” said another. “Grisly custom. Can you imagine? Being buried, I mean! Unhealthy! All them germs!”
“Sort of a shame. Romantic, kind of. I mean, leaving just this one graveyard untouched all these centuries. The other graveyards were cleaned out, what year was it, Jim?”

“About 2260, I think. Yeah, that was it, 2260, almost a hundred years ago. But some Salem Committee they got on their high horse and they said, ‘Look here, let’s have just one graveyard left, to remind us of the customs of the barbarians.’ And the gover’ment scratched its head, thunk it over, and said, ‘Okay. Salem it is. But all other graveyards go, you understand, all!’ ”
“And away they went,” said Jim.
“Sure, they sucked out ’em with fire and steam shovels and rocket-cleaners. If they knew a man was buried in a cow-pasture, they fixed him! Evacuated them, they did. Sort of cruel, I say.”
“I hate to sound old-fashioned, but still there were a lot of tourists came here every year, just to see what a real graveyard was like.”

“Right. We had nearly a million people in the last three years visiting. A good revenue. But⁠—a government order is an order. The government says no more morbidity, so flush her out we do! Here we go. Hand me that spade, Bill.”

William Lantry stood in the autumn wind, on the hill. It was good to walk again, to feel the wind and to hear the leaves scuttling like mice on the road ahead of him. It was good to see the bitter cold stars almost blown away by the wind.
It was even good to know fear again.

For fear rose in him now, and he could not put it away. The very fact that he was walking made him an enemy. And there was not another friend, another dead man, in all of the world, to whom one could turn for help or consolation. It was the whole melodramatic living world against one William Lantry. It was the whole vampire-disbelieving, body-burning, graveyard-annihilating world against a man in a dark suit on a dark autumn hill. He put out his pale cold hands into the city illumination. You have pulled the tombstones, like teeth, from the yard, he thought. Now I will find some way to push your damnable Incinerators down into rubble. I will make dead people again, and I will make friends in so doing. I cannot be alone and lonely. I must start manufacturing friends very soon. Tonight.
“War is declared,” he said, and laughed. It was pretty silly, one man declaring war on an entire world.
The world did not answer back. A rocket crossed the sky on a rush of flame, like an Incinerator taking wing.
Footsteps. Lantry hastened to the edge of the cemetery. The diggers, coming back to finish up their work? No. Just someone, a man, walking by.
As the man came abreast the cemetery gate, Lantry stepped swiftly out. “Good evening,” said the man, smiling.
Lantry struck the man in the face. The man fell. Lantry bent quietly down and hit the man a killing blow across the neck with the side of his hand.

Dragging the body back into shadow, he stripped it, changed clothes with it. It wouldn’t do for a fellow to go wandering about this future world with ancient clothing on. He found a small pocket knife in the man’s coat; not much of a knife, but enough if you knew how to handle it properly. He knew how.

He rolled the body down into one of the already opened and exhumed graves. In a minute he had shoveled dirt down upon it, just enough to hide it. There was little chance of it being found. They wouldn’t dig the same grave twice.
He adjusted himself in his new loose-fitting metallic suit. Fine, fine.
Hating, William Lantry walked down into town, to do battle with the Earth.

The incinerator was open. It never closed. There was a wide entrance, all lighted up with hidden illumination, there was a helicopter landing table and a beetle drive. The town itself was dying down after another day of the dynamo. The lights were going dim, and the only quiet, lighted spot in the town now was the Incinerator. God, what a practical name, what an unromantic name.

William Lantry entered the wide, well-lighted door. It was an entrance, really; there were no doors to open or shut. People could go in and out, summer or winter, the inside was always warm. Warm from the fire that rushed whispering up the high round flue to where the whirlers, the propellors, the air-jets pushed the leafy grey ashes on away for a ten mile ride down the sky.

There was the warmth of the bakery here. The halls were floored with rubber parquet. You couldn’t make a noise if you wanted to. Music played in hidden throats somewhere. Not music of death at all, but music of life and the way the sun lived inside the Incinerator; or the sun’s brother, anyway. You could hear the flame floating inside the heavy brick wall.

William Lantry descended a ramp. Behind him he heard a whisper and turned in time to see a beetle stop before the entrance way. A bell rang. The music, as if at a signal, rose to ecstatic heights. There was joy in it.

From the beetle, which opened from the rear, some attendants stepped carrying a golden box. It was six feet long and there were sun symbols on it. From another beetle the relatives of the man in the box stepped and followed as the attendants took the golden box down a ramp to a kind of altar.
