“Here.” He made adjustments on the machine that had just finished cutting the river bed in the rock floor of the valley. He lifted the smooth snout of the gun, pressed the lever, left it down. A gout of fire shot toward the cliffs. He fingered the range control, focused the flame end three miles from its source. Done. He turned to Lyte. “But I don’t understand,” she said.

He opened the airlock door. “It’s bitter cold out, and half an hour yet till dawn. If I run parallel to the flame from the machine, close enough to it, there’ll not be much heat but enough to sustain life, anyway.”
“It doesn’t sound safe,” Lyte protested.
“Nothing does, on this world.” He moved forward. “I’ll have a half hour start. That should be enough to reach the cliffs.”
“But if the machine should fail while you’re still running near its beam?”
“Let’s not think of that,” he said.

A moment later he was outside. He staggered as if kicked in the stomach. His heart almost exploded in him. The environment of his world forced him into swift living again. He felt his pulse rise, kicking through his veins.
The night was cold as death. The heat ray from the ship sliced across the valley, humming, solid and warm. He moved next to it, very close. One misstep in his running and⁠—
“I’ll be back,” he called to Lyte.
He and the ray of light went together.
In the early morning the peoples in the caves saw the long finger of orange incandescence and the weird whitish apparition floating, running along beside it. There was muttering and superstition.

So when Sim finally reached the cliffs of his childhood he saw alien peoples swarming there. There were no familiar faces. Then he realized how foolish it was to expect familiar faces. One of the older men glared down at him. “Who’re you?” he shouted. “Are you from the enemy cliff? What’s your name?”
“I am Sim, the son of Sim!”
“Sim!”
An old woman shrieked from the cliff above him. She came hobbling down the stone pathway. “Sim, Sim, it is you!”
He looked at her, frankly bewildered. “But I don’t know you,” he murmured.
“Sim, don’t you recognize me? Oh, Sim, it’s me! Dark!”
“Dark!”
He felt sick at his stomach. She fell into his arms. This old, trembling woman with the half-blind eyes, his sister.

Another face appeared above. That of an old man. A cruel, bitter face. It looked down at Sim and snarled. “Drive him away!” cried the old man. “He comes from the cliff of the enemy. He’s lived there! He’s still young! Those who go there can never come back among us. Disloyal beast!” And a rock hurtled down.
Sim leaped aside, pulling the old woman with him.
A roar came from the people. They ran toward Sim, shaking their fists. “Kill him, kill him!” raved the old man, and Sim did not know who he was.
“Stop!” Sim held out his hands. “I come from the ship!”
“The ship?” The people slowed. Dark clung to him, looking up into his young face, puzzling over its smoothness.
“Kill him, kill him, kill him!” croaked the old man, and picked up another rock.
“I offer you ten days, twenty days, thirty more days of life!”
The people stopped. Their mouths hung open. Their eyes were incredulous.
“Thirty days?” It was repeated again and again. “How?”
“Come back to the ship with me. Inside it, one can live forever!”
The old man lifted high a rock, then, choking, fell forward in an apoplectic fit, and tumbled down the rocks to lie at Sim’s feet.
Sim bent to peer at the ancient one, at the bleary, dead eyes, the loose, sneering lips, the crumpled, quiet body.
“Chion!”
“Yes,” said Dark behind him, in a croaking, strange voice. “Your enemy. Chion.”

That night a thousand warriors started for the ship as if going to war. The water ran in the new channel. Five hundred of them were drowned or lost behind in the cold. The others, with Sim, got through to the ship.
Lyte awaited them, and threw wide the metal door.
The weeks passed. Generations lived and died in the cliffs, while the five hundred workers labored over the ship, learning its functions and its parts.
On the last day they disbanded. Each ran to his station. Now there was a destiny of travel who still remained behind.
Sim touched the control plates under his fingers.

Lyte, rubbing her eyes, came and sat on the floor next to him, resting her head against his knee, drowsily. “I had a dream,” she said, looking off at something far away. “I dreamed I lived in caves in a cliff on a cold-hot planet where people grew old and died in eight days and were burnt.”
“What an impossible dream,” said Sim. “People couldn’t possibly live in such a nightmare. Forget it. You’re awake now.”
He touched the plates gently. The ship rose and moved into space. Sim was right. The nightmare was over at last.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The premise is a single bold image. On a planet next to the sun, where the nights burn with cold and the days are like torches of fire, people live exactly eight days. The story opens with a baby, Sim, who is born in a cave and understands everything almost at once. In his first hour he sees the elders around him melting like wax as they die, and his own father, half mad with age, trying to kill him with a stone knife because he thinks it is kinder than letting him live such a short, brutal life. Sim's mother stops him. In that opening Bradbury establishes the central tension: a child who can think faster than he can live, and parents who have already given up.

The next scenes follow Sim through his whole life in a rush. On his first morning there is an avalanche. By nightfall there are funerals. He learns that the people live in the cliffs to escape the deadly sun and the killing ice of night, and that their ancestors came in ships, metal seeds that crashed long ago. One ship, undamaged, still sits on a distant mountain. The Scientists, a small group of the community's best minds, believe that if anyone can reach the ship, its machinery might hold the key to a longer life. But eight days is too short to cross the valley, and the Scientists are dismissed by most as fools. Meanwhile the warriors, led by the rival Chion, fight a war over cliffs whose minerals might add three days to a life. Sim, who is drawn to the girl Lyte, joins the war, almost dies, wins a duel against a champion in the burning sun, and then, with Lyte, makes a desperate run for the ship across rain, river and cold.

The meaning of the run is the heart of the story. The ship works, but in an unexpected way: inside it time passes more slowly, and Sim and Lyte recover and discover that days pass for them while, outside, generations die. That is the story's big idea. The community that fought over three extra days could have had a whole life, if they had only believed in the dream. When Sim returns, he finds that his own sister is an old woman and that the people do not know him. They want to kill him. He offers them more days, and when he promises that inside the ship one might live forever, they follow.

The ending makes a quiet, ironic point. After the generations have worked to repair the ship, Lyte dreams of a terrible planet where people lived eight days and were burned. Sim tells her it is an impossible dream. They have forgotten. It is a fable about how escaping a nightmare can mean forgetting the people who made the escape possible.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
This is an ambitious and often thrilling story with a first-rate idea, but it is also uneven, and it is worth taking both sides seriously.

The best part is the conception. A short life is an old theme in literature, but here it becomes an engine for story. Because every stage of Sim's life is compressed into hours, Bradbury can do things few writers can, such as showing childhood, adolescence, love, ambition and old age in a single short narrative, and the pace of the telling matches the pace of the life. The writing is propulsive, with a pounding rhythm of short, urgent sentences, and the sense of a clock ticking down is built into every page. The detail of the people living in cliffs, hiding from sun and ice, gives the world a vivid, almost mythical quality, and the images, such as the sun plunging into the valley like molten lava or the funerals in which the dead are laid out for the sun to cremate, are memorable. The duel in the burning heat is a fine set piece, as Sim wins not by skill alone but by outlasting an opponent in the sun's test, and the run across the valley in the storm has real urgency.

The main idea of the ship, in which time runs more slowly, is also clever and gives the ending its sting. The moment when Sim wakes inside it and watches Lyte grow younger instead of older, and the temptation to stay inside while others die, gives the story real moral weight.

The weaknesses are of two kinds. The first is the science. The planet, the eight-day lifespan, the babies who think and talk almost from birth, and the ship that slows aging are all accepted on faith, and some of the story's mechanics, such as how a newborn can understand language and customs in an hour, are explained only by the vague word of accelerated impressions. A reader who wants the pieces to fit will be left with questions, such as why a species so short-lived could build and repair complex machines, or how an entire war and a scientific tradition could occur in a few days of life.

The second is the writing. The prose is sometimes overwrought, full of exclamation marks and breathless declarations, and a lot of emotional states are described in abstractions. The villain, Chion, is a thin figure who exists mostly to threaten, and the romance with Lyte is conventional, with Lyte supplying encouragement and rescue in familiar ways. The final section, which covers generations in a few paragraphs, feels rushed, as though Bradbury were as short of time as his characters.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The story's influence is modest and mostly through Bradbury himself. It was not a landmark in the way that The Martian Chronicles was, and it is not widely taught. But it has had a long life in his work, and some of its ideas belong to a larger conversation about time.

It first appeared in Planet Stories in the fall of 1946, in the pulp magazine's usual mixture of adventure and wonder. Planet Stories specialized in colorful tales of other planets, and many of its writers, like Leigh Brackett, were known for romantic, vividly imagined worlds. Bradbury, who by this time was selling regularly to the pulps, brought to this market a poetic intensity that set his work apart. Later it was retitled Frost and Fire, and under that name it became the opening story of R Is for Rocket in 1962, a collection of stories aimed at younger readers. That placement is telling. It shows that Bradbury considered the story strong enough to open a book, and it introduced a generation of young readers to his work.

In the larger world, the story gave expression to an idea that would recur in science fiction: that the experience of time is not fixed, and that a society's whole outlook can be shaped by how long its members live. Writers have explored similar ideas in many forms. Brian Aldiss's Hothouse, in 1962, imagines a distant Earth with a scorching sun and a lush, dangerous ecology, and the question of what lives, short or long, mean in a hostile place appears again and again in later fiction. The notion that a ship can be a refuge where time slows, with the dilation of time of relativity, was also developed in much later science fiction, which would use the effect in a more rigorously scientific way.

The story also contributed to the picture of Bradbury as a writer interested in human limits, in how we face death and how we choose what to do with limited time. This is the theme underlying works like The Martian Chronicles, which looks at a whole civilization's passing, and the later novel Something Wicked This Way Comes, which looks at the fear of aging. In that sense, Frost and Fire is an early and compact version of what he returned to again and again.

It is also used in the classroom, especially in the younger grades, where its central metaphor of compressed life is easy to grasp. Teachers can use it to prompt discussion about how we value time, and it has found a modest second life among younger readers.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Because this is a lesser-known story, there is no long list of famous reviews. What I can describe is what readers have tended to enjoy in it, and why it has stayed in print for so long.

Perhaps the most common source of delight is the central image of a person living an entire life in eight days. Many readers have said, in one way or another, that it makes them think of their own lives. The story compresses everything into a fable that is easy to take in at one sitting: birth, fear, family, love, ambition and death. By making the span so short, it forces the reader to see how much we do in what is, in cosmic terms, a very short time. The opening is especially striking, with a baby born into a cave and suddenly aware of the cruelty of his world. Readers often remember that first scene, the father with the knife and the mother who beats him back, as one of the most powerful in Bradbury's early work.

A second appeal is the speed and drive. The story moves like a chase, and each section brings a new danger, a new rule of the world and a new ambition. The avalanche, the funeral on the hill, the war, the duel in the sun, the run through the storm: these are the kind of vivid episodes that adventure readers love, and Bradbury's imagery gives each of them a physical, sensory force. The sun that plunges into the valley, the cliffs that groan and the river that cuts a new bed each night give the world a mythic feel.

A third appeal is the love story. Sim and Lyte have only days, and the story plays on that urgency. When Sim, in the middle of battle, regrets that he never cupped her mouth with his own, the line hits with the force of real loss. Readers often respond to the combination of tenderness and haste.

A fourth is the ending. The ship, the slowed time, and the final ironic forgetting make for a satisfying twist. Readers who like their science fiction with a moral edge enjoy that the victory is bittersweet. The people escape, but they do so by leaving behind the memory of what they suffered, and there is something poignant in Lyte's half-remembered dream. It is the kind of ending that makes you want to go back and read the beginning again.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Again, I will be cautious. This is not a story that has attracted a large body of formal criticism, so there are no famous reviews or detailed critical debates to cite. The following are the sorts of objections that thoughtful readers have raised or would reasonably raise, many of them common to Bradbury's pulp-era science fiction.

The most obvious is the scientific logic. Bradbury was never a hard science fiction writer, and in this story the physics and biology are fanciful. A planet close enough to the sun to scorch by day and freeze by night is hard to reconcile with real planetary science, and a human lifespan of eight days is, by any biological standard, impossible. The idea that newborn babies can speak, reason and feel complex emotions within an hour is a poetic device, not a scientific one. Readers who prefer their science rigorous may find these elements hard to accept, and the story does not make much effort to justify them. The mechanism of the ship, which slows time, is also vague. Why should a ship's interior slow aging, and why would the ship's makers have designed it that way? The story's answer is essentially a shrug.

The second is the writing. Bradbury's early prose can be feverish, and in this story it often tips over into melodrama. The use of exclamation points, the repeated cries and the somewhat stilted dialogue can feel overdone. The characters tend toward types: the cynical sister, the brutish rival, the loyal sweetheart, the wise old scientist. The villain, Chion, is little more than an obstacle, and the portrayal of Lyte, though sympathetic, is conventional, as she mostly supports the hero and is rescued in return.

The third is structural. The story covers a vast amount of ground in a small space, and the last third, in which Sim returns, convinces the people and organizes the building of the ship's machinery, passes in a few brisk paragraphs. Some readers feel that the biggest idea, the passage of generations, deserved more room, and that the quick ending cheats the reader of the full effect.

There is also the moral question. The story presents a world in which war is fought over a few extra days of life, and its answer, the ship, seems to be a technological fix, without much consideration of what happens to the culture left behind. This is less a flaw than a limit of the form. It is a pulp fable, and it plays by pulp rules.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
The Creatures That Time Forgot, or Frost and Fire as it later became, sits in the tradition of the planetary romance and the survival fable, and it shows Bradbury fitting his lyrical voice into the shape of pulp adventure.

The planetary romance was the signature form of Planet Stories: a story set on another world, usually hot, strange and dangerous, featuring heroic figures and a quest. Writers like Leigh Brackett and Edmond Hamilton made it a staple of the magazines. Bradbury's story follows the pattern, with its alien environment, its tribal warfare and its quest to reach a distant goal, but it twists it by making the strangeness a matter of time. The hostile planet is hostile not only in its climate but in its clock.

It also belongs to an old tradition of stories about the lost colony. A group of humans, stranded on a hostile world, forget their origins and live as primitives, while a few cling to the memory of what they once were. Robert Heinlein's Orphans of the Sky, published in book form in 1963 from magazine stories of 1941, tells of a generation ship whose people have forgotten that they are on a ship at all, and Bradbury's story shares that sense of a technological inheritance mistaken for myth. The Scientists in Bradbury's tale, who preserve fragments of knowledge in the face of general scorn, are echoes of the same figure, the keeper of a forgotten truth.

The theme of time has deeper roots. Poets and philosophers have long wondered what to do with a limited span of life, from the biblical Ecclesiastes to the carpe diem poets of the Renaissance. The story is a speeded-up version of the same meditation, and its ironic ending, in which the survivors forget the suffering that made their escape possible, recalls tragic myths in which gifts come at a cost. Later science fiction would explore the same idea with more technical detail, using time dilation, a consequence of relativity, to create stories of travelers who return to find their world changed.

Why read it today? Because it is short, vivid and original, and because it makes a familiar thought, that life is brief, feel sharp again. It also provides a glimpse of the young Bradbury, working within the pulp mold but already pushing against it, with a poet's eye for images and a fabulist's love of the big idea. It is not his best work, but it is a clear and exciting example of what happens when a lyrical writer takes up a pulp premise and runs with it.

stories.title: Beyond Lies the Wub
stories.author: Philip K. Dick
stories.epigraph: “The slovenly wub might well have said: Many men talk like philosophers and live like fools.”
stories.keyContext: In 1952, a twenty-three-year-old Californian named Philip K. Dick saw this story, his first professional publication, printed in the pulp magazine Planet Stories. He was writing fast, for pennies a word, but he was already doing something stranger than most of his rivals. The setup is standard space adventure: a freighter crew loads up with Martian animals and picks up one extra, a huge, sleepy, pig-like creature called a wub. Then the wub starts talking. Dick would spend the rest of his career asking what makes someone a real person, what counts as alive, and who gets to decide, and all three questions are already here, wrapped in a joke about dinner. The story also belongs to the early Cold War, an age of atomic fear and suspicion of anything unfamiliar. Listen for how it plays appetite against philosophy, and for how its last few lines turn the whole thing around. It is short, funny, and quietly unsettling.
paragraphs: The slovenly wub might well have said: Many men talk like philosophers and live like fools.
They had almost finished with the loading. Outside stood the Optus, his arms folded, his face sunk in gloom. Captain Franco walked leisurely down the gangplank, grinning.
“What’s the matter?” he said. “You’re getting paid for all this.”
The Optus said nothing. He turned away, collecting his robes. The Captain put his boot on the hem of the robe.
“Just a minute. Don’t go off. I’m not finished.”
“Oh?” The Optus turned with dignity. “I am going back to the village.” He looked toward the animals and birds being driven up the gangplank into the spaceship. “I must organize new hunts.”
Franco lit a cigarette. “Why not? You people can go out into the veldt and track it all down again. But when we run out halfway between Mars and Earth⁠—”
The Optus went off, wordless. Franco joined the first mate at the bottom of the gangplank.
“How’s it coming?” he said. He looked at his watch. “We got a good bargain here.”
The mate glanced at him sourly. “How do you explain that?”
“What’s the matter with you? We need it more than they do.”

“I’ll see you later, Captain.” The mate threaded his way up the plank, between the long-legged Martian go-birds, into the ship. Franco watched him disappear. He was just starting up after him, up the plank toward the port, when he saw it.
“My God!” He stood staring, his hands on his hips. Peterson was walking along the path, his face red, leading it by a string.
“I’m sorry, Captain,” he said, tugging at the string. Franco walked toward him.
“What is it?”
The wub stood sagging, its great body settling slowly. It was sitting down, its eyes half shut. A few flies buzzed about its flank, and it switched its tail.
It sat. There was silence.
“It’s a wub,” Peterson said. “I got it from a native for fifty cents. He said it was a very unusual animal. Very respected.”
“This?” Franco poked the great sloping side of the wub. “It’s a pig! A huge dirty pig!”
“Yes sir, it’s a pig. The natives call it a wub.”
“A huge pig. It must weigh four hundred pounds.” Franco grabbed a tuft of the rough hair. The wub gasped. Its eyes opened, small and moist. Then its great mouth twitched.
A tear rolled down the wub’s cheek and splashed on the floor.
“Maybe it’s good to eat,” Peterson said nervously.
“We’ll soon find out,” Franco said.

The wub survived the takeoff, sound asleep in the hold of the ship. When they were out in space and everything was running smoothly, Captain Franco bade his men fetch the wub upstairs so that he might perceive what manner of beast it was.
The wub grunted and wheezed, squeezing up the passageway.
“Come on,” Jones grated, pulling at the rope. The wub twisted, rubbing its skin off on the smooth chrome walls. It burst into the anteroom, tumbling down in a heap. The men leaped up.
“Good Lord,” French said. “What is it?”
“Peterson says it’s a wub,” Jones said. “It belongs to him.” He kicked at the wub. The wub stood up unsteadily, panting.
“What’s the matter with it?” French came over. “Is it going to be sick?”
They watched. The wub rolled its eyes mournfully. It gazed around at the men.
“I think it’s thirsty,” Peterson said. He went to get some water. French shook his head.
“No wonder we had so much trouble taking off. I had to reset all my ballast calculations.”
Peterson came back with the water. The wub began to lap gratefully, splashing the men.
Captain Franco appeared at the door.
“Let’s have a look at it.” He advanced, squinting critically. “You got this for fifty cents?”

“Yes, sir,” Peterson said. “It eats almost anything. I fed it on grain and it liked that. And then potatoes, and mash, and scraps from the table, and milk. It seems to enjoy eating. After it eats it lies down and goes to sleep.”

“I see,” Captain Franco said. “Now, as to its taste. That’s the real question. I doubt if there’s much point in fattening it up any more. It seems fat enough to me already. Where’s the cook? I want him here. I want to find out⁠—”
The wub stopped lapping and looked up at the Captain.
“Really, Captain,” the wub said. “I suggest we talk of other matters.”
The room was silent.
“What was that?” Franco said. “Just now.”
“The wub, sir,” Peterson said. “It spoke.”
They all looked at the wub.
“What did it say? What did it say?”
“It suggested we talk about other things.”
Franco walked toward the wub. He went all around it, examining it from every side. Then he came back over and stood with the men.
“I wonder if there’s a native inside it,” he said thoughtfully. “Maybe we should open it up and have a look.”
“Oh, goodness!” the wub cried. “Is that all you people can think of, killing and cutting?”
Franco clenched his fists. “Come out of there! Whoever you are, come out!”
Nothing stirred. The men stood together, their faces blank, staring at the wub. The wub swished its tail. It belched suddenly.
“I beg your pardon,” the wub said.
“I don’t think there’s anyone in there,” Jones said in a low voice. They all looked at each other.
The cook came in.
“You wanted me, Captain?” he said. “What’s this thing?”
“This is a wub,” Franco said. “It’s to be eaten. Will you measure it and figure out⁠—”
“I think we should have a talk,” the wub said. “I’d like to discuss this with you, Captain, if I might. I can see that you and I do not agree on some basic issues.”
The Captain took a long time to answer. The wub waited good-naturedly, licking the water from its jowls.
“Come into my office,” the Captain said at last. He turned and walked out of the room. The wub rose and padded after him. The men watched it go out. They heard it climbing the stairs.
“I wonder what the outcome will be,” the cook said. “Well, I’ll be in the kitchen. Let me know as soon as you hear.”
“Sure,” Jones said. “Sure.”
The wub eased itself down in the corner with a sigh. “You must forgive me,” it said. “I’m afraid I’m addicted to various forms of relaxation. When one is as large as I⁠—”
The Captain nodded impatiently. He sat down at his desk and folded his hands.
“All right,” he said. “Let’s get started. You’re a wub? Is that correct?”
The wub shrugged. “I suppose so. That’s what they call us, the natives, I mean. We have our own term.”
“And you speak English? You’ve been in contact with Earthmen before?”
“No.”
“Then how do you do it?”
“Speak English? Am I speaking English? I’m not conscious of speaking anything in particular. I examined your mind⁠—”
“My mind?”
“I studied the contents, especially the semantic warehouse, as I refer to it⁠—”
“I see,” the Captain said. “Telepathy. Of course.”

“We are a very old race,” the wub said. “Very old and very ponderous. It is difficult for us to move around. You can appreciate that anything so slow and heavy would be at the mercy of more agile forms of life. There was no use in our relying on physical defenses. How could we win? Too heavy to run, too soft to fight, too good-natured to hunt for game⁠—”
“How do you live?”
“Plants. Vegetables. We can eat almost anything. We’re very catholic. Tolerant, eclectic, catholic. We live and let live. That’s how we’ve gotten along.”
The wub eyed the Captain.

“And that’s why I so violently objected to this business about having me boiled. I could see the image in your mind⁠—most of me in the frozen food locker, some of me in the kettle, a bit for your pet cat⁠—”
“So you read minds?” the Captain said. “How interesting. Anything else? I mean, what else can you do along those lines?”

“A few odds and ends,” the wub said absently, staring around the room. “A nice apartment you have here, Captain. You keep it quite neat. I respect life-forms that are tidy. Some Martian birds are quite tidy. They throw things out of their nests and sweep them⁠—”
“Indeed.” The Captain nodded. “But to get back to the problem⁠—”

“Quite so. You spoke of dining on me. The taste, I am told, is good. A little fatty, but tender. But how can any lasting contact be established between your people and mine if you resort to such barbaric attitudes? Eat me? Rather you should discuss questions with me, philosophy, the arts⁠—”
The Captain stood up. “Philosophy. It might interest you to know that we will be hard put to find something to eat for the next month. An unfortunate spoilage⁠—”

“I know.” The wub nodded. “But wouldn’t it be more in accord with your principles of democracy if we all drew straws, or something along that line? After all, democracy is to protect the minority from just such infringements. Now, if each of us casts one vote⁠—”
The Captain walked to the door.
“Nuts to you,” he said. He opened the door. He opened his mouth.
He stood frozen, his mouth wide, his eyes staring, his fingers still on the knob.
The wub watched him. Presently it padded out of the room, edging past the Captain. It went down the hall, deep in meditation.
The room was quiet.
“So you see,” the wub said, “we have a common myth. Your mind contains many familiar myth symbols. Ishtar, Odysseus⁠—”
Peterson sat silently, staring at the floor. He shifted in his chair.
“Go on,” he said. “Please go on.”

“I find in your Odysseus a figure common to the mythology of most self-conscious races. As I interpret it, Odysseus wanders as an individual, aware of himself as such. This is the idea of separation, of separation from family and country. The process of individuation.”
“But Odysseus returns to his home.” Peterson looked out the port window, at the stars, endless stars, burning intently in the empty universe. “Finally he goes home.”
“As must all creatures. The moment of separation is a temporary period, a brief journey of the soul. It begins, it ends. The wanderer returns to land and race.⁠ ⁠…”
The door opened. The wub stopped, turning its great head.
Captain Franco came into the room, the men behind him. They hesitated at the door.
“Are you all right?” French said.
“Do you mean me?” Peterson said, surprised. “Why me?”
Franco lowered his gun. “Come over here,” he said to Peterson. “Get up and come here.”
There was silence.
“Go ahead,” the wub said. “It doesn’t matter.”
Peterson stood up. “What for?”
“It’s an order.”
Peterson walked to the door. French caught his arm.
“What’s going on?” Peterson wrenched loose. “What’s the matter with you?”
Captain Franco moved toward the wub. The wub looked up from where it lay in the corner, pressed against the wall.
“It is interesting,” the wub said, “that you are obsessed with the idea of eating me. I wonder why.”
“Get up,” Franco said.
“If you wish.” The wub rose, grunting. “Be patient. It is difficult for me.” It stood, gasping, its tongue lolling foolishly.
“Shoot it now,” French said.
“For God’s sake!” Peterson exclaimed. Jones turned to him quickly, his eyes gray with fear.
“You didn’t see him⁠—like a statue, standing there, his mouth open. If we hadn’t come down, he’d still be there.”
“Who? The Captain?” Peterson stared around. “But he’s all right now.”
They looked at the wub, standing in the middle of the room, its great chest rising and falling.
“Come on,” Franco said. “Out of the way.”
The men pulled aside toward the door.

“You are quite afraid, aren’t you?” the wub said. “Have I done anything to you? I am against the idea of hurting. All I have done is try to protect myself. Can you expect me to rush eagerly to my death? I am a sensible being like yourselves. I was curious to see your ship, learn about you. I suggested to the native⁠—”
The gun jerked.
“See,” Franco said. “I thought so.”
The wub settled down, panting. It put its paw out, pulling its tail around it.

“It is very warm,” the wub said. “I understand that we are close to the jets. Atomic power. You have done many wonderful things with it⁠—technically. Apparently, your scientific hierarchy is not equipped to solve moral, ethical⁠—”
Franco turned to the men, crowding behind him, wide-eyed, silent.
“I’ll do it. You can watch.”
French nodded. “Try to hit the brain. It’s no good for eating. Don’t hit the chest. If the rib cage shatters, we’ll have to pick bones out.”
“Listen,” Peterson said, licking his lips. “Has it done anything? What harm has it done? I’m asking you. And anyhow, it’s still mine. You have no right to shoot it. It doesn’t belong to you.”
Franco raised his gun.
“I’m going out,” Jones said, his face white and sick. “I don’t want to see it.”
“Me, too,” French said. The men straggled out, murmuring. Peterson lingered at the door.
“It was talking to me about myths,” he said. “It wouldn’t hurt anyone.”
He went outside.
Franco walked toward the wub. The wub looked up slowly. It swallowed.
“A very foolish thing,” it said. “I am sorry that you want to do it. There was a parable that your Saviour related⁠—”
It stopped, staring at the gun.
“Can you look me in the eye and do it?” the wub said. “Can you do that?”
The Captain gazed down. “I can look you in the eye,” he said. “Back on the farm we had hogs, dirty razorback hogs. I can do it.”
Staring down at the wub, into the gleaming, moist eyes, he pressed the trigger.
The taste was excellent.
They sat glumly around the table, some of them hardly eating at all. The only one who seemed to be enjoying himself was Captain Franco.
“More?” he said, looking around. “More? And some wine, perhaps.”
“Not me,” French said. “I think I’ll go back to the chart room.”
“Me, too.” Jones stood up, pushing his chair back. “I’ll see you later.”
The Captain watched them go. Some of the others excused themselves.
“What do you suppose the matter is?” the Captain said. He turned to Peterson. Peterson sat staring down at his plate, at the potatoes, the green peas, and at the thick slab of tender, warm meat.
He opened his mouth. No sound came.
The Captain put his hand on Peterson’s shoulder.

“It is only organic matter, now,” he said. “The life essence is gone.” He ate, spooning up the gravy with some bread. “I, myself, love to eat. It is one of the greatest things that a living creature can enjoy. Eating, resting, meditation, discussing things.”
Peterson nodded. Two more men got up and went out. The Captain drank some water and sighed.

“Well,” he said. “I must say that this was a very enjoyable meal. All the reports I had heard were quite true⁠—the taste of wub. Very fine. But I was prevented from enjoying this pleasure in times past.”
He dabbed at his lips with his napkin and leaned back in his chair. Peterson stared dejectedly at the table.
The Captain watched him intently. He leaned over.
“Come, come,” he said. “Cheer up! Let’s discuss things.”
He smiled.
“As I was saying before I was interrupted, the role of Odysseus in the myths⁠—”
Peterson jerked up, staring.
“To go on,” the Captain said. “Odysseus, as I understand him⁠—”

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
On its surface, this is a very simple tale. A spaceship has been loading up on a Martian trading stop, and a crewman named Peterson buys a wub from a native for fifty cents. It is a four-hundred-pound pig-like animal that sags, sleeps, and eats almost anything. The ship's captain, Franco, looks at it and sees one thing: meat. The crew is short on food, and the wub looks fat enough. Then the wub speaks, politely suggesting that they talk about other matters, and the story becomes a debate about whether you can eat something that can argue with you.

The debate is lopsided, and that is the point. The wub is gentle, patient, and wise. It explains that its people are old and ponderous, too heavy to run and too soft to fight, so they survived by being tolerant. It talks about democracy and suggests the crew draw straws instead of simply picking the victim. It talks about myth, and especially about the Odyssey, reading Odysseus as a figure who stands for separation and return, the individual who wanders and finally goes home. Peterson, the one crewman who listens, is plainly moved. Franco, meanwhile, gets more irritated with every reasonable sentence. His answer to philosophy is a gun. "Back on the farm we had hogs, dirty razorback hogs. I can do it." He looks the wub in the eye and shoots it.

The first layer, then, is a moral fable about cruelty and appetite. Franco cannot afford to see the wub as a person, because a person would be murder and a pig would be dinner. He picks the label that lets him do what he already wants to do. Notice how often the wub notes this itself: it wonders aloud why Franco is so obsessed with eating it.

The second layer is the ending, which is the cleverest part. At dinner the crew can barely eat. Only the Captain enjoys himself. He announces that the meat is only organic matter now, that the life essence is gone, and then he leans toward Peterson and begins, "As I was saying before I was interrupted, the role of Odysseus in the myths." Franco is now talking in the wub's voice, with the wub's ideas. Peterson jerks up and stares, and the story ends.

What exactly happened is left open. Perhaps the wub's mind survived death and moved into the man who ate its body. Perhaps it took over earlier, when Franco stood frozen with his mouth open at his office door. Either way, the person Franco killed has not been removed from the world. He has been swallowed and is still talking. The deepest joke is that the captain who insisted the wub was nothing but food has become, quite literally, what he ate.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
As craft, this is a remarkably confident piece for a first publication, and it is worth being specific about why. The strongest quality is tone. Dick keeps the surface pulpy, with a gruff captain, a ship, and a hold full of animals, and then lets an absurdly articulate pig take over the conversation. The comedy depends on the wub's mildness. It belches and says "I beg your pardon." It admits it is addicted to relaxation. It compliments the captain on how tidy his office is. A creature this courteous makes the humans look worse with each exchange, and Dick never has to underline it.

The structure is also well made. The story moves in clean steps: the discovery, the first conversation, the Captain's paralysis, the second conversation with Peterson, the execution, the dinner, the last line. It is short and nothing is wasted. The ending lands because everything before it has set up the wub's habit of drifting toward Odysseus whenever it is left alone with a listener. When Franco picks up that thread, the reader hears it before Peterson does.

There are weaknesses, and they should be named. The characters are thin. Franco is a blustering brute with a farm-boy past, and the crew members French and Jones are barely distinguishable from each other. Peterson is mainly a conscience with a name. That is partly the nature of the form, since a pulp magazine story of a few thousand words has little room for portraiture, but it means the story works more as a fable than as a drama.

The science is also loose in a way modern readers may find distracting. Telepathy is invoked without explanation. The wub's ability to freeze the Captain with a look is never accounted for, and the final possession happens by magic, not by any mechanism. Dick clearly did not care, and he was right not to, because the story is about ideas and not machinery. Still, the wub's philosophizing can run a little neat. Its remarks about democracy protecting the minority and its ethical complaints about atomic power are slightly on the nose, as if the author were making sure the reader got the message. Dick is subtler when the wub just talks about Odysseus.

One more point of balance: the story is sometimes praised for its horror, but it is hardly frightening. It is closer to a dark joke with a shudder at the end. That is part of its charm, and also a limit. The twist works as a punchline more than as an emotional blow, and the death of the wub, which should hurt, is handled quickly and slightly coldly. For all that, it is an unusually good example of how much a skilled writer can fit into a tiny box.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
Within Dick's career, this story matters first of all as a beginning. It was his first professional publication, in Planet Stories in July 1952, at the start of an astonishing burst of short fiction. Over the next few years he wrote and sold a huge number of stories, often for a penny or two a word, and this one shows nearly all the themes he would return to for the rest of his life. The idea that identity can be hijacked, that a mind may inhabit the wrong body, that the line between human and not human is unstable, and that authority figures often confuse their own appetites with principle: all of these run through his later novels, from the paranoid worlds of the 1960s to the late religious experiments.

The story's influence has been quieter than that of Dick's famous novels, which is natural. Nobody films a short, odd pulp story the way they film a full-length book. But it has been reprinted in many collections of his stories and remains one of his best-known early pieces. It is often the story people are handed when they want to see what Dick was like before the great novels. Teachers of science fiction use it as an example of the genre doing philosophy, because it is easy to read, funny, and short enough to discuss in a single class.

Its ideas have also seeped into later popular culture without much credit. The notion of an alien creature that argues for its own life in perfect reasonable language, and so forces its captors to face what they are doing, recurs in many later stories, as does the notion of a visitor who is gentler than the people who capture it. The refusal to say what the possession means, leaving the reader with an uneasy last image, is a technique that later writers of short horror and science fiction have used often.

There is a larger effect that is harder to measure. Dick helped teach science fiction readers to be suspicious of the point of view of the person with the gun. In a great deal of earlier pulp fiction, the human spaceship crew was the hero and the alien was the threat. Here, the humans are the ones with something to be ashamed of, and the alien is a better thinker and a better person. Dick was not the first to do this. But he did it with such good humor that it was easy to take in.

Finally, it fits the mood of its time. Published as the Korean War was grinding on and Americans were worrying about atomic weapons and spies, it asks what a society is willing to destroy simply because it is strange. Readers in the early 1950s did not need that spelled out, and Dick did not spell it out.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
What do readers love about this story? The short answer is the wub. It is one of the most endearing creatures in early science fiction, and much of its appeal is that it is so unheroic. It is fat, tired, and polite. It does not fight back. It does not even try very hard to escape. It simply keeps talking, and the more it talks, the more likable it becomes. Readers feel the injustice of its fate because it is so good-natured. A more dramatic alien would have been easier to dislike and so would have made the captain's choice less shameful.

Many readers also enjoy the humor. Dick has a natural comic ear. The wub's discussion of his own taste, "a little fatty, but tender", and the captain's grunted "Nuts to you" as he opens the door are funny precisely because the characters take themselves so seriously. Franco has a pulp hero's jaw and a pulp hero's lines, and the story quietly lets the air out of him. The exchange where the wub suggests that democracy should protect it from being eaten, and the Captain simply stops listening, is a small gem of satire.

The ending gets its own share of admiration. Readers who encounter the story for the first time often say they felt a jolt at the last line, when Franco begins to speak about Odysseus. It is the kind of ending that makes you go back to the beginning to see how it was done. Dick's contemporaries in the magazines were fond of twist endings, but many of them were mechanical. This one has an emotional logic, because it is built from the wub's character. The creature is a talker, and in the end it talks.

There is also a real affection for the story among people who care about Dick's whole body of work. For them it carries a particular pleasure of recognition. Here is the writer, twenty-three years old and not yet famous, already asking what makes a mind a mind, already worried about the way ordinary people turn other beings into things so as to use them. Readers who know the later novels often describe the story as a seed. It is small, but you can find the whole plant in it.

Finally, a good number of readers simply appreciate its kindness toward the idea of thinking. The wub's greatest enthusiasm is for myth and meaning, not for power. In a magazine full of rayguns and rocket ships, it is a pleasure to meet an alien whose weapon is conversation, and whose idea of a good evening is a long talk about Homer.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
There are not many famous attacks on this story, and it is fair to say so. It was a pulp tale in a pulp magazine, and the kind of detailed contemporary reviewing that a novel might receive was not given to a short piece in Planet Stories. So most of what can be said about its weaknesses comes from later readers and critics looking back at Dick's early work, not from any big public controversy.

The most common criticism of this kind concerns depth. Some readers feel that the story is clever without being truly moving. It has a neat idea and a neat twist, but the characters are sketched rather than felt, and the wub's death does not carry the weight it might. Critics who prefer Dick's novels often say that the early stories are more like jokes with philosophical punchlines than like finished fiction. They find the writing serviceable and the plotting tidy, but they miss the strangeness and personal anguish that fill the later work.

A second line of criticism has to do with the message. The moral is delivered rather heavily, in that the wub itself explains the ethics of the situation: its remarks about democracy, killing, and technology are close to speeches. Some readers feel that a better version would let the actions speak and trust the audience to draw the conclusion. Others point out that a story where the animal is more articulate than every human in the room risks sentimentality. The wub is almost too good, and the crew almost too bad, so that the moral comfort of the reader is never really tested.

There is also a more modern objection that a few readers raise. The story asks us to feel sympathy for the wub because it can talk and reason, and the argument it makes is, in effect, that intelligence makes killing wrong. Some readers have noted that this sits uneasily with the fact that the wub is, at first, just an animal that looks like a pig, and that the story does not ask whether the pig would deserve mercy if it did not speak. The Captain's farm memories of razorback hogs hint at this, but the story does not follow the thought. It might be read as a plea for vegetarianism, or merely as a plea for tolerance, and Dick does not choose.

Finally, a handful of readers find the ending a little too easy. The possession is unexplained and a bit magical, and one can argue that it undercuts the moral of the story, since the wub gets its revenge. If the creature survives anyway, was its killing really a tragedy? Dick seems to want both effects at once, and that is slightly greedy. Whether you find that a flaw or a strength is a matter of taste.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
To place this story, begin with the tradition it comes from. In the late 1940s and early 1950s, American science fiction was mostly written for cheap magazines, and the typical story was about men with ray guns exploring or conquering planets. Planet Stories, where this appeared, was famous for brash adventure. But the genre also had a thoughtful side, represented by writers such as Ray Bradbury, Theodore Sturgeon, and Clifford Simak, who used the alien to talk about what is human. Dick belongs to that second tradition. His wub is a cousin of the gentle Martians and sympathetic visitors found in that kind of story.

Behind them all is an older line of satire, which uses a visitor from elsewhere to expose the absurdity and cruelty of ordinary society. Jonathan Swift, in Gulliver's Travels, did this by sending a man among giants and wise horses. The wise animal who is more rational than the people who capture it is directly in that line, and the wub's ironic manners would not have shocked Swift. There is also a hint of the old fable, where animals talk so that humans may be reminded of their own behavior.

Looking forward, the story points toward the central obsessions of Dick's later work. In novels such as Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, written in the 1960s, the question of whether a being deserves moral treatment depends on whether it has an inner life, and the humans who deny that inner life are often the ones who have lost their own. The idea of identity being taken over, which closes this story, appears again and again in his fiction, in the replacement of humans by imposters or machines. Seen this way, the wub is an early draft of the android: a being that looks like a thing and turns out to be a person.

It can also be compared with other stories that ask who counts as a person. Later fiction about intelligent animals, uploaded minds, and artificial intelligence keeps returning to the same awkward question, and this story is an economical early version. It does not have the scale of a novel, but it has a purity that bigger works sometimes lose.

Why read it today? Partly because it is quick and funny, which makes it an ideal entrance into Dick's world. Partly because the central question has not gone away. We still decide, often with great speed and little thought, which creatures deserve our attention and which are only material, and we still tend to reach for the label that justifies what we already wanted to do. Dick saw that very early, in a story about a pig that would not stop talking. It is worth the ten minutes it takes.

stories.title: The Eyes Have It
stories.author: Philip K. Dick
stories.epigraph: “… his eyes slowly roved about the room.”
stories.keyContext: Here is one of the shortest and silliest pieces Philip K. Dick ever published, and one of the most reprinted. It appeared in a pulp magazine called Science Fiction Stories in 1953, when Dick was in his mid-twenties and turning out stories at a furious pace in Berkeley, California. It is a joke, and it is built on a single trick. A man finds a paperback novel on a bus and reads it with total literal-mindedness, so that every ordinary figure of speech becomes proof of a secret alien invasion. The date matters. Early-1950s America was thick with stories and rumors about hidden infiltrators, from Martians to communists, and the narrator is a perfect portrait of the fearful mind that sees conspiracy everywhere. Listen to how the language itself becomes the villain, and to how a story this small can poke fun at paranoia, at bureaucracy, and at the way science fiction itself was written. And watch for the last line.
paragraphs: It was quite by accident I discovered this incredible invasion of Earth by lifeforms from another planet. As yet, I haven’t done anything about it; I can’t think of anything to do. I wrote to the Government, and they sent back a pamphlet on the repair and maintenance of frame houses. Anyhow, the whole thing is known; I’m not the first to discover it. Maybe it’s even under control.

I was sitting in my easy-chair, idly turning the pages of a paperbacked book someone had left on the bus, when I came across the reference that first put me on the trail. For a moment I didn’t respond. It took some time for the full import to sink in. After I’d comprehended, it seemed odd I hadn’t noticed it right away.

The reference was clearly to a nonhuman species of incredible properties, not indigenous to Earth. A species, I hasten to point out, customarily masquerading as ordinary human beings. Their disguise, however, became transparent in the face of the following observations by the author. It was at once obvious the author knew everything. Knew everything⁠—and was taking it in his stride. The line (and I tremble remembering it even now) read:
… his eyes slowly roved about the room.

Vague chills assailed me. I tried to picture the eyes. Did they roll like dimes? The passage indicated not; they seemed to move through the air, not over the surface. Rather rapidly, apparently. No one in the story was surprised. That’s what tipped me off. No sign of amazement at such an outrageous thing. Later the matter was amplified.
… his eyes moved from person to person.

There it was in a nutshell. The eyes had clearly come apart from the rest of him and were on their own. My heart pounded and my breath choked in my windpipe. I had stumbled on an accidental mention of a totally unfamiliar race. Obviously non-Terrestrial. Yet, to the characters in the book, it was perfectly natural⁠—which suggested they belonged to the same species.

And the author? A slow suspicion burned in my mind. The author was taking it rather too easily in his stride. Evidently, he felt this was quite a usual thing. He made absolutely no attempt to conceal this knowledge. The story continued:
… presently his eyes fastened on Julia.

Julia, being a lady, had at least the breeding to feel indignant. She is described as blushing and knitting her brows angrily. At this, I sighed with relief. They weren’t all non-Terrestrials. The narrative continues:
… slowly, calmly, his eyes examined every inch of her.
Great Scott! But here the girl turned and stomped off and the matter ended. I lay back in my chair gasping with horror. My wife and family regarded me in wonder.
“What’s wrong, dear?” my wife asked.

I couldn’t tell her. Knowledge like this was too much for the ordinary run-of-the-mill person. I had to keep it to myself. “Nothing,” I gasped. I leaped up, snatched the book, and hurried out of the room.
In the garage, I continued reading. There was more. Trembling, I read the next revealing passage:
… he put his arm around Julia. Presently she asked him if he would remove his arm. He immediately did so, with a smile.

It’s not said what was done with the arm after the fellow had removed it. Maybe it was left standing upright in the corner. Maybe it was thrown away. I don’t care. In any case, the full meaning was there, staring me right in the face.

Here was a race of creatures capable of removing portions of their anatomy at will. Eyes, arms⁠—and maybe more. Without batting an eyelash. My knowledge of biology came in handy, at this point. Obviously they were simple beings, unicellular, some sort of primitive single-celled things. Beings no more developed than starfish. Starfish can do the same thing, you know.
I read on. And came to this incredible revelation, tossed off coolly by the author without the faintest tremor:
… outside the movie theater we split up. Part of us went inside, part over to the café for dinner.

Binary fission, obviously. Splitting in half and forming two entities. Probably each lower half went to the café, it being farther, and the upper halves to the movies. I read on, hands shaking. I had really stumbled onto something here. My mind reeled as I made out this passage:
… I’m afraid there’s no doubt about it. Poor Bibney has lost his head again.
Which was followed by:
… and Bob says he has utterly no guts.
Yet Bibney got around as well as the next person. The next person, however, was just as strange. He was soon described as:
… totally lacking in brains.
There was no doubt of the thing in the next passage. Julia, whom I had thought to be the one normal person, reveals herself as also being an alien life form, similar to the rest:
… quite deliberately, Julia had given her heart to the young man.

It didn’t relate what the final disposition of the organ was, but I didn’t really care. It was evident Julia had gone right on living in her usual manner, like all the others in the book. Without heart, arms, eyes, brains, viscera, dividing up in two when the occasion demanded. Without a qualm.
… thereupon she gave him her hand.
I sickened. The rascal now had her hand, as well as her heart. I shudder to think what he’s done with them, by this time.
… he took her arm.

Not content to wait, he had to start dismantling her on his own. Flushing crimson, I slammed the book shut and leaped to my feet. But not in time to escape one last reference to those carefree bits of anatomy whose travels had originally thrown me on the track:
… her eyes followed him all the way down the road and across the meadow.

I rushed from the garage and back inside the warm house, as if the accursed things were following me. My wife and children were playing Monopoly in the kitchen. I joined them and played with frantic fervor, brow feverish, teeth chattering.
I had had enough of the thing. I want to hear no more about it. Let them come on. Let them invade Earth. I don’t want to get mixed up in it.
I have absolutely no stomach for it.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The story is a monologue from a man who believes he has discovered an invasion of Earth. He tells us he found a paperback book that someone left on a bus, and that while idly turning the pages he came across a reference that "first put me on the trail." The reference is the sentence "his eyes slowly roved about the room."

The joke is in how he reads it. Ordinary readers know that to say someone's eyes roved is just a way of saying he looked around. The narrator takes it at face value. He pictures the eyes themselves, detached from the head, floating through the air. He notices that nobody in the book seems surprised, and this, he says, "is what tipped me off." The characters must be of the same strange species, and the author must be in on it too.

From that single misreading, he builds an entire theory. "His eyes moved from person to person" proves the eyes are on their own. An arm put around a girl and then "removed" shows that these beings can detach their limbs at will. Someone "lost his head," someone else has "utterly no guts," a third is "totally lacking in brains," and Julia "had given her heart to the young man." The narrator concludes that these creatures are primitive, single-celled things, no more developed than starfish. When the characters say that outside the movie theater "we split up," he decides they reproduce by dividing in two, with the upper halves presumably going to the film and the lower halves to the cafe. Every idiom of ordinary English is turned, line by line, into a clinical observation.

The pleasure is that the reader is always one step ahead. We know what each phrase really means, and we enjoy watching a mind that cannot see it. But there is a second layer. The narrator is not stupid in the usual way. His reasoning is orderly, even scientific in tone. He cites biology and he tracks clues. What is wrong is his starting point, the unshakable belief that something sinister is hidden and that the evidence is staring him in the face. Once you assume that, everything confirms it.

The opening and ending carry the real satire. He wrote to the Government and received a pamphlet on the maintenance of frame houses, which tells us how seriously the authorities treat him. He then says it is possibly "under control" already, a line that shows how readily the paranoid mind accepts that someone else must be in charge. At the end he runs home, joins his family playing Monopoly, and declares that he wants no more to do with it. "I have absolutely no stomach for it." That last sentence is a final pun, and also a final comment on the comedy: the man cannot even end his panic without using the kind of figure of speech that began it.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
As a piece of craft, this is a clever, tightly controlled trick, and the main thing to admire is its discipline. Dick finds one joke and never lets it go. Every example of the narrator's "evidence" is a stock phrase of the sort that fills cheap fiction, and he chooses them with an expert ear: eyes that roved, a heart given away, a head lost, a fellow with no guts. The progression is smart, too. It begins with the most obviously odd one, the roving eyes, builds through arms and splitting in half, and ends on organs that cannot sensibly be given away. The pace is brisk and there is a new twist on nearly every paragraph.

The voice is the second asset. The narrator is pompous and breathless in just the right mixture. He announces that he "hasten[s] to point out" certain details, he says he trembles at the memory of a sentence, he congratulates himself on his knowledge of biology. The staid, scientific diction clashes beautifully with the absurd content. Dick does not wink at us. He lets the narrator be entirely serious, and that is where the comedy comes from.

There are also weaknesses, and a fair assessment has to admit them. The piece is one idea, stretched. After the first several examples the pattern is clear, and a reader may feel the later ones are only repetition with different body parts. Some of the jokes are slightly strained, such as the business about which half of a person goes to the cafe, and the wordplay can feel more like a list than a story. There is no real plot and no character other than the narrator. The wife and children are shadows who exist to be kept in the dark.

The satire is also fairly gentle. The narrator is harmless, so the story never has to face what real paranoia can do. A sharper writer could have shown a man whose delusion hurts someone. Dick prefers to keep it light, which is entirely his right, but it means the piece is amusing rather than deep.

There is also an issue of dating. The comedy depends on the reader's knowing the set phrases of pulp romance and adventure. Most people still know these expressions, but the sort of paperback that would be full of them is a little remote now, and some of the references, like the family gathered around Monopoly, mark the story as a period piece. That said, the piece is short enough that none of this does much damage. It is a sketch, and a sketch is judged by whether it makes you laugh. For most readers, this one does, and it does so more reliably than many longer comic stories from the same magazines.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
It is difficult to measure the impact of a very short comic story, but a few things can be said with confidence. First, it is one of the pieces by which many readers first meet Dick's humor. He is mostly known for his dark and anxious novels, and a reader who comes to him through the movies based on his work may be surprised to find that he could be genuinely funny. This story is a standard example of that other side, and it appears in many collections of his short fiction.

Second, it is a fixture in discussions of science fiction humor. Because it is so short and so easy to grasp, it has been used in classrooms to illustrate several things at once: how language can mislead, how point of view shapes what we see, and how a genre can parody itself. A teacher can read it aloud in three minutes and have a discussion ready. That teaching life is probably its most lasting practical influence.

Third, the story fits into a long tradition of jokes about literal-mindedness. Comedy built on taking figures of speech at face value was not new, and it has remained popular, from children's books about a housekeeper who does exactly what her instructions say, to sketches and sitcom routines in which a character misunderstands an idiom. It would be wrong to claim that this story caused any of those. But it is an early and unusually pure example of the device applied to a science fiction premise, and it has the advantage of an actual argument underneath the gag.

Fourth, the story shows early signs of themes that would grow in Dick's work. The unreliable narrator whose version of reality is cracked, but who is entirely sincere, is central to his later novels. The sense that a hidden truth lies behind ordinary appearances, and that no one in authority will help, is the engine of countless Dick plots. Here it is treated as farce, but the structure of the thought is the same, and it is striking how easily the farce turns serious when later stories adopt the same shape. In the decades after it appeared, as Dick's reputation grew, readers went back to early pieces like this one and found in them a miniature version of his concerns.

There is little documented about how the story was received at the time, beyond the fact that it was published and has since been reprinted often. Like most of his early magazine work, it was a modest piece in a modest venue. Its reputation has grown slowly, through anthologies and collections, not through any single famous event.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
What readers love most about this story is how quickly it makes them feel clever. Almost everyone gets the joke within the first two paragraphs, and then the pleasure becomes one of anticipation. Each new phrase, such as "lost his head" or "gave her his heart", is a small test. You see it coming, and then you watch the narrator misread it in exactly the way you expected, and that confirmation feels good. A story that lets the reader be one step ahead and then rewards that foresight is a very satisfying thing.

People also enjoy the narrator's voice. He is absurd, but he is also oddly lovable. He is a husband and father who gets frightened, hides in the garage with the book, and then rushes back to the warm kitchen to play a board game with his family. That image, the man shaking with fear over a paperback and gripping a Monopoly piece "with frantic fervor," is the human heart of the story. It would be easy to dislike a character who sees monsters everywhere, but Dick makes him a figure of fun rather than scorn. We laugh at him and also recognize a little of ourselves in him, because everyone has at some point jumped to a ridiculous conclusion and then dug in.

The wordplay is another joy. Readers who love language tend to love this story, because it shows how rich and strange ordinary speech is. We say that people lose their heads, split up, or give their hearts away without ever thinking about what we are saying. The story makes us hear our own language as a foreigner might, and that is a kind of delight. It reminds us that English is full of dead metaphors that only seem normal because we have forgotten how weird they are.

Science fiction fans in particular tend to enjoy the way the story pokes at their own genre. Pulp magazines of the period were full of tales of hidden invasions and secret alien infiltrators, and the narrator's solemn deductions read like a parody of those stories. The deadpan treatment, in which the narrator treats his discovery as grave and cosmic, is exactly the tone that many real stories of the time adopted without irony. Fans who know the type appreciate being let in on the joke.

And finally, readers like the economy. It takes only a few minutes. Nothing is wasted, and the closing pun gives the whole thing a neat snap. A story that knows exactly how long it should be is rarer than it seems.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
There is little record of serious public criticism of this story, which is not surprising for a light comic piece in a pulp magazine. It was not the kind of work that attracted reviews in newspapers or provoked debate. So the objections that follow are mostly the sort that later readers and critics make when they discuss Dick's early work, and they are mild.

The most obvious complaint is that the story is slight. It is a single gag developed over a page or two. Readers who go to Dick for the large, disorienting visions of his novels may feel that this is a throwaway, amusing but of little consequence. Critics who take a stern view of his short fiction sometimes treat pieces like this as exercises, evidence of a young writer's wit and facility but not of his depth. There is a reasonable case for that view. Nothing in the story is at stake. No one is changed, and there is no moment of feeling.

A second objection concerns repetition. The humor is based on a pattern, and patterns wear thin. Some readers feel the narrator's catalog of body parts goes on a few examples longer than it needs to, and that the later examples are weaker than the early ones. A tighter version might have stopped sooner or varied the structure.

A third is about the target. The story makes fun of paranoia, but it does so in a way that is safe. The narrator is an obvious fool, and no one is threatened by his delusion, so the satire has no teeth. Compared with real-world paranoia in the early 1950s, which ruined careers and lives, this is very mild stuff. A reader who wants satire to bite may be disappointed. Similarly, someone might say the story fits a condescending habit of mocking the ordinary reader, the man in his easy chair with a paperback, as a gullible dolt. That is a stretch, since the narrator is so clearly a comic invention, but it is the kind of objection that can be raised.

Finally, some readers have noted that the joke has become easier to anticipate over time. Literalist humor is now so common that the story can feel familiar even on first reading. That is a sign of how successful the device became, but it means the story has less of the freshness it once had. None of this is a serious indictment. It simply places the story honestly: it is a good joke, well told, and a good joke does not need to carry more weight than that.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
The simplest way to place this story is as a parody. Science fiction in the 1950s was awash in tales of secret alien invasions, stories in which ordinary people were not what they seemed and a lone hero discovered the truth. The cultural moment encouraged them. The Cold War, the fear of hidden communist infiltrators, and a general sense that enemies might look just like neighbors fed a whole genre of paranoid fiction. The most famous examples came a little later, such as Jack Finney's novel The Body Snatchers, serialized in 1954, which became the classic film Invasion of the Body Snatchers. Dick's story is a comic cousin of these works. It takes their central premise, that the invaders are among us and that only one observant person has noticed, and shows what that premise looks like from the inside of a mind that wants it to be true.

The story also belongs to a tradition of wordplay and literal-mindedness in comedy. Writers from Lewis Carroll onward have enjoyed taking language at its word, and the technique has been used by humorists in every period. In science fiction, a number of short-story writers of the same era, such as Fredric Brown and Robert Sheckley, specialized in brief, witty pieces built on a single twist. Dick's story is among the best of that family. Later comic science fiction, including the work of Douglas Adams, shares its delight in what happens when strange ideas are treated with a straight face.

There is also a faint echo of something larger. The story is, in a way, about reading itself. The narrator is a reader who misreads, and the story asks how much the meaning of any text depends on what the reader brings to it. That concern with interpretation, and with the gap between what is written and what is understood, connects the piece to broader literary themes, and in particular to the long tradition of unreliable narrators, from Poe's raving murderers to the self-deceiving voices of modern fiction. Dick's narrator is a lightweight member of that family, but he belongs to it.

Looking at Dick's own career, the story sits at the lighter end of the early work. It lacks the grandeur of the novels, but it exhibits the same suspicion that reality is not what it appears and that the person describing it cannot be trusted. In his later fiction that suspicion would turn dark and personal. Here it is purely comic.

As for why to read it now, the answer is easy. It takes less than five minutes, it is genuinely funny, and it carries a small lasting lesson. In an age when every conspiracy theory comes with its own set of confident clues, a story about a man who assembles a grand theory out of misread phrases feels remarkably current. The story reminds us that a pattern found by someone determined to find it is not the same as a truth.

stories.title: Beyond the Door
stories.author: Philip K. Dick
stories.epigraph: “It’s made in Germany,” Larry said. After a moment he added, “Carl got it for me wholesale. He knows some guy in the clock business. Otherwise I wouldn’t have⁠—” He stopped.
stories.keyContext: Philip K. Dick is remembered for science fiction, but this story, published in the magazine Fantastic Universe in January 1954, has no spaceships and no aliens. It has a house, a marriage gone sour, and a cuckoo clock. Dick was in his mid-twenties, living in Berkeley, California, married for the first time, and writing at astonishing speed to pay the bills. The magazines of the time wanted a touch of the weird, and he often gave them the weird in the form of everyday objects behaving strangely. Here the object is a little carved bird that will come out for one person and not for another. Underneath, it is a story about a husband who treats his wife as property, and about what happens when affection, which he cannot buy or command, goes somewhere else. Listen for how the clock seems to take sides, and for how the last line leaves one question deliberately unanswered.
paragraphs: That night at the dinner table he brought it out and set it down beside her plate. Doris stared at it, her hand to her mouth. “My God, what is it?” She looked up at him, bright-eyed.
“Well, open it.”

Doris tore the ribbon and paper from the square package with her sharp nails, her bosom rising and falling. Larry stood watching her as she lifted the lid. He lit a cigarette and leaned against the wall.
“A cuckoo clock!” Doris cried. “A real old cuckoo clock like my mother had.” She turned the clock over and over. “Just like my mother had, when Pete was still alive.” Her eyes sparkled with tears.
“It’s made in Germany,” Larry said. After a moment he added, “Carl got it for me wholesale. He knows some guy in the clock business. Otherwise I wouldn’t have⁠—” He stopped.
Doris made a funny little sound.
“I mean, otherwise I wouldn’t have been able to afford it.” He scowled. “What’s the matter with you? You’ve got your clock, haven’t you? Isn’t that what you want?”
Doris sat holding onto the clock, her fingers pressed against the brown wood.
“Well,” Larry said, “what’s the matter?”
He watched in amazement as she leaped up and ran from the room, still clutching the clock. He shook his head. “Never satisfied. They’re all that way. Never get enough.”
He sat down at the table and finished his meal.

The cuckoo clock was not very large. It was handmade, however, and there were countless frets on it, little indentations and ornaments scored in the soft wood. Doris sat on the bed drying her eyes and winding the clock. She set the hands by her wristwatch. Presently she carefully moved the hands to two minutes of ten. She carried the clock over to the dresser and propped it up.
Then she sat waiting, her hands twisted together in her lap⁠—waiting for the cuckoo to come out, for the hour to strike.

As she sat she thought about Larry and what he had said. And what she had said, too, for that matter⁠—not that she could be blamed for any of it. After all, she couldn’t keep listening to him forever without defending herself; you had to blow your own trumpet in the world.

She touched her handkerchief to her eyes suddenly. Why did he have to say that, about getting it wholesale? Why did he have to spoil it all? If he felt that way he needn’t have got it in the first place. She clenched her fists. He was so mean, so damn mean.

But she was glad of the little clock sitting there ticking to itself, with its funny grilled edges and the door. Inside the door was the cuckoo, waiting to come out. Was he listening, his head cocked on one side, listening to hear the clock strike so that he would know to come out?

Did he sleep between hours? Well, she would soon see him: she could ask him. And she would show the clock to Bob. He would love it; Bob loved old things, even old stamps and buttons. He liked to go with her to the stores. Of course, it was a little awkward, but Larry had been staying at the office so much, and that helped. If only Larry didn’t call up sometimes to⁠—
There was a whirr. The clock shuddered and all at once the door opened. The cuckoo came out, sliding swiftly. He paused and looked around solemnly, scrutinizing her, the room, the furniture.
It was the first time he had seen her, she realized, smiling to herself in pleasure. She stood up, coming toward him shyly. “Go on,” she said. “I’m waiting.”
The cuckoo opened his bill. He whirred and chirped, quickly, rhythmically. Then, after a moment of contemplation, he retired. And the door snapped shut.

She was delighted. She clapped her hands and spun in a little circle. He was marvelous, perfect! And the way he had looked around, studying her, sizing her up. He liked her; she was certain of it. And she, of course, loved him at once, completely. He was just what she had hoped would come out of the little door.

Doris went to the clock. She bent over the little door, her lips close to the wood. “Do you hear me?” she whispered. “I think you’re the most wonderful cuckoo in the world.” She paused, embarrassed. “I hope you’ll like it here.”
Then she went downstairs again, slowly, her head high.

Larry and the cuckoo clock really never got along well from the start. Doris said it was because he didn’t wind it right, and it didn’t like being only half-wound all the time. Larry turned the job of winding over to her; the cuckoo came out every quarter hour and ran the spring down without remorse, and someone had to be ever after it, winding it up again.

Doris did her best, but she forgot a good deal of the time. Then Larry would throw his newspaper down with an elaborate weary motion and stand up. He would go into the dining-room where the clock was mounted on the wall over the fireplace. He would take the clock down and making sure that he had his thumb over the little door, he would wind it up.
“Why do you put your thumb over the door?” Doris asked once.
“You’re supposed to.”
She raised an eyebrow. “Are you sure? I wonder if it isn’t that you don’t want him to come out while you’re standing so close.”
“Why not?”
“Maybe you’re afraid of him.”
