There was no light revealed above, and as my hands went higher I knew that my climb was for the nonce ended; since the slab was the trapdoor of an aperture leading to a level stone surface of greater circumference than the lower tower, no doubt the floor of some lofty and capacious observation chamber. I crawled through carefully, and tried to prevent the heavy slab from falling back into place; but failed in the latter attempt. As I lay exhausted on the stone floor I heard the eerie echoes of its fall, but hoped when necessary to pry it up again.

Believing I was now at a prodigious height, far above the accursed branches of the wood, I dragged myself up from the floor and fumbled about for windows, that I might look for the first time upon the sky, and the moon and stars of which I had read. But on every hand I was disappointed; since all that I found were vast shelves of marble, bearing odious oblong boxes of disturbing size. More and more I reflected, and wondered what hoary secrets might abide in this high apartment so many eons cut off from the castle below. Then unexpectedly my hands came upon a doorway, where hung a portal of stone, rough with strange chiseling. Trying it, I found it locked; but with a supreme burst of strength I overcame all obstacles and dragged it open inward. As I did so there came to me the purest ecstasy I have ever known; for shining tranquilly through an ornate grating of iron, and down a short stone passageway of steps that ascended from the newly found doorway, was the radiant full moon, which I had never before seen save in dreams and in vague visions I dared not call memories.

Fancying now that I had attained the very pinnacle of the castle, I commenced to rush up the few steps beyond the door; but the sudden veiling of the moon by a cloud caused me to stumble, and I felt my way more slowly in the dark. It was still very dark when I reached the grating⁠—which I tried carefully and found unlocked, but which I did not open for fear of falling from the amazing height to which I had climbed. Then the moon came out.

Most demoniacal of all shocks is that of the abysmally unexpected and grotesquely unbelievable. Nothing I had before undergone could compare in terror with what I now saw; with the bizarre marvels that sight implied. The sight itself was as simple as it was stupefying, for it was merely this: instead of a dizzying prospect of treetops seen from a lofty eminence, there stretched around me on a level through the grating nothing less than the solid ground, decked and diversified by marble slabs and columns, and overshadowed by an ancient stone church, whose ruined spire gleamed spectrally in the moonlight.

Half unconscious, I opened the grating and staggered out upon the white gravel path that stretched away in two directions. My mind, stunned and chaotic as it was, still held the frantic craving for light; and not even the fantastic wonder which had happened could stay my course. I neither knew nor cared whether my experience was insanity, dreaming, or magic; but was determined to gaze on brilliance and gayety at any cost. I knew not who I was or what I was, or what my surroundings might be; though as I continued to stumble along I became conscious of a kind of fearsome latent memory that made my progress not wholly fortuitous. I passed under an arch out of that region of slabs and columns, and wandered through the open country; sometimes following the visible road, but sometimes leaving it curiously to tread across meadows where only occasional ruins bespoke the ancient presence of a forgotten road. Once I swam across a swift river where crumbling, mossy masonry told of a bridge long vanished.

Over two hours must have passed before I reached what seemed to be my goal, a venerable ivied castle in a thickly wooded park; maddeningly familiar, yet full of perplexing strangeness to me. I saw that the moat was filled in, and that some of the well-known towers were demolished; whilst new wings existed to confuse the beholder. But what I observed with chief interest and delight were the open windows⁠—gorgeously ablaze with light and sending forth sound of the gayest revelry. Advancing to one of these I looked in and saw an oddly dressed company, indeed; making merry, and speaking brightly to one another. I had never, seemingly, heard human speech before; and could guess only vaguely what was said. Some of the faces seemed to hold expressions that brought up incredibly remote recollections; others were utterly alien.

I now stepped through the low window into the brilliantly lighted room, stepping as I did so from my single bright moment of hope to my blackest convulsion of despair and realization. The nightmare was quick to come, for as I entered, there occurred immediately one of the most terrifying demonstrations I had ever conceived. Scarcely had I crossed the sill when there descended upon the whole company a sudden and unheralded fear of hideous intensity, distorting every face and evoking the most horrible screams from nearly every throat. Flight was universal, and in the clamor and panic several fell in a swoon and were dragged away by their madly fleeing companions. Many covered their eyes with their hands, and plunged blindly and awkwardly in their race to escape, overturning furniture and stumbling against the walls before they managed to reach one of the many doors.

The cries were shocking; and as I stood in the brilliant apartment alone and dazed, listening to their vanishing echoes, I trembled at the thought of what might be lurking near me unseen. At a casual inspection the room seemed deserted, but when I moved toward one of the alcoves I thought I detected a presence there⁠—a hint of motion beyond the golden-arched doorway leading to another and somewhat similar room. As I approached the arch I began to perceive the presence more clearly; and then, with the first and last sound I ever uttered⁠—a ghastly ululation that revolted me almost as poignantly as its noxious cause⁠—I beheld in full, frightful vividness the inconceivable, indescribable, and unmentionable monstrosity which had by its simple appearance changed a merry company to a herd of delirious fugitives.

I can not even hint what it was like, for it was a compound of all that is unclean, uncanny, unwelcome, abnormal, and detestable. It was the ghoulish shade of decay, antiquity, and desolation; the putrid, dripping eidolon of unwholesome revelation; the awful baring of that which the merciful earth should always hide. God knows it was not of this world⁠—or no longer of this world⁠—yet to my horror I saw in its eaten-away and bone-revealing outlines a leering, abhorrent travesty on the human shape; and in its moldy, disintegrating apparel an unspeakable quality that chilled me even more.

I was almost paralyzed, but not too much so to make a feeble effort toward flight; a backward stumble which failed to break the spell in which the nameless, voiceless monster held me. My eyes, bewitched by the glassy orbs which stared loathsomely into them, refused to close; though they were mercifully blurred, and showed the terrible object but indistinctly after the first shock. I tried to raise my hand to shut out the sight, yet so stunned were my nerves that my arm could not fully obey my will. The attempt, however, was enough to disturb my balance; so that I had to stagger forward several steps to avoid falling. As I did so I became suddenly and agonizingly aware of the nearness of the carrion thing, whose hideous hollow breathing I half fancied I could hear. Nearly mad, I found myself yet able to throw out a hand to ward off the fetid apparition which pressed so close; when in one cataclysmic second of cosmic nightmarishness and hellish accident my fingers touched the rotting outstretched paw of the monster beneath the golden arch.

I did not shriek, but all the fiendish ghouls that ride the night-wind shrieked for me as in that same second there crashed down upon my mind a single and fleeting avalanche of soul-annihilating memory. I knew in that second all that had been; I remembered beyond the frightful castle and the trees, and recognized the altered edifice in which I now stood; I recognized, most terrible of all, the unholy abomination that stood leering before me as I withdrew my sullied fingers from its own.

But in the cosmos there is balm as well as bitterness, and that balm is nepenthe. In the supreme horror of that second I forgot what had horrified me, and the burst of black memory vanished in a chaos of echoing images. In a dream I fled from that haunted and accursed pile, and ran swiftly and silently in the moonlight. When I returned to the churchyard place of marble and went down the steps I found the stone trapdoor immovable; but I was not sorry, for I had hated the antique castle and the trees. Now I ride with the mocking and friendly ghouls on the night-wind, and play by day amongst the catacombs of Nephren-Ka in the sealed and unknown valley of Hadoth by the Nile. I know that light is not for me, save that of the moon over the rock tombs of Neb, nor any gayety save the unnamed feasts of Nitokris beneath the Great Pyramid; yet in my new wildness and freedom I almost welcome the bitterness of alienage.

For although nepenthe has calmed me, I know always that I am an outsider; a stranger in this century and among those who are still men. This I have known ever since I stretched out my fingers to the abomination within that great gilded frame; stretched out my fingers and touched a cold and unyielding surface of polished glass.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The story begins like a nightmare with a very polite narrator. He tells us he was raised in an enormous, ancient castle, in perpetual gloom, under trees so tall that no sunlight ever reaches the ground. He has no memory of parents, teachers, or friends. He remembers no living person except himself, and the only creatures he can name are rats, bats, and spiders. He learned everything he knows from moldy books, and he has never heard a human voice, not even his own. Notice a small, chilling detail early on. He says he felt conscious of youth, and then explains why: "because I remembered so little." That is not how a young person reasons. It is how someone reasons who has lost the thread of his own history, and it is the first hint that something is wrong with his picture of himself.

Then comes the great decision. Starved for light, he climbs the single black tower that rises above the forest, a climb the text calls well-nigh impossible. Inside the dark he crawls up an endless inner wall, pushes through a trapdoor, and finds himself not in the sky but in a vault of marble shelves and strange boxes. He is, without knowing it, underground, and the trapdoor has led him up into the cellar of another building. He climbs out into a moonlit churchyard, and there he sees at last the sky and stars he had only read about. The meaning of that image is easy to feel: the way up and the way out turn out to be the same as the way into the grave.

Eventually he enters a bright, crowded castle where a party is going on. The guests see him and flee in screaming panic. Baffled, he looks for the horror that has frightened them, and sees a hideous thing inside a gilded archway, a rotted, shapeless, ghastly figure. He reaches out toward it, and his fingers touch cold glass. The monster is his own reflection. He had never seen a mirror, never seen his own face, and had believed himself to resemble the youthful figures in his books.

This final twist is the center of the story, and it is worth reading slowly. The narrator is a corpse, or something close to one, who has lost the memory of his own death. The castle of his childhood was a tomb, the books were all the company he had, and the world of the living is a world he has no right to rejoin. His instinct to climb, to want light and company, is the most human thing about him, and it is exactly what destroys him.

The ending adds a note of bitter consolation. The narrator says that in the cosmos there is "balm as well as bitterness, and that balm is nepenthe," an old word for a drug of forgetfulness taken from Homer's Odyssey. He forgets the horror and runs off to join friendly ghouls, riding the night wind and playing among Egyptian catacombs. But he can never forget what he is. He stays, in his own word, an outsider, a stranger in this century and among those who are still men. So the story is not only a shock. It is a portrait of permanent exile, told by someone who has learned to live with it.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
The Outsider is a model of economy, and that is where it is most masterful. It runs only a few pages, and almost every sentence is working. The opening paragraph sets up an unusual emotional position. Most horror narrators beg us to believe they are sane. This one begins by declaring that he is "strangely content" and clinging to his sere memories, and the strangeness of that contentment does half the work of creating dread. The long first half, in which almost nothing happens except atmosphere, is crucial, because it makes the final breakthrough feel like a lurch of terror and hope.

The twist works better than most twist endings because it is not only a trick. It reverses the meaning of a whole life. Everything we have read has been told by someone who could not see himself, and when he finally does, the sympathy we felt turns into something more complicated. We pity him. We are also, for an instant, forced to see him as the partygoers do. That double view, from inside and from outside at once, is the real achievement. The mirror is not a gimmick; it is the whole theme made visible, because the story is about the gap between how we feel inside and how the world sees us.

Still, the story has real weaknesses, and a fair critic should say so. Lovecraft's prose here is in its most overheated mode. The narration is thick with adjectives like accursed, hideous, nameless, and fiendish, and the opening paragraph's gloom can feel like a costume party for the word list of a Gothic novel. When every wall is damp and every tree gigantic, the sense of specific detail can blur. Modern readers who prefer restrained, concrete writing may find the first pages ornate to the point of parody, and the story can read as an exercise in an inherited style rather than a fresh voice.

There is also a problem of predictability. Readers who know Poe will guess early that the castle is a tomb, and the mirror twist, although elegantly executed, has since been used so often in horror and in comedy that it can feel familiar. In its defense, that familiarity is partly a measure of its influence, and a reader encountering it for the first time can still be thrown. The final ghoul paragraph is also a bit uneven. The names Nephren-Ka, Nitokris, and Hadoth, with their Egyptian color, are fun for a Lovecraft enthusiast, but they dissolve the intensity of the mirror moment into a kind of exotic tour. It is the one place where the story's focus softens.

Finally, the moral shape is unusually ambiguous, and that is a strength. The story does not tell us whether the narrator is a victim, a monster, or both. It offers no villain, no rescue, and no explanation, only an exquisitely sad portrait. That restraint, combined with the compression of the writing, makes The Outsider more affecting than much of Lovecraft's longer work, even if its ornamental language will always divide readers.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The Outsider did not make a splash on publication in the way a bestseller might. It appeared in Weird Tales in April 1926, years after it was written, and it was one of the stories that helped establish Lovecraft's reputation inside the small world of pulp horror. Once it appeared, it became one of the pieces that readers of the magazine remembered, and later it gave its name to the first hardcover collection of his fiction, The Outsider and Others, published by Arkham House in 1939 after his death. That book was assembled by his devoted friends August Derleth and Donald Wandrei, who founded their own publishing house expressly to keep his work in print. In that sense the story helped carry Lovecraft's name into permanence.

Its influence on later writers is considerable, though often as a mood rather than a plot. The idea of the narrator who discovers he is the monster, the ghost who does not know he is dead, and the reflection that reveals the truth are all staples of later horror, and this story is one of the clearest early examples. The term "outsider" has also entered the language of Lovecraft criticism, where it describes a whole type of Lovecraft protagonist: the solitary scholar, set apart from the human community by knowledge, inheritance, or simple strangeness.

Biography has shaped the story's afterlife. Lovecraft's life invites an autobiographical reading. He was a withdrawn, bookish child in a household dominated by anxious relatives, a man who felt out of step with the twentieth century and often said so. Biographers, including S. T. Joshi, have noted how well the story expresses that sensibility, and many readers treat the narrator as a kind of self-portrait. The story is therefore often a starting point for the question of how much of Lovecraft's horror comes from the real feelings of an isolated man.

The Outsider has been anthologized widely and is often taught in courses on Gothic literature and on the American weird tale, partly because it is short enough to read in a single sitting and rich enough to discuss for an hour. It has been adapted into comics, audio dramas, and short films. It is also a favorite recommendation for newcomers to Lovecraft, because it shows his gift for atmosphere without the heavy mythology of the later cosmic stories.

For many readers, it is the moment when his fiction stops being about a creature outside and starts being about the creature within.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers have loved The Outsider for several overlapping reasons, and the first is simple intensity. In just a few pages it delivers a complete emotional arc: yearning, struggle, breakthrough, shock, and a sad acceptance. Many people who read it for the first time remember the moment of the mirror for years afterward. The reveal lands because the whole story has trained us to see through the narrator's eyes, and the sudden shift of perspective feels like a physical drop.

A second reason is its tenderness. Lovecraft is often thought of as a cold writer, a builder of indifferent universes and tentacled gods. Here, by contrast, the narrator is genuinely moving. His longing to see the sky, to hear another voice, to be among gay crowds is touching, and his bruised dignity at the end, living on as a ghoul among ghouls, can bring a lump to the throat. Readers who feel like outsiders themselves, whether from shyness, difference, illness, or circumstance, have often found in the story a surprising comfort. It names a feeling that is hard to describe: the sense that you are watching life from behind glass, and that the glass is part of you.

Third, it is a showcase for atmosphere. Fans of Gothic fiction treasure the passages where the narrator describes the damp stones, the dead trees, the impossible climb up the tower, and the dreamlike experience of emerging from the vault into moonlight. These passages are excellent read aloud, which is part of why the story works so well as an audio piece. The rhythm of the long sentences, the repeated words like dark and silent, and the build-up toward the climb give it an almost hypnotic quality.

Fellow writers have also admired the story. Horror authors have often named Lovecraft as an influence, and The Outsider in particular is a favorite among those who value the short, concentrated tale. Some readers regard it as the nearest Lovecraft came to a perfect short story.

Finally, readers like that the story leaves room to think. Is the narrator dead, undead, or simply a monstrous being who never knew? Is the castle he escapes his own tomb, or somewhere else entirely? The story gives hints but never settles the question, and the mystery has fed decades of discussion. That openness is a gift, because it lets different readers bring their own fears to the final image. For some it is a story about death, for some about disability or deformity, for some about growing up and discovering that the world is not made for you. The range of meanings people find in a few pages is, in itself, a measure of its appeal.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
The Outsider has not escaped criticism, and the most common complaint is about style. Lovecraft's critics, from his own era to the present, have often found his prose overwritten. The critic Edmund Wilson, in a famous and scornful 1945 essay in The New Yorker, dismissed Lovecraft as bad art, and complaints about adjective-heavy, melodramatic writing have followed him ever since. This story, with its accursed, noisome, and fiendish vocabulary, is one of the most frequent examples. Critics argue that the words announce horror rather than create it, and that a more restrained approach would hit harder.

A second objection is derivativeness. The Outsider wears its Poe influence on its sleeve. The ruined castle, the gloom, the narrator who sees too late, and the closing note of damnation all echo stories like The Fall of the House of Usher and The Masque of the Red Death. The epigraph, drawn from John Keats, underscores the literary pedigree. Some critics have said the story is more a skilled pastiche than a new creation, and Lovecraft himself, in his own essays, acknowledged how deeply he admired and borrowed from Poe. Others reply that originality lies in the twist on Poe's formula, the inside view of the monster, but the charge of imitation has stuck.

A third line of criticism concerns the ending. The mirror reveal is clever, but some find it too neat, as though the entire story were built for a single punchline. There is also the question of whether the story withholds so much that it frustrates. We never learn who the narrator was, how he died, or why he was in the castle, and some readers want more than an atmosphere.

Finally, there is the broader and unavoidable issue of Lovecraft's reputation. Lovecraft held hateful racist views, which he expressed in letters and which surface in some of his stories. The Outsider is among the least affected by that, since it contains no overt racial content, but readers today often approach his whole body of work with that knowledge. Some critics have argued that his fear of the outsider, the stranger, the other, is entangled with his own prejudices, and that a story about an alienated monster should be read in that uncomfortable light. Others take the opposite view, that the story is the rare place where he extends real sympathy to the monstrous. Either way, the discussion shows that the story cannot be separated from its author, and that honest readers should keep both the artistry and the shadows of his thinking in view.

None of these objections is fatal, but they explain why the story is loved and argued over in roughly equal measure.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
The Outsider belongs to the tradition of the Gothic and the weird tale, a lineage that runs from Horace Walpole's The Castle of Otranto in the eighteenth century, through Mary Shelley, Poe, and Hawthorne, and on to Lovecraft's own era. It descends most directly from Poe, whose first-person narrators, haunted houses, and doomed sensibilities supply the template. But there is a deeper comparison with Mary Shelley's Frankenstein. Shelley's creature also teaches himself about the world from books, also longs for human company, also approaches the human world with hope, and is also driven away by horror at his appearance, and one famous moment even involves him seeing his reflection and understanding what he is. Lovecraft's narrator is a sort of ghostly cousin of that creature, told with the sympathy turned all the way up and the explanation stripped all the way out.

The story also looks forward. It anticipates the modern horror tale in which we are asked to identify with the monster, a mode that runs through later fiction and film, from stories of vampires who suffer in secret to novels of ghosts who do not know they are dead. It shares an emotional world with writers such as Shirley Jackson, whose lonely, house-bound characters long to be accepted, and with stories like Kafka's, in which a protagonist is cut off from human beings by an unexplained change. The comparison with Kafka is not exact, but both writers turn alienation into a physical fact.

Within Lovecraft's own work, The Outsider sits at the border between his early Poe-style tales and the cosmic horror for which he is now best known. It is not part of the Cthulhu mythology in the strict sense, although it mentions ghouls and Egyptian names that recur elsewhere. It is closer in feeling to stories like The Rats in the Walls and The Shadow over Innsmouth, in which the discovery of a terrible inheritance or identity becomes the central horror. In all of these, the true monster lives in the narrator's own blood or body, and the outside universe is simply the place where that truth gets exposed.

Why read it today? One reason is its brevity and force: it can be absorbed in about fifteen minutes and remembered for a lifetime. Another is how freshly it speaks about a modern feeling. Loneliness, the sense of not belonging, and the dread of seeing oneself from outside are not old-fashioned concerns. The story gives them a form that is both extravagant and strangely intimate.

It is also a good way to understand Lovecraft honestly. Here you can see his gifts, a mastery of mood, an instinct for the climactic image, and a feel for the pathos of isolation, and you can see his limits, including the heavy language and the debt to Poe. A reader who finishes it will understand why he inspired such devotion, and why the argument about him continues.

stories.title: The Cats of Ulthar
stories.author: H. P. Lovecraft
stories.epigraph: “It is said that in Ulthar, which lies beyond the river Skai, no man may kill a cat; and this I can verily believe as I gaze upon him who sitteth purring before the fire.”
stories.keyContext: The Cats of Ulthar is a tiny fable by H. P. Lovecraft, and it is a good place to meet him at his gentlest. Lovecraft was a reclusive writer from Providence, Rhode Island, now famous for cosmic horror, but in 1920, when he wrote this, he was deeply under the spell of an Irish fantasy author named Lord Dunsany, who wrote dreamy, invented-world tales in a grave, biblical voice. The result is not a story about tentacled gods. It is a short legend, told like something repeated by travelers, that explains why in the imaginary town of Ulthar it is against the law to kill a cat. It first appeared in a small amateur magazine called Tryout in late 1920. Lovecraft adored cats, and you can feel it. At heart it is a tale about cruelty getting its comeuppance, and about the quiet, mysterious power of the creatures we think of as simply pets. Listen for the old-fashioned storytelling voice, and for how little it explains.
paragraphs: It is said that in Ulthar, which lies beyond the river Skai, no man may kill a cat; and this I can verily believe as I gaze upon him who sitteth purring before the fire. For the cat is cryptic, and close to strange things which men can not see. He is the soul of antique Aegyptus, and bearer of tales from forgotten cities in Meroë and Ophir. He is the kin of the jungle’s lords, and heir to the secrets of hoary and sinister Africa. The Sphinx is his cousin, and he speaks her language; but he is more ancient than the Sphinx, and remembers that which she hath forgotten.

In Ulthar, before ever the burgesses forbade the killing of cats, there dwelt an old cotter and his wife who delighted to trap and slay the cats of their neighbors. Why they did this I know not; save that many hate the voice of the cat in the night, and take it ill that cats should run stealthily about yards and gardens at twilight. But whatever the reason, this old man and woman took pleasure in trapping and slaying every cat which came near to their hovel; and from some of the sounds heard after dark, many villagers fancied that the manner of slaying was exceedingly peculiar. But the villagers did not discuss such things with the old man and his wife; because of the habitual expression on the withered faces of the two, and because their cottage was so small and so darkly hidden under spreading oaks at the back of a neglected yard. In truth, much as the owners of cats hated these odd folk, they feared them more; and instead of berating them as brutal assassins, merely took care that no cherished pet or mouser should stray toward the remote hovel under the dark trees. When through some unavoidable oversight a cat was missed, and sounds heard after dark, the loser would lament impotently; or console himself by thanking Fate that it was not one of his children who had thus vanished. For the people of Ulthar were simple, and knew not whence it is that all cats first came.

One day a caravan of strange wanderers from the South entered the narrow cobbled streets of Ulthar. Dark wanderers they were, and unlike the other roving folk who passed through the village twice every year. In the marketplace they told fortunes for silver, and bought gay beads from the merchants. What was the land of these wanderers none could tell; but it was seen that they were given to strange prayers, and that they had painted on the sides of their wagons strange figures with human bodies and the heads of cats, hawks, rams, and lions. And the leader of the caravan wore a headdress with two horns and a curious disk betwixt the horns.

There was in this singular caravan a little boy with no father or mother, but only a tiny black kitten to cherish. The plague had not been kind to him, yet had left him this small furry thing to mitigate his sorrow; and when one is very young, one can find great relief in the lively antics of a black kitten. So the boy whom the dark people called Menes smiled more often than he wept as he sat playing with his graceful kitten on the steps of an oddly painted wagon.

On the third morning of the wanderers’ stay in Ulthar, Menes could not find his kitten; and as he sobbed aloud in the marketplace certain villagers told him of the old man and his wife, and of sounds heard in the night. And when he heard these things his sobbing gave place to meditation, and finally to prayer. He stretched out his arms toward the sun and prayed in a tongue no villager could understand; though indeed the villagers did not try very hard to understand, since their attention was mostly taken up by the sky and the odd shapes the clouds were assuming. It was very peculiar, but as the little boy uttered his petition there seemed to form overhead the shadowy, nebulous figures of exotic things; of hybrid creatures crowned with horn-flanked disks. Nature is full of such illusions to impress the imaginative.

That night the wanderers left Ulthar, and were never seen again. And the householders were troubled when they noticed that in all the village there was not a cat to be found. From each hearth the familiar cat had vanished; cats large and small, black, gray, striped, yellow and white. Old Kranon, the burgomaster, swore that the dark folk had taken the cats away in revenge for the killing of Menes’ kitten; and cursed the caravan and the little boy. But Nith, the lean notary, declared that the old cotter and his wife were more likely persons to suspect; for their hatred of cats was notorious and increasingly bold. Still, no one durst complain to the sinister couple; even when little Atal, the innkeeper’s son, vowed that he had at twilight seen all the cats of Ulthar in that accursed yard under the trees, pacing very slowly and solemnly in a circle around the cottage, two abreast, as if in performance of some unheard-of rite of beasts. The villagers did not know how much to believe from so small a boy; and though they feared that the evil pair had charmed the cats to their death, they preferred not to chide the old cotter till they met him outside his dark and repellent yard.

So Ulthar went to sleep in vain anger; and when the people awaked at dawn⁠—behold! every cat was back at his accustomed hearth! Large and small, black, gray, striped, yellow and white, none was missing. Very sleek and fat did the cats appear, and sonorous with purring content. The citizens talked with one another of the affair, and marveled not a little. Old Kranon again insisted that it was the dark folk who had taken them, since cats did not return alive from the cottage of the ancient man and his wife. But all agreed on one thing; that the refusal of all the cats to eat their portions of meat or drink their saucers of milk was exceedingly curious. And for two whole days the sleek, lazy cats of Ulthar would touch no food, but only doze by the fire or in the sun.

It was fully a week before the villagers noticed that no lights were appearing at dusk in the windows of the cottage under the trees. Then the lean Nith remarked that no one had seen the old man or his wife since the night the cats were away. In another week the burgomaster decided to overcome his fears and call at the strangely silent dwelling as a matter of duty, though in doing so he was careful to take with him Shang the blacksmith and Thul the cutter of stone as witnesses. And when they had broken down the frail door they found only this: two cleanly picked human skeletons on the earthen floor, and a number of singular beetles crawling in the shadowy corners.

There was subsequently much talk amongst the burgesses of Ulthar. Zath, the coroner, disputed at length with Nith, the lean notary; and Kranon and Shang and Thul were overwhelmed with questions. Even little Atal, the innkeeper’s son, was closely questioned and given a sweetmeat as reward. They talked of the old cotter and his wife, of the caravan of dark wanderers, of small Menes and his black kitten, of the prayer of Menes and of the sky during that prayer, of the doings of the cats on the night the caravan left, and of what was later found in the cottage under the dark trees in the repellent yard.
And in the end the burgesses passed that remarkable law which is told of by traders in Hatheg and discussed by travelers in Nir; namely, that in Ulthar no man may kill a cat.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
On the surface, The Cats of Ulthar is a revenge story told as a legend. It opens with a narrator saying that in the town of Ulthar, no man may kill a cat, and that he can believe it as he watches his own cat purring by the fire. Then he tells us how the law came to be. An old man and his wife, who live in a dark hovel under oak trees, take pleasure in trapping and killing the cats of their neighbors. The villagers hate them but fear them even more, so no one confronts them. They simply keep their pets away and quietly accept the losses.

Then a caravan of dark wanderers arrives from the South. Among them is an orphaned boy named Menes, who has only a black kitten left to him after the plague took his family. When the kitten disappears, the villagers tell him about the old couple. Menes first weeps, then thinks, and then prays, stretching his arms to the sun in a tongue the villagers cannot understand. The caravan leaves the next morning, and that evening, strange things happen. The sky takes on unusual shapes, and every cat in the village vanishes. When the cats return the next day, they are sleek and well-fed, and they refuse their food for two days. Soon after, the villagers notice that the cottage under the trees is dark. When the burgomaster finally breaks in, he finds two cleanly picked human skeletons and some strange beetles. The town then passes its law.

The story never says exactly what happened, and that gap is the point. We are asked to infer that Menes's prayer, offered to some ancient power, summoned the cats to take vengeance, and that the cats ate the old couple. The strange figures painted on the caravan wagons, human bodies with the heads of cats, hawks, rams, and lions, and the leader's horned headdress with a disk between the horns, point toward ancient Egypt, where cats were sacred and animal-headed gods were worshipped. The boy's name, Menes, is the name traditionally given to the first pharaoh of a united Egypt. Lovecraft is telling us, without lecturing, that the wanderers carry an old faith, and that the cats are not just animals but servants of something older than the town.

The opening paragraph gives the key to the story's mood. Lovecraft says the cat is "cryptic, and close to strange things which men can not see," the soul of ancient Egypt and kin to the lords of the jungle. This sets up the idea that cats hold a secret knowledge.

There is also a quieter moral reading. The old couple are not punished because they are wicked in some dramatic way, but because they are casually cruel to those who cannot defend themselves, and because the community around them allows it. The villagers hate what the couple does, yet they merely lament and look away. When justice finally comes, it comes from outside, from a grieving child and the creatures he loved. Read this way, the story is about what happens when kindness is silent and cruelty goes unchecked, and about the fairy-tale idea that the small and powerless are never as helpless as they seem.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
As craft, The Cats of Ulthar is charming and uneven, and it is worth separating what works from what does not. Its greatest strength is tone. Lovecraft borrows the stately cadence of a very old tale, with phrases like "I know not" and "sitteth purring," and the voice does a lot of work. By telling the story as hearsay, something traders in Hatheg and travelers in Nir repeat, he makes it feel like folklore. The final sentence, which simply states the law, lands with the satisfaction of a proverb. That sense of an authentic legend is hard to fake, and he fakes it well.

The story is also admirably economical. In about thirteen hundred words we get a villain pair, a sympathetic child, a mystery, a climax, and a coda. The climactic episode is smartly handled by leaving it off the page. We never see what the cats do. We see only their sleek, full-bellied laziness afterward, the untouched milk, and the two clean skeletons. A more explicit writer would have staged a gory scene. Lovecraft lets the reader's imagination do it, and the quiet details, especially the cats refusing to eat, are more chilling than any description. The beetles in the corner are a perfectly odd final touch, suggesting something strange beyond the obvious.

On the other hand, it has real limitations. The characters are barely characters. The old couple are cruel because the story requires cruelty, and the text frankly admits it does not know why they do it. Menes is a sketch of a sad child, not a person. Readers wanting psychological depth will not find it. The story is also thin on suspense: because the narrator announces from the first line that cats are protected by law, and because the structure is a legend, there is little doubt about where it is going. It is more a mood piece than a thriller.

There is also the matter of ornament. The Dunsanian style, with its invented place names and its archaic grammar, is lovely in small doses but can feel precious. The quick tour of names at the end, Zath the coroner, Nith the notary, Kranon, Shang, Thul, and little Atal, is a deliberate imitation of Dunsany's fondness for exotic names, but it also exposes the story's thinness, since these characters exist only as sounds.

More troubling is the portrayal of the caravan. The "dark wanderers" are presented as mysterious, vaguely sinister foreigners, and the story relies on a stereotype of the exotic outsider, even if it grants them the moral high ground and a sympathetic child. Readers today often notice this, and it sits uneasily with an otherwise light tale. Overall, the story succeeds as a miniature, a clever, atmospheric, deliberately small piece, but it is not among Lovecraft's deepest work, and it was not meant to be.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The Cats of Ulthar was never a blockbuster, and its influence is gentle and specific rather than sweeping. Lovecraft wrote it in June 1920 and it appeared in the amateur journal Tryout in November of that year, a very small publication circulated among hobbyist writers. It was reprinted in Weird Tales in 1926, which gave it a far wider audience in the pulp world, and eventually it became part of the standard Lovecraft collections, so that generations of readers have met it early.

Its most important impact is on the shape of Lovecraft's own imagination. The story belongs to what scholars call his Dunsanian phase, a period in which he wrote dreamlike, myth-flavored tales in the manner of Lord Dunsany. The invented geography here, Ulthar, the river Skai, Nir, and Hatheg, would return in Lovecraft's longer fantasy, The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, written in the 1920s, in which cats play an important and clever role and the town of Ulthar appears again. In that sense the story is a seed. It helped create the Dreamlands, a shared imaginary world that Lovecraft and later writers used for stories unlike his better-known cosmic horror. For readers who prefer wonder to dread, this strand of his work has stayed beloved.

The story also contributed to Lovecraft's lasting image as a cat person. He was well known in his circle for his affection for cats, and the story is often cited in discussions of his personality. A fan of Lovecraft will often point to it as proof that the author of so much cold, bleak fiction had a warm, almost sentimental side. It is routinely quoted, adapted, and referenced in cat-themed anthologies and in discussions of cats in fantasy, and the phrase that in Ulthar no man may kill a cat has become a kind of motto among Lovecraft fans.

In the larger culture, the story has been adapted into short films, audio readings, comics, and tabletop gaming material, and the town of Ulthar appears in role-playing games based on Lovecraft's Dreamlands. Fantasy writers have borrowed its premise of cats as keepers of old secrets, and the idea of the cat as a quiet, supernatural guardian pops up widely in fantasy fiction. A few later authors have written explicitly in its shadow, producing stories in which cats avenge abuse or guard humans from unseen dangers.

Finally, the story is taught and anthologized less as a masterpiece than as an accessible introduction. Teachers and fans like it because it is brief, readable, and carries many of the features of Lovecraft's craft without the heavy vocabulary or the hostility of his later work. It is a gentle doorway into a writer who is often approached with caution.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
What do readers love about The Cats of Ulthar? The first answer is the cats, of course. Anyone who has shared a home with a cat knows the mix of affection and mystery that animal can inspire, the sense that it is looking at something we cannot see. Lovecraft captures that feeling in the opening lines, and readers who love cats recognize themselves in his narrator watching his own pet by the fire. The story gives a literary form to a very common experience: the cat who sits and stares, apparently aware of things no one else notices.

The second answer is the satisfaction of justice. Readers like stories where cruelty is punished, and this one delivers its payoff with little fuss. There is something deeply pleasing about an orphan with nothing but a kitten calling on higher powers, and the powers answering. It is a revenge fantasy for people who love animals, and it has the tidy, fairy-tale morality of a story in which the bad are devoured and the good are left in peace. The fact that the vengeance is handled so calmly, with the cats simply returning and refusing their dinner, makes the justice feel both fierce and strangely elegant.

Third, readers enjoy its voice. The storyteller's tone is warm, dry, and slightly archaic, like an elder speaking by a fire. Many Lovecraft fans appreciate a break from his usual narrators, who sweat and shudder and gibber. Here, the narrator is calm and amused, and the sentences have a natural musical rhythm. Read aloud, which is how many people will hear it, the story has the pleasing shape of a bedtime legend, with its repeating names, its leisurely opening, and its crisp last line.

Fourth, the story is a treat for those who like creeping, understated horror. Because it never shows the killing, it leaves a delicious chill. The image of two clean skeletons on a dirt floor is stark enough to stay in the mind, and the beetles hint at something unsettling without overexplaining it. Readers have often noted that the story manages a lot of menace in a very small space.

Finally, it has the charm of discovery. Many readers meet it as an early, short Lovecraft, an easy path into the larger world of the Dreamlands. They find that this author who has a reputation for dark gloom can also write something light-footed, funny, and humane. That surprise is part of its affection. People often return to it when they want a short, atmospheric story that is more cozy than frightening, a story to be read before sleep without fear of nightmares, and perhaps with a cat nearby.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Because the story is slight and not widely reviewed in its own time, there is no famous body of contemporary criticism to cite. It appeared first in a tiny amateur magazine, and most of what has been said about it comes from later Lovecraft scholars and readers. So the criticisms that follow are the ones that have commonly been raised in later discussion, rather than a documented battle.

The most frequent complaint is that the story is minor. Even its admirers tend to call it a charming trifle. Compared with the great weight of Lovecraft's later fiction, such as The Call of Cthulhu or At the Mountains of Madness, it seems light, and critics sometimes say that it is pleasant but not memorable on its own. It lacks the cosmic scale and the philosophical edge that make his best work stand out. Some readers find the plot too thin, a single idea stretched into a short anecdote, and the lack of suspense a weakness.

A second complaint concerns its derivativeness. The Dunsany influence is so strong that some critics regard the story as pastiche, an exercise in borrowed style rather than an original work. The archaic diction, the invented names, and the legend structure all come directly from Dunsany's model, and Lovecraft himself later moved away from this manner toward his own kind of horror. Those who prefer his mature voice sometimes see this story as an apprenticeship piece.

A third and increasingly important criticism concerns race and stereotype. The caravan of dark wanderers from the South, with their strange prayers and exotic gods, belongs to a familiar pattern in which foreign people are presented as mysterious and faintly menacing. Lovecraft's racism is well documented, and readers who know that background tend to read his portrayals of outsiders with suspicion. In this story the foreigners are treated sympathetically, in that the boy is a victim and his cause is just, but they are still exoticized, and their power is described as strange rather than understood. Some critics argue that the story, for all its kindness, is shaped by the same habits of mind as his harsher work. Others contend that the story is generous to the wanderers and that its sympathies are clear.

Finally, a few readers have objected to the violence, finding the idea of cats devouring people unpleasant, or have questioned the moral logic of a punishment so extreme for what is, after all, cruelty to animals. That reaction is probably an overreading of a fable, in which exaggeration is part of the form, but it is real. The story invites us to cheer, and not everyone cheers.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
The Cats of Ulthar sits in a long tradition of the animal fable and the legend that explains a custom. Humans have told stories for ages about why a place has a strange rule, from tales of the origins of festivals to local folklore of cursed fields. Lovecraft's story is a literary version of this, with an ancient, mysterious explanation attached to a simple law. It also belongs to the old and widespread tradition of cats as magical or sacred beings, from the cat goddess Bastet of ancient Egypt to the many witch-and-cat tales of European folklore.

It also descends from a specific literary lineage: the fantasy of Lord Dunsany, whose collections such as The Gods of Pegana and Time and the Gods created invented worlds with their own gods, kings, and customs, told in a lofty, simple voice. Lovecraft discovered Dunsany around 1919 and was strongly influenced by him for years. The Cats of Ulthar is one of the clearest examples. Through Dunsany it also touches earlier traditions of the fairy tale and the prose poem.

Another interesting comparison is with Edgar Allan Poe's The Black Cat, which Lovecraft admired. Poe's story is about a man who cruelly harms a cat and is destroyed by his guilt and by the animal's return, and the cat there is a force of retribution. Lovecraft shifts the tone from guilt-ridden Gothic to cool fable, but the underlying idea, that cruelty to a cat invites a reckoning, is shared. Later fantasy and horror writers have returned to the same pattern, from stories of vengeful pets to modern fantasy in which cats are cunning and half-magical creatures. The pulp writer Fritz Leiber, who corresponded with Lovecraft and loved cats, wrote warm fantasy stories about them, and you can see a kinship.

Within Lovecraft's body of work, the story is an early outpost of the Dreamlands, the strand of his writing that stands apart from the Cthulhu stories. It shows another side of him, wonder and whimsy rather than dread, and it connects forward to the longer Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath and to many shorter dream tales.

Why read it now? First, it is short and graceful, a ten-minute story that leaves a distinct picture. Second, it offers an unusually human Lovecraft, one with a sense of humor and a real affection for animals. Third, it is a good example of how a story can be effective by implying rather than showing. And finally, it is a reminder that fantasy and horror can be playful. A reader who finishes it with a cat in the lap will understand why the old line still feels right: that the cat is close to strange things which men cannot see.

stories.title: Dagon
stories.author: H. P. Lovecraft
stories.epigraph: “I am writing this under an appreciable mental strain, since by tonight I shall be no more.”
stories.keyContext: Dagon is the story where H. P. Lovecraft first found the voice that made him famous. He wrote it in the summer of 1917, in Providence, Rhode Island, while the First World War was raging and he was just returning to fiction after years of nervous retreat. It was published in a small amateur magazine in 1919, and in 1923 it became one of the first Lovecraft stories to appear in the pulp magazine Weird Tales. The title refers to an ancient fish god of the Philistines, mentioned in the Bible. The story is a confession, written by a desperate man on the last night of his life, describing what he saw after escaping a German ship and drifting in a lifeboat across the Pacific. It is short, and its ideas are enormous: that humanity is a recent, fragile accident, and that older things may be waiting beneath the sea. Pay attention to the narrator's growing panic, and to how much he refuses to describe.
paragraphs: I am writing this under an appreciable mental strain, since by tonight I shall be no more. Penniless, and at the end of my supply of the drug which alone makes life endurable, I can bear the torture no longer; and shall cast myself from this garret window into the squalid street below. Do not think from my slavery to morphine that I am a weakling or a degenerate. When you have read these hastily scrawled pages you may guess, though never fully realize, why it is that I must have forgetfulness or death.

It was in one of the most open and least frequented parts of the Pacific that the packet of which I was supercargo fell a victim to the German sea-raider. The great war was then at its very beginning, and the enemy’s navy had not reached its later degree of ruthlessness, so that our vessel was made a legitimate prize, whilst we of her crew were treated with all the fairness and consideration due us as naval prisoners. So liberal, indeed, was the discipline of our captors, that five days after we were taken I managed to escape alone in a small boat with water and provisions for a good length of time.

When I finally found myself adrift and free, I had but little idea of my surroundings. Never a competent navigator, I could only guess vaguely by the sun and stars that I was somewhat south of the equator. Of the longitude I knew nothing, and no island or coastline was in sight. The weather kept fair, and for uncounted days I drifted aimlessly beneath the scorching sun; waiting either for some passing ship, or to be cast on the shores of some habitable land. But neither ship nor land appeared, and I began to despair in my solitude upon the heaving vastness of unbroken blue.

The change happened whilst I slept. Its details I shall never know; for my slumber, though troubled and dream-infested, was continuous. When at last I awaked, it was to discover myself half sucked into a slimy expanse of hellish black mire which extended about me in monotonous undulations as far as I could see, and in which my boat lay grounded some distance away.

Though one might well imagine that my first sensation would be of wonder at so prodigious and unexpected a transformation of scenery, I was in reality more horrified than astonished, for there was in the air and in the rotting soil a sinister quality which chilled me to the very core. The region was putrid with the carcasses of decaying fish, and of other less describable things which I saw protruding from the nasty mud of the unending plain. Perhaps I should not hope to convey in mere words the unutterable hideousness that can dwell in absolute silence and barren immensity. There was nothing within hearing, and nothing in sight save a vast reach of black slime; yet the very completeness of the stillness and the homogeneity of the landscape oppressed me with a nauseating fear.

The sun was blazing down from a sky which seemed to me almost black in its cloudless cruelty; as though reflecting the inky marsh beneath my feet. As I crawled into the stranded boat I realized that only one theory could explain my position. Through some unprecedented volcanic upheaval, a portion of the ocean floor must have been thrown to the surface, exposing regions which for innumerable millions of years had lain hidden under unfathomable watery depths. So great was the extent of the new land which had risen under me, that I could not detect the faintest noise of the surging ocean, strain my ears as I might. Nor were there any sea-fowl to prey upon the dead things.

For several hours I sat thinking or brooding in the boat, which lay on its side and afforded a slight shade as the sun moved across the heavens. As the day progressed, the ground lost some of its stickiness, and seemed likely to dry sufficiently for traveling purposes in a short time. That night I slept but little, and the next day I made for myself a pack containing food and water, preparatory to an overland journey in search of the vanished sea and possible rescue.

On the third morning I found the soil dry enough to walk upon with ease. The odor of the fish was maddening; but I was too much concerned with graver things to mind so slight an evil, and set out boldly for an unknown goal. All day I forged steadily westward, guided by a faraway hummock which rose higher than any other elevation on the rolling desert. That night I camped, and on the following day still traveled toward the hummock, though that object seemed scarcely nearer than when I had first spied it. By the fourth evening I attained the base of the mound, which turned out to be much higher than it had appeared from a distance; an intervening valley setting it out in sharper relief from the general surface. Too weary to ascend, I slept in the shadow of the hill.

I do not know why my dreams were so wild that night, but before the waning and fantastically gibbous moon had risen far above the eastern plain, I was awake in a cold perspiration, determined to sleep no more. Such visions as I had experienced were too much for me to endure again. And in the glow of the moon I saw how unwise I had been to travel by day. Without the glare of the parching sun, my journey would have cost me less energy; indeed, I now felt quite able to perform the ascent which had deterred me at sunset. Picking up my pack, I started for the crest of the eminence.

I have said that the unbroken monotony of the rolling plain was a source of vague horror to me; but I think my horror was greater when I gained the summit of the mound and looked down the other side into an immeasurable pit or canyon, whose black recesses the moon had not yet soared high enough to illumine. I felt myself on the edge of the world; peering over the rim into a fathomless chaos of eternal night. Through my terror ran curious reminiscences of Paradise Lost, and of Satan’s hideous climb through the unfashioned realms of darkness.

As the moon climbed higher in the sky, I began to see that the slopes of the valley were not quite so perpendicular as I had imagined. Ledges and outcroppings of rock afforded fairly easy footholds for a descent, whilst after a drop of a few hundred feet, the declivity became very gradual. Urged on by an impulse which I cannot definitely analyze, I scrambled with difficulty down the rocks and stood on the gentler slope beneath, gazing into the Stygian deeps where no light had yet penetrated.

All at once my attention was captured by a vast and singular object on the opposite slope, which rose steeply about a hundred yards ahead of me; an object that gleamed whitely in the newly bestowed rays of the ascending moon. That it was merely a gigantic piece of stone, I soon assured myself; but I was conscious of a distinct impression that its contour and position were not altogether the work of Nature. A closer scrutiny filled me with sensations I cannot express; for despite its enormous magnitude, and its location in an abyss which had yawned at the bottom of the sea since the world was young, I perceived beyond a doubt that the strange object was a well-shaped monolith whose massive bulk had known the workmanship and perhaps the worship of living and thinking creatures.

Dazed and frightened, yet not without a certain thrill of the scientist’s or archaeologist’s delight, I examined my surroundings more closely. The moon, now near the zenith, shone weirdly and vividly above the towering steeps that hemmed in the chasm, and revealed the fact that a far-flung body of water flowed at the bottom, winding out of sight in both directions, and almost lapping my feet as I stood on the slope.

Across the chasm, the wavelets washed the base of the Cyclopean monolith; on whose surface I could now trace both inscriptions and crude sculptures. The writing was in a system of hieroglyphics unknown to me, and unlike anything I had ever seen in books; consisting for the most part of conventionalized aquatic symbols such as fishes, eels, octopi, crustaceans, molluscs, whales, and the like. Several characters obviously represented marine things which are unknown to the modern world, but whose decomposing forms I had observed on the ocean-risen plain.

It was the pictorial carving, however, that did most to hold me spellbound. Plainly visible across the intervening water on account of their enormous size, were an array of bas-reliefs whose subjects would have excited the envy of a Doré. I think that these things were supposed to depict men⁠—at least, a certain sort of men; though the creatures were shown disporting like fishes in the waters of some marine grotto, or paying homage at some monolithic shrine which appeared to be under the waves as well. Of their faces and forms I dare not speak in detail; for the mere remembrance makes me grow faint. Grotesque beyond the imagination of a Poe or a Bulwer, they were damnably human in general outline despite webbed hands and feet, shockingly wide and flabby lips, glassy, bulging eyes, and other features less pleasant to recall. Curiously enough, they seemed to have been chiseled badly out of proportion with their scenic background; for one of the creatures was shown in the act of killing a whale represented as but little larger than himself.

I remarked, as I say, their grotesqueness and strange size; but in a moment decided that they were merely the imaginary gods of some primitive fishing or seafaring tribe; some tribe whose last descendant had perished eras before the first ancestor of the Piltdown or Neanderthal man was born. Awestruck at this unexpected glimpse into a past beyond the conception of the most daring anthropologist, I stood musing, whilst the moon cast queer reflections on the silent channel before me.

Then suddenly I saw it. With only a slight churning to mark its rise to the surface, the thing slid into view above the dark waters. Vast, Polyphemus-like, and loathsome, it darted like a stupendous monster of nightmares to the monolith, about which it flung its gigantic scaly arms, the while it bowed its hideous head and gave vent to certain measured sounds. I think I went mad then.

Of my frantic ascent of the slope and cliff, and of my delirious journey back to the stranded boat, I remember little. I believe I sang a great deal, and laughed oddly when I was unable to sing. I have indistinct recollections of a great storm some time after I reached the boat; at any rate, I know that I heard peals of thunder and other tones which Nature utters only in wild and terrible moods.

When I came out of the shadows I was in a San Francisco hospital; brought thither by the captain of the American ship which had picked up my boat in mid-ocean. In my delirium I had said much, but found that my words had been given scant attention. Of any land upheaval in the Pacific, my rescuers knew nothing; nor did I deem it necessary to insist upon a thing which I knew they could not believe. Once I sought out a celebrated ethnologist, and amused him with peculiar questions regarding the ancient Philistine legend of Dagon, the Fish-God; but, soon perceiving that he was hopelessly conventional, I did not press my inquiries.

It is at night, especially when the moon is gibbous and waning, that I see the thing. I tried morphine, but the drug has given only transient surcease, and has drawn me into its clutches as a hopeless slave. So now I am going to end matters, having written a full account for the information or the contemptuous amusement of my fellow-men. Often I ask myself if it could not all have been a pure phantasm⁠—a mere freak of fever as I lay sun-stricken and raving in the open boat after my escape from the German man-of-war.

This I ask myself, but ever does there come before me a hideously vivid vision in reply. I cannot think of the deep sea without shuddering at the nameless things that may at this very moment be crawling and floundering on its slimy bed, worshipping their ancient stone idols and carving their own detestable likenesses on submarine obelisks of water-soaked granite. I dream of a day when they may rise above the billows to drag down in their reeking talons the remnants of puny, war-exhausted mankind⁠—of a day when the land shall sink, and the dark ocean floor shall ascend amidst universal pandemonium.
The end is near. I hear a noise at the door, as of some immense slippery body lumbering against it. It shall not find me. God, that hand! The window! The window!

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
Dagon is a confession written by a man who has already decided to die. In the first lines he tells us that he is penniless, addicted to morphine, and about to throw himself from a garret window. He insists that he is not a weakling, and promises that once we have read his pages, we may guess why he needs either forgetfulness or death. This opening matters because it frames everything that follows as the testimony of a damaged man, and it plants the question the story never quite answers: did this really happen, or is he mad?

His account begins in the First World War. He was a ship's officer, a supercargo, whose vessel was captured by a German sea raider in the Pacific. He escapes in a small boat and drifts for days under the sun, with no idea where he is. Then, while he sleeps, something changes. He wakes half-sunk in a vast plain of black, stinking mud, strewn with rotting fish and other things he cannot name. His boat lies stranded, and there is no sound of the ocean at all. He reasons that a volcanic upheaval has pushed part of the sea floor to the surface, exposing what had been hidden for millions of years.

After some days the mud hardens, and he walks across it toward a distant rise. Beyond it lies a chasm with a great monolith on the far side, covered with carvings and hieroglyphs unlike any he has seen. The carvings show aquatic creatures and enormous bas-reliefs of beings that are almost men but behave like fish. Then, in the moonlight, something rises out of the water. It is described as "Vast, Polyphemus-like, and loathsome," and it wraps its arms around the monolith, bowing its head and making measured sounds, as though in worship. The narrator says simply, "I think I went mad then."

The meaning of this scene is the beating heart of the story. The creature is not acting as a monster would, attacking or hunting. It is praying. The monolith is an altar, and the sea creature a worshipper, perhaps of Dagon himself. What horrifies the narrator is not just the size of the thing but the realization that these beings have beliefs, history, and art that predate humanity by an unthinkable span of time. The universe contains minds older and larger than ours, and they do not know or care that we exist.

That is why the ending is so bleak. The narrator is rescued and goes home, but he cannot forget. He asks a scholar about Dagon, finds him hopelessly conventional, and gives up trying to be believed. He imagines the creatures rising one day to drag down "puny, war-exhausted mankind." The story ends with a sound at his door, as of an immense slippery body, and the broken cry, "God, that hand! The window! The window!" There is no escape, no explanation, and no comfort. The horror is not simply that something is coming for him, but that the world is not the safe, human-centered place he believed it to be.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
Dagon is a landmark and also a rough draft, and it is best read as both. Its greatest virtue is the way it builds dread out of emptiness. The central stretch, in which the narrator wakes on an endless plain of black mud under an inky sky, is genuinely unsettling. Lovecraft makes silence and sameness into the enemy. The line about the "unutterable hideousness that can dwell in absolute silence and barren immensity" captures his whole approach: the true terror is not a monster but the scale of a space that does not care about us. In a few paragraphs he gives us a landscape that feels both physically vivid and psychologically bottomless.

The framing device also works. By beginning with a suicide note, Lovecraft gives the narrator authority and urgency. He is not telling us a ghost story for entertainment, but leaving a final statement. The addiction detail adds ambiguity, because the reader can never be certain whether he has seen the truth or the results of fever and drugs. That doubt helps the story, since it lets the horror remain just outside proof, a method Lovecraft would use for the rest of his career.

But the story has weaknesses that readers should recognize. The prose is already heavily ornamented, with adjectives like hideous, loathsome, and nameless carrying a lot of the weight. When the narrator keeps telling us that things are beyond description, it can start to feel like a way of avoiding the work of description. Some readers feel that the crucial creature is introduced with a rush and a shrug, a big scaly thing that appears, hugs a rock, and sends the narrator running. After the careful build-up, the climax is brief and somewhat conventional, and the big reveal, a giant fish-man, can feel less frightening than the empty landscape that preceded it.

The ending is also uneven. The final, abrupt cry about the hand and the window is dramatic, but it comes close to melodrama. It resembles the closing lines of a pulp tale, ending on an exclamation rather than on a resonant image. Lovecraft would later refine this technique, often letting his narrators trail off in more subtle ways.

There is also an issue of plausibility within the story's own terms. The narrator's journey, from lifeboat to risen sea floor to hospital, is skimmed through quickly, and the suicide framing means that we are left wondering how he finds the energy to write so thoroughly. These are small points, and a reader swept along by the mood will forgive them. But they show that Dagon is a young writer's work: strong in concept and atmosphere, a little rushed in execution. Its power lies in the idea and the first great landscape, not in finish. What makes it worth reading is that the seeds of the later, more polished work are so clearly visible.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
Dagon's importance is largely in what it started. Written in July 1917, it is usually considered the first of Lovecraft's mature stories, the point where he moved from the Poe-style apprenticeship of his teenage years to the cosmic outlook that defines his reputation. He had stopped writing fiction for several years, partly because of ill health and a sense of failure. Encouraged by involvement in the amateur press, a network of hobbyist writers and small magazines, he returned to storytelling with Dagon and its companion, The Tomb. The story appeared in the amateur magazine The Vagrant in November 1919, and its reprint in Weird Tales in October 1923 was among his first appearances in the magazine that would make him famous.

Its content became a template. The idea of an ancient, aquatic race worshipping a sea god, the stone monuments risen from the deep, and the narrator who learns an unbearable truth all return in later work. The most famous descendants are The Call of Cthulhu, with its sunken city of R'lyeh and its worship of a vast creature, and The Shadow over Innsmouth, which develops the fish-people idea into a full tale of a town of hybrid worshippers. Lovecraft's later writers and fans often take the term Deep Ones from the latter story to describe such beings, and Dagon is regularly cited as an early appearance of the concept. The god Dagon himself later becomes part of the wider Cthulhu mythos, a collective name for the shared world of stories by Lovecraft and his followers.

Beyond Lovecraft, the story has had a wide cultural reach. Stories of ancient sea cults and monstrous ocean depths have become a staple of horror in film, games, and fiction. The idea that the deep sea hides something older than us has echoes in countless later tales. There is a 2001 film called Dagon, a Spanish production directed by Stuart Gordon, which borrows mainly from The Shadow over Innsmouth but carries the title. Role-playing games and comic adaptations have also drawn on the story, and the notion of the unwitting witness driven to despair has become a Lovecraftian signature.

For Lovecraft's own career, Dagon is a milestone. It was the first story in which he expressed the idea that would later be called cosmic horror, a fear based not on ghosts or curses but on the insignificance of humanity in an ancient, indifferent universe. He had always been drawn to science, especially astronomy, and the story reflects a worldview shaped by that, one in which humanity is a recent accident and the world is far stranger than we imagine.

Today, Dagon is regularly anthologized, taught as an introduction to Lovecraft, and read as the first clear statement of his central themes. Its brevity makes it a favorite entry point for readers curious about the writer who shaped modern horror.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers have admired Dagon for a few key qualities, and the first is its concept. The notion that the ocean floor might be thrown up and reveal the remains of a vanished, monstrous civilization is both simple and spectacular. Many people who encounter the story remember the image of the black mud plain and the towering monolith long after they forget the details. It feels like something between a geological catastrophe and a religious vision, and it taps a fear many of us share about the deep sea: that vast, dark, unseen world beneath the waves.

Second, they love its mood of dread. Lovecraft was a master at making emptiness frightening, and Dagon is an early demonstration. The silence of the plain, the putrid smell, the black sky, and the narrator's creeping sense of being watched give the story a nightmarish pull that can feel more real than a conventional ghost story. Many horror fans find that the first half, before any monster appears, is the most gripping part.

Third, readers appreciate the human voice of the narrator. His desperation and his strange, formal politeness make him a haunting figure. He addresses us directly, insists on his sanity, and pleads for a hearing, and the mix of dignity and despair is moving. His final, broken lines, written as something presses against the door, are among the most memorable endings in short horror fiction. Many people can recite them from memory.

Fourth, the story is compact. At about two thousand words, it delivers a complete experience quickly, which suits readers who want atmosphere without long commitments. It is also a perfect test case for the cosmic horror idea: after reading it, you understand what Lovecraft meant when people say his horror is about scale rather than gore.

Finally, readers like that it opens a door. A great many fans of Lovecraft came to him through this story, and then followed its hints toward the Cthulhu stories, the Deep Ones, and the whole mythology. Because the story leaves so much unexplained, it invites imagination. What are those creatures? What did they build? What were they praying to? The questions are part of the pleasure, and many writers and gamers have taken up the invitation to answer them. For readers who enjoy a story that opens up a world rather than closes it, Dagon is endlessly generous.

It also benefits from its historical timing. Written in the middle of a devastating world war, it carries a sense of civilization exhausted and fragile, and that mood speaks to readers who sense that modern life rests on thin ground.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Dagon has received a fair amount of criticism over the years, much of it from fans who still love it. The most common complaint is that it is derivative. The influence of Edgar Allan Poe is plain, in the confessional narrator, the doomed tone, and the use of an unnamed, unspeakable horror. There is also a strong debt to the fantasy writer Lord Dunsany and to the sea stories of William Hope Hodgson, whose tales of terrifying ocean depths cover similar ground. Some critics regard Dagon as a promising apprentice work that borrows more than it invents.

A second criticism is about style. The language is heavy and often melodramatic. The narrator repeatedly tells us what we should feel, using words like loathsome, hideous, and unutterable, rather than letting events carry the weight. The strongest example is the climactic creature, described in vague, grandiose terms, which some find unsatisfying. Critics who prefer restraint see this as the weakness Lovecraft never fully overcame.

A third criticism concerns structure and logic. The story depends on a number of conveniences: an unexplained geological upheaval, a lucky escape, a sudden rescue, and a narrator who survives long enough to write it all down. Some readers feel the story's plot is held together by hand-waving, and that the supernatural and scientific explanations pull in different directions. The question of whether the whole thing is a delusion caused by morphine or fever is raised but not resolved, and for some readers that is a smart ambiguity while for others it is a cop-out.

A fourth concern is the broader set of attitudes in Lovecraft's work. His fears of degeneration, of mixing between kinds, and of ancient hybrid beings are tied to his well-documented racial anxieties, which become more visible in later stories like The Shadow over Innsmouth. In Dagon the theme is mild, but the fish-men, drawn as almost-human creatures that provoke disgust, belong to a pattern in which the strange and foreign are presented as horrifying. Modern critics often point this out, and it is a reason some readers approach Lovecraft with caution.

Finally, there is the matter of how it ends. The suicide frame, in which the narrator kills himself because of what he has seen, can strike some readers as sensational. It is an old pulp device, and it is used here in a quick and slightly theatrical way. Readers today may also feel uneasy about the treatment of addiction as a plot device rather than as a real condition. None of these objections cancels the story's power, but they explain why it is generally described as important and effective rather than perfect.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
Dagon belongs to the tradition of weird fiction and the Gothic, with a strong link to the sea story. The sea has long been a place of horror in literature, from the voyage tales of Poe, such as The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym, to Herman Melville's Moby-Dick, in which the ocean is both beautiful and terrifying, to the nightmare sea tales of William Hope Hodgson. Lovecraft borrows that sense of the ocean as a vast, uncaring other world, then pushes it further by suggesting that it holds a hidden history.

It also belongs to the literature of the unreliable witness. The narrator who may or may not be sane, who has seen something no one will believe, is a staple of Gothic fiction, and Poe in particular used it again and again. But Lovecraft gives the device a new twist. The horror is not a personal guilt or a haunted house but a fact about the universe, and the narrator's despair comes from knowledge rather than from sin.
