When she put him to bed, she would stay a long time making the Cross over him and murmuring a prayer; then she would go to bed and dream of that faraway misty future when Sasha would finish his studies and become a doctor or an engineer, would have a big house of his own with horses and a carriage, would get married and have children.⁠ ⁠… She would fall asleep still thinking of the same thing, and tears would run down her cheeks from her closed eyes, while the black cat lay purring beside her: “Mrr, mrr, mrr.”
Suddenly there would come a loud knock at the gate.
Olenka would wake up breathless with alarm, her heart throbbing. Half a minute later would come another knock.
“It must be a telegram from Harkov,” she would think, beginning to tremble from head to foot. “Sasha’s mother is sending for him from Harkov.⁠ ⁠… Oh, mercy on us!”

She was in despair. Her head, her hands, and her feet would turn chill, and she would feel that she was the most unhappy woman in the world. But another minute would pass, voices would be heard: it would turn out to be the veterinary surgeon coming home from the club.
“Well, thank God!” she would think.
And gradually the load in her heart would pass off, and she would feel at ease. She would go back to bed thinking of Sasha, who lay sound asleep in the next room, sometimes crying out in his sleep:
“I’ll give it you! Get away! Shut up!”

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
Olenka is the daughter of a retired minor official, sitting on her porch in a small provincial town. She is a gentle, pleasant, sweet-faced woman, and everyone who knows her calls her Darling. The story follows her through four attachments. First comes Kukin, the harried manager of an open-air theatre called the Tivoli, who complains constantly about the weather and the vulgar public. Olenka marries him and adopts his worries as her own, talking of nothing but the theatre and the theatre's tragedies. When he dies suddenly in Moscow, she mourns. Then she marries Pustovalov, a quiet, sober manager at a timber yard, and instantly becomes a woman who talks only of timber, prices and the wickedness of dealers. When he too dies, she falls in with Smirnin, a veterinary surgeon, and suddenly speaks only of cattle plague and the need for sanitary inspections of animals. He is then transferred away, and Olenka is left alone, with no opinions at all. Finally she finds a new object of love in the veterinarian's young son, Sasha, whose schoolwork and moods she makes her entire life.

The core meaning is hinted at in a line near the story's low point, when she is alone: the awful thing is that she had no opinions of any sort. She sees a bottle or the rain, understands what she sees, but cannot say anything about it. Olenka has no self that is independent of the person she loves. Her thoughts, speech, even her way of laughing are borrowed. When the man goes, the borrowed content goes with him, and she is empty, a vessel with nothing in it.

On one level, Chekhov is poking fun. There is something comic in the way she repeats her husband's words, in the speed with which she converts from theatre to timber to veterinary medicine. On a deeper level, the story is wondering about what love is. Olenka's capacity to give herself to another is overwhelming and entirely sincere. She asks for nothing. But is it love, or is it dependence that looks like love? The story lets both readings stand.

The layer that readers often miss lies in the ending. With Sasha, Olenka's affection finally takes a form that is selfless in the fullest sense, a mother's love for a child who is not her own. She is torn with anxiety, defends him from imagined dangers, repeats his teachers' opinions as though they were scripture, and sits awake worrying. The story ends not with a verdict but with Olenka lying awake after a knock at the gate, fearing it is a telegram calling the boy away, until she hears it is only the veterinarian coming home from the club. The relief that follows is the closest thing she has to happiness, and the final image of the sleeping boy shouting threats in his dreams is a perfect, slightly comic touch. We are left with a woman who has finally found, in a child's chatter, something that will outlast her borrowed opinions, and with the open question of whether the child will repay or release her.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
The craft in The Darling is deceptively simple. Chekhov relies on repetition and variation: Olenka falls in love, takes on her husband's language, loses him, and starts again. The structure is almost a fable or a comic song with four verses, and the repetition does the work of satire. We learn to anticipate each transformation, and the humor comes from watching how thoroughly she mirrors each new partner. The shift from the theatre to timber is the best joke, because she does not simply adopt the new interest, she takes it up with the same solemn intensity as she had the last one. Yet Chekhov never lets the humor tip over into cruelty. The moments of grief, when Kukin dies and when she is left alone, are described with such plain sympathy that the laughter catches in the throat.

The prose is crisp and unadorned, with a gift for the telling particular. Olenka's plump, white neck, her soft smile, and the way she looks at people with such innocence that they cannot help responding with warmth are rendered in a few strokes. The description of her emptiness, with the yard overgrown and the house falling to ruin as she sits without opinions, is quietly devastating. The cat, the old cook and the empty yard are all that remain.

The great achievement is tonal balance, and it is also the source of the story's problems. Chekhov wants to hold satire and tenderness together, and for most of the story he does. But the final section, the love for Sasha, drifts toward sentimentality. Olenka's maternal passion is described in glowing terms, and the story seems to approve of it with less irony than before. The boy himself is thinly drawn, a vehicle for her feelings more than a person. Some readers feel the ending is almost too warm, too redeeming, and that it softens the question the earlier parts posed. If Olenka's vacancy is a tragic flaw, the tenderness of the last section seems to excuse it a little too easily.

There is also something slightly schematic about the four men. They are distinct, but each is mostly a type, there to supply Olenka with her opinions. Kukin, with his theatrical misery, is vivid and funny, but Pustovalov and Smirnin are sketches. The women of the story are even more sketchy. In the whole narrative, the interest focuses on a single quality in a single character, and a reader hungry for plot or for social texture may find it thin.

And yet, the compression is remarkable. In under five thousand words, Chekhov creates a character who has entered the language, so that someone is called a darling in the sense of a person who has no independent views. He also invents a structure, the comic cycle that deepens into pathos, that few writers have managed so cleanly. It is a minor Chekhov in scale, but a nearly perfect one in execution, with its main flaw being a gentleness that some feel goes slightly too far.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The Darling appeared in Russian magazines at the end of the nineteenth century, a period of great productivity for Chekhov. He was living in Yalta for his health, writing stories like The Lady with the Dog, and had begun a close association with the Moscow Art Theatre that would produce his major plays. Within this body of work, The Darling quickly became one of his most popular and most discussed stories, in part because it seemed to be about a figure everyone recognized.

Its single most famous episode of reception is the response of Leo Tolstoy. Tolstoy loved the story and read it aloud to friends and family. Later, in 1905, he wrote a commentary on it, arguing that Chekhov had set out to mock Olenka but had been overcome by the poetry of her nature, so that, as Tolstoy put it, the author meant to curse and ended by blessing. Tolstoy argued that her capacity for love was a great gift, misdirected only because it was given to unworthy objects, and that the right object would have been something higher. Whether or not one accepts his reading, which was heavily colored by Tolstoy's own religious and moral views, it set the terms for debates about the story for generations. The fact that the era's greatest novelist wrote a commentary on a short story is itself a measure of its impact.

The story also became a point of reference in discussions of gender. In Russia and abroad, the word darling, in English translations, became shorthand for a woman who defines herself through her relationships. Feminist critics in the twentieth century revisited the story, some reading it as a satire of women's enforced dependence in a society that gave them no independent roles, others as a warning against the habits that dependence produced. The debate over whether Olenka is a victim of her circumstances or a woman of unusual virtue continues.

In literature, The Darling helped establish Chekhov's reputation as a writer who could draw a complete character in a brief space. It influenced later writers of the short story who focused on single, oddly specific personalities, and its mixture of comedy and compassion was a model for Katherine Mansfield, Isaac Babel and others. It has been adapted for stage and screen, including a Soviet film in 1966 directed by Samson Samsonov, and it remains a staple of anthologies and classrooms.

It is also taught as a case study in ambiguous authorial intention. Students are asked whether Chekhov is satirizing Olenka or celebrating her, and the answer, that he does both, becomes a lesson in how stories can exceed their authors' plans. It is a standard example in discussions of irony, characterization and the role of the reader in making meaning.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
What readers have most often loved about The Darling is Olenka herself. She is one of those characters who feels entirely alive, even though she is a type. People recognize her. Almost everyone has met someone who agrees warmly with whoever spoke last, or has noticed that tendency in themselves. Chekhov catches the way she shifts without any sense of hypocrisy, since she is utterly sincere each time. That sincerity is the key. She is not a flatterer or a schemer; she simply gives herself fully, and readers find that both funny and moving.

They love the comedy too. The episode in which she lectures guests about the price of timber, repeating her husband's phrases, is the kind of gentle humor that Chekhov did better than almost anyone. The transformation of her views is delightfully quick. Her sudden concern about veterinary matters, expressed with total authority, gets a laugh without cruelty. The humor makes the sadness more bearable and the sadness makes the humor richer.

Another strength readers admire is the final movement, with the boy Sasha. Many readers report being moved by the picture of Olenka's anxious devotion, her sleeplessness and her awe at his lessons. The woman who has nothing to say about the world suddenly has a whole world in a child. For some, this is the story's real discovery: that love, even love without self, can give life its meaning. The last image, of the boy murmuring in his sleep and the woman listening with a full heart, is often cited as one of the most affecting moments in Chekhov.

Writers and critics have praised the tact of the story. Chekhov does not tell us what to think about Olenka. He trusts the reader to feel the complexity. That trust has made the story a favorite among writers, who often single it out as an example of how to handle a character who might otherwise be reduced to a joke. The fact that Tolstoy, so often severe in his views, found in it a revelation of the soul is part of the admiration it has inspired.

Finally, readers like its brevity and shape. It can be read in twenty minutes, and it contains a whole life. Its simplicity makes it a favorite introduction to Chekhov, and its depth rewards rereading. Many people describe reading it first as a young person, finding it funny, and returning to it as an adult, finding it painful, which may be the best sign that a story is doing something real.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
The most persistent objection to The Darling concerns its view of women. From the beginning, some readers felt that the story was condescending, that Olenka is a portrait of a woman with no mind of her own, drawn by a male author with a mixture of affection and amusement. The suggestion that a woman is nothing without a man to define her can feel like a stereotype. Later feminist critics have argued that Chekhov mistakes the effects of a restricted social position for a feature of feminine nature. Olenka has no education, no profession and few options, so her dependence is not a character flaw so much as a condition. Other critics reply that Chekhov was well aware of this, and that the story's sympathy is a form of critique, but the question of how far a male author can be trusted with this subject has not gone away.

Contemporary critics also disagreed about the author's intent. Some read the story as straightforward satire, an exercise in mocking a silly, empty-headed woman. Others thought the satire collapsed under the weight of the author's affection. Tolstoy's reading, that the story blessed what it meant to curse, was itself challenged. Some critics argued that Tolstoy twisted the story into a vehicle for his own moral teaching about love and God, and that Chekhov, a skeptical doctor with no religious program, would not have shared that interpretation. The disagreement shows that readers project their own values onto Olenka.

A third criticism is about sentimentality. The last section, in which Olenka's love finds its fullest expression in the care of a child, has been called too soft. Critics have argued that Chekhov flinches from the harder implication of his own premise, that a person without a self is in some way diminished, by rewarding her with a happy ending. The suggestion that a woman is fulfilled by caring for a child is, to a modern reader, a little conventional, and the boy's own wishes are left unexamined. There is a hint of danger in her devotion, since a child may not want to be the entire world to another person, but the story does not follow it.

Some have also suggested that the story's structure, with its four loves and its circular pattern, is too neat for Chekhov's own principles. The repetition can make the moral feel mechanical, and the brisk summary of whole marriages and bereavements gives them little emotional weight. A reader looking for the subtle, open-ended texture of The Lady with the Dog may find The Darling more schematic.

Still, these objections are made against a story that most readers like, and many of them are part of its enduring interest, since they keep the debate alive.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
The Darling belongs to the great tradition of nineteenth-century realism, in which writers drew ordinary people with fidelity and sympathy. It follows a line of portraits of provincial life in Russian literature, from Gogol's gallery of small-town characters to Turgenev's sketches and Leskov's stories. But it is distinctive in focusing on a single psychological peculiarity, a self formed entirely in relation to others, and in treating it with a delicate balance of comedy and compassion.

In the broader history of the short story, it is an example of the character study, a form that depends on a single vivid personality rather than plot. Flaubert's A Simple Heart, written in 1877, is a close relative, telling of a humble servant, Félicité, whose capacity for devotion attaches itself to a series of objects, ending with a parrot. Chekhov's story differs in its gentle humor and in the fact that Olenka's devotion is more social than religious, but the kinship is strong. Both stories ask whether a life of pure giving is a failure or a kind of grace. Later stories of the self-effacing, from Mansfield to Elizabeth Taylor to Alice Munro, often follow in this lineage.

The Darling also anticipates themes of identity that became central in the twentieth century. The idea that a self is built from the opinions of others, that we speak in borrowed words and have no inner core, is at the heart of modernist and later social-psychological thought. Olenka is a comic version of a question that modern writers treat with grim seriousness: what is a person when the roles are stripped away? Compared with the existential despair of a Kafka or a Beckett, she is a gentle, domestic case, but the question is the same.

It also belongs to the long conversation between Chekhov and Tolstoy about love and morality. Tolstoy's own stories and novels, from Family Happiness to Anna Karenina, are full of women whose lives are shaped by their love for others. His reading of the story as a blessing places it within his own search for the right object of love. Chekhov's looser, more skeptical outlook gives the story its characteristic openness.

Why read it now? Because the question it asks has not become less pressing. In an age of social media and constant opinion, many people shape their views to fit the groups around them. Olenka is both a warning and a comfort: a warning about a self that borrows everything, and a comfort in the reminder that the ability to love is not nothing. The story leaves us unsure whether to laugh, to weep or to admire, and that uncertainty, handled with such lightness, is what makes it great.

stories.title: Misery
stories.author: Anton Chekhov
stories.epigraph: “To Whom Shall I Tell My Grief?”
stories.keyContext: Anton Chekhov wrote Misery in 1886, when he was twenty-five or twenty-six, a young medical student and doctor turning out comic sketches for newspapers to make a living. It was one of the first stories in which he showed the quieter, sadder voice that would make him famous. It is short, only a few pages, and its situation could hardly be simpler. On a snowy night in Saint Petersburg, an old cab driver named Iona Potapov is grieving for his son, who died a few days ago, and he wants to tell someone. Nobody will listen. The story is a test of how much feeling a very small scene can carry. It asks what happens to grief that finds no one to receive it, and it suggests, without raising its voice, that the sorrow of an ordinary poor man deserves as much attention as any tragedy in a grand novel.
paragraphs: “To Whom Shall I Tell My Grief?”

The twilight of evening. Big flakes of wet snow are whirling lazily about the street lamps, which have just been lighted, and lying in a thin soft layer on roofs, horses’ backs, shoulders, caps. Iona Potapov, the sledge-driver, is all white like a ghost. He sits on the box without stirring, bent as double as the living body can be bent. If a regular snowdrift fell on him it seems as though even then he would not think it necessary to shake it off.⁠ ⁠… His little mare is white and motionless too. Her stillness, the angularity of her lines, and the stick-like straightness of her legs make her look like a halfpenny gingerbread horse. She is probably lost in thought. Anyone who has been torn away from the plough, from the familiar gray landscapes, and cast into this slough, full of monstrous lights, of unceasing uproar and hurrying people, is bound to think.

It is a long time since Iona and his nag have budged. They came out of the yard before dinnertime and not a single fare yet. But now the shades of evening are falling on the town. The pale light of the street lamps changes to a vivid color, and the bustle of the street grows noisier.
“Sledge to Vyborgskaya!” Iona hears. “Sledge!”
Iona starts, and through his snow-plastered eyelashes sees an officer in a military overcoat with a hood over his head.
“To Vyborgskaya,” repeats the officer. “Are you asleep? To Vyborgskaya!”

In token of assent Iona gives a tug at the reins which sends cakes of snow flying from the horse’s back and shoulders. The officer gets into the sledge. The sledge-driver clicks to the horse, cranes his neck like a swan, rises in his seat, and more from habit than necessity brandishes his whip. The mare cranes her neck, too, crooks her stick-like legs, and hesitatingly sets of.⁠ ⁠…
“Where are you shoving, you devil?” Iona immediately hears shouts from the dark mass shifting to and fro before him. “Where the devil are you going? Keep to the r-right!”
“You don’t know how to drive! Keep to the right,” says the officer angrily.

A coachman driving a carriage swears at him; a pedestrian crossing the road and brushing the horse’s nose with his shoulder looks at him angrily and shakes the snow off his sleeve. Iona fidgets on the box as though he were sitting on thorns, jerks his elbows, and turns his eyes about like one possessed as though he did not know where he was or why he was there.
“What rascals they all are!” says the officer jocosely. “They are simply doing their best to run up against you or fall under the horse’s feet. They must be doing it on purpose.”
Iona looks as his fare and moves his lips.⁠ ⁠… Apparently he means to say something, but nothing comes but a sniff.
“What?” inquires the officer.
Iona gives a wry smile, and straining his throat, brings out huskily: “My son⁠ ⁠… er⁠ ⁠… my son died this week, sir.”
“H’m! What did he die of?”
Iona turns his whole body round to his fare, and says:
“Who can tell! It must have been from fever.⁠ ⁠… He lay three days in the hospital and then he died.⁠ ⁠… God’s will.”
“Turn round, you devil!” comes out of the darkness. “Have you gone cracked, you old dog? Look where you are going!”
“Drive on! drive on!⁠ ⁠…” says the officer. “We shan’t get there till tomorrow going on like this. Hurry up!”

The sledge-driver cranes his neck again, rises in his seat, and with heavy grace swings his whip. Several times he looks round at the officer, but the latter keeps his eyes shut and is apparently disinclined to listen. Putting his fare down at Vyborgskaya, Iona stops by a restaurant, and again sits huddled up on the box.⁠ ⁠… Again the wet snow paints him and his horse white. One hour passes, and then another.⁠ ⁠…
Three young men, two tall and thin, one short and hunchbacked, come up, railing at each other and loudly stamping on the pavement with their goloshes.
“Cabby, to the Police Bridge!” the hunchback cries in a cracked voice. “The three of us,⁠ ⁠… twenty kopecks!”

Iona tugs at the reins and clicks to his horse. Twenty kopecks is not a fair price, but he has no thoughts for that. Whether it is a rouble or whether it is five kopecks does not matter to him now so long as he has a fare.⁠ ⁠… The three young men, shoving each other and using bad language, go up to the sledge, and all three try to sit down at once. The question remains to be settled: Which are to sit down and which one is to stand? After a long altercation, ill-temper, and abuse, they come to the conclusion that the hunchback must stand because he is the shortest.

“Well, drive on,” says the hunchback in his cracked voice, settling himself and breathing down Iona’s neck. “Cut along! What a cap you’ve got, my friend! You wouldn’t find a worse one in all Petersburg.⁠ ⁠…”
“He-he!⁠ ⁠… he-he!⁠ ⁠…” laughs Iona. “It’s nothing to boast of!”
“Well, then, nothing to boast of, drive on! Are you going to drive like this all the way? Eh? Shall I give you one in the neck?”
“My head aches,” says one of the tall ones. “At the Dukmasovs’ yesterday Vaska and I drank four bottles of brandy between us.”
“I can’t make out why you talk such stuff,” says the other tall one angrily. “You lie like a brute.”
“Strike me dead, it’s the truth!⁠ ⁠…”
“It’s about as true as that a louse coughs.”
“He-he!” grins Iona. “Me-er-ry gentlemen!”
“Tfoo! the devil take you!” cries the hunchback indignantly. “Will you get on, you old plague, or won’t you? Is that the way to drive? Give her one with the whip. Hang it all, give it her well.”

Iona feels behind his back the jolting person and quivering voice of the hunchback. He hears abuse addressed to him, he sees people, and the feeling of loneliness begins little by little to be less heavy on his heart. The hunchback swears at him, till he chokes over some elaborately whimsical string of epithets and is overpowered by his cough. His tall companions begin talking of a certain Nadyezhda Petrovna. Iona looks round at them. Waiting till there is a brief pause, he looks round once more and says:
“This week⁠ ⁠… er⁠ ⁠… my⁠ ⁠… er⁠ ⁠… son died!”
“We shall all die,⁠ ⁠…” says the hunchback with a sigh, wiping his lips after coughing. “Come, drive on! drive on! My friends, I simply cannot stand crawling like this! When will he get us there?”
“Well, you give him a little encouragement⁠ ⁠… one in the neck!”
“Do you hear, you old plague? I’ll make you smart. If one stands on ceremony with fellows like you one may as well walk. Do you hear, you old dragon? Or don’t you care a hang what we say?”
And Iona hears rather than feels a slap on the back of his neck.
“He-he!⁠ ⁠…” he laughs. “Merry gentlemen.⁠ ⁠… God give you health!”
“Cabman, are you married?” asks one of the tall ones.

“I? He he! Me-er-ry gentlemen. The only wife for me now is the damp earth.⁠ ⁠… He-ho-ho!⁠ ⁠… The grave that is!⁠ ⁠… Here my son’s dead and I am alive.⁠ ⁠… It’s a strange thing, death has come in at the wrong door.⁠ ⁠… Instead of coming for me it went for my son.⁠ ⁠…”

And Iona turns round to tell them how his son died, but at that point the hunchback gives a faint sigh and announces that, thank God! they have arrived at last. After taking his twenty kopecks, Iona gazes for a long while after the revelers, who disappear into a dark entry. Again he is alone and again there is silence for him.⁠ ⁠… The misery which has been for a brief space eased comes back again and tears his heart more cruelly than ever. With a look of anxiety and suffering Iona’s eyes stray restlessly among the crowds moving to and fro on both sides of the street: can he not find among those thousands someone who will listen to him? But the crowds flit by heedless of him and his misery.⁠ ⁠… His misery is immense, beyond all bounds. If Iona’s heart were to burst and his misery to flow out, it would flood the whole world, it seems, but yet it is not seen. It has found a hiding-place in such an insignificant shell that one would not have found it with a candle by daylight.⁠ ⁠…
Iona sees a house-porter with a parcel and makes up his mind to address him.
“What time will it be, friend?” he asks.
“Going on for ten.⁠ ⁠… Why have you stopped here? Drive on!”

Iona drives a few paces away, bends himself double, and gives himself up to his misery. He feels it is no good to appeal to people. But before five minutes have passed he draws himself up, shakes his head as though he feels a sharp pain, and tugs at the reins.⁠ ⁠… He can bear it no longer.
“Back to the yard!” he thinks. “To the yard!”

And his little mare, as though she knew his thoughts, falls to trotting. An hour and a half later Iona is sitting by a big dirty stove. On the stove, on the floor, and on the benches are people snoring. The air is full of smells and stuffiness. Iona looks at the sleeping figures, scratches himself, and regrets that he has come home so early.⁠ ⁠…

“I have not earned enough to pay for the oats, even,” he thinks. “That’s why I am so miserable. A man who knows how to do his work,⁠ ⁠… who has had enough to eat, and whose horse has had enough to eat, is always at ease.⁠ ⁠…”
In one of the corners a young cabman gets up, clears his throat sleepily, and makes for the water-bucket.
“Want a drink?” Iona asks him.
“Seems so.”
“May it do you good.⁠ ⁠… But my son is dead, mate.⁠ ⁠… Do you hear? This week in the hospital.⁠ ⁠… It’s a queer business.⁠ ⁠…”

Iona looks to see the effect produced by his words, but he sees nothing. The young man has covered his head over and is already asleep. The old man sighs and scratches himself.⁠ ⁠… Just as the young man had been thirsty for water, he thirsts for speech. His son will soon have been dead a week, and he has not really talked to anybody yet.⁠ ⁠… He wants to talk of it properly, with deliberation.⁠ ⁠… He wants to tell how his son was taken ill, how he suffered, what he said before he died, how he died.⁠ ⁠… He wants to describe the funeral, and how he went to the hospital to get his son’s clothes. He still has his daughter Anisya in the country.⁠ ⁠… And he wants to talk about her too.⁠ ⁠… Yes, he has plenty to talk about now. His listener ought to sigh and exclaim and lament.⁠ ⁠… It would be even better to talk to women. Though they are silly creatures, they blubber at the first word.
“Let’s go out and have a look at the mare,” Iona thinks. “There is always time for sleep.⁠ ⁠… You’ll have sleep enough, no fear.⁠ ⁠…”

He puts on his coat and goes into the stables where his mare is standing. He thinks about oats, about hay, about the weather.⁠ ⁠… He cannot think about his son when he is alone.⁠ ⁠… To talk about him with someone is possible, but to think of him and picture him is insufferable anguish.⁠ ⁠…

“Are you munching?” Iona asks his mare, seeing her shining eyes. “There, munch away, munch away.⁠ ⁠… Since we have not earned enough for oats, we will eat hay.⁠ ⁠… Yes,⁠ ⁠… I have grown too old to drive.⁠ ⁠… My son ought to be driving, not I.⁠ ⁠… He was a real cabman.⁠ ⁠… He ought to have lived.⁠ ⁠…”
Iona is silent for a while, and then he goes on:

“That’s how it is, old girl.⁠ ⁠… Kuzma Ionitch is gone.⁠ ⁠… He said goodbye to me.⁠ ⁠… He went and died for no reason.⁠ ⁠… Now, suppose you had a little colt, and you were own mother to that little colt.⁠ ⁠… And all at once that same little colt went and died.⁠ ⁠… You’d be sorry, wouldn’t you?⁠ ⁠…”
The little mare munches, listens, and breathes on her master’s hands. Iona is carried away and tells her all about it.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The story begins in the twilight of a winter evening. Wet snow falls on the street lamps and settles on the roofs, on the backs of horses, and on the cab driver, Iona Potapov, who sits so still on his sledge that he is white like a ghost. His little mare is just as white and motionless. He has had no fare since before dinner. Then an officer climbs in and asks to be driven to the Vyborg district. As they go, Iona tries to speak. All he can say is that his son died this week. The officer asks idly what he died of, then tells him to hurry. Later, three young men, two tall and one short and hunchbacked, take his sledge, joking and swearing and arguing about a drinking party. Iona tries again to speak, and again he is mocked and brushed aside. They get out. Finally, in the stable yard late at night, a young driver wakes briefly to ask for water, and Iona tries once more. The younger man turns over and goes back to sleep. In the end, Iona goes out to the stable and tells the whole story to his mare.

On the surface, nothing happens. That is the point. The story is built around a series of failed conversations, each one a small refusal. The officer's brief question is a reflex; the young men are too busy with their own talk; the porter and the younger driver are too tired or indifferent. Each person is not cruel, exactly. They are simply absorbed in themselves, as most of us are most of the time, and they cannot make room for a stranger's grief. Chekhov shows how loneliness is not the absence of people, since Iona is surrounded by a roaring city, but the absence of anyone who will listen.

The original title in Russian, usually translated as Misery, is also rendered as Grief or Anguish, and the story also carries the phrase To Whom Shall I Tell My Grief? as a kind of subtitle That question is the story's whole subject. There is an echo here of a religious tradition, in which sorrow is brought to God, and the final scene has a quiet irony: the only one who listens is an animal.

Notice the details. The mare is compared to a gingerbread horse, a cheap toy, so that Iona and his animal seem like discarded figures in the city's lights. Notice also how Iona's attempts to talk grow more urgent as the story proceeds. The first is a sentence to an officer, the last a whole outpouring. Notice, too, how the story avoids describing the son in much detail. We know he was a cabman, that he died of fever after three days in the hospital, and that Iona thinks he ought to have lived. Chekhov lets the reader supply the rest. The story ends with Iona carried away, telling the mare everything while she munches and breathes on his hands. The tenderness of that last gesture is the only comfort the story allows, and it is both beautiful and almost unbearable.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
The most impressive thing about Misery is its economy. In a very short space, Chekhov builds a complete emotional arc. The structure is a series of attempts, each slightly longer and more desperate than the last, with the climax coming not in a dramatic event but in a release. The repetition has the feel of a musical piece, with variations on a single theme, and the escalating rhythm makes the reader want Iona to succeed, which makes each rebuff hurt more. By the end, the reader is almost ready to be the listener that Iona needs, which is exactly what Chekhov wants.

His restraint is another strength. Chekhov never tells us that Iona's heart is breaking, and he never has Iona deliver a speech about the injustice of the world. The narrator keeps a calm, almost clinical distance, noting the snow, the lamp light and the slowness of the horse. This coolness does not weaken the feeling; it concentrates it. The famous opening image, in which a man is so bent under his sorrow that a snowdrift falling on him would make no difference, communicates the whole state of mind in a single picture. The cold detail of the officer shutting his eyes to avoid listening is another example of fact doing the work of emotion.

The story is also well observed in social terms. The sledge-drivers, the porters and the passengers are drawn with convincing humor and without condescension. The young men's bickering, the hunchback's cracked voice and the rude comments about Iona's cap make a lively, noisy contrast with the old man's silence. Chekhov also gives Iona small dignities, such as his wry laugh at the abuse and his steady care for the horse.

There are weaknesses, and they come mostly from the story's youth. The ending is potentially sentimental. A grieving man confiding in a faithful animal is a familiar device and could easily become mawkish. Chekhov largely avoids this by keeping Iona's speech plain and halting, and by letting the mare munch, but a stricter reader might feel that the last paragraph pushes slightly too hard, as though Chekhov wants to be sure we have felt it. The story is also quite schematic. The passengers are types, each designed to be a different kind of indifference. At times the structure feels a little too orderly, a little like a demonstration of a thesis.

And some of the shorthand about city life, with the monstrous lights and the horse torn from the plough, belongs to an older, more conventional style of social sympathy. It is not as subtle as the mature Chekhov, who would learn to leave even such comments out.

Even so, Misery is remarkable for a writer of his age. It shows what he could do with a few hundred words and a simple situation. If it is not as layered as The Lady with the Dog, it has an immediacy and a purity that the later stories only sometimes match. Its flaws are the flaws of a young master finding his voice, and its virtues are exactly the virtues that would define his mature art.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
Misery was published in a Saint Petersburg newspaper in January 1886, when Chekhov was still known mainly as a humorist who wrote under a comic pseudonym for small magazines. He had begun to find a wider audience, and in that same year the established writer Dmitry Grigorovich wrote to urge him to take his talent seriously and to stop dashing off work for quick pay. Misery belongs to the group of stories from this time that showed a more serious side. It is often cited as one of the early signs that Chekhov was becoming the writer we know, one who could make a whole world from a slight incident.

The story's influence on later fiction has been wide. It is one of the clearest early examples of a type of story that Chekhov helped to define, in which the plot is minimal, the emotion is carried by small details and the ending is a quiet note rather than a twist. Writers of the modern short story, including Katherine Mansfield, James Joyce and Raymond Carver, are in debt to this method. The Irish writer Frank O'Connor, in his well-known study of the short story, argued that the form often gives voice to what he called submerged populations, people on the margins of society, and Chekhov's cab driver is a perfect example.

Misery also belongs to a Russian tradition of sympathy for the small man, descending from Pushkin's The Station Master and Gogol's The Overcoat. In The Overcoat, a poor clerk is robbed of his coat, ignored by the authorities and dies. Chekhov takes the same compassion and strips away the supernatural coda and the broad comedy, leaving only the truth of loneliness. This continuity of Russian humane realism is a favorite topic in courses on the literature.

In popular and educational life, the story has been a mainstay. It is widely anthologized, taught in schools as an introduction to Chekhov because of its brevity, and used in classes on point of view and on showing rather than telling. It is also a frequent choice for translators, with versions by Constance Garnett and many later hands. The image of the old man talking to his horse has become an emblem of unspoken grief.

Another form of impact is the way it has been used outside literature. Its central image, of a person who cannot find a listener, is often cited in discussions of loneliness, bereavement and the importance of simply listening. Though this reception is informal rather than scholarly, it shows how the story's meaning spills beyond its time and place.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers have loved Misery, above all, for its emotional truth. Almost everyone has had the experience of needing to tell someone about a loss and sensing that the other person has no room to hear it. The officer's mild, absent-minded question about the cause of death, followed by an instant return to his own concerns, is painfully familiar. We have all been the officer at one time or another, and we have all been Iona. The story makes both recognitions possible, and readers often say they finish it wanting to be a better listener.

They also love the horse. There is something deeply touching in the old man's turning to the one creature that will stay with him, and in the small, solemn domestic details, such as the hay in place of oats and the mare's warm breath on his hands. The animal is neither a symbol nor a joke. She is simply present, and her presence is what Iona needs. Many readers find the last lines among the most moving in the whole of Chekhov, precisely because they refuse to tell us that it is enough.

The story's quietness is another source of admiration. It does not shout. It lets the snow fall and the lamps burn and the old man sit. In a literary culture that often prized dramatic effects, this modest approach felt fresh and true. Later writers have praised it for what it leaves out, for example the mother, the wife or the funeral, and for the dignity it grants a character who in life would be invisible. A cab driver in a threadbare cap, treated with such attention, became for many readers a proof that no life is too small for literature.

The humor, perhaps surprisingly, is something readers value too. The young men's banter, the hunchback's cracked voice and the clumsy argument over who will stand give the middle of the story a lively comic energy. This is the young Chekhov, the humorist, at work, and the contrast with Iona's silence heightens the sadness. The cruelty is never melodramatic. It is just the ordinary cruelty of busy, careless people, which is why it feels real.

Finally, readers like how short it is. It can be read in minutes, yet it stays in the mind for years. Many people remember the first time they read it. Teachers say students respond to it right away, even those who find older literature remote, because the situation, a person who wants to be heard, is immediate. That directness is rare and valuable.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Little detailed contemporary criticism of Misery has been recorded in English-language sources, and it is difficult to point to specific reviews of the 1886 publication. What can be said is that Chekhov's early work in general met a mixed reception in Russia. Critics of the time, especially those who expected literature to carry a clear social or political message, accused him of lacking convictions and of merely recording moods. A story like Misery, which shows suffering but proposes no cure and blames no one, was exactly the kind of work these critics found inadequate. The suggestion was that Chekhov's compassion was passive. A later generation of Soviet critics sometimes praised him as a witness to social injustice, while others found him insufficiently engaged.

The most common modern objection is sentimentality. Some readers feel that the device of a lonely man confiding in an animal is a stock sentimental image, and that the story tugs at the heartstrings more openly than the mature Chekhov would have done. The deliberate piling-up of rejections, officer, young men, porter, younger driver, can feel engineered, a bit like a machine for producing pathos. The tone of the opening, with its observations about the city's monstrous lights and the peasant torn from the plough, can seem a little too readily sympathetic. It is fair to say that Misery lacks the ambiguity of the later pieces.

Another line of criticism concerns its simplicity. Because the story has no twist and little psychological complexity, some readers find it slight, a sketch rather than a fully developed tale. Iona is a figure of pure suffering, with little else to him, and some critics have suggested that he is more an emblem than a person. The passengers, likewise, are types of indifference rather than rounded characters. This is a fair point, and it is why the story is often seen as a prelude to the greater stories.

There is also the question of whether the story's view of human indifference is too bleak or too accusatory. By presenting everyone but the horse as callous, Chekhov may seem to condemn his society wholesale, yet the story also acknowledges that these people are tired, cold and caught up in their own lives. Some readers feel this balance tips toward a slightly self-righteous pity. Others argue that the story's gentleness toward everyone, even the cruel hunchback, is what saves it.

None of these objections has diminished the story's standing. They mark it as an early work, strong in feeling and economy, and not yet the full subtlety of the later masterpieces.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
In the history of literature, Misery occupies the early stretch of Chekhov's career, before the great stories of the 1890s and the plays. It belongs to the broader movement of Russian realism, which sought to portray ordinary life truthfully, and to the more specific tradition of the humane story about the poor and powerless. Its ancestors include Pushkin's The Station Master, a tale of a lowly postmaster whose daughter is taken from him, and Gogol's The Overcoat, about a clerk whose life is destroyed by the loss of a garment. The Russian habit of looking at the small man with pity runs through Dostoevsky's Poor Folk and through Turgenev's sketches. Chekhov is distinctive in the lightness of his touch. He has none of Gogol's fantasy and none of Dostoevsky's feverish intensity; he offers instead a patient, clear-eyed attention.

Looking forward, the story is a step toward the modern short story. The idea that a story might consist of nothing more than a state of feeling, dramatized through a few encounters, and end without resolution, became a core principle of the form. It points toward Mansfield's quiet stories, Joyce's epiphanies, Hemingway's understatement and the contemporary tradition of Carver, Munro and William Trevor. Even outside fiction, its approach to showing suffering without commentary has parallels in documentary photography and film.

Comparison with Tolstoy is instructive. Tolstoy's The Death of Ivan Ilyich also considers the loneliness of someone facing death surrounded by uncomprehending people. But Tolstoy's story is long, philosophical and intensely moral, while Chekhov's is tiny, unsermonizing and rooted in an ordinary working man. Chekhov himself, in his story Vanka from the same year, portrays a boy's letter to his grandfather that will never arrive, another instance of an unheard voice. These pieces share a central image of communication failing, and they rank among the most affecting expressions of this theme in the literature.

There is also a link to modern drama. The way characters in Chekhov's plays talk past one another, each locked in private concerns, is already visible here in miniature, and the hunger to be heard is a driving force in The Three Sisters and Uncle Vanya. In that sense, Misery is a seed of his theatre.

Why read it today? Because its subject is as pressing as ever. In a world of constant noise and instant messages, loneliness is still the experience of not being heard. The story takes only a few minutes, and it asks nothing of us except attention, which is exactly what Iona needs and cannot find. Reading it is a small practice of the thing it recommends. When we finish it, we might want to turn to the next person and say, go on, I am listening.

stories.title: Vanka
stories.author: Anton Chekhov
stories.epigraph: “How about a pinch of snuff?” he was saying, offering the women his snuffbox.
stories.keyContext: Anton Chekhov wrote Vanka in 1886, when he was twenty-six, a young doctor in Moscow turning out comic sketches for newspapers under a joking pen name. It appeared in a Christmas issue, and it is one of the shortest and most quietly devastating stories he ever wrote. Chekhov knew this world. His grandfather had been a serf, born into bondage until his family bought its freedom, and Chekhov himself had watched children treated as cheap labor. Russia had freed its serfs only twenty-five years earlier, and freedom had left many poor families with few choices except to send their children away to work. The story follows a nine-year-old apprentice who writes a letter on Christmas Eve to the one person who loves him. Listen for the way Chekhov never begs you to cry. He simply lets a child describe his misery in a child's words, and then he lets you notice what the boy does not understand. Pay particular attention to the address on the envelope.
paragraphs: Vanka Zhukov, a boy of nine, who had been for three months apprenticed to Alyahin the shoemaker, was sitting up on Christmas Eve. Waiting till his master and mistress and their workmen had gone to the midnight service, he took out of his master’s cupboard a bottle of ink and a pen with a rusty nib, and, spreading out a crumpled sheet of paper in front of him, began writing. Before forming the first letter he several times looked round fearfully at the door and the windows, stole a glance at the dark icon, on both sides of which stretched shelves full of lasts, and heaved a broken sigh. The paper lay on the bench while he knelt before it.

“Dear grandfather, Konstantin Makaritch,” he wrote, “I am writing you a letter. I wish you a happy Christmas, and all blessings from God Almighty. I have neither father nor mother, you are the only one left me.”

Vanka raised his eyes to the dark icon on which the light of his candle was reflected, and vividly recalled his grandfather, Konstantin Makaritch, who was night watchman to a family called Zhivarev. He was a thin but extraordinarily nimble and lively little old man of sixty-five, with an everlastingly laughing face and drunken eyes. By day he slept in the servants’ kitchen, or made jokes with the cooks; at night, wrapped in an ample sheepskin, he walked round the grounds and tapped with his little mallet. Old Kashtanka and Eel, so-called on account of his dark colour and his long body like a weasel’s, followed him with hanging heads. This Eel was exceptionally polite and affectionate, and looked with equal kindness on strangers and his own masters, but had not a very good reputation. Under his politeness and meekness was hidden the most Jesuitical cunning. No one knew better how to creep up on occasion and snap at one’s legs, to slip into the storeroom, or steal a hen from a peasant. His hind legs had been nearly pulled off more than once, twice he had been hanged, every week he was thrashed till he was half dead, but he always revived.

At this moment grandfather was, no doubt, standing at the gate, screwing up his eyes at the red windows of the church, stamping with his high felt boots, and joking with the servants. His little mallet was hanging on his belt. He was clasping his hands, shrugging with the cold, and, with an aged chuckle, pinching first the housemaid, then the cook.
“How about a pinch of snuff?” he was saying, offering the women his snuffbox.
The women would take a sniff and sneeze. Grandfather would be indescribably delighted, go off into a merry chuckle, and cry:
“Tear it off, it has frozen on!”

They give the dogs a sniff of snuff too. Kashtanka sneezes, wriggles her head, and walks away offended. Eel does not sneeze, from politeness, but wags his tail. And the weather is glorious. The air is still, fresh, and transparent. The night is dark, but one can see the whole village with its white roofs and coils of smoke coming from the chimneys, the trees silvered with hoar frost, the snowdrifts. The whole sky spangled with gay twinkling stars, and the Milky Way is as distinct as though it had been washed and rubbed with snow for a holiday.⁠ ⁠…
Vanka sighed, dipped his pen, and went on writing:

“And yesterday I had a wigging. The master pulled me out into the yard by my hair, and whacked me with a boot-stretcher because I accidentally fell asleep while I was rocking their brat in the cradle. And a week ago the mistress told me to clean a herring, and I began from the tail end, and she took the herring and thrust its head in my face. The workmen laugh at me and send me to the tavern for vodka, and tell me to steal the master’s cucumbers for them, and the master beats me with anything that comes to hand. And there is nothing to eat. In the morning they give me bread, for dinner, porridge, and in the evening, bread again; but as for tea, or soup, the master and mistress gobble it all up themselves. And I am put to sleep in the passage, and when their wretched brat cries I get no sleep at all, but have to rock the cradle. Dear grandfather, show the Divine Mercy, take me away from here, home to the village. It’s more than I can bear. I bow down to your feet, and will pray to God for you forever, take me away from here or I shall die.”
Vanka’s mouth worked, he rubbed his eyes with his black fist, and gave a sob.

“I will powder your snuff for you,” he went on. “I will pray for you, and if I do anything you can thrash me like Sidor’s goat. And if you think I’ve no job, then I will beg the steward for Christ’s sake to let me clean his boots, or I’ll go for a shepherd-boy instead of Fedka. Dear grandfather, it is more than I can bear, it’s simply no life at all. I wanted to run away to the village, but I have no boots, and I am afraid of the frost. When I grow up big I will take care of you for this, and not let anyone annoy you, and when you die I will pray for the rest of your soul, just as for my mammy’s.”

“Moscow is a big town. It’s all gentlemen’s houses, and there are lots of horses, but there are no sheep, and the dogs are not spiteful. The lads here don’t go out with the star, and they don’t let anyone go into the choir, and once I saw in a shop window fishing-hooks for sale, fitted ready with the line and for all sorts of fish, awfully good ones, there was even one hook that would hold a forty-pound sheatfish. And I have seen shops where there are guns of all sorts, after the pattern of the master’s guns at home, so that I shouldn’t wonder if they are a hundred roubles each.⁠ ⁠… And in the butchers’ shops there are grouse and woodcocks and fish and hares, but the shopmen don’t say where they shoot them.”
“Dear grandfather, when they have the Christmas tree at the big house, get me a gilt walnut, and put it away in the green trunk. Ask the young lady Olga Ignatyevna, say it’s for Vanka.”

Vanka gave a tremulous sigh, and again stared at the window. He remembered how his grandfather always went into the forest to get the Christmas tree for his master’s family, and took his grandson with him. It was a merry time! Grandfather made a noise in his throat, the forest crackled with the frost, and looking at them Vanka chortled too. Before chopping down the Christmas tree, grandfather would smoke a pipe, slowly take a pinch of snuff, and laugh at frozen Vanka.⁠ ⁠… The young fir trees, covered with hoar frost, stood motionless, waiting to see which of them was to die. Wherever one looked, a hare flew like an arrow over the snowdrifts.⁠ ⁠… Grandfather could not refrain from shouting: “Hold him, hold him⁠ ⁠… hold him! Ah, the bobtailed devil!”

When he had cut down the Christmas tree, grandfather used to drag it to the big house, and there set to work to decorate it.⁠ ⁠… The young lady, who was Vanka’s favourite, Olga Ignatyevna, was the busiest of all. When Vanka’s mother Pelageya was alive, and a servant in the big house, Olga Ignatyevna used to give him goodies, and having nothing better to do, taught him to read and write, to count up to a hundred, and even to dance a quadrille. When Pelageya died, Vanka had been transferred to the servants’ kitchen to be with his grandfather, and from the kitchen to the shoemaker’s in Moscow.

“Do come, dear grandfather,” Vanka went on with his letter. “For Christ’s sake, I beg you, take me away. Have pity on an unhappy orphan like me; here everyone knocks me about, and I am fearfully hungry; I can’t tell you what misery it is, I am always crying. And the other day the master hit me on the head with a last, so that I fell down. My life is wretched, worse than any dog’s.⁠ ⁠… I send greetings to Alyona, one-eyed Yegorka, and the coachman, and don’t give my concertina to anyone. I remain, your grandson, Ivan Zhukov. Dear grandfather, do come.”
Vanka folded the sheet of writing-paper twice, and put it into an envelope he had bought the day before for a kopeck.⁠ ⁠… After thinking a little, he dipped the pen and wrote the address:
To grandfather in the village.

Then he scratched his head, thought a little, and added: Konstantin Makaritch. Glad that he had not been prevented from writing, he put on his cap and, without putting on his little greatcoat, ran out into the street as he was in his shirt.⁠ ⁠…

The shopmen at the butcher’s, whom he had questioned the day before, told him that letters were put in postboxes, and from the boxes were carried about all over the earth in mailcarts with drunken drivers and ringing bells. Vanka ran to the nearest postbox, and thrust the precious letter in the slit.⁠ ⁠…
An hour later, lulled by sweet hopes, he was sound asleep.⁠ ⁠… He dreamed of the stove. On the stove was sitting his grandfather, swinging his bare legs, and reading the letter to the cooks.⁠ ⁠…
By the stove was Eel, wagging his tail.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
On its surface, Vanka is almost nothing. A nine-year-old boy, apprenticed to a shoemaker in Moscow, waits until his master and mistress have gone to the Christmas Eve service, steals a little ink and a rusty pen, and writes to his grandfather in the countryside. He begs to be taken away. He seals the letter, drops it into a postbox, and falls asleep dreaming that his grandfather is reading it aloud in the kitchen. That is the whole plot. The meaning lives in the gap between what Vanka believes he has done and what the reader knows he has done.

The key moment is the address. After all the pages of misery, Vanka writes on the envelope: "To grandfather in the village." Then he scratches his head, thinks, and adds the name Konstantin Makaritch. No village is named. No province. The letter will go nowhere, and the boy, who has been taught only a little reading and writing by a kind young lady in the big house, has no way to know that. The tenderness of that small afterthought, the added name, is exactly what breaks the heart. He believes the name is the missing piece, and it is not the piece that matters at all.

Chekhov builds the story by braiding two worlds. In the shoemaker's room, in the cold and the dark, Vanka is beaten with a strap, hit on the head with a shoemaker's last, fed scraps, and made to rock the baby. In the letter, and in the long memory that interrupts it, there is the village: the grandfather with his sheepskin and his snuff and his laughing face, the dogs Kashtanka and Eel, the frosty forest where they cut down the Christmas tree. The memory is so vivid that it threatens to become a rescue in itself. But notice that even the memory is not purely happy. The grandfather is a night watchman who lives in a servants' kitchen, hardly a free man himself. The old man is not a savior. He is another poor servant at the mercy of others, and he is nowhere near able to take in a grandson.

Some readers also catch the quiet detail that Vanka runs out to the postbox without his coat, in his shirt, in a Russian winter. The story lets the reader feel the cold the boy ignores. And the very last line, "By the stove was Eel, wagging his tail," is a perfect piece of misdirection. The dream is warm, and the dog, once a symbol of sly cunning in the memory, is simply glad. The reader leaves the story inside the dream, which makes the waking reality, the one only we can see, even harder to bear.

So the story is about hope without a means. It is about how the powerless reach for the only route they can imagine, and how the systems around them, in this case a postal system and a social order, cannot carry their cry. It is a story about a letter that cannot be delivered, and about the many people in every era whose cries are real but are addressed to nowhere.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
Judged purely as craft, Vanka is close to flawless, and its great virtue is restraint. Chekhov could have narrated the boy's suffering in his own adult voice. Instead he mostly hands the page to Vanka, whose letter is full of childish priorities. In the middle of begging for rescue, he sends greetings to the coachman and says not to give his concertina to anyone. That detail is the kind of thing a writer cannot invent without having listened to real children. It makes the boy a specific child rather than an emblem of poverty, and it shows that the sorrow has not erased his sense of what is his.

The structure is also elegant. The story begins in the sad room, pulls back into a long and loving memory of the village, returns to the letter, and ends with the mailbox and the dream. The memory section is the story's secret engine. It does two jobs at once: it makes the grandfather real enough that we want the rescue, and it supplies the contrast that lets us feel the boy's present pain without a single speech about injustice. The pace is steady, and nothing is wasted. Even the dog Eel, who is introduced with a paragraph about his reputation for sly meekness, comes back at the end, and that small circle closes the story like a lid.

Where does it falter? Some readers find the ending a little too neatly engineered. The sleeping boy, the sweet dream, the wagging tail, the irony of the address: all of it is arranged to deliver one final pang, and a tougher reader might feel the hand of the writer pulling the string. Chekhov himself was suspicious of stories that tell you exactly when to cry, and this one comes closer to that line than most of his later work. It also deals in a classic type, the suffering orphan at Christmas, that Dickens and many sentimental writers of the era had worked heavily. The difference is that Chekhov refuses the consoling lie: nobody comes, the master is not redeemed, and the dream is only a dream. But the story can still feel, at moments, like a perfectly cut small gem rather than a deep investigation of anything.

There is also a limit of scale. The boy has no inner life beyond longing and fear, and the masters are shown only through blows. That is arguably the point, since the story is told from a child's low vantage, but it means there is no moral complexity. In Chekhov's best longer stories, the people who cause harm are as muddled and human as the people who endure it. Here, the shoemaker is a shadow with a strap.

Still, it is hard to complain much. The story is a few pages long, and in those pages it gets a whole social order, a whole childhood, and a whole kind of loneliness onto the page, without a single false note. If it is a minor work by Chekhov's later standards, it is minor in the way a perfectly tuned small instrument is minor.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
Vanka was written early, in the stretch of Chekhov's career when he was supporting his family by writing quick humorous pieces for papers under the name Antosha Chekhonte. A few months before this story, the respected older writer Dmitry Grigorovich had written him a famous letter urging him to take his talent seriously and slow down. Vanka belongs to the moment when Chekhov began to do exactly that. It still carries his comic training, in its economy and its timing, but it uses those tools for something quieter and sadder. In that sense it is one of the early signs of the mature Chekhov, the writer who would go on to produce The Lady with the Dog, Ward No. 6, and the great plays.

Its larger impact is as a model for how to write about suffering without shouting. The story became a staple of Russian schoolrooms and has been taught for generations, often to children not much older than Vanka. It has been widely translated, and it is one of the most frequently anthologized of all Chekhov's stories in English. Because it is short, plain, and emotionally immediate, it is often a reader's first Chekhov, and for many readers it sets up an expectation of what he does: small events, deep consequences, and an ending that opens rather than closes.

In Russia it also had a life as a cultural reference. The phrase "to grandfather in the village" became a proverb of sorts for a message sent to no one, a plea that cannot arrive, or a hopelessly vague address. People who have never read the story use the phrase. That kind of absorption into everyday speech is a rare achievement for a short story.

The story also fits into a long conversation about child labor and the legacy of serfdom. Russia abolished serfdom in 1861, and the decades afterward were full of writing, from reformers and novelists alike, about the poverty and exploitation that survived the legal change. Chekhov did not write a polemic, and he generally avoided stating political positions in his fiction. Yet stories like this fed the same moral current as the reformers, simply by making a nine-year-old's cold room unforgettable. Later Soviet criticism, unsurprisingly, prized the story as an indictment of the old order, and that is one reason it was so widely taught in the twentieth century.

It has also been adapted: there have been Russian and other animated and live film versions, and the story has inspired stage readings and illustrated editions. Among writers, its mark can be seen wherever a short story trusts a child's limited understanding to carry a much larger adult truth. The device of dramatic irony, where the reader knows more than the narrator's central figure, is hardly Chekhov's alone, but Vanka is one of the cleanest examples in the form.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
The first thing readers tend to say about Vanka is that it hurts, and that it hurts without seeming to try. People who read it as children remember the address on the envelope for decades. That is a remarkable thing for a story to leave behind: a single line, a few words long, that detonates years later when a reader realizes what the boy did not.

Part of the love is for the child himself. Vanka is not a saint. He is hungry, scared, a little proud of his concertina, and capable of mixed-up thoughts, like his fierce protectiveness of his concertina. He remembers the village with complete affection but also with the odd, vivid, comic details only a real child would remember: the grandfather laughing at him shivering in the forest, the hare shooting across the snow, the shout of "the bobtailed devil." The warmth of those memories makes the story feel generous even as it is cruel. Readers admire that Chekhov lets the village be vivid and funny, rather than turning it into a stale paradise.

Fellow writers have long admired the story's economy. Chekhov's reputation among other writers is enormous, and short fiction writers from Katherine Mansfield to Raymond Carver to Alice Munro have been associated with his influence. For them Vanka represents a certain discipline: no commentary, no lecture, no summary of meaning, just a scene and a gesture. Teachers like it because it is easy to read yet hard to exhaust. You can read it in ten minutes and think about it for a week.

Readers also respond to the emotional honesty of the ending. A sentimental writer would have sent the grandfather to the rescue, or at least hinted that he might. Chekhov leaves the reader with a sweet dream and no help. The story does not tell you what to feel, but it does not let you off easily either. The pleasure of the dream, shared briefly by the reader, makes the reality hit harder, and many readers say that this gap between wish and fact is exactly what stays with them.

There is also a simple, durable appeal in its subject. Anyone who has ever been far from home, scared, and sure that one person could fix everything has some of Vanka in them. The story speaks across cultures and centuries because the feeling is so basic. A child alone at night, writing to someone who loves him, is a figure that needs very little cultural translation, and Chekhov draws him with such precise love that he stays in memory long after the plot is forgotten.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Vanka has not been a lightning rod for controversy, and it is worth saying so plainly. It is a short, early, widely loved story, and little has been written attacking it. But there are real reservations that critics and readers have raised over time, and they are worth taking seriously.

The most common one is sentimentality. The orphan boy, the beloved grandfather, the Christmas setting, the ill-addressed letter: these are the ingredients of Victorian-era pathos, and some critics have felt that Chekhov, for all his cool manner, is operating the machinery of tears here. This criticism has a respectable pedigree. Chekhov himself was famously allergic to overt emotional manipulation and is reported to have advised younger writers to keep a cool head when telling sad stories, so that the reader's own feeling would do the work. Vanka mostly follows that advice, but its final dream sequence and the pointed irony of the address do feel designed to make a reader's throat tighten. Some critics see it as a lesser work for exactly that reason, a polished piece of affecting craft rather than a deeper exploration of the human condition.

A second reservation concerns the political use made of it. In the Soviet period especially, the story was taught as a straightforward indictment of the pre-revolutionary order, and a good deal of later commentary pushed back on that flattening. Chekhov was not a political writer in that sense. He distrusted ideology, and his stories typically refuse to assign blame to a single class or system. Reading Vanka only as a sermon about capitalist or tsarist cruelty can miss its subtler subject, which is loneliness and the limits of the means people have for reaching one another. Critics have also pointed out that the story does not really explore the master and mistress as people, which makes it a more limited instrument for social analysis than the label suggests.

A third objection, more of an aesthetic quibble, is that the story is slight. By the time Chekhov wrote his great works, he was exploring psychological ambiguity and the quiet failures of ordinary lives in a way that makes this early piece look simple. It is a story with a single note, however beautifully sustained. Readers who want the layered irony and moral uncertainty of his later work may find Vanka too clean.

It is fair to say that these criticisms are mild. Few serious readers dismiss the story. The usual verdict is that it is an early masterpiece of compression, with a touch more sentiment than the mature Chekhov would permit himself, and that its weaknesses are the weaknesses of a very small form handled very well.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
Vanka sits at the meeting point of several traditions. One is the Russian literature of social conscience, running from Gogol's The Overcoat and Turgenev's sketches of peasant life through Dostoevsky's tormented children. Dostoevsky, in particular, wrote harrowing scenes of suffering kids, including a famous story about a boy at a Christmas tree, and his work in this vein is a clear ancestor. But where Dostoevsky works at fever pitch, philosophizing and weeping, Chekhov takes the same material and cools it down to something almost conversational. That choice of temperature is his signature.

Another tradition is the Christmas story of misery and mercy that Dickens, Hans Christian Andersen, and others made popular in the nineteenth century. Andersen's The Little Match Girl is the obvious relative: a poor child, a holiday, a consoling vision at the end. The comparison is revealing. Andersen's child is gathered into a heavenly consolation, and the story is steeped in religious comfort. Chekhov offers a worldly dream instead, the grandfather reading by the stove, and withholds any promise of ultimate justice. His story is therefore a secular, skeptical descendant of that older form.

It also belongs to the broader birth of the modern short story. Chekhov, along with Maupassant and, later, Joyce, Mansfield, and Hemingway, helped move the short story away from tidy plots with twist endings and toward moments of revelation and suggestion. The idea that a story can end without a resolution, trusting an image to carry the meaning, flows through the twentieth century. You can hear Chekhov in the quiet, open-ended endings of Mansfield, in Carver's flat domestic stories, and in much contemporary literary fiction. Vanka is an early, tidy demonstration of the method, which makes it a good place to see how the machinery works before it gets more complicated.

Among works that might be compared, readers sometimes pair it with Chekhov's own Sleepy, a much darker story about a young girl worked to exhaustion who commits a terrible act, and with Dickens's treatment of apprentices and workhouse children in Oliver Twist. Compared with these, Vanka is gentler and shorter, but it shares their insistence that childhood in the lower ranks of society is a form of captivity.

Why read it now? Because the situation it describes has not vanished. Children are still sent away to work, still separated from the people who love them, still writing messages that no system is built to deliver. And because it is an easy, quick, humane demonstration of how much a short story can do with almost nothing. It takes five minutes to read. It teaches you that restraint can be louder than shouting, that a detail like a misaddressed envelope can carry a whole society's failure, and that the people at the bottom of history are not abstractions. They are boys in their shirtsleeves, running to a postbox in the cold.

stories.title: A Chameleon
stories.author: Anton Chekhov
stories.epigraph: “So you bite, you damned brute?” Otchumyelov hears suddenly. “Lads, don’t let him go! Biting is prohibited nowadays! Hold him! ah⁠ ⁠… ah!”
stories.keyContext: A Chameleon is a comic sketch from 1884, written when Anton Chekhov was twenty-four, still a medical student and then a young doctor, writing funny pieces for humor magazines under the pen name Antosha Chekhonte. It runs only a few pages, but it has lasted because its target is so durable. In a dusty Russian market square, a police superintendent has to decide what to do about a dog that has bitten a man's finger. The facts never change, yet the verdict keeps changing, depending on a single question: who owns the dog? Russia in those years was ruled by a rigid ladder of rank, in which a petty official's judgment could depend less on right and wrong than on who stood above him. Chekhov turns that servile habit into a farce. Watch the superintendent's overcoat as you listen. The title tells you the animal that matters, and it is not the dog.
paragraphs: The police superintendent Otchumyelov is walking across the market square wearing a new overcoat and carrying a parcel under his arm. A red-haired policeman strides after him with a sieve full of confiscated gooseberries in his hands. There is silence all around. Not a soul in the square.⁠ ⁠… The open doors of the shops and taverns look out upon God’s world disconsolately, like hungry mouths; there is not even a beggar near them.
“So you bite, you damned brute?” Otchumyelov hears suddenly. “Lads, don’t let him go! Biting is prohibited nowadays! Hold him! ah⁠ ⁠… ah!”

There is the sound of a dog yelping. Otchumyelov looks in the direction of the sound and sees a dog, hopping on three legs and looking about her, run out of Pitchugin’s timber-yard. A man in a starched cotton shirt, with his waistcoat unbuttoned, is chasing her. He runs after her, and throwing his body forward falls down and seizes the dog by her hind legs. Once more there is a yelping and a shout of “Don’t let go!” Sleepy countenances are protruded from the shops, and soon a crowd, which seems to have sprung out of the earth, is gathered round the timber-yard.
“It looks like a row, your honour⁠ ⁠…” says the policeman.
Otchumyelov makes a half turn to the left and strides towards the crowd.

He sees the aforementioned man in the unbuttoned waistcoat standing close by the gate of the timber-yard, holding his right hand in the air and displaying a bleeding finger to the crowd. On his half-drunken face there is plainly written: “I’ll pay you out, you rogue!” and indeed the very finger has the look of a flag of victory. In this man Otchumyelov recognises Hryukin, the goldsmith. The culprit who has caused the sensation, a white borzoy puppy with a sharp muzzle and a yellow patch on her back, is sitting on the ground with her forepaws outstretched in the middle of the crowd, trembling all over. There is an expression of misery and terror in her tearful eyes.
“What’s it all about?” Otchumyelov inquires, pushing his way through the crowd. “What are you here for? Why are you waving your finger⁠ ⁠… ? Who was it shouted?”

“I was walking along here, not interfering with anyone, your honour,” Hryukin begins, coughing into his fist. “I was talking about firewood to Mitry Mitritch, when this low brute for no rhyme or reason bit my finger.⁠ ⁠… You must excuse me, I am a working man.⁠ ⁠… Mine is fine work. I must have damages, for I shan’t be able to use this finger for a week, may be.⁠ ⁠… It’s not even the law, your honour, that one should put up with it from a beast.⁠ ⁠… If everyone is going to be bitten, life won’t be worth living.⁠ ⁠…”

“H’m. Very good,” says Otchumyelov sternly, coughing and raising his eyebrows. “Very good. Whose dog is it? I won’t let this pass! I’ll teach them to let their dogs run all over the place! It’s time these gentry were looked after, if they won’t obey the regulations! When he’s fined, the blackguard, I’ll teach him what it means to keep dogs and such stray cattle! I’ll give him a lesson!⁠ ⁠… Yeldyrin,” cries the superintendent, addressing the policeman, “find out whose dog this is and draw up a report! And the dog must be strangled. Without delay! It’s sure to be mad.⁠ ⁠… Whose dog is it, I ask?”
“I fancy it’s General Zhigalov’s,” says someone in the crowd.

“General Zhigalov’s, h’m.⁠ ⁠… Help me off with my coat, Yeldyrin⁠ ⁠… it’s frightfully hot! It must be a sign of rain.⁠ ⁠… There’s one thing I can’t make out, how it came to bite you?” Otchumyelov turns to Hryukin. “Surely it couldn’t reach your finger. It’s a little dog, and you are a great hulking fellow! You must have scratched your finger with a nail, and then the idea struck you to get damages for it. We all know⁠ ⁠… your sort! I know you devils!”
“He put a cigarette in her face, your honour, for a joke, and she had the sense to snap at him.⁠ ⁠… He is a nonsensical fellow, your honour!”

“That’s a lie, Squinteye! You didn’t see, so why tell lies about it? His honour is a wise gentleman, and will see who is telling lies and who is telling the truth, as in God’s sight.⁠ ⁠… And if I am lying let the court decide. It’s written in the law.⁠ ⁠… We are all equal nowadays. My own brother is in the gendarmes⁠ ⁠… let me tell you.⁠ ⁠…”
“Don’t argue!”
“No, that’s not the General’s dog,” says the policeman, with profound conviction, “the General hasn’t got one like that. His are mostly setters.”
“Do you know that for a fact?”
“Yes, your honour.”

“I know it, too. The General has valuable dogs, thoroughbred, and this is goodness knows what! No coat, no shape.⁠ ⁠… A low creature. And to keep a dog like that!⁠ ⁠… where’s the sense of it. If a dog like that were to turn up in Petersburg or Moscow, do you know what would happen? They would not worry about the law, they would strangle it in a twinkling! You’ve been injured, Hryukin, and we can’t let the matter drop.⁠ ⁠… We must give them a lesson! It is high time.⁠ ⁠… !”
“Yet maybe it is the General’s,” says the policeman, thinking aloud. “It’s not written on its face.⁠ ⁠… I saw one like it the other day in his yard.”
“It is the General’s, that’s certain!” says a voice in the crowd.

“H’m, help me on with my overcoat, Yeldyrin, my lad⁠ ⁠… the wind’s getting up.⁠ ⁠… I am cold.⁠ ⁠… You take it to the General’s, and inquire there. Say I found it and sent it. And tell them not to let it out into the street.⁠ ⁠… It may be a valuable dog, and if every swine goes sticking a cigar in its mouth, it will soon be ruined.
