A dog is a delicate animal.⁠ ⁠… And you put your hand down, you blockhead. It’s no use your displaying your fool of a finger. It’s your own fault.⁠ ⁠…”
“Here comes the General’s cook, ask him⁠ ⁠… Hi, Prohor! Come here, my dear man! Look at this dog.⁠ ⁠… Is it one of yours?”
“What an idea! We have never had one like that!”

“There’s no need to waste time asking,” says Otchumyelov. “It’s a stray dog! There’s no need to waste time talking about it.⁠ ⁠… Since he says it’s a stray dog, a stray dog it is.⁠ ⁠… It must be destroyed, that’s all about it.”
“It is not our dog,” Prohor goes on. “It belongs to the General’s brother, who arrived the other day. Our master does not care for hounds. But his honour is fond of them.⁠ ⁠…”
“You don’t say his Excellency’s brother is here? Vladimir Ivanitch?” inquires Otchumyelov, and his whole face beams with an ecstatic smile. “Well, I never! And I didn’t know! Has he come on a visit?”
“Yes.”

“Well, I never.⁠ ⁠… He couldn’t stay away from his brother.⁠ ⁠… And there I didn’t know! So this is his honour’s dog? Delighted to hear it.⁠ ⁠… Take it. It’s not a bad pup.⁠ ⁠… A lively creature.⁠ ⁠… Snapped at this fellow’s finger! Ha-ha-ha.⁠ ⁠… Come, why are you shivering? Rrr⁠ ⁠… Rrrr.⁠ ⁠… The rogue’s angry⁠ ⁠… a nice little pup.”
Prohor calls the dog, and walks away from the timber-yard with her. The crowd laughs at Hryukin.
“I’ll make you smart yet!” Otchumyelov threatens him, and wrapping himself in his greatcoat, goes on his way across the square.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The story takes place in a single scene, in a single place, in perhaps a quarter of an hour. Police Superintendent Otchumyelov crosses a quiet market square in a new overcoat. A policeman follows him carrying a sieve of confiscated gooseberries. Suddenly there is a commotion: a goldsmith named Hryukin is holding up a bleeding finger and shouting that a dog has bitten him. A crowd gathers. The superintendent takes charge, and at first his judgment is swift and stern. Whoever owns the dog will pay, and the dog, if it is a stray, will be destroyed.

Then a voice in the crowd says the dog looks like General Zhigalov's. The superintendent's tone reverses at once. Perhaps the man provoked the dog. Perhaps he stuck a cigar in its mouth. Look at the poor little creature, and look at that fool's finger. Then someone says no, the General has no such dog. Back swings the verdict: a wretched, mangy brute, to be destroyed. Then the policeman thinks he saw one like it in the General's yard. Around and around it goes, with the superintendent calling for his coat to be taken off when he feels hot with righteous anger toward the dog's owner, and put back on when the dog is revealed to belong to someone powerful, and he feels a chill of fear. At last the General's cook arrives and says it belongs to the General's brother, a visitor. At that, the superintendent is all smiles. A lively pup. A nice little thing. And the goldsmith, the actual victim, is threatened for his trouble.

The meaning is not about dogs. It is about how authority behaves when it has no principle of its own. Otchumyelov does not weigh evidence. He has an inner weathervane that points toward power. Right and wrong are whatever the ranks above him would prefer. The overcoat is the visible sign of this: the coat goes on and off like a mood, and in the final line he wraps himself in it again and walks on, unembarrassed. The man who, a moment before, threatened to have a dog strangled now melts into tenderness, and neither the crowd nor he himself seems troubled by the contradiction.

A layer worth noticing is the role of the crowd. The bystanders are not neutral. Each shout from the crowd is a small push on the weathervane, and each is delivered with the same confidence, whether it helps the victim or the dog. They laugh at the goldsmith at the end. The story hints that the superintendent is not a lone monster but the natural product of a society where everyone watches the person above and nobody asks what is fair. The name itself is a joke on this: Otchumyelov echoes a Russian word for being addled or going mad, and Hryukin's name echoes a grunting sound, as in a pig's. Chekhov names his characters like the comic types of old stage farce, and then lets them turn out to be disturbingly real.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
As pure comic machinery, A Chameleon is superb. The whole story is built on a single repeated gesture, a reversal, and Chekhov is wise enough to repeat it exactly the right number of times: about five. Any fewer and the pattern would not register; any more and it would turn tiresome. Each flip is triggered by a fresh scrap of information, usually a throwaway line from a bystander or the policeman, which keeps the reversals believable and quick. The overcoat adds a physical rhythm to the verbal one, so the reader sees the switch as well as hears it. This is the work of a young writer who understood comedy as timing.

The prose is also remarkably lean. The opening sentences establish the empty square, the open shop doors that look "like hungry mouths," the sieve of gooseberries, and the silence, and then the first shout breaks it. There is almost no description after that, only dialogue and the superintendent's reactions. That economy is partly a product of the circumstances: Chekhov was writing for humor magazines that wanted very short pieces, and he learned to deliver a whole world in a few hundred words. He took the constraint and made it a style.

Where is the weakness? The characters are types. Otchumyelov is a satirical figure, a puffed-up tyrant who is also a coward, and we learn nothing of his life outside the incident. The goldsmith Hryukin is merely a victim, and the crowd is a chorus. The story has no interest in inwardness, and so it cannot offer the surprise that comes when a character turns out to contain more than we expected. For readers who love Chekhov for his psychological subtlety, this early work can feel like a clever sketch rather than a story.

The satire can also seem a little blunt. The dog is a nearly perfect device, since it cannot speak and is entirely at the mercy of the humans' shifting judgment, but the point is made so explicitly, with such constant shouting about rank and the General, that the sly reader may feel nudged. A subtler writer, which Chekhov would later become, might have let one reversal go unremarked. And the ending, with the superintendent threatening the victim after all, is a tidy button on the joke. It lands, but it is the kind of ending a comic writer reaches for, a final punishing twist.

Even so, the story pays back its small ambitions in full. It does exactly one thing, does it in about a thousand words, and does it so cleanly that the title has entered the language as a stock description of a person who changes colors to suit the room. There is real virtue in a perfectly made small thing, and this is one.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
A Chameleon was published in 1884 in a humor magazine of the time, the St. Petersburg weekly Oskolki, which means Fragments, one of the outlets that paid Chekhov a few kopecks a line. He wrote hundreds of such pieces in his twenties. Most are forgotten, and a few, including this one, became classics. It belongs to the early period that made him a known name in Russia before he turned to his more serious stories and plays, and it demonstrates how much craft he had already acquired.

Its most lasting impact is linguistic and cultural. In Russian, the word for chameleon, and the story's title, became shorthand for a turncoat, a person who adapts shamelessly to whoever holds power. Russian readers use the word without needing to have read the story. Otchumyelov himself became a reference figure: a type of petty official who bends with the wind. In the Soviet period the story was widely taught in school, and its portrait of a servile bureaucrat could be read in more than one way, as a critique of the old tsarist order but also, for the attentive, as a description of timeservers under any regime.

The story also contributed to a particular strain of Russian satire, the tradition of mocking small officials and their absurd hierarchies, which runs from Gogol's The Government Inspector and The Overcoat through Saltykov-Shchedrin to Chekhov's own The Death of a Government Clerk, and onward to twentieth-century satirists such as Zoshchenko and, in a darker register, Bulgakov. It helped establish the idea that the real subject of satire is not villainy but obsequiousness, the small, constant, ordinary bending of the spine.

It has been adapted many times in Russia, for stage, film, and television, and is frequently performed as a short theatrical piece, because its single-scene structure and strong physical business, the overcoat on and off, are made for actors. It has also been animated, and the dog is a popular role. Outside Russia, it is a standard item in anthologies of Chekhov's early comic stories and is used in classrooms as a model of how a story can be built on a single repeated reversal.

For Chekhov's career, the story is a marker of his apprenticeship. He later said, in a number of letters, that he wrote his early comic pieces fast and sometimes carelessly. But A Chameleon shows him already in command of a method he would never abandon: take an ordinary event, strip away commentary, and let the behavior of the characters reveal everything. The humorous sketches taught him compression, and compression is the foundation of his mature style.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
The great pleasure of A Chameleon is recognition. Almost everyone has met an Otchumyelov: the manager who agrees with whoever spoke last, the official who is a bully to the weak and a pushover to the strong, the colleague whose opinion changes the moment the boss walks in. Readers across languages and generations have laughed at the story because they can attach a face to the type, often more than one. That is why the title has traveled so well. The word chameleon already hints at the idea, and the story fills it with a vivid example.

Readers also love how physical the comedy is. The superintendent's coat, which he wants off because he is hot with anger and wants on because he is suddenly cold with worry, is a perfect comic prop. It makes an invisible moral shift visible. Audiences who hear the story read aloud, which is how many Russians first met it, often laugh at each flip, because Chekhov arranges the rhythm so well. The bystanders' interjections feel like a chorus in a farce, and the final image of the crowd laughing at the poor goldsmith adds a bitter edge to the laughter that many readers find irresistible.

Another thing admirers prize is the story's tact. Chekhov never says that the system is corrupt or that servility is a national disease. He never has a narrator lecture. He simply sets up the situation and lets it run, trusting that the reader will recognize the truth. That trust is part of what fellow writers admire. Chekhov's later insistence that a writer should not be a judge but a witness is already visible here in embryo.

Younger readers often love it for a more basic reason: it is short, funny, and easy to follow. It makes a good introduction to Chekhov because there is no need for background about nineteenth-century Russia beyond the most basic idea of rank and deference. A reader who finishes it in five minutes has understood the whole thing and can still go back for the finer details, such as the way the overcoat motif frames the story or the careful placement of the gooseberries in the opening.

There is also the dog. Readers who care about animals often note, with some affection, that the little dog is the one character with entirely consistent behavior. She bites when bothered, she shivers when frightened, and she goes back to her owners. Every human in the story changes color except her. It is a small joke inside the large one, and it is part of why the story feels warm even as it mocks. The satire is aimed at human weakness, and it is delivered with a smile rather than with contempt.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Because A Chameleon is a short comic sketch from the start of Chekhov's career, it has attracted less critical argument than his mature work, and it would be dishonest to pretend there is a large body of famous attacks on it. What exists is a set of reservations that readers and critics have voiced over time.

The first is that the story is thin. Compared with the great later works, it offers a single joke and a single target. Critics who prize Chekhov for his ambiguity, his refusal to settle on a verdict, sometimes treat his early humorous pieces as juvenilia, clever but lacking the weight that makes his later fiction astonishing. In the late nineteenth century, some Russian critics also complained, more generally, that Chekhov seemed to lack a clear social position or message, and that his stories were mere impressions. A Chameleon, with its sharp point, escaped that charge, but it did not escape the sense that such pieces were light entertainment.

The second reservation is about the satire's bluntness. The characters are broad. The superintendent is almost a cartoon, and the story's punch depends on that exaggeration. A reader who wants social satire to feel rooted in real, complicated people may find it too schematic. It makes its point by caricature, and caricature is a form some critics regard as limited, since it flatters the reader into feeling superior to the target. In the story, we are invited to laugh at Otchumyelov, but we are less often invited to see ourselves in him, though the story does gesture in that direction.

A third line of criticism involves the political readings that have been laid on the story. In the Soviet era it was sometimes taught as a straightforward denunciation of tsarist bureaucrats, and later commentators have pointed out that this reading flattens Chekhov's more general interest in human weakness. Chekhov did not write a protest piece. Reading him as a social crusader can miss the fact that servility is portrayed as a timeless human habit rather than the product of a single regime.

Finally, a few readers and translators have remarked on how much of the comedy depends on Russian ranks, titles, and forms of address, which can be hard to convey in English. Names like Otchumyelov and Hryukin carry comic sounds that do not survive translation, and the system of deference can seem remote. That is not a flaw in the story so much as a limit on how much of it travels, but it is a real difference between how Russian readers and foreign readers experience it.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
A Chameleon sits in the long tradition of satire about officialdom, and in Russia that tradition is unusually rich. Gogol's play The Government Inspector, from 1836, shows an entire town of officials groveling before a man they mistake for an important visitor. His story The Overcoat gives us a clerk crushed by the ranks above him. Chekhov borrows that sensibility but trims away the fantasy and the grandeur. Where Gogol builds elaborate comic worlds, Chekhov gives you a single square and a single dog. In this sense the story is a miniature, a distilled version of a tradition.

It also has a relative in Chekhov's own sketches of the same period, such as The Death of a Government Clerk, in which a man dies from the embarrassment of having sneezed on a general, and Fat and Thin, in which two old schoolmates' friendship collapses the moment one learns the other's rank. All of these treat the same disease: the way hierarchy distorts human feeling. A Chameleon is the purest example because it has no sentiment in it at all. There is no pathos, only the machinery.

Looking forward, the story's descendants are numerous. Any later fiction that mocks the petty tyrant who tailors his judgments to the powerful owes something to this model. You can see echoes in the satire of Zoshchenko, in the bureaucratic comedy of Czech and Polish writers, and in English-language works such as Orwell's depictions of servility. In a different register, the figure of the opportunist who changes sides to suit the hour is a staple of political fiction, and Otchumyelov is an early, memorable portrait.

The story also connects to the idea of the chameleon in literature generally, which reaches back to antiquity. The animal that changes color to suit its surroundings has long stood for flattery and inconstancy. Chekhov's achievement is to make the metaphor concrete by letting us watch a man do it in real time, and to attach it to a specific social disease, deference to power.

Why read it now? Because the behavior it describes is not historical. Anywhere there is a hierarchy, there is someone adjusting his judgment according to who owns the dog. The story is also a good lesson in how comedy can carry moral observation without sermonizing, and it takes only a few minutes. It reminds us that the question of who is wrong often gets replaced, in institutions and in ordinary life, by the question of who is important, and that the replacement is often invisible to the person making it. Chekhov makes it visible by giving him an overcoat.

stories.title: Hills Like White Elephants
stories.author: Ernest Hemingway
stories.epigraph: “What should we drink?” the girl asked. She had taken off her hat and put it on the table.
stories.keyContext: Hills Like White Elephants was published in 1927, when Ernest Hemingway was in his late twenties and already known as the leading voice of a new, stripped-down American style. It is one of the most famous examples of what he called the iceberg idea: tell only the part above the water, and trust the bulk beneath to be felt. The story is almost entirely dialogue. An American man and a young woman wait at a Spanish railway junction for a train to Madrid, drink beer and anise liqueur, and talk about something that the story never names. The setting is the aftermath of the First World War, a time when many young people, Hemingway among them, felt cut loose from older rules about marriage, religion, and what a life was supposed to look like. As you listen, pay attention to what the two characters avoid saying, and to how differently each of them uses the word fine.
paragraphs: The hills across the valley of the Ebro were long and white. On this side there was no shade and no trees and the station was between two lines of rails in the sun. Close against the side of the station there was the warm shadow of the building and a curtain, made of strings of bamboo beads, hung across the open door into the bar, to keep out flies. The American and the girl with him sat at a table in the shade, outside the building. It was very hot and the express from Barcelona would come in forty minutes. It stopped at this junction for two minutes and went on to Madrid.
“What should we drink?” the girl asked. She had taken off her hat and put it on the table.
“It’s pretty hot,” the man said.
“Let’s drink beer.”
“Dos cervezas,” the man said into the curtain.
“Big ones?” a woman asked from the doorway.
“Yes. Two big ones.”

The woman brought two glasses of beer and two felt pads. She put the felt pads and the beer glasses on the table and looked at the man and the girl. The girl was looking off at the line of hills. They were white in the sun and the country was brown and dry.
“They look like white elephants,” she said.
“I’ve never seen one,” the man drank his beer.
“No, you wouldn’t have.”
“I might have,” the man said. “Just because you say I wouldn’t have doesn’t prove anything.”
The girl looked at the bead curtain. “They’ve painted something on it,” she said. “What does it say?”
“Anis del Toro. It’s a drink.”
“Could we try it?”
The man called “Listen” through the curtain. The woman came out from the bar.
“Four reales.”
“We want two Anis del Toro.”
“With water?”
“Do you want it with water?”
“I don’t know,” the girl said. “Is it good with water?”
“It’s all right.”
“You want them with water?” asked the woman.
“Yes, with water.”
“It tastes like licorice,” the girl said and put the glass down.
“That’s the way with everything.”
“Yes,” said the girl. “Everything tastes of licorice. Especially all the things you’ve waited so long for, like absinthe.”
“Oh, cut it out.”
“You started it,” the girl said. “I was being amused. I was having a fine time.”
“Well, let’s try and have a fine time.”
“All right. I was trying. I said the mountains looked like white elephants. Wasn’t that bright?”
“That was bright.”
“I wanted to try this new drink. That’s all we do, isn’t it⁠—look at things and try new drinks?”
“I guess so.”
The girl looked across at the hills.
“They’re lovely hills,” she said. “They don’t really look like white elephants. I just meant the coloring of their skin through the trees.”
“Should we have another drink?”
“All right.”
The warm wind blew the bead curtain against the table.
“The beer’s nice and cool,” the man said.
“It’s lovely,” the girl said.
“It’s really an awfully simple operation, Jig,” the man said. “It’s not really an operation at all.”
The girl looked at the ground the table legs rested on.
“I know you wouldn’t mind it, Jig. It’s really not anything. It’s just to let the air in.”
The girl did not say anything.
“I’ll go with you and I’ll stay with you all the time. They just let the air in and then it’s all perfectly natural.”
“Then what will we do afterward?”
“We’ll be fine afterward. Just like we were before.”
“What makes you think so?”
“That’s the only thing that bothers us. It’s the only thing that’s made us unhappy.”
The girl looked at the bead curtain, put her hand out and took hold of two of the strings of beads.
“And you think then we’ll be all right and be happy.”
“I know we will. You don’t have to be afraid. I’ve known lots of people that have done it.”
“So have I,” said the girl. “And afterward they were all so happy.”
“Well,” the man said, “if you don’t want to you don’t have to. I wouldn’t have you do it if you didn’t want to. But I know it’s perfectly simple.”
“And you really want to?”
“I think it’s the best thing to do. But I don’t want you to do it if you don’t really want to.”
“And if I do it you’ll be happy and things will be like they were and you’ll love me?”
“I love you now. You know I love you.”
“I know. But if I do it, then it will be nice again if I say things are like white elephants, and you’ll like it?”
“I’ll love it. I love it now but I just can’t think about it. You know how I get when I worry.”
“If I do it you won’t ever worry?”
“I won’t worry about that because it’s perfectly simple.”
“Then I’ll do it. Because I don’t care about me.”
“What do you mean?”
“I don’t care about me.”
“Well, I care about you.”
“Oh, yes. But I don’t care about me. And I’ll do it and then everything will be fine.”
“I don’t want you to do it if you feel that way.”

The girl stood up and walked to the end of the station. Across, on the other side, were fields of grain and trees along the banks of the Ebro. Far away, beyond the river, were mountains. The shadow of a cloud moved across the field of grain and she saw the river through the trees.
“And we could have all this,” she said. “And we could have everything and every day we make it more impossible.”
“What did you say?”
“I said we could have everything.”
“We can have everything.”
“No, we can’t.”
“We can have the whole world.”
“No, we can’t.”
“We can go everywhere.”
“No, we can’t. It isn’t ours any more.”
“It’s ours.”
“No, it isn’t. And once they take it away, you never get it back.”
“But they haven’t taken it away.”
“We’ll wait and see.”
“Come on back in the shade,” he said. “You mustn’t feel that way.”
“I don’t feel any way,” the girl said. “I just know things.”
“I don’t want you to do anything that you don’t want to do⁠—”
“Nor that isn’t good for me,” she said. “I know. Could we have another beer?”
“All right. But you’ve got to realize⁠—”
“I realize,” the girl said. “Can’t we maybe stop talking?”
They sat down at the table and the girl looked across at the hills on the dry side of the valley and the man looked at her and at the table.
“You’ve got to realize,” he said, “that I don’t want you to do it if you don’t want to. I’m perfectly willing to go through with it if it means anything to you.”
“Doesn’t it mean anything to you? We could get along.”
“Of course it does. But I don’t want anybody but you. I don’t want anyone else. And I know it’s perfectly simple.”
“Yes, you know it’s perfectly simple.”
“It’s all right for you to say that, but I do know it.”
“Would you do something for me now?”
“I’d do anything for you.”
“Would you please please please please please please please stop talking?”
He did not say anything but looked at the bags against the wall of the station. There were labels on them from all the hotels where they had spent nights.
“But I don’t want you to,” he said, “I don’t care anything about it.”
“I’ll scream,” the girl said.
The woman came out through the curtains with two glasses of beer and put them down on the damp felt pads. “The train comes in five minutes,” she said.
“What did she say?” asked the girl.
“That the train is coming in five minutes.”
The girl smiled brightly at the woman, to thank her.
“I’d better take the bags over to the other side of the station,” the man said. She smiled at him.
“All right. Then come back and we’ll finish the beer.”

He picked up the two heavy bags and carried them around the station to the other tracks. He looked up the tracks but could not see the train. Coming back, he walked through the barroom, where people waiting for the train were drinking. He drank an Anis at the bar and looked at the people. They were all waiting reasonably for the train. He went out through the bead curtain. She was sitting at the table and smiled at him.
“Do you feel better?” he asked.
“I feel fine,” she said. “There’s nothing wrong with me. I feel fine.”

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
On the surface, nothing happens. A man and a woman wait forty minutes for a train in a hot Spanish station, order drinks, and talk. The hills across the valley are long and white. She says they look like white elephants. He says he has never seen one. And so the conversation goes, apparently about nothing, until you notice how tightly everything they say is wound around one unspoken thing.

The unspoken thing is an abortion. The word never appears in the story. The man keeps calling it "an awfully simple operation" and says it is "just to let the air in." The woman, whom he calls Jig, has been brought to this station to catch a train to a city where it will be done. He insists he does not want her to do it unless she wants to. But everything he says pushes in one direction. He is perfectly willing, he says, to "go through with it" if it means anything to her, and yet he describes how simple it is, how many people have done it, how happy they all were afterward. She hears the pressure beneath the reassurance, and the story is the record of her hearing it.

Look at the way the big images work. The white hills are fertile, round, like the body of a pregnant woman, and on the other side of the station, the dry side, is a barren plain. The woman looks across the valley and sees the fields of grain and the river and says, "And we could have all this." The man answers, "We can have everything." She replies, "No, we can't." They are talking about the child, but also about a whole way of living that he does not want and she is starting to want. Their bags carry labels from all the hotels where they have spent nights. That is the life he is protecting, endless travel and drinks and no tie. The white elephant itself is an old English idiom for a gift that is more burden than benefit, and the joke may be on him as much as her: perhaps the thing he treats as a burden is the one valuable thing between them.

Notice also the drinks. They order beer, then Anis del Toro, which she says tastes like licorice, and she adds that everything tastes like licorice, especially the things you have waited so long for, like absinthe. The ordering of drinks fills silences, and it shows a couple used to drowning difficult subjects in pleasure.

The last lines are the most chilling. The man carries the bags to the other side, drinks an Anis, and comes back. "Do you feel better?" he asks. "I feel fine," she says. "There's nothing wrong with me. I feel fine." The repetition is the entire tragedy in miniature. She has stopped arguing, and what she says is not a report but a closing of a door. We never learn what she decides. The story is not about the decision. It is about a relationship in which one person talks past the other until the other falls silent.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
Hills Like White Elephants is, by almost any measure, one of the most carefully built short stories in English. Its first virtue is control. Everything is rendered in short, plain sentences, with almost no interior access. We are never told what either character thinks. Instead the story gives us physical things, such as the bamboo bead curtain, the bags with their hotel labels, the damp felt pads under the beer glasses, and the station standing between two lines of rails, and it trusts those to carry the weight. The setting itself is an argument: a junction, a place of transit, where nobody belongs, positioned precisely between two options.

The dialogue is the real achievement. Listen to how the pattern shifts. In the early lines the woman is playful, almost teasing, and the man is patient. As the subject is gradually approached, her sentences shorten and her sarcasm sharpens. "Yes, you know it's perfectly simple." Then she explodes into the famous plea: "Would you please please please please please please please stop talking?" The stacking of pleases is a small miracle of rhythm, and it reads as exhaustion and rage in one breath. Meanwhile the man's speech becomes more and more circular, repeating the same reassurance in slightly different words. Hemingway lets repetition do what a lesser writer would do with adjectives.

There are weaknesses worth admitting. The first is that the man is drawn as somewhat too smoothly selfish, and some readers feel that the woman, by contrast, is mostly a vessel for pain. She is perceptive and bitter, but we learn little about what she actually wants beyond what she says in a few lines. The imbalance can make the story feel like a scenario with a built-in moral rather than a fully lived encounter. Secondly, a few of the symbolic touches, the fertile hills against the barren plain, the elephant as unwanted burden, are so neatly placed that they can feel like the author's hand arranging a still life.

There is also the question of the iceberg itself. Hemingway's method works best when the submerged part is felt and not merely hidden. Here, some argue, the story is so reticent that readers must reconstruct the subject from cues, which means the experience depends heavily on a certain background knowledge. A reader with no sense of what is going on can finish the story thinking it is a quarrel about a trip. Whether that is a flaw or a feature depends on taste; many admirers feel the difficulty is part of the point, since the characters themselves are avoiding the subject.

And yet the story's concision is so extreme and its emotional result so large that its flaws seem like the shadow of its strengths. It takes perhaps ten minutes to read and an afternoon to stop thinking about.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The story first appeared in 1927 in the Paris magazine transition, an avant-garde journal, and was soon collected in Hemingway's book Men Without Women, which came out in October of that year. By then Hemingway was already famous for The Sun Also Rises, published the previous year, and this story reinforced his standing as the most influential new prose stylist in America. It showed what his method could do in a very small space: a whole relationship, a moral crisis, and a social era, compressed into a few pages of speech.

Its most important legacy is as the model of what Hemingway later described, in his book on bullfighting, Death in the Afternoon, as the theory of omission. A writer who knows enough about the subject, he said, may leave things out, and the reader will feel them as strongly as if they had been stated. The image of the iceberg, with only an eighth above water, comes from there, and Hills Like White Elephants has become the textbook illustration. It is routinely used in writing classes to teach subtext: how dialogue can carry meaning that the words themselves avoid.

The story's effect on later short fiction has been enormous. The spare, dialogue-driven, reticent realism associated with writers like Raymond Carver, whose characters talk around the things that matter most, owes a great deal to this model. So do countless minimalist stories and, for that matter, screenwriting. The rhythm of overlapping, evasive conversation can be traced into film and television drama.

It also has a cultural and political afterlife. The story deals with abortion without ever naming it, at a time when the subject was legally and socially taboo, and it has been taught, argued over, and read in many different ways as the public debate has changed. Some readers see it as sympathetic to a woman pressured into a choice, others as a story about a couple's divergence of values, and still others as a study in male evasion. The fact that it can support these readings is part of why it endures.

It has been adapted for the screen and stage a number of times, including a 1990 cable television version, and it has been staged as a short theater piece. Few of these adaptations keep the bare, unforced feeling of the original, which is a kind of tribute to how much depends on the text's silences. In Hemingway's career, the story sits near the height of his early style, before the more public persona of the war correspondent and big-game hunter overshadowed the quiet, exacting craftsman who wrote it.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers and writers have loved Hills Like White Elephants above all for its nerve. It dares to leave the biggest subject unsaid, and it does so with such confidence that the reader is drawn into collaboration. You feel clever when you catch on, and then you feel the weight of what you have caught. That experience of discovery, of slowly realizing that this idle chatter is a life-changing conversation, is part of what people remember. Many readers say they first read it as a puzzle and finished it as a heartbreak.

They also love how true the dialogue feels. Anyone who has been in a relationship where one person is pressing and the other is retreating will recognize the rhythm: the "I don't want you to do anything you don't want to do" followed immediately by more pressure; the "I'm perfectly willing" that is nothing of the kind. The man's gentle, reasonable tone is, in some ways, the most unsettling part, because it is how real coercion often sounds. It is rarely a shout. It is a patient voice repeating that everything will be fine.

Another thing admirers cherish is the woman's quiet intelligence. She is witty and sharp, and she hears everything. Her remark about the hills and her small bitter jokes show a mind that has outpaced the man's. At the end, her insistence that she feels fine is a performance, and readers love the dignity and the sorrow of it. Many say she is among the most memorable women in Hemingway's work, a character who stays vivid even though she is rarely given the narrative's sympathy outright.

Fellow writers admire the story as a masterclass in technique. It is frequently named in discussions of the best American short stories, and it is a favorite of teachers because every detail, down to the beaded curtain, rewards close reading. The sheer compression of it, a whole drama in a few pages and almost no action, is a source of awe. Even people who dislike Hemingway's public persona tend to concede that this story shows him at his most disciplined.

Finally, readers respond to the setting, which is almost a character. The heat, the white hills, the dry side and the green side, the clinking of beer glasses, the sense of a train that will take them somewhere: it is a landscape in which a decision hangs in the air. The atmosphere does the emotional work. A reader who has never been to Spain can feel the stillness of that platform and the pressure of the clock ticking toward a train.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Because the story is so open, much of the criticism has been about how to read it, and some of it is sharply divided. The central dispute concerns whose side the story is on. One group of readers, many of them feminist critics, see it as an indictment of a man who manipulates a woman into an abortion she does not want while claiming to leave the choice to her. Another group reads it more ambiguously, as a portrait of a couple in which both are at fault, or as a story about a woman who has already decided and is simply waiting for the man to catch up. A third strain argues that the story is, in the end, more concerned with the man's emotional limits than with the woman's, and that Hemingway's sympathies, as in much of his work, lie more with male experience. Reasonable readers have landed everywhere in this range, and the text does not settle it.

A related criticism is that the woman, for all her vividness, has little agency or inner life in the story. We see her only through speech and through the man's eyes, and she is reduced at times to a symbol, the fertile landscape, the vessel of pain. Some critics find that this reproduces the very objectification the story seems to deplore. Others reply that this is the point, that the story shows how a woman can be silenced by a conversation, and that the form enacts the problem.

There is also the broader criticism of Hemingway's style that this story sometimes attracts. The famous reticence can look like a pose. Critics from his own time onward have charged that his clipped, repetitive prose, imitated by countless lesser writers, can degrade into mannerism, with a tough-guy simplicity that conceals thinness. Hills Like White Elephants largely escapes that charge, but it is the kind of story that spawned a thousand imitators who did not escape it.

Finally, some readers object to the symbolism as too schematic: the two sides of the valley, the white elephant, the barren versus fertile imagery. They feel that a story pledged to understatement should not be quite so careful about its metaphors, and that the arrangement shows the writer's hand more than he intended. Others defend the images as natural, since people notice such things when they are anxious.

What stands out is that few critics dispute the story's quality. The argument is almost entirely about its meaning and its politics, which is often the sign of a work that has genuinely gotten under the skin of its readers.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
Hills Like White Elephants belongs to the modernist moment of the 1920s, when writers in Paris, London, and New York were trying to break with Victorian fullness and moralizing and to find a language equal to the shock of the First World War. Hemingway was part of the group of American expatriates in Paris, and he was mentored in compression by Ezra Pound and Gertrude Stein. The idea that a story should drop its explanations and present things as they are, with feeling carried by objects and gestures, is a modernist principle shared by Pound's imagist poetry and by Joyce and Eliot in different ways.

Within that movement, Hemingway's contribution was a particular kind of plainness. His ancestors include Mark Twain's vernacular in Huckleberry Finn, which he once called the source of all modern American literature, and the compression of Chekhov, whose stories also end on an open note and trust subtext. The comparison with Chekhov is useful: both writers show an unresolved moment and let the reader supply the rest, though Chekhov is warmer and more interested in the sorrow of ordinary lives, while Hemingway is colder and more concerned with stoic endurance.

Descendants are everywhere. Raymond Carver's minimalist stories, with their halting, evasive speech, are one obvious line. Another runs through writers like Grace Paley, Alice Munro, and Lorrie Moore, who work with subtext in different keys. In drama, Harold Pinter's famous pauses and menace beneath polite talk have something in common with the story's method. And in film, the idea that the most important part of a scene may be what is not said is now commonplace.

Placed beside Hemingway's other work, the story shows a side of him that is less swaggering than his reputation. It belongs with his quieter tales of failing intimacy and dread, rather than with the big-game and war material. It is also comparable to Joyce's The Dead, which ends with a revelation between husband and wife, though Joyce works in a lush, lyrical register and Hemingway in a bare one.

Why read it now? Because the subject remains charged, and because the story's real subject, how a conversation can be a struggle for power disguised as concern, is permanent. It is also one of the cleanest lessons in how fiction works: how a handful of objects and a bit of dialogue can create a whole moral situation, and how silence can be louder than speech. After reading it, you may start listening differently to the way people say that they are fine.

stories.title: The Killers
stories.author: Ernest Hemingway
stories.epigraph: “The door of Henry’s lunchroom opened and two men came in. They sat down at the counter.”
stories.keyContext: The Killers, published in 1927 and collected in Ernest Hemingway's book Men Without Women, is one of the most famous crime stories ever written, though it contains almost no crime. Two hired gunmen walk into a small-town lunchroom in Illinois, tie up the cook and a teenage boy named Nick Adams, and wait for a retired boxer who never shows up. Hemingway was in his twenties, living in Europe, and by then known as the leader of a new, spare way of writing in which feeling is carried by what people do and say rather than by what the narrator explains. The setting is Prohibition-era America, when gangsters from Chicago were becoming a national legend and a national fear. The story's surprise is that the real subject is not violence but what it does to a young person who sees it up close. Listen for the way the dialogue loops and repeats, and for how the story ends not with a bang but with a boy making a quiet decision.
paragraphs: The door of Henry’s lunchroom opened and two men came in. They sat down at the counter.
“What’s yours?” George asked them.
“I don’t know,” one of the men said. “What do you want to eat, Al?”
“I don’t know,” said Al. “I don’t know what I want to eat.”

Outside it was getting dark. The streetlight came on outside the window. The two men at the counter read the menu. From the other end of the counter Nick Adams watched them. He had been talking to George when they came in.
“I’ll have a roast pork tenderloin with apple sauce and mashed potatoes,” the first man said.
“It isn’t ready yet.”
“What the hell do you put it on the card for?”
“That’s the dinner,” George explained. “You can get that at six o’clock.”
George looked at the clock on the wall behind the counter.
“It’s five o’clock.”
“The clock says twenty minutes past five,” the second man said.
“It’s twenty minutes fast.”
“Oh, to hell with the clock,” the first man said. “What have you got to eat?”
“I can give you any kind of sandwiches,” George said. “You can have ham and eggs, bacon and eggs, liver and bacon, or a steak.”
“Give me chicken croquettes with green peas and cream sauce and mashed potatoes.”
“That’s the dinner.”
“Everything we want’s the dinner, eh? That’s the way you work it.”
“I can give you ham and eggs, bacon and eggs, liver⁠—”

“I’ll take ham and eggs,” the man called Al said. He wore a derby hat and a black overcoat buttoned across the chest. His face was small and white and he had tight lips. He wore a silk muffler and gloves.

“Give me bacon and eggs,” said the other man. He was about the same size as Al. Their faces were different, but they were dressed like twins. Both wore overcoats too tight for them. They sat leaning forward, their elbows on the counter.
“Got anything to drink?” Al asked.
“Silver beer, bevo, ginger-ale,” George said.
“I mean you got anything to drink?”
“Just those I said.”
“This is a hot town,” said the other. “What do they call it?”
“Summit.”
“Ever hear of it?” Al asked his friend.
“No,” said the friend.
“What do you do here nights?” Al asked.
“They eat the dinner,” his friend said. “They all come here and eat the big dinner.”
“That’s right,” George said.
“So you think that’s right?” Al asked George.
“Sure.”
“You’re a pretty bright boy, aren’t you?”
“Sure,” said George.
“Well, you’re not,” said the other little man. “Is he, Al?”
“He’s dumb,” said Al. He turned to Nick. “What’s your name?”
“Adams.”
“Another bright boy,” Al said. “Ain’t he a bright boy, Max?”
“The town’s full of bright boys,” Max said.
George put the two platters, one of ham and eggs, the other of bacon and eggs, on the counter. He set down two side-dishes of fried potatoes and closed the wicket into the kitchen.
“Which is yours?” he asked Al.
“Don’t you remember?”
“Ham and eggs.”
“Just a bright boy,” Max said. He leaned forward and took the ham and eggs. Both men ate with their gloves on. George watched them eat.
“What are you looking at?” Max looked at George.
“Nothing.”
“The hell you were. You were looking at me.”
“Maybe the boy meant it for a joke, Max,” Al said.
George laughed.
“You don’t have to laugh,” Max said to him. “You don’t have to laugh at all, see?”
“All right,” said George.
“So he thinks it’s all right.” Max turned to Al. “He thinks it’s all right. That’s a good one.”
“Oh, he’s a thinker,” Al said. They went on eating.
“What’s the bright boy’s name down the counter?” Al asked Max.
“Hey, bright boy,” Max said to Nick. “You go around on the other side of the counter with your boy friend.”
“What’s the idea?” Nick asked.
“There isn’t any idea.”
“You better go around, bright boy,” Al said. Nick went around behind the counter.
“What’s the idea?” George asked.
“None of your damn business,” Al said. “Who’s out in the kitchen?”
“The nigger.”
“What do you mean the nigger?”
“The nigger that cooks.”
“Tell him to come in.”
“What’s the idea?”
“Tell him to come in.”
“Where do you think you are?”
“We know damn well where we are,” the man called Max said. “Do we look silly?”
“You talk silly,” Al said to him. “What the hell do you argue with this kid for? Listen,” he said to George, “tell the nigger to come out here.”
“What are you going to do to him?”
“Nothing. Use your head, bright boy. What would we do to a nigger?”
George opened the slit that opened back into the kitchen. “Sam,” he called. “Come in here a minute.”
The door to the kitchen opened and the nigger came in. “What was it?” he asked. The two men at the counter took a look at him.
“All right, nigger. You stand right there,” Al said.
Sam, the nigger, standing in his apron, looked at the two men sitting at the counter. “Yes, sir,” he said. Al got down from his stool.

“I’m going back to the kitchen with the nigger and bright boy,” he said. “Go on back to the kitchen, nigger. You go with him, bright boy.” The little man walked after Nick and Sam, the cook, back into the kitchen. The door shut after them. The man called Max sat at the counter opposite George. He didn’t look at George but looked in the mirror that ran along back of the counter. Henry’s had been made over from a saloon into a lunch-counter.
“Well, bright boy,” Max said, looking into the mirror, “why don’t you say something?”
“What’s it all about?”
“Hey, Al,” Max called, “bright boy wants to know what it’s all about.”
“Why don’t you tell him?” Al’s voice came from the kitchen.
“What do you think it’s all about?”
“I don’t know.”
“What do you think?”
Max looked into the mirror all the time he was talking.
“I wouldn’t say.”
“Hey, Al, bright boy says he wouldn’t say what he thinks it’s all about.”

“I can hear you, all right,” Al said from the kitchen. He had propped open the slit that dishes passed through into the kitchen with a catsup bottle. “Listen, bright boy,” he said from the kitchen to George. “Stand a little further along the bar. You move a little to the left, Max.” He was like a photographer arranging for a group picture.
“Talk to me, bright boy,” Max said. “What do you think’s going to happen?”
George did not say anything.
“I’ll tell you,” Max said. “We’re going to kill a Swede. Do you know a big Swede named Ole Andreson?”
“Yes.”
“He comes here to eat every night, don’t he?”
“Sometimes he comes here.”
“He comes here at six o’clock, don’t he?”
“If he comes.”
“We know all that, bright boy,” Max said. “Talk about something else. Ever go to the movies?”
“Once in a while.”
“You ought to go to the movies more. The movies are fine for a bright boy like you.”
“What are you going to kill Ole Andreson for? What did he ever do to you?”
“He never had a chance to do anything to us. He never even seen us.”
“And he’s only going to see us once,” Al said from the kitchen.
“What are you going to kill him for, then?” George asked.
“We’re killing him for a friend. Just to oblige a friend, bright boy.”
“Shut up,” said Al from the kitchen. “You talk too goddam much.”
“Well, I got to keep bright boy amused. Don’t I, bright boy?”
“You talk too damn much,” Al said. “The nigger and my bright boy are amused by themselves. I got them tied up like a couple of girl friends in the convent.”
“I suppose you were in a convent.”
“You never know.”
“You were in a kosher convent. That’s where you were.”
George looked up at the clock.
“If anybody comes in you tell them the cook is off, and if they keep after it, you tell them you’ll go back and cook yourself. Do you get that, bright boy?”
“All right,” George said. “What you going to do with us afterward?”
“That’ll depend,” Max said. “That’s one of those things you never know at the time.”
George looked up at the clock. It was a quarter past six. The door from the street opened. A streetcar motorman came in.
“Hello, George,” he said. “Can I get supper?”
“Sam’s gone out,” George said. “He’ll be back in about half an hour.”
“I’d better go up the street,” the motorman said. George looked at the clock. It was twenty minutes past six.
“That was nice, bright boy,” Max said. “You’re a regular little gentleman.”
“He knew I’d blow his head off,” Al said from the kitchen.
“No,” said Max. “It ain’t that. Bright boy is nice. He’s a nice boy. I like him.”
At six-fifty-five George said: “He’s not coming.”

Two other people had been in the lunchroom. Once George had gone out to the kitchen and made a ham-and-egg sandwich “to go” that a man wanted to take with him. Inside the kitchen he saw Al, his derby hat tipped back, sitting on a stool beside the wicket with the muzzle of a sawed-off shotgun resting on the ledge. Nick and the cook were back to back in the corner, a towel tied in each of their mouths. George had cooked the sandwich, wrapped it up in oiled paper, put it in a bag, brought it in, and the man had paid for it and gone out.
“Bright boy can do everything,” Max said. “He can cook and everything. You’d make some girl a nice wife, bright boy.”
“Yes?” George said. “Your friend, Ole Andreson, isn’t going to come.”
“We’ll give him ten minutes,” Max said.
Max watched the mirror and the clock. The hands of the clock marked seven o’clock, and then five minutes past seven.
“Come on, Al,” said Max. “We better go. He’s not coming.”
“Better give him five minutes,” Al said from the kitchen.
In the five minutes a man came in, and George explained that the cook was sick.
“Why the hell don’t you get another cook?” the man asked. “Aren’t you running a lunch-counter?” He went out.
“Come on, Al,” Max said.
“What about the two bright boys and the nigger?”
“They’re all right.”
“You think so?”
“Sure. We’re through with it.”
“I don’t like it,” said Al. “It’s sloppy. You talk too much.”
“Oh, what the hell,” said Max. “We got to keep amused, haven’t we?”

“You talk too much, all the same,” Al said. He came out from the kitchen. The cutoff barrels of the shotgun made a slight bulge under the waist of his too tight-fitting overcoat. He straightened his coat with his gloved hands.
“So long, bright boy,” he said to George. “You got a lot of luck.”
“That’s the truth,” Max said. “You ought to play the races, bright boy.”

The two of them went out the door. George watched them, through the window, pass under the arc-light and cross the street. In their tight overcoats and derby hats they looked like a vaudeville team. George went back through the swinging-door into the kitchen and untied Nick and the cook.
“I don’t want any more of that,” said Sam, the cook. “I don’t want any more of that.”
Nick stood up. He had never had a towel in his mouth before.
“Say,” he said. “What the hell?” He was trying to swagger it off.
“They were going to kill Ole Andreson,” George said. “They were going to shoot him when he came in to eat.”
“Ole Andreson?”
“Sure.”
The cook felt the corners of his mouth with his thumbs.
“They all gone?” he asked.
“Yeah,” said George. “They’re gone now.”
“I don’t like it,” said the cook. “I don’t like any of it at all.”
“Listen,” George said to Nick. “You better go see Ole Andreson.”
“All right.”
“You better not have anything to do with it at all,” Sam, the cook, said. “You better stay way out of it.”
“Don’t go if you don’t want to,” George said.
“Mixing up in this ain’t going to get you anywhere,” the cook said. “You stay out of it.”
“I’ll go see him,” Nick said to George. “Where does he live?”
The cook turned away.
“Little boys always know what they want to do,” he said.
“He lives up at Hirsch’s rooming-house,” George said to Nick.
“I’ll go up there.”

Outside the arc-light shone through the bare branches of a tree. Nick walked up the street beside the car-tracks and turned at the next arc-light down a side-street. Three houses up the street was Hirsch’s rooming-house. Nick walked up the two steps and pushed the bell. A woman came to the door.
“Is Ole Andreson here?”
“Do you want to see him?”
“Yes, if he’s in.”
Nick followed the woman up a flight of stairs and back to the end of a corridor. She knocked on the door.
“Who is it?”
“It’s somebody to see you, Mr. Andreson,” the woman said.
“It’s Nick Adams.”
“Come in.”

Nick opened the door and went into the room. Ole Andreson was lying on the bed with all his clothes on. He had been a heavyweight prizefighter and he was too long for the bed. He lay with his head on two pillows. He did not look at Nick.
“What was it?” he asked.
“I was up at Henry’s,” Nick said, “and two fellows came in and tied up me and the cook, and they said they were going to kill you.”
It sounded silly when he said it. Ole Andreson said nothing.
“They put us out in the kitchen,” Nick went on. “They were going to shoot you when you came in to supper.”
Ole Andreson looked at the wall and did not say anything.
“George thought I better come and tell you about it.”
“There isn’t anything I can do about it,” Ole Andreson said.
“I’ll tell you what they were like.”
“I don’t want to know what they were like,” Ole Andreson said. He looked at the wall. “Thanks for coming to tell me about it.”
“That’s all right.”
Nick looked at the big man lying on the bed.
“Don’t you want me to go and see the police?”
“No,” Ole Andreson said. “That wouldn’t do any good.”
“Isn’t there something I could do?”
“No. There ain’t anything to do.”
“Maybe it was just a bluff.”
“No. It ain’t just a bluff.”
Ole Andreson rolled over toward the wall.
“The only thing is,” he said, talking toward the wall, “I just can’t make up my mind to go out. I been in here all day.”
“Couldn’t you get out of town?”
“No,” Ole Andreson said. “I’m through with all that running around.”
He looked at the wall.
“There ain’t anything to do now.”
“Couldn’t you fix it up some way?”
“No. I got in wrong.” He talked in the same flat voice. “There ain’t anything to do. After a while I’ll make up my mind to go out.”
“I better go back and see George,” Nick said.
“So long,” said Ole Andreson. He did not look toward Nick. “Thanks for coming around.”
Nick went out. As he shut the door he saw Ole Andreson with all his clothes on, lying on the bed looking at the wall.

“He’s been in his room all day,” the landlady said downstairs. “I guess he don’t feel well. I said to him: ‘Mr. Andreson, you ought to go out and take a walk on a nice fall day like this,’ but he didn’t feel like it.”
“He doesn’t want to go out.”
“I’m sorry he don’t feel well,” the woman said. “He’s an awfully nice man. He was in the ring, you know.”
“I know it.”
“You’d never know it except from the way his face is,” the woman said. They stood talking just inside the street door. “He’s just as gentle.”
“Well, good night, Mrs. Hirsch,” Nick said.
“I’m not Mrs. Hirsch,” the woman said. “She owns the place. I just look after it for her. I’m Mrs. Bell.”
“Well, good night, Mrs. Bell,” Nick said.
“Good night,” the woman said.
Nick walked up the dark street to the corner under the arc-light, and then along the car-tracks to Henry’s eating-house. George was inside, back of the counter.
“Did you see Ole?”
“Yes,” said Nick. “He’s in his room and he won’t go out.”
The cook opened the door from the kitchen when he heard Nick’s voice.
“I don’t even listen to it,” he said and shut the door.
“Did you tell him about it?” George asked.
“Sure. I told him but he knows what it’s all about.”
“What’s he going to do?”
“Nothing.”
“They’ll kill him.”
“I guess they will.”
“He must have got mixed up in something in Chicago.”
“I guess so,” said Nick.
“It’s a hell of a thing.”
“It’s an awful thing,” Nick said.
They did not say anything. George reached down for a towel and wiped the counter.
“I wonder what he did?” Nick said.
“Double-crossed somebody. That’s what they kill them for.”
“I’m going to get out of this town,” Nick said.
“Yes,” said George. “That’s a good thing to do.”
“I can’t stand to think about him waiting in the room and knowing he’s going to get it. It’s too damned awful.”
“Well,” said George, “you better not think about it.”

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The Killers is built in three movements. First comes the scene in Henry's lunchroom, the longest part by far, in which two men in tight black overcoats and derby hats, Al and Max, order dinner, make fun of the staff, and finally reveal that they have come to kill a man named Ole Andreson, a big Swede who usually eats there at six. They tie up Nick and the cook, Sam, in the kitchen, hold George at the counter, and wait. Ole does not come. At last they give up, walk out, and leave the others alive. In the second movement, Nick runs to the rooming house to warn Ole. He finds him lying on his bed, fully dressed, facing the wall, and Ole refuses to do anything. In the third, Nick returns to the lunchroom and says he is going to leave town.

What is it about? The most obvious answer is fear, but a more careful reading says it is about a collision between innocence and a world that does not care. The killers are almost comic at first. They bicker about the menu, call George and Nick "bright boys," and say they are killing Ole "just to oblige a friend." That phrase is a chilling joke: to them murder is a favor, a piece of business. They have nothing against him. He never did them any harm. The violence is utterly impersonal, which is what makes it terrifying. Nothing in the universe of the story gives it a reason.

Then there is Ole Andreson. Once a heavyweight prizefighter, he lies on the bed and says, "There ain't anything to do." He has stopped running. He says he got "in wrong," and he is waiting for the thing to happen. This surrender is what truly shakes Nick. A big man, a man who once fought for a living, has been reduced to a body turned toward a wall. The story suggests that some doom cannot be argued with, and that some people, when it finds them, simply stop.

Nick is the real center. At the start he is a boy who watches. At the end he says he cannot stand to think about Ole waiting in his room, "knowing he's going to get it. It's too damned awful." George, older and more settled, gives the answer of the world: "Well, you better not think about it." That is the story's final line, and it is the cold truth of how adults cope. Nick has crossed a line from a boy who didn't know to a young man who does. The story is an initiation, a loss of innocence told without a single speech about it. It also carries, in the background, the presence of casual racism in the era's language, which the story records without comment and which modern readers will notice.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
The craft of The Killers is spectacular, and its first great strength is tension built from almost nothing. For nearly half the story, the menace comes entirely from dialogue and delay. The men's refusal to order, their mocking repetition, their small cruelties, and the patience of their waiting produce a quiet dread that action rarely achieves. The famous opening exchange, with Al and Max each saying "I don't know what I want to eat," sets the pattern: speech that circles and circles, and under it a threat.

Hemingway's ear for dialogue is the engine. The killers talk in a stylized, almost vaudeville way. They echo each other and slide from comedy into threat. "The town's full of bright boys," says Max. Their repetition is reminiscent of the routine of a comedy double act, which is part of the horror, since menace delivered as a routine seems to have no human feeling at all. George's cautious replies and Nick's silence form a counterpoint. Nobody says what he feels, and so everything is felt. The scene in the kitchen, where Nick and Sam sit tied while Al sits with a sawed-off shotgun on the ledge of the serving hatch, is a model of controlled physical description: simple facts that make the reader's pulse rise.

The structure is also admirable. The story spends a great deal of time on the scene where nothing is accomplished and then moves quickly through the aftermath. That imbalance is deliberate. The waiting is the story, and the killers' failure to find their victim denies the reader the satisfaction of a crime plot, replacing it with something harder: knowledge.

There are real weaknesses to consider. The killers are drawn so stylishly that some readers feel Hemingway admires them, or at least that they become more vivid than the people they threaten. The dialogue can tip into mannerism, with its relentless repetition, and in the hands of imitators it became a parody. Ole's passivity is a mystery the story deliberately refuses to solve, but some readers find his fatalism too convenient, a device to produce the final shock rather than a convincing human response. The ending, with Nick's decision, is slightly more explicit about its meaning than the best of Hemingway's work, since the boy practically states the theme.

Finally, the casual racist language applied to the cook, and the way Sam is treated as a minor figure who simply wants to avoid trouble, are features a present-day reader cannot ignore. The story is recording the attitudes of its time and its characters, but it records them without any visible critical perspective, and that deserves honest notice.

Even so, the story's mastery is plain. It is rare to find a piece of fiction that creates so much fear from so little, and does it with such discipline.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
When The Killers appeared in Scribner's Magazine in March 1927, and then in Men Without Women in October, it was greeted as a demonstration of what American short fiction could now do. It helped cement Hemingway's reputation as the leading stylist of his generation, and it became one of the most widely reprinted short stories in the language. It is also the story where Nick Adams, the semi-autobiographical young man who runs through Hemingway's early work, appears in one of his most dramatic roles.

Its influence on crime writing was immediate and lasting. The hard-boiled school of American detective fiction, led by writers like Dashiell Hammett and later Raymond Chandler, shared Hemingway's taste for plain, vernacular speech and his refusal to sentimentalize violence. James M. Cain, Jim Thompson, and a whole tradition of noir fiction follow in the wake. More specifically, the image of two professional killers who chat idly before work has been borrowed again and again. It is hard to watch a later scene of hit men talking about nothing, whether in the films of Quentin Tarantino or the Coen brothers, without thinking of Al and Max.

The story has been adapted for the screen repeatedly. The best known is the 1946 film directed by Robert Siodmak, which expands the story into a full film noir: the opening twenty minutes follow Hemingway's story closely, and then the film spins a long investigation of why Ole, here played by Burt Lancaster in his debut, was marked for death. A second adaptation, directed by Don Siegel in 1964, reshaped the material again, and it has the distinction of featuring Lee Marvin as a hit man. A short student film of the story was also made in 1956 by the young Andrei Tarkovsky, before he became one of the great directors of world cinema.

Within the history of the short story, The Killers became a staple of teaching. It is a classic example of dramatic, objective narration, in which the author remains outside the characters' minds and the reader is forced to infer. It is used to illustrate subtext, repetition, tone, and the structure of an initiation story.

For Hemingway's career, it was a high point of his early period, showing that his method worked not just on quiet domestic dilemmas but on high-tension material. It is part of the body of work that supported his later Nobel Prize and the extraordinary force of his example on twentieth-century prose.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers have always responded to the sheer suspense of The Killers. Even people who know nothing about Hemingway or modernism find the lunchroom scene gripping. The menace is physical and immediate, and the humor of the gunmen, their weird hospitality and their taunting, makes the reader both laugh and shiver. There is an old observation that the most frightening villains are the ones who talk like comedians, and Al and Max are the proof.

Readers also love the story's economy. In a few thousand words it creates a town, a decor, a set of people, and a crisis. Henry's lunchroom, made over from a saloon, with the mirror along the back and the arc light outside, is a complete place. The reader feels the clock on the wall, which George says runs twenty minutes fast, and the streetlight coming on at dusk. The details are chosen so tightly that readers who return to the story often discover a new one each time.

Many admire the ending. Instead of a burst of violence, the story gives a moral pivot: a young man deciding to leave a town where such a thing can happen. People find it resonant because it suggests how most of us meet cruelty, not by fighting it but by trying to look away, and by being unable to stop thinking about it. George's advice not to think about it is, for many readers, the saddest line, because it is what practical adults really say, and it shows how a community absorbs horror by refusing to look.

Writers in particular admire how well the story demonstrates what Hemingway could do with speech. Teachers of fiction often use it to show how dialogue can characterize, advance a plot, and build tension all at once. Crime writers revere it. Film directors have loved it for its visual, theatrical staging: a single room, a few actors, and a ticking threat. It plays almost like a one-act play.

And then there is Ole Andreson, who has been a source of fascination ever since. The scene in the rooming house, with the huge, gentle man facing the wall, is regarded by many as the emotional peak of the story. His flat refusal to run, and the quiet way the landlady says "he's just as gentle," humanize a figure who might have been a mere target. Readers are moved by that dignity and that despair, and they often find the unexplained mystery of what he did to be more haunting than any answer could be.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
The Killers has been largely admired, but a number of reservations have been voiced. One is the old complaint about the Hemingway mannerism. The clipped, repetitive speech of the killers and the plain declarative narration are so distinctive that, even at the time, some reviewers worried they were becoming a formula. Later critics have said that Hemingway's style, so fresh in its first appearances, could harden into a pose of toughness, and that the killers' routine is a little too stylized to be fully believable as speech. Real gangsters, the objection goes, do not talk like a vaudeville act. This is a fair point about realism, though defenders reply that the story is not aiming at documentary realism but at a heightened, almost ritual effect.

A second line of criticism concerns the story's unexplained center. We never learn what Ole did. Some readers find the lack of explanation frustrating, a mystery that is also an evasion. Others, as with the Siodmak film, have felt the need to supply a backstory, which is a kind of critical verdict in itself. Hemingway's view, consistent with his theory of leaving out what the reader can feel, was that the explanation would weaken the story. But the story's fatalism, in which Ole simply lies down to wait for death, has struck some critics as an unconvincing passivity.

A third area is the treatment of race and class. The cook, Sam, is described with a racial slur in the narration and in George's speech, and is a figure of fear and compliance. Modern readers rightly note that the story records this without any critical frame. Whether the author is merely reflecting the world he wrote about or sharing its blind spots is debated, and it is one of the reasons the story is taught today with some care.

There are also criticisms of the story's moral vision. Some have found its treatment of violence as an inexplicable fact, to be endured and avoided, too bleak or too resigned. The story offers no justice, no redemption, and no counterforce. Readers who want some sense of moral order may feel that the story, however brilliantly made, is a shrug. Others say that this is exactly the honesty that makes it great.

Finally, a few critics have observed that the story is more admired than any one of its parts. The famous opening dialogue is often cited as the best part, and the rooming house scene and the ending, while powerful, have drawn comparatively less attention and sometimes feel like a necessary epilogue to an extraordinary first movement.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
The Killers stands at a crossroads between literary fiction and genre fiction. Its materials come from the crime tale, with hit men, a doomed victim, and a Chicago background, but its method comes from modernist literature, with its objectivity, compression, and refusal to explain. This fusion is one of the most productive in twentieth-century writing. It helped open the way for the literary respectability of crime fiction and for the hard-boiled style of Hammett, Chandler, Cain, and later writers, while also showing literary writers that violence and menace could be handled with great subtlety.

In Hemingway's own work, it belongs with the early Nick Adams stories and with the collection In Our Time. Together they trace a young man's education in a violent world: the Indian camp where a baby is born and a father kills himself, the war stories, the fishing trips that are really recoveries. In those, as in this, Nick is the observer to whom something terrible happens, and the lesson is not articulated but absorbed. The story is also in conversation with a long American tradition of the innocent encountering evil, from Hawthorne and Melville to Twain.

Among comparisons, it resembles in some ways Shirley Jackson's The Lottery, in which a small town carries out a ritual violence in a flat, everyday tone, and Flannery O'Connor's A Good Man Is Hard to Find, in which a family meets a killer. Each uses plain, cheerful surface detail to contrast with horror. It also has kinship with Chekhov's method of ending on an open note and with Joyce's technique in Dubliners, where a small event produces a moment of realization.

Its descendants are everywhere: in the films of Tarantino, whose hit men chatter about hamburgers, in Harold Pinter's play The Dumb Waiter, in which two killers wait in a basement room and bicker, in the Coen brothers' No Country for Old Men, and in the grim, understated tone of countless crime dramas on screen. Whenever violence is presented as routine, delivered by people who talk about lunch, the lineage leads back to Henry's lunchroom.

Why read it today? Because it is a model of suspense that does not depend on gimmicks, a lesson in how to write dialogue, and an enduring portrait of the moment when a young person realizes that the world contains forces that cannot be reasoned with and that most adults handle by looking away. It takes twenty minutes to read. It will teach you to hear what a conversation hides, and it will probably make you slightly uneasy the next time two strangers walk into a quiet diner.

stories.title: Cat in the Rain
stories.author: Ernest Hemingway
stories.epigraph: “I’m going down and get that kitty,” the American wife said.
stories.keyContext: Cat in the Rain is a short, quiet story by Ernest Hemingway, first published in 1925 in his collection In Our Time. It is one of the clearest early examples of his method: very simple sentences, almost nothing that looks like an event, and a great deal of feeling pressed beneath the surface. An American couple is staying in an Italian seaside hotel on a rainy day. The wife sees a cat outside, wants to rescue it, and returns to a husband who is more interested in his book. Hemingway wrote it in his mid twenties, as a young American living in Europe after the First World War, married and soon to be a father, and trying to find a form for the unspoken disappointments of ordinary intimacy. Many readers take it as a story about a marriage in which one person's needs go unheard. Listen to how often the wife says what she wants, and to who is actually listening.
paragraphs: There were only two Americans stopping at the hotel. They did not know any of the people they passed on the stairs on their way to and from their room. Their room was on the second floor facing the sea. It also faced the public garden and the war monument. There were big palms and green benches in the public garden. In the good weather there was always an artist with his easel. Artists liked the way the palms grew and the bright colors of the hotels facing the gardens and the sea. Italians came from a long way off to look up at the war monument. It was made of bronze and glistened in the rain. It was raining. The rain dripped from the palm trees. Water stood in pools on the gravel paths. The sea broke in a long line in the rain and slipped back down the beach to come up and break again in a long line in the rain. The motor cars were gone from the square by the war monument. Across the square in the doorway of the café a waiter stood looking out at the empty square.

The American wife stood at the window looking out. Outside right under their window a cat was crouched under one of the dripping green tables. The cat was trying to make herself so compact that she would not be dripped on.
“I’m going down and get that kitty,” the American wife said.
“I’ll do it,” her husband offered from the bed.
“No, I’ll get it. The poor kitty out trying to keep dry under a table.”
The husband went on reading, lying propped up with the two pillows at the foot of the bed.
“Don’t get wet,” he said.
The wife went downstairs and the hotel owner stood up and bowed to her as she passed the office. His desk was at the far end of the office. He was an old man and very tall.
“Il piove,” the wife said. She liked the hotelkeeper.
“Si, si, Signora, brutto tempo. It is very bad weather.”

He stood behind his desk in the far end of the dim room. The wife liked him. She liked the deadly serious way he received any complaints. She liked his dignity. She liked the way he wanted to serve her. She liked the way he felt about being a hotelkeeper. She liked his old, heavy face and big hands.

Liking him she opened the door and looked out. It was raining harder. A man in a rubber cape was crossing the empty square to the café. The cat would be around to the right. Perhaps she could go along under the eaves. As she stood in the doorway an umbrella opened behind her. It was the maid who looked after their room.
“You must not get wet,” she smiled, speaking Italian. Of course, the hotelkeeper had sent her.

With the maid holding the umbrella over her, she walked along the gravel path until she was under their window. The table was there, washed bright green in the rain, but the cat was gone. She was suddenly disappointed. The maid looked up at her.
“Ha perduto qualque cosa, Signora?”
“There was a cat,” said the American girl.
“A cat?”
“Si, il gatto.”
“A cat?” the maid laughed. “A cat in the rain?”
“Yes,” she said, “under the table.” Then, “Oh, I wanted it so much. I wanted a kitty.”
When she talked English the maid’s face tightened.
“Come, Signora,” she said. “We must get back inside. You will be wet.”
“I suppose so,” said the American girl.

They went back along the gravel path and passed in the door. The maid stayed outside to close the umbrella. As the American girl passed the office, the padrone bowed from his desk. Something felt very small and tight inside the girl. The padrone made her feel very small and at the same time really important. She had a momentary feeling of being of supreme importance. She went on up the stairs. She opened the door of the room. George was on the bed, reading.
“Did you get the cat?” he asked, putting the book down.
“It was gone.”
“Wonder where it went to,” he said, resting his eyes from reading.
She sat down on the bed.
“I wanted it so much,” she said. “I don’t know why I wanted it so much. I wanted that poor kitty. It isn’t any fun to be a poor kitty out in the rain.”
George was reading again.

She went over and sat in front of the mirror of the dressing table looking at herself with the hand glass. She studied her profile, first one side and then the other. Then she studied the back of her head and her neck.
“Don’t you think it would be a good idea if I let my hair grow out?” she asked, looking at her profile again.
George looked up and saw the back of her neck, clipped close like a boy’s.
“I like it the way it is.”
“I get so tired of it,” she said. “I get so tired of looking like a boy.”
