George shifted his position in the bed. He hadn’t looked away from her since she started to speak.
“You look pretty darn nice,” he said.
She laid the mirror down on the dresser and went over to the window and looked out. It was getting dark.
“I want to pull my hair back tight and smooth and make a big knot at the back that I can feel,” she said. “I want to have a kitty to sit on my lap and purr when I stroke her.”
“Yeah?” George said from the bed.
“And I want to eat at a table with my own silver and I want candles. And I want it to be spring and I want to brush my hair out in front of a mirror and I want a kitty and I want some new clothes.”
“Oh, shut up and get something to read,” George said. He was reading again.
His wife was looking out of the window. It was quite dark now and still raining in the palm trees.
“Anyway, I want a cat,” she said, “I want a cat. I want a cat now. If I can’t have long hair or any fun, I can have a cat.”
George was not listening. He was reading his book. His wife looked out of the window where the light had come on in the square.
Someone knocked at the door.
“Avanti,” George said. He looked up from his book.
In the doorway stood the maid. She held a big tortoiseshell cat pressed tight against her and swung down against her body.
“Excuse me,” she said, “the padrone asked me to bring this for the Signora.”

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The plot can be told in a breath. Two Americans are staying at a hotel in Italy. It is raining. From their window, the wife sees a cat crouched under a dripping green table in the garden, trying to make itself small enough not to get wet. She announces she will go down and get it. Her husband George, lying on the bed reading, says only "Don't get wet." She goes out, accompanied by an umbrella-bearing maid sent by the hotelkeeper, but the cat is gone. She goes back upstairs. And then, in front of a mirror, she begins to say what she really wants: long hair, a kitten, candles, her own silver, spring, new clothes. George tells her to shut up and get something to read. At the very end, there is a knock, and the maid arrives carrying a big tortoiseshell cat, sent by the padrone for the Signora.

The cat is the key, but it is not just a cat. It is a stand-in for everything the wife feels is missing. Think of what the animal is doing when we first see it: trying to make itself so compact that it will not be dripped on. That is a portrait of a creature making itself small to survive bad weather, and the wife, who is stuck in a hotel room with a husband who does not look up, is doing much the same. She says it plainly: "It isn't any fun to be a poor kitty out in the rain." She is talking about herself.

The second great image is her hair. She has it cropped short, like a boy's. She says she gets tired of looking like a boy, and wants to pull it back tight and smooth into a big knot she can feel. In the 1920s, bobbed hair was fashionable and a sign of modern freedom, but here it has become a sort of disguise or a loss. She wants to be a woman with a home, with a domestic, settled life, and the story suggests that she feels that life slipping away in the rootless world of hotels and travel. The husband's reply, "I like it the way it is," is not cruel, but it is entirely beside the point.

Then there is the padrone. The wife is touched by him. She likes his dignity, his seriousness, the way he takes her complaints. She likes the way he wants to serve her. When she passes his desk, she feels both small and important. He is the only person in the story who pays attention to her, and it is a stately, formal kind of attention. In the ending, his gift of the cat is a gesture of care, but it is ironic, because the thing she needed was not a cat. The story leaves us unsure whether she will be consoled, or whether the cat is a substitute that makes the loneliness plainer. The point is the gap between a want and the person who ought to answer it.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
The first thing to admire in Cat in the Rain is how much it does with how little. It opens with a flat statement: "There were only two Americans stopping at the hotel." From there, Hemingway describes the setting in short sentences that seem to be doing nothing: the palms, the war monument glistening in the rain, the empty square, the café. But the setting is precisely chosen. The war monument, in a seaside town in the shadow of recent war, hints at a world that has lost something. The empty square and the rain create isolation. The detail that the Americans do not know anyone on the stairs tells us they are cut off. The outer world mirrors the inner one.

The most skillful part is the handling of point of view. The narrator does not tell us what the wife feels; instead the story calls her, at different moments, the American wife, the American girl, and the wife. That shifting label is subtle. It shows how she is seen, as a function in a marriage, as a young person, as a foreign visitor, and it makes her feel unnamed, almost anonymous. The story is also careful with repetition. The word "like" echoes through the passage on the hotelkeeper, and "I want" echoes at the climax. The sheer repetition produces a kind of pressure that builds without a single raised voice.

Now the weaknesses. The story is, frankly, slight. It can feel like a sketch. Because Hemingway is so reticent, we learn almost nothing about George beyond his reading and his minimal replies. Is he cruel, tired, absorbed, or simply oblivious? The story does not say, and some readers find him a too-convenient cardboard figure, a stock inattentive husband. The wife, meanwhile, is a collection of wants that are easy to caricature: a kitten, long hair, silver, candles. A hostile reader might see her as petulant, and the story arguably does not give her enough interior depth to resist that reading.

The ending is also debatable. The maid's arrival with the cat is a clever turn, and many critics find it ambiguous in a productive way. But it can also feel a little contrived, an irony delivered a bit too neatly, and one wonders if the story gains or loses from its tidy final image. And the symbolism, with the cat as longing, the hair as lost femininity, and the rain as gloom, is clear enough that some readers feel the story is making its points too deliberately for something that pretends to be so offhand.

Still, the achievement is real. There is something remarkable about a story in which a woman looks out a window and says she wants a cat, and the reader's heart sinks. That is the accomplishment: a vast ache created from the barest materials.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
Cat in the Rain came out in the United States in October 1925, in In Our Time, published by Boni and Liveright. That book, combining stories with very short prose sketches, was Hemingway's first major work in America and the one that announced him. It was widely noticed by critics as a new voice, and it helped bring him to the attention of his future publisher, Scribner's, and the editor Maxwell Perkins. Cat in the Rain is one of the quietest stories in that book, sitting among tales of war, hunting, and the Michigan woods, and it shows the same style turned on domestic life.

The story is often read in connection with Hemingway's own life. He and his first wife, Hadley, spent time in Rapallo, on the Italian coast, in early 1923, and later biographers have linked the story to that period and to tensions in their marriage, including questions about children and about the cut of Hadley's hair. The links are plausible and have been argued over, but the story does not require them, and critics caution against reducing it to biography. What is clear is that Hemingway was already thinking about marriage as a place where two people can be physically close and emotionally far apart.

The larger influence of the story lies in how it demonstrated that a short story could be built on a nearly invisible event. It became a standard teaching text, widely anthologized and used to introduce students to subtext, point of view, symbolism, and Hemingway's theory of omission. It is also a favorite example in discussions of gender and domestic life in modernist fiction, since it can be read as a portrait of a woman's frustrated desire for agency, recognition, and a home.

Later writers who wrote about quiet failures of intimacy, from Raymond Carver and his American domestic realists to Alice Munro and Lorrie Moore, work within a space that Hemingway helped open. The story has been adapted on a smaller scale than some of his work, but it is a frequent choice for short films, stage readings, and classroom performances.

In his own career, the story marks a stage in which Hemingway's reputation as a writer of men's adventures was balanced by his skill as an observer of intimate emotional life. That aspect is sometimes underplayed in the public image of the hunter and soldier, and this story is one of the best correctives.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
The usual first response to Cat in the Rain is an odd kind of ache. Readers say they finish it and feel they have witnessed something sad but are not sure what. That ambiguity is what many love about it. It sets a small human scene in front of you and trusts you to feel its edges.

Many readers love the wife, even though she is thinly sketched. She is observant and tender, and her little bursts of longing, the way she looks at herself in the mirror and studies her profile and the back of her neck, are completely recognizable. The line "I want a cat. I want a cat now," has a childlike honesty that goes straight to the heart. It is a moment of rawness that cuts through the story's careful reserve. Readers who have felt unheard in a relationship, or who have wanted something small and been told to be quiet, find the scene piercing.

They also love the ending for its quiet irony. The cat arrives, delivered by a servant at the request of a man who has barely spoken to the wife, while the husband who should have noticed is deaf to her. People respond to the contrast. A stranger, an old hotelkeeper with a heavy face, has understood what the husband could not. The story's gentleness toward the padrone is part of its warmth.

Fellow writers admire the story's technical control and its calm. The descriptions are clean, the sentences are short, and the story ends without commentary. Teachers love it because every detail can be discussed: why is the cat under a green table, why does the maid's face tighten when the wife speaks English, why is the monument glistening, why is the wife called by several names. Readers often say they notice new things on each rereading.

There is also something to be said for how contemporary it feels. The story does not belong to a distant period; its situation, of a person who wants more attention than she is getting, in a relationship where each is in a different mood and a different room, is timeless. And the small, specific longings, a kitten, a candle, spring, are the kind that make the reader see the character as an individual rather than a type. The story's power lies in the fact that no one in it is a villain, and yet someone is clearly hurting.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Cat in the Rain has not been a controversial story in the sense of provoking scandal, but it has provoked a lasting debate about how to read it, and it has drawn some pointed criticisms.

The central question is about the wife, and critics have long disagreed. Some read her as a sympathetic figure, a woman who feels trapped and unheard, and see George as a symbol of male indifference. Others find her petulant, a woman who confuses a series of whims with deep need, and see the story as an ironic portrait of dissatisfaction that cannot be satisfied. Still others emphasize the possibility that the story is about a deeper unspoken matter, such as the question of whether the couple will have a child, or a dissatisfaction rooted in the couple's rootless life. The fact that all these readings are available is a mark of the story's openness, but it is also, for some critics, a mark of its vagueness. They argue that the story withholds so much that it invites any interpretation, and that it is not clear it has a definite achievement of its own.

A second reservation concerns gender. Feminist critics have noted that the story gives its female character no resources except desire, and that its treatment of her wanting, with its repeated list of things she feels deprived of, can be read as faintly condescending, as if a woman's longing were charming but trivial. Others have defended the story as a sympathetic account of a woman's invisibility within a marriage, and still others see the author as quietly criticizing the husband. The disagreement continues.

There are also criticisms of its slightness. Some readers feel that in this story the Hemingway technique tips into something almost empty, that nothing is at stake beyond a mood, and that the symbolism is the only thing holding it together. The cat and the hair, they say, are too tidy as signs. Compared with the force of his war and violent stories, this one can seem a minor exercise.

Finally, the ending has been questioned. Some readers find the arrival of the cat a sentimental softening, an unexpected kindness that sits oddly with the story's coolness. Others say it is the opposite, a devastating irony. The dispute shows that readers do not agree about the story's final tone.

It is worth saying that much of this criticism is a matter of taste and interpretation, not of dismissal. The story is broadly respected, and the debates have, if anything, kept it alive.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
Cat in the Rain belongs to the modernist short story of the early twentieth century, the form shaped by Chekhov, Joyce, and Katherine Mansfield, in which a small incident or a moment of mood replaces the plot with its twists. Mansfield's stories of women's unspoken longings, such as Bliss and The Garden Party, are close relatives, as is Joyce's Eveline, in which a young woman stands at a crossroads and cannot act. What Hemingway adds is the extreme bareness of his surface and the refusal even to hint at inner life.

It also has a place in the long literary tradition of the marriage story, from Chekhov's tales of tired marriages to Ibsen's A Doll's House, in which a wife's needs are overlooked until she insists on being heard. Ibsen's heroine leaves, while Hemingway's wife only asks for a cat. The comparison shows the difference between the older, openly dramatic treatment and the new understatement. In the world of the story, the explosion has been replaced by a quiet request, and the request is not met in kind.

Within Hemingway's own work, the story shows a side of him often overshadowed by the war and hunting material: the observer of couples who sit in the same room and cannot say what matters. A woman asks, in her own way, to be heard, and a man with the best intentions replies in a way that misses her.

Looking forward, its descendants include the domestic minimalism of Raymond Carver, the quiet, observant fiction of Alice Munro, William Trevor, and others, and many contemporary stories that locate a whole emotional drama in a gesture or an object. The fundamental technique, in which an ordinary desire stands for a deep, unnamed loss, is now so common that it can be hard to remember someone had to invent it.

Why read it now? Because it is short, because it rewards rereading, and because it captures a feeling that is hard to name and easy to recognize: wanting something small and being unable to explain that it is not small. In a few paragraphs, it shows how a person can be lonely in a room with someone she loves, and how a stranger's small kindness can both comfort and wound. The next time it rains and someone near you is looking out the window, you may find yourself wondering what they want.

stories.title: In Another Country
stories.author: Ernest Hemingway
stories.epigraph: “The doctor came up to the machine where I was sitting and said: “What did you like best to do before the war? Did you practise a sport?””
stories.keyContext:
Ernest Hemingway published In Another Country in 1927, in a collection called Men Without Women, and it is one of the quietest and most devastating stories he ever wrote. Hemingway was badly wounded as a very young man in Italy in the First World War, and he spent months recovering in a Milan hospital. The story is not really about heroics. It is about what happens after the fighting, when wounded men sit in machines meant to repair their bodies, and try not to think about what cannot be repaired.

The writing is spare and plain, with short sentences and almost no explanation of feelings. Hemingway believed that what you leave out can hit harder than what you say, and this story is a good test of that idea. The title echoes an old line from Christopher Marlowe about a distant country and a dead woman. Listen for the Italian major with the withered hand, and for what he says about marriage.
paragraphs: In the fall the war was always there, but we did not go to it any more. It was cold in the fall in Milan and the dark came very early. Then the electric lights came on, and it was pleasant along the streets looking in the windows. There was much game hanging outside the shops, and the snow powdered in the fur of the foxes and the wind blew their tails. The deer hung stiff and heavy and empty, and small birds blew in the wind and the wind turned their feathers. It was a cold fall and the wind came down from the mountains.

We were all at the hospital every afternoon, and there were different ways of walking across the town through the dusk to the hospital. Two of the ways were alongside canals, but they were long. Always, though, you crossed a bridge across a canal to enter the hospital. There was a choice of three bridges. On one of them a woman sold roasted chestnuts. It was warm, standing in front of her charcoal fire, and the chestnuts were warm afterward in your pocket. The hospital was very old and very beautiful, and you entered through a gate and walked across a courtyard and out a gate on the other side. There were usually funerals starting from the courtyard. Beyond the old hospital were the new brick pavilions, and there we met every afternoon and were all very polite and interested in what was the matter, and sat in the machines that were to make so much difference.
The doctor came up to the machine where I was sitting and said: “What did you like best to do before the war? Did you practise a sport?”
I said: “Yes, football.”
“Good,” he said. “You will be able to play football again better than ever.”

My knee did not bend and the leg dropped straight from the knee to the ankle without a calf, and the machine was to bend the knee and make it move as in riding a tricycle. But it did not bend yet, and instead the machine lurched when it came to the bending part. The doctor said: “That will all pass. You are a fortunate young man. You will play football again like a champion.”

In the next machine was a major who had a little hand like a baby’s. He winked at me when the doctor examined his hand, which was between two leather straps that bounced up and down and flapped the stiff fingers, and said: “And will I too play football, captain-doctor?” He had been a very great fencer, and before the war the greatest fencer in Italy.

The doctor went to his office in a back room and brought a photograph which showed a hand that had been withered almost as small as the major’s, before it had taken a machine course, and after was a little larger. The major held the photograph with his good hand and looked at it very carefully. “A wound?” he asked.
“An industrial accident,” the doctor said.
“Very interesting, very interesting,” the major said, and handed it back to the doctor.
“You have confidence?”
“No,” said the major.

There were three boys who came each day who were about the same age I was. They were all three from Milan, and one of them was to be a lawyer, and one was to be a painter, and one had intended to be a soldier, and after we were finished with the machines, sometimes we walked back together to the Café Cova, which was next door to the Scala. We walked the short way through the communist quarter because we were four together. The people hated us because we were officers, and from a wine-shop someone would call out, “A basso gli ufficiali!” as we passed. Another boy who walked with us sometimes and made us five wore a black silk handkerchief across his face because he had no nose then and his face was to be rebuilt. He had gone out to the front from the military academy and been wounded within an hour after he had gone into the front line for the first time. They rebuilt his face, but he came from a very old family and they could never get the nose exactly right. He went to South America and worked in a bank. But this was a long time ago, and then we did not any of us know how it was going to be afterward. We only knew then that there was always the war, but that we were not going to it any more.

We all had the same medals, except the boy with the black silk bandage across his face, and he had not been at the front long enough to get any medals. The tall boy with a very pale face who was to be a lawyer had been a lieutenant of Arditi and had three medals of the sort we each had only one of. He had lived a very long time with death and was a little detached. We were all a little detached, and there was nothing that held us together except that we met every afternoon at the hospital. Although, as we walked to the Cova through the tough part of town, walking in the dark, with light and singing coming out of the wine-shops, and sometimes having to walk into the street when the men and women would crowd together on the sidewalk so that we would have had to jostle them to get by, we felt held together by there being something that had happened that they, the people who disliked us, did not understand.

We ourselves all understood the Cova, where it was rich and warm and not too brightly lighted, and noisy and smoky at certain hours, and there were always girls at the tables and the illustrated papers on a rack on the wall. The girls at the Cova were very patriotic, and I found that the most patriotic people in Italy were the café girls⁠—and I believe they are still patriotic.

The boys at first were very polite about my medals and asked me what I had done to get them. I showed them the papers, which were written in very beautiful language and full of fratellanza and abnegazione, but which really said, with the adjectives removed, that I had been given the medals because I was an American. After that their manner changed a little toward me, although I was their friend against outsiders. I was a friend, but I was never really one of them after they had read the citations, because it had been different with them and they had done very different things to get their medals. I had been wounded, it was true; but we all knew that being wounded, after all, was really an accident. I was never ashamed of the ribbons, though, and sometimes, after the cocktail hour, I would imagine myself having done all the things they had done to get their medals; but walking home at night through the empty streets with the cold wind and all the shops closed, trying to keep near the street lights, I knew that I would never have done such things, and I was very much afraid to die, and often lay in bed at night by myself, afraid to die and wondering how I would be when I went back to the front again.

The three with the medals were like hunting-hawks; and I was not a hawk, although I might seem a hawk to those who had never hunted; they, the three, knew better and so we drifted apart. But I stayed good friends with the boy who had been wounded his first day at the front, because he would never know now how he would have turned out; so he could never be accepted either, and I liked him because I thought perhaps he would not have turned out to be a hawk either.

The major, who had been the great fencer, did not believe in bravery, and spent much time while we sat in the machines correcting my grammar. He had complimented me on how I spoke Italian, and we talked together very easily. One day I had said that Italian seemed such an easy language to me that I could not take a great interest in it; everything was so easy to say. “Ah, yes,” the major said. “Why, then, do you not take up the use of grammar?” So we took up the use of grammar, and soon Italian was such a difficult language that I was afraid to talk to him until I had the grammar straight in my mind.

The major came very regularly to the hospital. I do not think he ever missed a day, although I am sure he did not believe in the machines. There was a time when none of us believed in the machines, and one day the major said it was all nonsense. The machines were new then and it was we who were to prove them. It was an idiotic idea, he said, “a theory, like another.” I had not learned my grammar, and he said I was a stupid impossible disgrace, and he was a fool to have bothered with me. He was a small man and he sat straight up in his chair with his right hand thrust into the machine and looked straight ahead at the wall while the straps thumped up and down with his fingers in them.
“What will you do when the war is over if it is over?” he asked me. “Speak grammatically!”
“I will go to the States.”
“Are you married?”
“No, but I hope to be.”
“The more of a fool you are,” he said. He seemed very angry. “A man must not marry.”
“Why, Signor Maggiore?”
“Don’t call me ‘Signor Maggiore.’ ”
“Why must not a man marry?”

“He cannot marry. He cannot marry,” he said angrily. “If he is to lose everything, he should not place himself in a position to lose that. He should not place himself in a position to lose. He should find things he cannot lose.”
He spoke very angrily and bitterly, and looked straight ahead while he talked.
“But why should he necessarily lose it?”

“He’ll lose it,” the major said. He was looking at the wall. Then he looked down at the machine and jerked his little hand out from between the straps and slapped it hard against his thigh. “He’ll lose it,” he almost shouted. “Don’t argue with me!” Then he called to the attendant who ran the machines. “Come and turn this damned thing off.”

He went back into the other room for the light treatment and the massage. Then I heard him ask the doctor if he might use his telephone and he shut the door. When he came back into the room, I was sitting in another machine. He was wearing his cape and had his cap on, and he came directly toward my machine and put his arm on my shoulder.
“I am so sorry,” he said, and patted me on the shoulder with his good hand. “I would not be rude. My wife has just died. You must forgive me.”
“Oh⁠—” I said, feeling sick for him. “I am so sorry.”
He stood there biting his lower lip. “It is very difficult,” he said. “I cannot resign myself.”

He looked straight past me and out through the window. Then he began to cry. “I am utterly unable to resign myself,” he said and choked. And then crying, his head up looking at nothing, carrying himself straight and soldierly, with tears on both his cheeks and biting his lips, he walked past the machines and out the door.

The doctor told me that the major’s wife, who was very young and whom he had not married until he was definitely invalided out of the war, had died of pneumonia. She had been sick only a few days. No one expected her to die. The major did not come to the hospital for three days. Then he came at the usual hour, wearing a black band on the sleeve of his uniform. When he came back, there were large framed photographs around the wall, of all sorts of wounds before and after they had been cured by the machines. In front of the machine the major used were three photographs of hands like his that were completely restored. I do not know where the doctor got them. I always understood we were the first to use the machines. The photographs did not make much difference to the major because he only looked out of the window.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
On the surface, almost nothing happens in this story. A young American officer, wounded in the knee, goes to a hospital in Milan every afternoon to sit in a machine that is supposed to bend his stiff leg. He walks there through the cold autumn dusk, past shops with game hanging in the windows, across bridges, through a courtyard where funerals often begin. He meets three young Italian officers who are also patients, and a major who used to be the finest fencer in Italy and now has a hand withered to the size of a baby's. The major corrects the narrator's grammar. And then, near the end, the major learns that his young wife has died of pneumonia, and falls apart in a stiff, upright, soldierly way.

The meaning lives in what the story refuses to say. Look at the opening. "In the fall the war was always there, but we did not go to it any more." The men are suspended between two worlds. The war is over for them, but they are not yet back in normal life, and the narrator keeps noticing death in the background: the funerals in the courtyard, the dead deer hanging in the shop windows, stiff and heavy and empty. The hospital's cheerful talk is a kind of lie. The doctor tells the narrator he will play football again like a champion, and tells the major that his hand will recover, and nobody in the room believes him. When the doctor asks the major, "You have confidence?" and the major answers with a flat "No," it is the most honest moment in the room.

The medals matter too. The narrator has one, but he is an American, and he knows his medal was given partly out of courtesy. The three Italian boys earned theirs by real bravery, and the narrator says they were like hunting hawks, while he was not a hawk, although he might seem like one to people who had never hunted. He is afraid to die, and he lies awake at night thinking about going back. This is not a story about brave men. It is about the gap between how courage looks from outside and how it feels from inside.

Then comes the major's speech about marriage. He is furious at the narrator for hoping to marry. "A man must not marry," he says, because a man who has already lost everything should not put himself in the position of losing anything else. He should find things he cannot lose. At that point the reader does not yet know why he is so angry. Then he takes a phone call, comes back in his cape, and tells the narrator that his wife has just died. The major's cruelty a minute earlier was grief he did not yet know about, or a dread he had always carried. Having lost his fencing and his hand, he put what remained of his hope into a young wife, and now she is gone.

The last image is the photographs. The doctor hangs framed pictures of healed hands on the wall, but the major simply looks out the window. Medicine can restore a hand, perhaps, but not a person, and the machines cannot fix what is actually broken. That is the whole story: a man who has been trained to endure everything, and finds the one thing he cannot endure.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
In Another Country is close to a perfect piece of short fiction, and its best qualities are also the ones that are easiest to take for granted. The first paragraph alone does a remarkable amount of work. The sentences are mostly plain and repetitive, built on the word "and," so the prose feels like a person walking: one step, another step, a bridge, a chestnut seller, a gate. Underneath that calm are the dead animals and the funerals, so that death is placed in the background of every pleasant detail. Hemingway never says "I am afraid" until the story is well underway, and by then the reader has felt it for pages.

The structure is just as smart. The story moves from general to specific. It begins with the narrator's habits and the whole group of wounded men, and only slowly narrows to the major, and then to a single afternoon. The announcement of the wife's death arrives almost offhandedly, with no musical build, and it is all the more powerful for that. The reversal is also fair. The major's rage about marriage is planted a few lines before the reader learns why, so that on a second reading his anger is heartbreaking rather than merely strange. The last two details, the black armband and the photographs he ignores, let the reader draw the conclusion without being told.

If the story has weaknesses, they are small and mostly matters of taste. Hemingway's narrator is deliberately blank. He is a camera with a conscience, but he is not much of a character, and readers who want more access to his inner life may find him thin. The story also leans on a few familiar Hemingway attitudes, such as the idea that real soldiers are quiet and tired of talk, and that the people who suffer most say least. That stoicism is moving here, but when imitated by lesser writers, and sometimes by Hemingway himself later on, it hardens into pose. The Italian dialogue is also simplified, with characters speaking in a kind of translated plainness that can sound stiff.

Still, these are the kind of objections one makes about a masterpiece. The story is short enough to read in fifteen minutes, yet it contains an entire theory of loss. Hemingway later described his method as showing only the tip of the iceberg while the rest stays beneath the surface. Here the iceberg is enormous, and the tip is a man looking out a window.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
In Another Country was published in Scribner's Magazine in April 1927 and then in Men Without Women, Hemingway's second collection of short stories, which came out that October. By then he was already famous. The Sun Also Rises had appeared the year before, and critics were arguing about whether he was the voice of a whole disillusioned generation. The stories in Men Without Women, including The Killers and Hills Like White Elephants, confirmed that his short fiction was at least as influential as his novels.

The story's greatest effect has been on the way writers handle emotion. Hemingway's approach, which he later described as the iceberg theory, holds that a writer who knows his subject well can leave out most of what he knows, and the reader will feel it anyway. Generations of writers have learned from that. Short story writers such as Raymond Carver, with his stripped-down domestic scenes, and many writers of the so-called minimalist school took lessons from Hemingway's habit of letting a plain surface carry enormous pressure. You can hear echoes of it in war fiction, from Tim O'Brien to many younger writers who write about veterans who cannot explain what they carry.

The story also helped shape how we think about the aftermath of war. Much earlier war writing was about glory or about battles. Hemingway, along with other writers of the 1920s, turned attention to the hospital, the long recovery, and the men who return unable to say what happened. Here the war is almost absent. We never see a battle. We see a waiting room full of broken men and a doctor offering false hope. That shift was important, and it has remained a standard way to tell war stories.

Teachers use the story constantly. It is a favorite in high school and college courses because it is short, because its images are concrete, and because it rewards close reading without needing much background. Students are often asked to explain what the major's speech about marriage reveals, or to trace how the opening paragraph prepares the ending.

Within Hemingway's own career, the story belongs to a group of pieces that draw on his Italian experience. He was wounded in July 1918 while serving as a Red Cross ambulance driver near the Piave River, and he recovered in Milan, where he fell in love with a nurse. That experience later fed A Farewell to Arms in 1929, a novel that carries many of the same moods: cold weather, rain, hospitals, and the sense that the world breaks everyone. The story can be read as a small, early version of the same sorrow, written with far less plot.

The title borrows from a line in Christopher Marlowe's play The Jew of Malta, which T. S. Eliot had also used in a poem, so Hemingway was placing his story inside a literary conversation about distance, memory, and the dead.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers have loved this story first for its restraint. It is hard to write about grief without sentimentality, and Hemingway does it by showing almost nothing. When the major cries, he is described as carrying himself straight and soldierly, with tears on both cheeks and biting his lips, and that is all. Readers tend to remember that image for years because it refuses to ask for pity. The man's dignity and his collapse exist at the same time.

Many readers also admire the way the story captures the strange mood of recovery. Anyone who has spent time in a hospital, or sat in a waiting room full of people with the same problem, will recognize the false politeness, the small jokes, and the way strangers become companions only because they are in the same place every afternoon. The narrator says there was nothing that held them together except that they met each day at the hospital. That sentence is true of many friendships formed in difficult places, and it is part of why the story feels so humane.

The atmosphere is another favorite. Milan in the fall, with the early dark, the lighted shop windows, the wind coming down from the mountains, the chestnut seller warming her hands over charcoal, gives the story a physical reality that readers often cite. It is a rare piece of fiction that makes you feel cold and warm at once. The detail of the game hanging outside the shops, with snow powdering the foxes, is often admired as an example of how a single image can suggest the whole mood of a book.

Fellow writers have praised its economy. Hemingway's reputation among other authors has been mixed at times, but this story, along with a few others from the same period, is often named as proof that his method really works. Critics who dislike his later bluster and macho posing usually exempt the early stories, which they find more vulnerable and more precise.

Finally, readers love the moral sensitivity of the story. The narrator does not judge the major for his harshness. He listens, he apologizes, he feels sick for him. He also admits his own fear, which is a quiet kind of honesty about courage. The story suggests that bravery is not the absence of fear, and that grief is not a failure of strength, which is a message many readers, especially those who have lost someone, find comforting rather than bleak. There is no lesson announced, but the reader leaves with a sense that being gentle with a hurting person is the right response.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Because In Another Country is so admired, it has received less direct criticism than many of Hemingway's longer works, but certain objections come up again and again. The first is the old complaint about his style. Some critics, since the 1920s, have found his short declarative sentences monotonous or mannered, and have accused him of mistaking blankness for depth. According to this view, a story that withholds feeling can sometimes simply withhold it, leaving the reader to supply what the author did not. Parodies of Hemingway's style, which have been popular for decades, make fun of exactly this habit of repeating the word "and" and describing simple actions with solemn seriousness.

Another line of criticism concerns the narrator. Because he is so reserved, some readers feel that the story never lets us into his mind in a way that earns the emotional payoff. We are told he is afraid to die, but we are not shown it dramatically. We are told he is feeling sick for the major, but the story prefers to report this in a sentence. Critics who prize interior life, as in Henry James or Virginia Woolf, have sometimes found the story distant for this reason.

There have also been broader complaints about Hemingway's view of the world. His fiction is often accused of treating suffering as something to be borne in silence, and of valuing a kind of stern stoicism that is not available to everyone. The major's advice that a man must not marry, or must find things he cannot lose, can be read as a bleak and self-protective philosophy, and some critics have wondered whether the story endorses it. The more usual reading is that the story pities the major for believing this, since the reader sees that his grief is exactly the price of love. Still, the ambiguity has bothered some.

Some critics have noted that women in the story are almost entirely absent. The major's wife never appears, and exists only as a loss. The chestnut seller is a background detail. This reflects a larger pattern in Hemingway's early work, in which women are often seen from outside, as objects of desire, comfort, or grief, rather than as people with their own inner lives. A story called Men Without Women, as the collection is titled, invites this criticism almost by design.

Finally, a few readers feel that the story's polish can seem too careful. The details of the walk, the symbolism of the funerals and the dead game, and the neat ending with the photographs can make the story feel designed. Even admirers sometimes admit that the effect is a little controlled. Still, most disagreements are about Hemingway's larger legacy, not about this particular piece.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
In Another Country belongs to the tradition of modernist fiction, the movement in the early twentieth century that broke away from long, explanatory Victorian storytelling in favor of compression, fragments, and hidden meaning. Hemingway learned a great deal in Paris from Gertrude Stein and Ezra Pound, who urged writers to cut the extra words and trust the concrete image. The story is a small triumph of that approach, and it sits alongside the poems of Pound and the early work of other modernists as an example of how little you need.

It also belongs to the great body of literature written after the First World War. That war shocked a generation of writers into new forms. Erich Maria Remarque's All Quiet on the Western Front, Wilfred Owen's poems, and Hemingway's own A Farewell to Arms all describe the damage of the war, not its glory. Hemingway's version is distinct because it moves away from the battlefield entirely. In a sense, it is a story about the war's long shadow, the injuries that last, and the loss that follows the soldiers home. The phrase "Lost Generation," which Hemingway used as an epigraph in his novel, connects to this feeling of people who survived but cannot return to what they were.

Going back, the story descends from older traditions of storytelling about stoic endurance, such as the Anglo-Saxon poems about warriors, and from nineteenth century realists such as Anton Chekhov and Stephen Crane, who also let small events carry large feeling. Chekhov in particular is a good comparison. Both writers trust that readers will notice what has been left unsaid. The title's allusion to Marlowe turns a cold Renaissance joke about a dead woman into an elegy.

What descends from it is a whole school of American short fiction. Writers as different as Raymond Carver, Ann Beattie, and many contemporary authors of quiet, domestic stories use some version of its approach, with an unadorned surface and a heavy emotional undertow. War writers keep returning to its model of the hospital and the aftermath.

It matters still because its subject has not gone out of date. Every war produces men and women who come home with bodies and minds that cannot be easily repaired, and the cheerful promises of doctors and governments often ring hollow. The story also speaks to everyone who has lost something dear, because it knows that people respond to loss with anger, with dignity, or with silence, and that none of these is a failure. If you want to understand why Hemingway mattered, begin here.

stories.title: Soldier’s Home
stories.author: Ernest Hemingway
stories.epigraph: “Krebs went to the war from a Methodist college in Kansas.”
stories.keyContext:
Soldier's Home, by Ernest Hemingway, first appeared in 1925 and was gathered into his first major book of stories, In Our Time. It is about a young Marine named Harold Krebs, who comes home to a small town in Oklahoma long after the parades are over, and finds that nobody wants to hear the truth about what he saw. Hemingway himself came home from the First World War wounded and restless, and moved back in with his parents in Illinois, so the story carries some of his own friction.

The writing is famously plain. Short sentences, repeated words, and almost no explanation of feelings let you sense the numbness that Krebs carries. This was a new way of writing about war, and it influenced many later authors. The story asks a quiet question that still matters: what happens to a person who has been through something enormous, when everyone around him wants life to go back to normal? Listen for the lies Krebs tells, and for the scene with his mother at the breakfast table.
paragraphs: Krebs went to the war from a Methodist college in Kansas. There is a picture which shows him among his fraternity brothers, all of them wearing exactly the same height and style collar. He enlisted in the Marines in 1917 and did not return to the United States until the second division returned from the Rhine in the summer of 1919.

There is a picture which shows him on the Rhine with two German girls and another corporal. Krebs and the corporal look too big for their uniforms. The German girls are not beautiful. The Rhine does not show in the picture.

By the time Krebs returned to his home town in Oklahoma the greeting of heroes was over. He came back much too late. The men from the town who had been drafted had all been welcomed elaborately on their return. There had been a great deal of hysteria. Now the reaction had set in. People seemed to think it was rather ridiculous for Krebs to be getting back so late, years after the war was over.

At first Krebs, who had been at Belleau Wood, Soissons, the Champagne, St. Mihiel and in the Argonne did not want to talk about the war at all. Later he felt the need to talk but no one wanted to hear about it. His town had heard too many atrocity stories to be thrilled by actualities. Krebs found that to be listened to at all he had to lie, and after he had done this twice he, too, had a reaction against the war and against talking about it. A distaste for everything that had happened to him in the war set in because of the lies he had told. All of the times that had been able to make him feel cool and clear inside himself when he thought of them; the times so long back when he had done the one thing, the only thing for a man to do, easily and naturally, when he might have done something else, now lost their cool, valuable quality and then were lost themselves.

His lies were quite unimportant lies and consisted in attributing to himself things other men had seen, done or heard of, and stating as facts certain apocryphal incidents familiar to all soldiers. Even his lies were not sensational at the pool room. His acquaintances, who had heard detailed accounts of German women found chained to machine guns in the Argonne forest and who could not comprehend, or were barred by their patriotism from interest in, any German machine gunners who were not chained, were not thrilled by his stories.

Krebs acquired the nausea in regard to experience that is the result of untruth or exaggeration, and when he occasionally met another man who had really been a soldier and they talked a few minutes in the dressing room at a dance he fell into the easy pose of the old soldier among other soldiers: that he had been badly, sickeningly frightened all the time. In this way he lost everything.

During this time, it was late summer, he was sleeping late in bed, getting up to walk down town to the library to get a book, eating lunch at home, reading on the front porch until he became bored and then walking down through the town to spend the hottest hours of the day in the cool dark of the pool room. He loved to play pool.

In the evening he practiced on his clarinet, strolled down town, read and went to bed. He was still a hero to his two young sisters. His mother would have given him breakfast in bed if he had wanted it. She often came in when he was in bed and asked him to tell her about the war, but her attention always wandered. His father was noncommittal.

Before Krebs went away to the war he had never been allowed to drive the family motor car. His father was in the real estate business and always wanted the car to be at his command when he required it to take clients out into the country to show them a piece of farm property. The car always stood outside the First National Bank building where his father had an office on the second floor. Now, after the war, it was still the same car.

Nothing was changed in the town except that the young girls had grown up. But they lived in such a complicated world of already defined alliances and shifting feuds that Krebs did not feel the energy or the courage to break into it. He liked to look at them, though. There were so many good-looking young girls. Most of them had their hair cut short. When he went away only little girls wore their hair like that or girls that were fast. They all wore sweaters and shirt waists with round Dutch collars. It was a pattern. He liked to look at them from the front porch as they walked on the other side of the street. He liked to watch them walking under the shade of the trees. He liked the round Dutch collars above their sweaters. He liked their silk stockings and flat shoes. He liked their bobbed hair and the way they walked.

When he was in town their appeal to him was not very strong. He did not like them when he saw them in the Greek’s ice cream parlor. He did not want them themselves really. They were too complicated. There was something else. Vaguely he wanted a girl but he did not want to have to work to get her. He would have liked to have a girl but he did not want to have to spend a long time getting her. He did not want to get into the intrigue and the politics. He did not want to have to do any courting. He did not want to tell any more lies. It wasn’t worth it.

He did not want any consequences. He did not want any consequences ever again. He wanted to live along without consequences. Besides he did not really need a girl. The army had taught him that. It was all right to pose as though you had to have a girl. Nearly everybody did that. But it wasn’t true. You did not need a girl. That was the funny thing. First a fellow boasted how girls mean nothing to him, that he never thought of them, that they could not touch him. Then a fellow boasted that he could not get along without girls, that he had to have them all the time, that he could not go to sleep without them.

That was all a lie. It was all a lie both ways. You did not need a girl unless you thought about them. He learned that in the army. Then sooner or later you always got one. When you were really ripe for a girl you always got one. You did not have to think about it. Sooner or later it would come. He had learned that in the army.

Now he would have liked a girl if she had come to him and not wanted to talk. But here at home it was all too complicated. He knew he could never get through it all again. It was not worth the trouble. That was the thing about French girls and German girls. There was not all this talking. You couldn’t talk much and you did not need to talk. It was simple and you were friends. He thought about France and then he began to think about Germany. On the whole he had liked Germany better. He did not want to leave Germany. He did not want to come home. Still, he had come home. He sat on the front porch.

He liked the girls that were walking along the other side of the street. He liked the look of them much better than the French girls or the German girls. But the world they were in was not the world he was in. He would like to have one of them. But it was not worth it. They were such a nice pattern. He liked the pattern. It was exciting. But he would not go through all the talking. He did not want one badly enough. He liked to look at them all, though. It was not worth it. Not now when things were getting good again.

He sat there on the porch reading a book on the war. It was a history and he was reading about all the engagements he had been in. It was the most interesting reading he had ever done. He wished there were more maps. He looked forward with a good feeling to reading all the really good histories when they would come out with good detail maps. Now he was really learning about the war. He had been a good soldier. That made a difference.
One morning after he had been home about a month his mother came into his bedroom and sat on the bed. She smoothed her apron.
“I had a talk with your father last night, Harold,” she said, “and he is willing for you to take the car out in the evenings.”
“Yeah?” said Krebs, who was not fully awake. “Take the car out? Yeah?”
“Yes. Your father has felt for some time that you should be able to take the car out in the evenings whenever you wished but we only talked it over last night.”
“I’ll bet you made him,” Krebs said.
“No. It was your father’s suggestion that we talk the matter over.”
“Yeah. I’ll bet you made him,” Krebs sat up in bed.
“Will you come down to breakfast, Harold?” his mother said.
“As soon as I get my clothes on,” Krebs said.

His mother went out of the room and he could hear her frying something downstairs while he washed, shaved and dressed to go down into the dining-room for breakfast. While he was eating breakfast his sister brought in the mail.
“Well, Hare,” she said. “You old sleepyhead. What do you ever get up for?”
Krebs looked at her. He liked her. She was his best sister.
“Have you got the paper?” he asked.

She handed him the Kansas City Star and he shucked off its brown wrapper and opened it to the sporting page. He folded the Star open and propped it against the water pitcher with his cereal dish to steady it, so he could read while he ate.
“Harold,” his mother stood in the kitchen doorway, “Harold, please don’t muss up the paper. Your father can’t read his Star if it’s been mussed.”
“I won’t muss it,” Krebs said.
His sister sat down at the table and watched him while he read.
“We’re playing indoor over at school this afternoon,” she said. “I’m going to pitch.”
“Good,” said Krebs. “How’s the old wing?”
“I can pitch better than lots of the boys. I tell them all you taught me. The other girls aren’t much good.”
“Yeah?” said Krebs.
“I tell them all you’re my beau. Aren’t you my beau, Hare?”
“You bet.”
“Couldn’t your brother really be your beau just because he’s your brother?”
“I don’t know.”
“Sure you know. Couldn’t you be my beau, Hare, if I was old enough and if you wanted to?”
“Sure. You’re my girl now.”
“Am I really your girl?”
“Sure.”
“Do you love me?”
“Uh, huh.”
“Will you love me always?”
“Sure.”
“Will you come over and watch me play indoor?”
“Maybe.”
“Aw, Hare, you don’t love me. If you loved me, you’d want to come over and watch me play indoor.”
Krebs’s mother came into the dining-room from the kitchen. She carried a plate with two fried eggs and some crisp bacon on it and a plate of buckwheat cakes.
“You run along, Helen,” she said. “I want to talk to Harold.”
She put the eggs and bacon down in front of him and brought in a jug of maple syrup for the buckwheat cakes. Then she sat down across the table from Krebs.
“I wish you’d put down the paper a minute, Harold,” she said.
Krebs took down the paper and folded it.
“Have you decided what you are going to do yet, Harold?” his mother said, taking off her glasses.
“No,” said Krebs.
“Don’t you think it’s about time?” His mother did not say this in a mean way. She seemed worried.
“I hadn’t thought about it,” Krebs said.
“God has some work for everyone to do,” his mother said. “There can be no idle hands in His Kingdom.”
“I’m not in His Kingdom,” Krebs said.
“We are all of us in His Kingdom.”
Krebs felt embarrassed and resentful as always.

“I’ve worried about you so much, Harold,” his mother went on. “I know the temptations you must have been exposed to. I know how weak men are. I know what your own dear grandfather, my own father, told us about the Civil War and I have prayed for you. I pray for you all day long, Harold.”
Krebs looked at the bacon fat hardening on his plate.

“Your father is worried, too,” his mother went on. “He thinks you have lost your ambition, that you haven’t got a definite aim in life. Charley Simmons, who is just your age, has a good job and is going to be married. The boys are all settling down; they’re all determined to get somewhere; you can see that boys like Charley Simmons are on their way to being really a credit to the community.”
Krebs said nothing.

“Don’t look that way, Harold,” his mother said. “You know we love you and I want to tell you for your own good how matters stand. Your father does not want to hamper your freedom. He thinks you should be allowed to drive the car. If you want to take some of the nice girls out riding with you, we are only too pleased. We want you to enjoy yourself. But you are going to have to settle down to work, Harold. Your father doesn’t care what you start in at. All work is honorable as he says. But you’ve got to make a start at something. He asked me to speak to you this morning and then you can stop in and see him at his office.”
“Is that all?” Krebs said.
“Yes. Don’t you love your mother, dear boy?”
“No,” Krebs said.
His mother looked at him across the table. Her eyes were shiny. She started crying.
“I don’t love anybody,” Krebs said.

It wasn’t any good. He couldn’t tell her, he couldn’t make her see it. It was silly to have said it. He had only hurt her. He went over and took hold of her arm. She was crying with her head in her hands.
“I didn’t mean it,” he said. “I was just angry at something. I didn’t mean I didn’t love you.”
His mother went on crying. Krebs put his arm on her shoulder.
“Can’t you believe me, mother?”
His mother shook her head.
“Please, please, mother. Please believe me.”
“All right,” his mother said chokily. She looked up at him. “I believe you, Harold.”
Krebs kissed her hair. She put her face up to him.
“I’m your mother,” she said. “I held you next to my heart when you were a tiny baby.”
Krebs felt sick and vaguely nauseated.
“I know, Mummy,” he said. “I’ll try and be a good boy for you.”
“Would you kneel and pray with me, Harold?” his mother asked.
They knelt down beside the dining-room table and Krebs’s mother prayed.
“Now, you pray, Harold,” she said.
“I can’t,” Krebs said.
“Try, Harold.”
“I can’t.”
“Do you want me to pray for you?”
“Yes.”

So his mother prayed for him and then they stood up and Krebs kissed his mother and went out of the house. He had tried so to keep his life from being complicated. Still, none of it had touched him. He had felt sorry for his mother and she had made him lie. He would go to Kansas City and get a job and she would feel all right about it. There would be one more scene maybe before he got away. He would not go down to his father’s office. He would miss that one. He wanted his life to go smoothly. It had just gotten going that way. Well, that was all over now, anyway. He would go over to the schoolyard and watch Helen play indoor baseball.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
Soldier's Home is about a man who has come home and cannot come all the way back. Harold Krebs went to war from a Methodist college in Kansas, fought in some of the worst battles of the American war in France, and returned in the summer of 1919, long after the town's welcome parties for the draftees had ended. The story is very careful about timing. Krebs "came back much too late." The hero's welcome has already been used up, and the town has moved on to feeling a little bored by the war.

The first problem is that nobody wants to listen. At first Krebs does not want to talk about the war. Later he feels the need to, but the town has heard so many atrocity stories that real experience seems dull. To be listened to at all, he has to lie. His lies are small. He borrows things other men saw and adopts stories that every soldier knows. But the lying poisons the memories. The moments in the war that had made him feel "cool and clear" inside, the times when he did the one thing a man should do, lose their value once he cheapens them by talking. This is the core of the story. Krebs is not damaged by violence alone. He is damaged by having no honest way to carry what happened.

Notice the opening paragraph, which describes two photographs. In one, he sits with his fraternity brothers, all in identical collars. In another, he is on the Rhine with two German girls, and the narrator notes that the Rhine does not show in the picture. That is the story in miniature: a surface that records almost nothing of the real experience.

The second problem is that Krebs wants a life without effort or consequences. He watches the young girls of the town from a distance and likes the look of them, but he does not want the "intrigue and the politics" of courting, and he does not want to tell any more lies. He says he wants "to live along without consequences." This is both honest and sad. It shows how thoroughly the war has drained his energy, and how he is hiding from anything that might require him to feel.

Then comes the breakfast scene, which is the emotional center. His mother, who loves him and wants to help, tells him that God has work for everyone and that there can be no idle hands in His Kingdom. She asks, "Don't you love your mother, dear boy?" He answers "No," and then "I don't love anybody." Then he apologizes, kisses her hair, and kneels to pray, but cannot. He lets his mother pray for him.

At the end, Krebs decides he will go to Kansas City and find a job. This is not triumph. It is escape. He does not want a scene. He wants his life to go smoothly. He will go and watch his sister Helen play indoor baseball, which is the one simple, uncomplicated pleasure in his world. The story ends on that small gesture, and the reader feels the loss behind it.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
Soldier's Home is one of the cleanest pieces of short fiction in the language, and its biggest strength is control. Nearly every sentence does two jobs. It tells you what is happening in the plainest possible words, and it also reveals a state of mind. Take the line about the photograph with the Rhine missing. It is flat, almost comic, and yet it tells us exactly how little the pictures capture. The same is true of the long sequence in which Krebs eats breakfast, reads the sports page, and walks to the library. The repetition of "he liked" and "he did not want" creates a rhythm of withdrawal. We feel his wish to be left alone without ever being told to.

The structure is also well judged. The first half describes Krebs's days and thoughts, building a mood of drift. The second half collapses that drift into a single scene, so that the abstract problem becomes a concrete conflict at a breakfast table. This is smart, and it prepares us to understand why he says what he says. The mother is drawn with real compassion. She is not a villain. She speaks in clichés about God and work, but she is frightened and loving, and the story lets us see that. That fairness keeps it from being a simple sermon against religion or small-town life.

There are weaknesses. The story's reliance on repetition can occasionally feel mechanical, particularly in the middle paragraphs, where Hemingway's "he liked" and "he did not want" sentences stack up almost like a formula. Some readers find the long middle section static, a series of statements rather than scenes. The mother's dialogue also tilts toward caricature in places, especially in the prayer, and the references to her father and the Civil War are slightly clumsy. The title is a subtle irony, since the soldier has no home, but it also announces the theme a bit loudly.

There is another problem of perspective. Krebs's numbness is presented as almost entirely a matter of the war and the town's indifference, but the story is slightly vague about what exactly happened to him. The narrator refuses to explain, which is part of the design. Yet some readers feel the vagueness protects Hemingway from the harder task of showing us a damaged mind from the inside. It is a story about trauma that never names it, and that restraint can be read as either wise or evasive.

Even so, the ending is hard to fault. The last sentences are almost cruelly simple, and they close the story without resolving it. Krebs will leave. He will watch Helen play. He will keep things simple. The reader knows he is still stuck. That is a tough, truthful ending, and it is why the story has lasted.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
When Soldier's Home appeared in 1925, it was part of a small, bold group of stories that announced a new voice in American writing. It was first printed in a collection of contemporary writers edited by Robert McAlmon, and then collected in In Our Time, Hemingway's first major book of stories, published in the United States by Boni and Liveright. At the time he was a young American in Paris, sharpening his style among a circle of experimental writers. The book established the approach that made him famous, and Soldier's Home showed it at its most disciplined.

The story's biggest impact was on how American writers dealt with war and its aftermath. Most earlier fiction about soldiers focused on battle, sacrifice, or patriotism. Hemingway focused instead on the quiet days after, when a man cannot explain himself. This shift helped create a whole tradition of postwar writing. It echoes in novels about veterans after the Second World War, and in stories about Vietnam and the later conflicts. Writers like Tim O'Brien and many others who write about the difficulty of telling the truth about war are working in a path Hemingway helped clear. The story's central insight, that telling war stories can corrupt the memory of them, appears again and again in veterans' writing.

It also played a major role in popularizing what became known as the iceberg theory. Hemingway later explained that a writer could omit things he knew, and the story would still feel their weight. In Soldier's Home, the omitted material is enormous, and the story depends on the reader's sense of it. Many later short story writers took the lesson, including those who wrote domestic and working-class stories in a stripped-down, minimalist style.

The story has also lived in classrooms. It is anthologized widely, taught in high schools and colleges, and often used to introduce close reading, because its techniques are easy to see. Students are asked to look at the repeated words, the absence of explanation, and the single decisive scene.

For Hemingway himself, the story belongs to a theme he returned to for years: the man who comes back from war and cannot fit into ordinary life. A related story in the same book, Big Two-Hearted River, shows another veteran seeking peace in nature. The two pieces together are often read as a pair, one showing the failure of home and the other the attempt at self-repair.

Finally, the story has fed a broader cultural conversation about how societies treat returning soldiers. The first line about the parades being over has become a kind of shorthand for the way a country can honor its soldiers in public and then ignore them in private. That idea remains painfully familiar.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers have loved Soldier's Home most of all for its honesty. It declines to make Krebs a hero or a victim. He is just a man who is tired, confused, and unable to explain it, and many readers recognize that feeling from their own lives, even if they have never been to war. The story's emotional truth is not confined to soldiers. Anyone who has returned from a transforming experience, whether a long illness, a hard time abroad, or a loss, and found that others cannot or will not listen, knows something of Krebs's predicament.

Many also love the story's treatment of lying. It is a startlingly accurate observation that talking about a precious experience in a way that pleases others can ruin it. The idea that Krebs's lies make the best memories lose their value is subtle, and readers often point to it as one of Hemingway's deepest insights. It is the sort of idea that you only realize is true after you read it.

The prose style has won countless admirers. Writers and readers who find the long sentences of other novelists exhausting have often found relief in Hemingway's directness. Admirers have praised how the plain sentences can carry feeling without decoration. The line about the German girls in the photograph, who were not beautiful, and the Rhine that does not show, is often quoted as a perfect example of understated irony.

The breakfast scene is another high point. Readers have long been moved by the mother's loving, suffocating pressure and by Krebs's unexpected cruelty and quick remorse. It feels like a real argument, in which both people are hurting and neither is entirely wrong. The moment when he cannot pray and asks his mother to pray for him is regularly singled out as unforgettable. It conveys so much about faith, family, and distance in a few words.

The ending also earns affection for its quiet tenderness. Krebs's sister Helen, who adores him, provides a ray of simple warmth, and the fact that he chooses to watch her play baseball suggests that he has not given up on human connection altogether. Readers like this because it is hopeful without being sentimental.

Taken together, these qualities explain why the story is so often named as one of the best American short stories of the twentieth century. It is short, accessible, and deeply felt, and it speaks to anyone who has ever felt like a stranger in the place they once called home.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Even a story as admired as Soldier's Home has attracted criticism. The most common objection concerns Hemingway's style. Critics from the 1920s onward have said that his plain, repetitive prose can be monotonous, and that what looks like depth is sometimes just blankness. Parodies of his manner often borrow the cadence of this very story, with its steady drumbeat of short statements. For some readers, the repeated phrases such as "he did not want" cross the line from effective rhythm into mannerism.

Another complaint is about the characters. Krebs's mother, in particular, can seem a type, the pious and smothering small-town woman, rather than a fully imagined person. Some readers feel Hemingway was settling scores with his own mother, and that the portrait is unfair. This is a reasonable reading, since Hemingway did have a difficult relationship with his mother after he returned from the war, and he later spoke harshly of her. The story's sympathy for her is real but limited.

Some critics have also questioned the moral outlook. Krebs's wish to live without consequences can look less like a wound and more like an immature refusal of responsibility. A reader who is less sympathetic may see a young man who is sulking at home, being supported by his parents, and refusing even to look for work. The story does not clearly resolve whether we should pity him or push him. Some find that ambiguity rich. Others find that it leaves the story a little too comfortable with his passivity.

There are also questions about how the war is handled. The story names battles, but we never see them. Some critics have said that this lets Hemingway borrow the authority of war experience without having to dramatize it. Others, particularly veterans, have argued the opposite, that the story gets the aftermath right. Both views are part of the continuing conversation.

The treatment of women is another point of criticism. The girls in the story are seen purely from the outside, as objects of Krebs's vague desire and his disinterest. Women have little interior life in the story apart from the mother, and even she is seen through Krebs's irritation. This pattern in Hemingway's work has drawn comment from feminist critics for decades.

Finally, a few readers argue that the story is overrated simply because it is a classroom favorite, and that its tidy symbolism and carefully planned omissions are easier to teach than to love. That seems unfair to me, but it is a view held by some.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
Soldier's Home sits at the center of modernist short fiction, the movement that, in the early twentieth century, rejected the long, explanatory, moralizing style of the nineteenth century. Modernists such as Hemingway, Ezra Pound, and Gertrude Stein believed that language should be stripped of ornament, and that the reader should be trusted to supply meaning. Hemingway learned this in Paris, and Soldier's Home is one of its purest products.

It also belongs to the large body of writing produced by the First World War. Along with Erich Maria Remarque's All Quiet on the Western Front, Wilfred Owen's poems, and Hemingway's own A Farewell to Arms, it helped define the idea of the Lost Generation, the young people who survived the war but found themselves unable to believe in the old promises. What sets Soldier's Home apart is that it is entirely set after the war, in a place that seems untouched by it. The distance between the quiet town and the unspeakable memory is the whole drama.

Looking backward, the story descends from the realism of writers such as Anton Chekhov and Stephen Crane. Chekhov's stories also hinge on small moments and unspoken pain. Sherwood Anderson, whose Winesburg, Ohio explores lonely small-town lives, was an early supporter of Hemingway and a clear influence on this kind of tale. The theme of the returning soldier goes back much further, to the Odyssey, in which Odysseus comes home to a place that has changed and a family that does not quite know him. Krebs is a modern, unheroic version of that figure.

Looking forward, the story's descendants are everywhere. After the Second World War, the film The Best Years of Our Lives and many novels dealt with returning veterans. Later writers about Vietnam, Iraq, and Afghanistan, including Tim O'Brien and many younger authors, have returned to the same problem of unshareable experience. Outside war, American short fiction from Raymond Carver to many contemporary writers continues to use Hemingway's lean, understated approach.

It matters today because the problem it describes has not changed. Societies still celebrate soldiers in ceremonies and then leave them to manage alone. People still struggle to explain extreme experiences to those who have not lived them. And families still try to help in ways that make things worse. The story is short enough to read in twenty minutes, and it offers no easy answers. What it gives is recognition. If you have ever felt that your inner life could not be shared, Krebs will feel familiar, and that is why it is worth reading.

stories.title: Bernice Bobs Her Hair
stories.author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
stories.epigraph: “After dark on Saturday night one could stand on the first tee of the golf-course and see the country-club windows as a yellow expanse over a very black and wavy ocean.”
stories.keyContext:
Bernice Bobs Her Hair, by F. Scott Fitzgerald, appeared in the Saturday Evening Post in May 1920, just weeks after his first novel, This Side of Paradise, made him famous at twenty-three. It was then collected in his first book of stories, Flappers and Philosophers. The story is a sharp, funny tale about a shy small-town girl who visits her glamorous cousin and is coached in the art of being popular. It is often credited with helping fix the image of the flapper in the public mind, the daring young woman of the early 1920s with her short hair and her contempt for old rules.

Fitzgerald reportedly built it, in part, on advice he had given his younger sister about popularity, and on the dance-floor social world he knew well from his own youth. Under the comedy, it is about how cruel and competitive teenage society can be, and what happens when someone finally fights back. Listen for the barbershop scene, and for the surprising final act.
paragraphs: After dark on Saturday night one could stand on the first tee of the golf-course and see the country-club windows as a yellow expanse over a very black and wavy ocean. The waves of this ocean, so to speak, were the heads of many curious caddies, a few of the more ingenious chauffeurs, the golf professional’s deaf sister⁠—and there were usually several stray, diffident waves who might have rolled inside had they so desired. This was the gallery.

The balcony was inside. It consisted of the circle of wicker chairs that lined the wall of the combination clubroom and ballroom. At these Saturday-night dances it was largely feminine; a great babel of middle-aged ladies with sharp eyes and icy hearts behind lorgnettes and large bosoms. The main function of the balcony was critical, it occasionally showed grudging admiration, but never approval, for it is well known among ladies over thirty-five that when the younger set dance in the summertime it is with the very worst intentions in the world, and if they are not bombarded with stony eyes stray couples will dance weird barbaric interludes in the corners, and the more popular, more dangerous, girls will sometimes be kissed in the parked limousines of unsuspecting dowagers.

But, after all, this critical circle is not close enough to the stage to see the actors’ faces and catch the subtler byplay. It can only frown and lean, ask questions and make satisfactory deductions from its set of postulates, such as the one which states that every young man with a large income leads the life of a hunted partridge. It never really appreciates the drama of the shifting, semi-cruel world of adolescence. No; boxes, orchestra-circle, principals, and chorus be represented by the medley of faces and voices that sway to the plaintive African rhythm of Dyer’s dance orchestra.

From sixteen-year-old Otis Ormonde, who has two more years at Hill School, to G. Reece Stoddard, over whose bureau at home hangs a Harvard law diploma; from little Madeleine Hogue, whose hair still feels strange and uncomfortable on top of her head, to Bessie MacRae, who has been the life of the party a little too long⁠—more than ten years⁠—the medley is not only the centre of the stage but contains the only people capable of getting an unobstructed view of it.
