Makár Semyónitch did not rise, but beat his head on the floor. “Iván Dmítritch, forgive me!” he cried. “When they flogged me with the knout it was not so hard to bear as it is to see you now⁠ ⁠… yet you had pity on me, and did not tell. For Christ’s sake forgive me, wretch that I am!” And he began to sob.
When Aksyónof heard him sobbing he, too, began to weep.

“God will forgive you!” said he. “Maybe I am a hundred times worse than you.” And at these words his heart grew light, and the longing for home left him. He no longer had any desire to leave the prison, but only hoped for his last hour to come.
In spite of what Aksyónof had said, Makár Semyónitch confessed his guilt. But when the order for his release came, Aksyónof was already dead.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
Ivan Dmitritch Aksyonov is a young merchant in the town of Vladimir, handsome, fair, fond of singing, and happily married. He is setting out for a trade fair when his wife begs him not to go, because she has dreamed that when he came back his hair had turned gray. He laughs it off. On the road he shares an inn with another merchant, leaves before dawn, and plays his guitar at the next stop. Then police arrive. The other merchant has been found with his throat cut, and a bloody knife turns up in Aksyonov's bag. He is frightened and tongue-tied, which makes him look guilty, and he is flogged and sent to Siberia. The wife's dream has come true in a way no one could have imagined.

The most painful moment is not in the courtroom but in the prison, when his wife visits with the children. She has petitioned the Tsar without result. Then she runs her fingers through his hair, remembers her dream, and asks, "Vanya dearest, tell your wife the truth; was it not you who did it?" He answers, "So you, too, suspect me!" and weeps. That is the real injury, since the loss of his family's trust takes more from him than the loss of his freedom. After that scene he stops petitioning and gives himself to prayer, deciding that only God can know the truth.

Twenty-six years pass. Aksyonov's hair is white, his laughter is gone, and he has become the prison's quiet saint, called Grandfather by the other convicts, who bring him their quarrels. He makes boots and reads the lives of the saints. Then a new prisoner arrives, Makar Semyonitch, who is from Vladimir and who reacts oddly when he hears Aksyonov's story. Aksyonov begins to suspect that this man is the real killer. When the guards discover that Makar has been digging a tunnel under the wall, the governor asks Aksyonov, the most trusted man in the prison, who did it. Aksyonov could have taken his revenge by telling. Instead he says, "It is not God's will that I should tell.

That night Makar kneels and confesses. He did kill the merchant, and he had planned to kill Aksyonov too, but a noise outside forced him to flee. He says the flogging he later suffered was nothing compared with seeing Aksyonov now, and that Aksyonov's mercy has crushed him. Aksyonov weeps with him, says God will forgive him, and adds that maybe he himself is a hundred times worse. In that moment his longing for home leaves him. Makar confesses publicly, and the order for Aksyonov's release arrives, but Aksyonov is already dead.

The title, God sees the truth, but waits, is a comfort and a rebuke at once. It promises that truth exists and is known, but it also says that truth is slow and does not owe us a happy ending. The story's meaning is what it does with that waiting. Aksyonov is not rewarded by freedom. He is freed in a different sense, from bitterness, which the story presents as the only release that was ever really available to him.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
This is a story of remarkable compression. In less than three thousand words Tolstoy gives us a whole life, its sudden fall, a quarter century of prison, and a final transformation. The first part moves like a trap closing. Every small, ordinary decision, leaving early, playing a guitar, answering questions honestly, helps convict him, and the frightening thing is how reasonable the police officer's logic is. The door was locked from inside, no one else was there, and the knife was in his bag. Tolstoy shows how innocence can look like guilt when a man is afraid.

The prison section is also superbly handled. Notice how Tolstoy avoids melodrama. There are no scenes of torture beyond a single sentence about the knout, no long speeches about injustice. We see Aksyonov change through small things, boots, a book, a voice still good enough for the choir, and his nickname. The conversation in which Makar casually tells his own story and then reacts strangely to Aksyonov's is a lovely piece of quiet suspense, since we can almost watch Makar's face change.

The turning point, the governor's question, works because it is so undramatized. Aksyonov's thoughts are given to us in two sides. He wonders why he should protect the man who ruined his life, and then he wonders whether he is mistaken, and what good revenge would do. He does not become suddenly noble. The decision is murky, which makes it believable.

There are weaknesses. The plot depends on a huge coincidence, that the real killer should be sent to the very same prison, decades later, and should happen to be a man from the same town. Folk tales run on this kind of fate, but a skeptical modern reader may feel the author's hand pushing the pieces together. The moral is also stated rather plainly, and the final line, that Aksyonov was already dead when the order came, has a bleak tidiness that some find too neat. And Makar's confession, with its quick repentance and tears, is thinner than the rest. We believe in Aksyonov's long suffering far more than in the murderer's sudden remorse.

Still, the story's plainness is its power. The language is stripped of ornament, the sentences simple, the emotions understated. Tolstoy trusts the situation, and he is right to.

A word on the narration is also in order. Tolstoy tells the story in a calm, almost reportorial voice that never tells us how to feel, and that calm makes the injustice more upsetting, not less. When the police officer says that Aksyonov's face and manner betray him, we know he is wrong, but the narrator does not rush to say so. We are left to feel what it is to be disbelieved, which is exactly the experience the story is about.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
This is early Tolstoy, written before Anna Karenina was finished and years before the crisis he described in A Confession. It came out when he was deeply involved in teaching village children and had produced a primer and a series of readers. Those books were for him as serious as any novel, and the simple stories in them, folk tales and moral anecdotes, taught him the style that would define his later work. So this tale belongs to the moment when the great novelist began to practice writing as plainly as a proverb.

The theme it develops, that goodness means forgiving and not resisting evil, runs straight into his later philosophy. After his religious conversion Tolstoy came to believe that the Sermon on the Mount should be taken literally, and that violence, even in self-defense, was wrong. That teaching influenced Mohandas Gandhi, who corresponded with him, and through Gandhi it reached Martin Luther King Jr. and the broader tradition of nonviolent protest. A story about a man who refuses to take revenge when he easily could is a small ancestor of that great idea, though I would not claim it shaped any of those movements directly.

The story has been widely translated and anthologized, and is a regular in collections of Tolstoy's short fiction. It is often given to students because of its brevity and its clarity of theme, and it is a favorite for discussions of justice, forgiveness, and faith. It also has a place in the history of the wrongful-conviction story, which has become a staple of modern fiction and film. The details differ, but a man shut away for a crime he did not commit and slowly finding a kind of freedom inside is an image that has recurred often since.

It is worth saying plainly how little is documented about its reception when it first appeared. In the early 1870s Tolstoy was already the famous author of War and Peace, so anything he published drew attention, but the attention was on his novels, and these children's-reader stories were treated by the literary world as a curious sideline. Their real audience was in the schools. Their lasting impact came later, once readers looked back and saw in these simple pieces the seed of the moral voice that would define his last decades.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers have loved the story's emotional honesty, especially the scene with the wife. Many people say that this is the moment that stays with them, since the pain of being doubted by the person closest to you is a feeling nearly everyone understands. It makes the injustice personal. Tolstoy knew that being punished by the state is terrible, but being disbelieved by a loved one is worse.

They have also loved the transformation. Aksyonov does not turn into a saint by going through a conversion. He grows into it over many years, and his quiet decency feels earned. His refusal to name Makar is a surprise, and the reader can only feel the difficulty of what he does. People often describe a sense of a weight lifting at that moment, even though nothing has changed in Aksyonov's circumstances.

The ending is another favorite. Because the release comes too late, the story refuses to console us with a typical reward. Instead it suggests that the inner change mattered more than the outer one. Many readers find that moving, and also somewhat unsettling, and the combination keeps the tale alive in memory.

And the story is easy to share. It can be read aloud in a quarter of an hour, and listeners find it as gripping as a thriller and as thoughtful as a sermon. Tolstoy wanted stories that anyone could follow, and this is a good example of how he succeeded.

Teachers and translators have also been fond of it, and that fondness says something. Because the vocabulary is plain and the events are clear, the story is a favorite for students learning Russian or English, and for classes that want to talk about big ideas without drowning in difficult prose. Many readers first meet Tolstoy this way, and report being surprised that the author of enormous novels could be so spare.

Another thing readers prize is its sense of time. We feel twenty-six years pass in a single sentence, and yet the weight of those years is present in every line afterward. The white hair, the stoop, the silence, and the unused laugh all tell us what the years have done. It is a model of how a short story can cover a lifetime without feeling rushed, and writers still study it for that reason.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
The first objection is that the story seems to recommend passivity. Aksyonov accepts an injustice for twenty-six years and never fights it, and when he finally has the chance to speak, he chooses silence. Some readers find this admirable, but others see a dangerous message, that suffering should be borne meekly and that wrongdoing may be forgiven without being answered. Critics of Tolstoyan nonviolence have long argued that it can leave victims at the mercy of the powerful.

A second objection is about realism. The coincidence that brings the murderer to the same prison is hard to accept, and the speed of Makar's repentance feels more like a moral device than a human reaction. Some critics have also said that the story's religious frame is so strong that it settles questions too easily. The title says that God sees the truth, but the story never tests whether that comfort is enough for a man who has lost everything.

There is also the matter of the wife. She has little role beyond her doubt, and some readers feel she is treated harshly by the story, which turns her one moment of uncertainty into a wound that Aksyonov never heals. We never learn how she fared or whether she believed him in the end. The children, too, vanish. A modern reader may find that the story's moral clarity comes at the expense of its women and its human complexity.

Finally, a few readers find the tale simply too schematic, a parable more than a story. That is a fair description, and it was what Tolstoy intended, but those who prefer the subtle psychological detail of his big novels sometimes feel that the short folk tales, for all their power, leave out too much.

A related complaint is the way the story handles guilt and innocence. Aksyonov, at the start, is described as someone who used to drink and be riotous, and the tale hints that his suffering may be partly a punishment for his sins. That reading, that the innocent man is secretly being paid back for something else, strikes many modern readers as troubling, since it can excuse an unjust system. Tolstoy leaves the idea open, but the unease remains, and it leads some to read the story as more consoling toward authority than it should be.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
The story belongs to the tradition of the moral tale, which stretches back to the parables of Jesus and the fables of every culture. It also draws on the Russian folk story and the Russian tradition of the holy fool and the suffering saint. Tolstoy was writing in a country where Orthodox Christianity shaped how people thought about suffering, and the idea that undeserved pain can purify the soul was widespread.

It invites comparison with other stories of wrongful imprisonment. Alexandre Dumas's The Count of Monte Cristo is the great opposite, since Edmond Dantes is jailed unjustly too, but he emerges to take an elaborate revenge. Victor Hugo's Les Miserables offers another view, in which mercy given to a convict transforms him. And Dostoevsky's House of the Dead, a fictionalized account of his own years in a Siberian prison camp, shows the same setting from a darker and more realistic angle. Tolstoy admired that book. More recently, tales such as Stephen King's Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption return to the idea of an innocent man finding a measure of freedom behind bars, though with a very different spirit.

It matters today because the question at its center is still uncomfortable. When you have been wronged, and you can name the wrongdoer, what do you owe him? Tolstoy's answer is radical and not everyone will accept it, but the story does not lecture. It gives us a man, a long time, and a choice, and lets us decide what we think. In a few pages it also shows how a life that begins in lightness, with a guitar and a joke about gray hair, can end in a different kind of lightness, which is a rare thing for a short story to manage.

One more connection is with Tolstoy's own later fiction. The mercy that Aksyonov shows to Makar is close to the mercy in Tolstoy's late tales, such as Where Love Is, God Is, and echoes in the novel Resurrection, where a nobleman follows a wrongly condemned woman to Siberia and slowly changes his own life. In that sense this early story is a small rehearsal for a theme that Tolstoy would return to for the rest of his career, the idea that suffering unjustly borne can give a person a kind of moral authority that no court can take away.

stories.title: The Three Hermits
stories.author: Leo Tolstoy
stories.epigraph: “An Old Legend Current in the Volga District”
stories.keyContext: Leo Tolstoy published The Three Hermits in 1886, and he labeled it an old legend from the Volga district, meaning a tale he had picked up from ordinary Russian storytellers rather than invented himself. By then he was one of the most famous writers alive, but he had broken with the Russian Orthodox Church and was writing stories meant for peasants, printed cheaply and sold by the hundreds of thousands. The tale opens with a line from Jesus in the Gospel of Matthew, a warning against praying with empty repetition, as if God had to be talked into listening. A bishop is sailing to a famous monastery when he learns of three old hermits living on a tiny island, and he decides to teach them to pray properly. Listen for who ends up teaching whom, and for what the story suggests about religion, humility, and the gap between rules and sincerity.
paragraphs: An Old Legend Current in the Volga District

“And in praying use not vain repetitions, as the Gentiles do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking. Be not therefore like unto them: for your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask Him.”

A Bishop was sailing from Archangel to the Solovétsk Monastery; and on the same vessel were a number of pilgrims on their way to visit the shrines at that place. The voyage was a smooth one. The wind favourable, and the weather fair. The pilgrims lay on deck, eating, or sat in groups talking to one another. The Bishop, too, came on deck, and as he was pacing up and down, he noticed a group of men standing near the prow and listening to a fisherman, who was pointing to the sea and telling them something. The Bishop stopped, and looked in the direction in which the man was pointing. He could see nothing, however, but the sea glistening in the sunshine. He drew nearer to listen, but when the man saw him, he took off his cap and was silent. The rest of the people also took off their caps, and bowed.
“Do not let me disturb you, friends,” said the Bishop. “I came to hear what this good man was saying.”
“The fisherman was telling us about the hermits,” replied one, a tradesman, rather bolder than the rest.
“What hermits?” asked the Bishop, going to the side of the vessel and seating himself on a box. “Tell me about them. I should like to hear. What were you pointing at?”

“Why, that little island you can just see over there,” answered the man, pointing to a spot ahead and a little to the right. “That is the island where the hermits live for the salvation of their souls.”
“Where is the island?” asked the Bishop. “I see nothing.”
“There, in the distance, if you will please look along my hand. Do you see that little cloud? Below it, and a bit to the left, there is just a faint streak. That is the island.”
The Bishop looked carefully, but his unaccustomed eyes could make out nothing but the water shimmering in the sun.
“I cannot see it,” he said. “But who are the hermits that live there?”
“They are holy men,” answered the fisherman. “I had long heard tell of them, but never chanced to see them myself till the year before last.”

And the fisherman related how once, when he was out fishing, he had been stranded at night upon that island, not knowing where he was. In the morning, as he wandered about the island, he came across an earth hut, and met an old man standing near it. Presently two others came out, and after having fed him, and dried his things, they helped him mend his boat.
“And what are they like?” asked the Bishop.

“One is a small man and his back is bent. He wears a priest’s cassock and is very old; he must be more than a hundred, I should say. He is so old that the white of his beard is taking a greenish tinge, but he is always smiling, and his face is as bright as an angel’s from heaven. The second is taller, but he also is very old. He wears a tattered, peasant coat. His beard is broad, and of a yellowish grey colour. He is a strong man. Before I had time to help him, he turned my boat over as if it were only a pail. He too, is kindly and cheerful. The third is tall, and has a beard as white as snow and reaching to his knees. He is stern, with overhanging eyebrows; and he wears nothing but a mat tied round his waist.”
“And did they speak to you?” asked the Bishop.

“For the most part they did everything in silence, and spoke but little even to one another. One of them would just give a glance, and the others would understand him. I asked the tallest whether they had lived there long. He frowned, and muttered something as if he were angry; but the oldest one took his hand and smiled, and then the tall one was quiet. The oldest one only said: ‘Have mercy upon us,’ and smiled.”
While the fisherman was talking, the ship had drawn nearer to the island.
“There, now you can see it plainly, if your Grace will please to look,” said the tradesman, pointing with his hand.
The Bishop looked, and now he really saw a dark streak⁠—which was the island. Having looked at it awhile, he left the prow of the vessel, and going to the stern, asked the helmsman:
“What island is that?”
“That one,” replied the man, “has no name. There are many such in this sea.”
“Is it true that there are hermits who live there for the salvation of their souls?”
“So it is said, your Grace, but I don’t know if it’s true. Fishermen say they have seen them; but of course they may only be spinning yarns.”
“I should like to land on the island and see these men,” said the Bishop. “How could I manage it?”
“The ship cannot get close to the island,” replied the helmsman, “but you might be rowed there in a boat. You had better speak to the captain.”
The captain was sent for and came.
“I should like to see these hermits,” said the Bishop. “Could I not be rowed ashore?”
The captain tried to dissuade him.

“Of course it could be done,” said he, “but we should lose much time. And if I might venture to say so to your Grace, the old men are not worth your pains. I have heard say that they are foolish old fellows, who understand nothing, and never speak a word, any more than the fish in the sea.”
“I wish to see them,” said the Bishop, “and I will pay you for your trouble and loss of time. Please let me have a boat.”

There was no help for it; so the order was given. The sailors trimmed the sails, the steersman put up the helm, and the ship’s course was set for the island. A chair was placed at the prow for the Bishop, and he sat there, looking ahead. The passengers all collected at the prow, and gazed at the island. Those who had the sharpest eyes could presently make out the rocks on it, and then a mud hut was seen. At last one man saw the hermits themselves. The captain brought a telescope and, after looking through it, handed it to the Bishop.
“It’s right enough. There are three men standing on the shore. There, a little to the right of that big rock.”
The Bishop took the telescope, got it into position, and he saw the three men: a tall one, a shorter one, and one very small and bent, standing on the shore and holding each other by the hand.
The captain turned to the Bishop.
“The vessel can get no nearer in than this, your Grace. If you wish to go ashore, we must ask you to go in the boat, while we anchor here.”

The cable was quickly let out, the anchor cast, and the sails furled. There was a jerk, and the vessel shook. Then a boat having been lowered, the oarsmen jumped in, and the Bishop descended the ladder and took his seat. The men pulled at their oars, and the boat moved rapidly towards the island. When they came within a stone’s throw, they saw three old men: a tall one with only a mat tied round his waist: a shorter one in a tattered peasant coat, and a very old one bent with age and wearing an old cassock⁠—all three standing hand in hand.
The oarsmen pulled in to the shore, and held on with the boathook while the Bishop got out.
The old men bowed to him, and he gave them his benediction, at which they bowed still lower. Then the Bishop began to speak to them.

“I have heard,” he said, “that you, godly men, live here saving your own souls, and praying to our Lord Christ for your fellow men. I, an unworthy servant of Christ, am called, by God’s mercy, to keep and teach His flock. I wished to see you, servants of God, and to do what I can to teach you, also.”
The old men looked at each other smiling, but remained silent.
“Tell me,” said the Bishop, “what you are doing to save your souls, and how you serve God on this island.”
The second hermit sighed, and looked at the oldest, the very ancient one. The latter smiled, and said:
“We do not know how to serve God. We only serve and support ourselves, servant of God.”
“But how do you pray to God?” asked the Bishop.
“We pray in this way,” replied the hermit. “Three are ye, three are we, have mercy upon us.”
And when the old man said this, all three raised their eyes to heaven, and repeated:
“Three are ye, three are we, have mercy upon us!”
The Bishop smiled.

“You have evidently heard something about the Holy Trinity,” said he. “But you do not pray aright. You have won my affection, godly men. I see you wish to please the Lord, but you do not know how to serve Him. That is not the way to pray; but listen to me, and I will teach you. I will teach you, not a way of my own, but the way in which God in the Holy Scriptures has commanded all men to pray to Him.”
And the Bishop began explaining to the hermits how God had revealed Himself to men; telling them of God the Father, and God the Son, and God the Holy Ghost.
“God the Son came down on earth,” said he, “to save men, and this is how He taught us all to pray. Listen, and repeat after me: ‘Our Father.’ ”
And the first old man repeated after him, “Our Father,” and the second said, “Our Father,” and the third said, “Our Father.”
“Which art in heaven,” continued the Bishop.

The first hermit repeated, “Which art in heaven,” but the second blundered over the words, and the tall hermit could not say them properly. His hair had grown over his mouth so that he could not speak plainly. The very old hermit, having no teeth, also mumbled indistinctly.

The Bishop repeated the words again, and the old men repeated them after him. The Bishop sat down on a stone, and the old men stood before him, watching his mouth, and repeating the words as he uttered them. And all day long the Bishop laboured, saying a word twenty, thirty, a hundred times over, and the old men repeated it after him. They blundered, and he corrected them, and made them begin again.

The Bishop did not leave off till he had taught them the whole of the Lord’s prayer so that they could not only repeat it after him, but could say it by themselves. The middle one was the first to know it, and to repeat the whole of it alone. The Bishop made him say it again and again, and at last the others could say it too.

It was getting dark, and the moon was appearing over the water, before the Bishop rose to return to the vessel. When he took leave of the old men, they all bowed down to the ground before him. He raised them, and kissed each of them, telling them to pray as he had taught them. Then he got into the boat and returned to the ship.

And as he sat in the boat and was rowed to the ship he could hear the three voices of the hermits loudly repeating the Lord’s prayer. As the boat drew near the vessel their voices could no longer be heard, but they could still be seen in the moonlight, standing as he had left them on the shore, the shortest in the middle, the tallest on the right, the middle one on the left. As soon as the Bishop had reached the vessel and got on board, the anchor was weighed and the sails unfurled. The wind filled them, and the ship sailed away, and the Bishop took a seat in the stern and watched the island they had left. For a time he could still see the hermits, but presently they disappeared from sight, though the island was still visible. At last it too vanished, and only the sea was to be seen, rippling in the moonlight.

The pilgrims lay down to sleep, and all was quiet on deck. The Bishop did not wish to sleep, but sat alone at the stern, gazing at the sea where the island was no longer visible, and thinking of the good old men. He thought how pleased they had been to learn the Lord’s prayer; and he thanked God for having sent him to teach and help such godly men.

So the Bishop sat, thinking, and gazing at the sea where the island had disappeared. And the moonlight flickered before his eyes, sparkling, now here, now there, upon the waves. Suddenly he saw something white and shining, on the bright path which the moon cast across the sea. Was it a seagull, or the little gleaming sail of some small boat? The Bishop fixed his eyes on it, wondering.

“It must be a boat sailing after us,” thought he, “but it is overtaking us very rapidly. It was far, far away a minute ago, but now it is much nearer. It cannot be a boat, for I can see no sail; but whatever it may be, it is following us, and catching us up.”

And he could not make out what it was. Not a boat, nor a bird, nor a fish! It was too large for a man, and besides a man could not be out there in the midst of the sea. The Bishop rose, and said to the helmsman:

“Look there, what is that, my friend? What is it?” the Bishop repeated, though he could now see plainly what it was⁠—the three hermits running upon the water, all gleaming white, their grey beards shining, and approaching the ship as quickly as though it were not moving.
The steersman looked and let go the helm in terror.
“Oh Lord! The hermits are running after us on the water as though it were dry land!”

The passengers hearing him, jumped up, and crowded to the stern. They saw the hermits coming along hand in hand, and the two outer ones beckoning the ship to stop. All three were gliding along upon the water without moving their feet. Before the ship could be stopped, the hermits had reached it, and raising their heads, all three as with one voice, began to say:

“We have forgotten your teaching, servant of God. As long as we kept repeating it we remembered, but when we stopped saying it for a time, a word dropped out, and now it has all gone to pieces. We can remember nothing of it. Teach us again.”
The Bishop crossed himself, and leaning over the ship’s side, said:
“Your own prayer will reach the Lord, men of God. It is not for me to teach you. Pray for us sinners.”
And the Bishop bowed low before the old men; and they turned and went back across the sea. And a light shone until daybreak on the spot where they were lost to sight.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The tale begins with a bishop on a calm sea, traveling with pilgrims to the Solovetsky Monastery, a famous holy place on islands in the far north. Out on deck he overhears a fisherman describing a small island where three hermits live, old men who are said to have saved their souls. The bishop is curious and a little condescending. He asks to be taken there and when the helmsman reluctantly agrees he is rowed ashore in a small boat.

The three hermits are touching. One is small and bent, one tall, and one very old, wearing nothing but a mat, and they greet him with simple smiles. When he asks how they serve God, they say they do not know how, they only serve and feed themselves. He asks how they pray, and they answer with their entire prayer, the words that Three are ye, three are we, have mercy upon us. The bishop is shocked at how crude this is, and sets out to teach them the Lord's Prayer. It is slow work. The hermits are old, toothless, and forgetful, and they keep stumbling, and he spends the whole day repeating each phrase until they can say it, then leaves them practicing.

That night, as his ship sails away, the bishop sits on deck and notes a glowing patch of moonlight on the water. Something is following the ship, moving fast, and it is not a boat or a bird. It is the three hermits, running over the water as if it were dry land, hand in hand, shining white. They call out that they have forgotten his teaching, that when they stopped repeating it a word dropped out and the whole thing fell apart, and they beg him to teach them again. The bishop crosses himself and bows low. He says that their own prayer will reach the Lord, and that it is not for him to teach them. They turn and go back across the sea, and a light shines at the spot until daybreak.

The meaning is in the reversal. The bishop is educated, powerful, and sure he knows the proper way to pray, and the hermits are ignorant of every formula. Yet the hermits can walk on water, an image that echoes Jesus and the apostle Peter in the Gospels, and the bishop cannot. The miracle is the story's way of saying which prayer God actually hears. The bishop's lesson was about words. The hermits' prayer, though clumsy, came from sincere hearts, and the bishop realizes that he has been trying to improve something that was not broken.

There are details worth noticing. The epigraph from Matthew warns against vain repetitions, yet the Lord's Prayer is itself repeated by the hermits until it goes to pieces, and in the end they rely on their own crude phrase. The story seems to put the weight on the heart behind the words, not on the words. Notice also that the bishop's humility comes at once. He does not argue, and he does not insist on his rank. That quick turning is what makes him, at the end, one of Tolstoy's rare attractive clergymen.

One last detail concerns the title word Old Legend. Tolstoy presents the story as something handed down, which gives it a certain authority and also places it at a distance. The bishop is no one in particular, the hermits have no names, and the island is simply an island. That anonymity is part of the meaning. Anyone could be the bishop, the one who is sure of the proper way, and anyone could be among the hermits, the ones whose own plain words may be enough.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
As a piece of craft this is nearly flawless, and the reason is that it uses every element it has. The setting, a calm ship with idle pilgrims, gives the bishop an audience, and so makes the visit to the island feel like an act of vanity as well as charity. The island scene is quick and visual, three figures as simple as children's drawings. The day of teaching is told with a light, affectionate humor, with the old men trying and failing, and the bishop's patience turning gradually into a kind of pride in his work.

The ending is the best part. Tolstoy builds the suspense with a single, clear image. A shape on the water, too large to be a bird, drawing near faster than a ship, and the narrator's refusal to name it until the bishop sees for himself. The helmsman lets go of the wheel in terror. The hermits' request, so humble and so anxious, makes the miracle feel intimate rather than grand. And the last image, the light staying until dawn, is quiet and exact.

There are weaknesses. The hermits are almost too perfect. They are childlike, always smiling, with no flaws and no inner life, and the story depends on a miracle to settle an argument that is really about the nature of faith. A skeptic may feel the case is rigged. The bishop is also a mild target. He is a decent man, only mistaken, so the story's critique of the clergy is less sharp than Tolstoy's other writing on the church, which could be harsh.

There is a subtler problem, and the story does not quite face it. Jesus, in the verses right after the one quoted in the epigraph, gives his followers the Lord's Prayer as a model, which is exactly what the bishop is teaching. The point against empty repetition is fair, but the story makes the prayer itself look like the problem when it is really the attitude that matters. And the idea that formal knowledge counts for nothing could easily be used to dismiss all teaching. Tolstoy leans hard into a particular view of simple faith, and a reader who disagrees may find the tale a bit one-sided.

Even so, its brevity helps it. In a few pages it gives us a complete arc, vanity, correction, humility, and does not stay a moment past the point where it has said what it wants.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The story came out in 1886, in the same stretch of years as The Death of Ivan Ilyich and How Much Land Does a Man Need?, and it belongs to the cheap-edition series that Tolstoy and a publisher friend ran to put good stories in the hands of ordinary readers. These little books sold in huge numbers for a few pennies, and for many people in Russia they were the first writing of Tolstoy's they ever saw. It helped establish the idea that the author of great novels might also be a teller of tales for the poor.

It also fed into his conflict with the church. Tolstoy believed that institutional religion, with its rituals, its hierarchy, and its doctrines, had buried the simple teaching of Jesus. A story in which a bishop is taught by uneducated hermits reads like an illustration of that belief. The Holy Synod of the Russian Orthodox Church excommunicated him in 1901, and while that had many causes, the attitude behind this story was part of it. I would be careful not to say that this one story caused anything, but it is a small, clear expression of the attitude that did.

Beyond Russia it has had a long life as a teaching story. It is retold in sermons, in collections of moral tales, and in books for children, and it has been included in many anthologies of Tolstoy's short work. Its central image, holy men running on water, has been borrowed and referred to in many places, and the idea that sincerity matters more than polish is one that many traditions have returned to. Its direct influence on other major writers is harder to trace, but its influence on how Tolstoy was read by general audiences is clear.

Because the story is so short and so easily retold, it is hard to separate its influence from the broader folk tradition it came from. Tolstoy was borrowing a legend rather than inventing one, and after he gave it a polished written form it re-entered oral circulation, passed along by preachers and teachers who may never have known where the version they told came from. That is arguably the best kind of influence a folk story can have, and it fits what Tolstoy wanted, which was for these stories to belong to everyone.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers have loved the story first for its images. The hermits running over the water, gleaming white with beards shining, is among the most memorable pictures in the whole of Tolstoy's short fiction, and it seems to stay with people who read the story only once. It is a miracle told without fuss, and that makes it feel truer.

They love the humor and warmth. The scene of the old men repeating the Lord's Prayer is funny, since we can see them struggling, and yet it never mocks them. The reader is on the hermits' side from the start, and gradually on the bishop's too, because he proves capable of changing his mind.

Many also admire the story's gentleness about a hard point. Tolstoy could be fierce in his attacks on the church, but this is not a fierce story. The bishop is neither a hypocrite nor a villain. He is a good man who must learn something, and the lesson is given to him without humiliation. Readers often say that this is what makes the story persuasive, since it invites us to see ourselves in the bishop rather than to feel superior to him. Anyone who has tried to teach, to correct, or to improve someone else can recognize the temptation.

And many just love its simplicity. It can be read in ten minutes, and it reads like a legend, with the rhythm of a story told aloud. That oral quality makes it ideal for listening, which is how many people have met it.

Teachers love how well it holds up in a classroom. A group can talk for an hour about what the hermits' prayer means, whether the bishop was right to teach them, and what the miracle is really saying. Because the story takes no cheap shots at the bishop, believers of many kinds, and nonbelievers too, can find something in it. People from very different traditions have said that it gave voice to something they already felt, that a heartfelt, imperfect prayer counts for more than a perfect one said without attention.

There is also a pleasure in how the story is built like a legend, with its triplets. Three hermits, three saying their prayer, three times they say they forgot, the number repeating throughout, and that almost musical structure helps it feel old and true. Listeners tend to remember it long after the details of other stories have gone, which is an achievement for something so short.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
The chief complaint from the religious side is that the story undervalues learning and tradition. Orthodox and other Christian critics have pointed out that liturgy and set prayers are not necessarily empty, and that the Lord's Prayer was given by Jesus himself. To them the story makes a false opposition between sincere feeling and shared forms of worship, and slights the church's role in preserving faith across generations.

From the literary side, critics have found the tale overly simple, a parable with a tidy message that leaves little room for the ambiguities of his great novels. The hermits are sometimes called sentimental figures, Tolstoy's idealized peasants in saintly form. This is a recurring complaint about his late work, that he romanticized the simple man while living in a manor house, and that the stories can feel like sermons wearing a costume.

There is also the doubt about the miracle. Tolstoy rejected miracles in his own theology, and some readers have wondered why a writer who thought the Gospels' supernatural events were later additions should end this story on a miracle. One answer is that the tale was a legend and he kept its form. Another is that the miracle works as a symbol rather than a claim. Either way, the question reveals a slight tension between Tolstoy's rational Christianity and his love of traditional storytelling.

Finally, there is the sheer ease of the lesson. Some find that the bishop gives up too easily, since a real cleric might have argued, and that the story's resolution comes before any real conflict has taken place.

A related objection concerns the portrait of the bishop's motives. The story suggests that the bishop is moved to visit the island partly out of curiosity and a sense of his own importance, but it never lets him be a real antagonist, and that mildness can feel like a dodge. A sharper story might have shown a bishop who truly resists the lesson, or a hermit who truly needs the instruction. As written, the conflict is settled by the hermits' miracle, and some readers want more of a struggle.

Others raise a social point, that the story flatters a particular picture of the poor as simple, holy, and content. In Tolstoy's Russia, many peasants were illiterate and desperately poor, and some later critics have worried about gentry writers who found spiritual perfection in other people's hardship. The hermits are not exactly peasants, but they belong to that tradition of the pure, uneducated saint, and the criticism applies. It is a fair question to ask what the hermits know that a bishop, with a lifetime of study and responsibility, cannot know.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
The Three Hermits belongs to an old family of stories about humble people who turn out to be holier than the learned. You find it in the Gospels, where Jesus says that the truth is hidden from the wise and revealed to little children, and in the lives of the saints, and in desert fathers' tales in which a famous teacher is corrected by an uneducated monk. Russian culture also has the figure of the holy fool, the person who seems foolish or simple but carries real spiritual insight.

Within Tolstoy's work it is part of the late short tales, with Where Love Is, God Is, and How Much Land Does a Man Need?, in which he used the folk tale to express his own version of Christianity. Its closest cousin in other literature may be the Hasidic tales told in the Jewish tradition, in which a simple man's honest prayer reaches heaven where a scholar's does not. There is also a resemblance to the story of the widow's mite in the Gospels. As to descendants, the idea of the learned person humbled by the simple one has become a staple of fable, children's stories, and films.

A small historical irony adds to its interest. The Solovetsky Monastery that the bishop is sailing to became, after the Russian Revolution, one of the first camps in the Soviet prison system, a place where many people suffered and died. A modern reader cannot help noticing that the holy island of the story would later become a place of terror. That has nothing to do with Tolstoy's intent, but it gives the opening an unexpected shadow.

It is worth reading now because its question remains alive. How much of religion, or any practice, is the form and how much is the sincerity behind it? The story does not settle that, but it poses it more gracefully than most arguments do, and in barely ten minutes. For listeners especially, its steady, almost chanted rhythm makes it a good companion for a quiet evening.

stories.title: Three Questions
stories.author: Leo Tolstoy
stories.epigraph: “And learned men came to the King, but they all answered his questions differently.”
stories.keyContext: Leo Tolstoy wrote Three Questions in 1903, when he was seventy-four, famous around the world, and officially an outcast from the Russian Orthodox Church, which had excommunicated him two years earlier. He had recently survived a serious illness, and he was thinking hard about how to spend whatever time he had left. The story is a fable, a short tale with a lesson, about a king who believes that if he could only answer three questions, he would never fail at anything. When should I act, whom should I listen to, and what matters most? The wise men of his kingdom all give different answers, so he goes to see a hermit in the forest. Tolstoy spent his whole late career trying to boil life down to a simple practice, and this tale is one of his clearest attempts. Listen for what the king ends up doing before anyone answers him.
paragraphs: It once occurred to a certain king, that if he always knew the right time to begin everything; if he knew who were the right people to listen to, and whom to avoid; and, above all, if he always knew what was the most important thing to do, he would never fail in anything he might undertake.

And this thought having occurred to him, he had it proclaimed throughout his kingdom that he would give a great reward to anyone who would teach him what was the right time for every action, and who were the most necessary people, and how he might know what was the most important thing to do.
And learned men came to the King, but they all answered his questions differently.

In reply to the first question, some said that to know the right time for every action, one must draw up in advance, a table of days, months and years, and must live strictly according to it. Only thus, said they, could everything be done at its proper time. Others declared that it was impossible to decide beforehand the right time for every action; but that, not letting oneself be absorbed in idle pastimes, one should always attend to all that was going on, and then do what was most needful. Others, again, said that however attentive the King might be to what was going on, it was impossible for one man to decide correctly the right time for every action, but that he should have a Council of wise men, who would help him to fix the proper time for everything.

But then again others said there were some things which could not wait to be laid before a Council, but about which one had at once to decide whether to undertake them or not. But in order to decide that, one must know beforehand what was going to happen. It is only magicians who know that; and, therefore, in order to know the right time for every action, one must consult magicians.

Equally various were the answers to the second question. Some said, the people the King most needed were his councillors; others, the priests; others, the doctors; while some said the warriors were the most necessary.

To the third question, as to what was the most important occupation: some replied that the most important thing in the world was science. Others said it was skill in warfare; and others, again, that it was religious worship.

All the answers being different, the King agreed with none of them, and gave the reward to none. But still wishing to find the right answers to his questions, he decided to consult a hermit, widely renowned for his wisdom.

The hermit lived in a wood which he never quitted, and he received none but common folk. So the King put on simple clothes, and before reaching the hermit’s cell dismounted from his horse, and, leaving his bodyguard behind, went on alone.

When the King approached, the hermit was digging the ground in front of his hut. Seeing the King, he greeted him and went on digging. The hermit was frail and weak, and each time he stuck his spade into the ground and turned a little earth, he breathed heavily.

The King went up to him and said: “I have come to you, wise hermit, to ask you to answer three questions: How can I learn to do the right thing at the right time? Who are the people I most need, and to whom should I, therefore, pay more attention than to the rest? And, what affairs are the most important, and need my first attention?”
The hermit listened to the King, but answered nothing. He just spat on his hand and recommenced digging.
“You are tired,” said the King, “let me take the spade and work awhile for you.”
“Thanks!” said the hermit, and, giving the spade to the King, he sat down on the ground.
When he had dug two beds, the King stopped and repeated his questions. The hermit again gave no answer, but rose, stretched out his hand for the spade, and said:
“Now rest awhile⁠—and let me work a bit.”
But the King did not give him the spade, and continued to dig. One hour passed, and another. The sun began to sink behind the trees, and the King at last stuck the spade into the ground, and said:
“I came to you, wise man, for an answer to my questions. If you can give me none, tell me so, and I will return home.”
“Here comes someone running,” said the hermit, “let us see who it is.”

The King turned round, and saw a bearded man come running out of the wood. The man held his hands pressed against his stomach, and blood was flowing from under them. When he reached the King, he fell fainting on the ground moaning feebly. The King and the hermit unfastened the man’s clothing. There was a large wound in his stomach. The King washed it as best he could, and bandaged it with his handkerchief and with a towel the hermit had. But the blood would not stop flowing, and the King again and again removed the bandage soaked with warm blood, and washed and rebandaged the wound. When at last the blood ceased flowing, the man revived and asked for something to drink. The King brought fresh water and gave it to him. Meanwhile the sun had set, and it had become cool. So the King, with the hermit’s help, carried the wounded man into the hut and laid him on the bed. Lying on the bed the man closed his eyes and was quiet; but the King was so tired with his walk and with the work he had done, that he crouched down on the threshold, and also fell asleep⁠—so soundly that he slept all through the short summer night. When he awoke in the morning, it was long before he could remember where he was, or who was the strange bearded man lying on the bed and gazing intently at him with shining eyes.
“Forgive me!” said the bearded man in a weak voice, when he saw that the King was awake and was looking at him.
“I do not know you, and have nothing to forgive you for,” said the King.

“You do not know me, but I know you. I am that enemy of yours who swore to revenge himself on you, because you executed his brother and seized his property. I knew you had gone alone to see the hermit, and I resolved to kill you on your way back. But the day passed and you did not return. So I came out from my ambush to find you, and I came upon your bodyguard, and they recognized me, and wounded me. I escaped from them, but should have bled to death had you not dressed my wound. I wished to kill you, and you have saved my life. Now, if I live, and if you wish it, I will serve you as your most faithful slave, and will bid my sons do the same. Forgive me!”

The King was very glad to have made peace with his enemy so easily, and to have gained him for a friend, and he not only forgave him, but said he would send his servants and his own physician to attend him, and promised to restore his property.

Having taken leave of the wounded man, the King went out into the porch and looked around for the hermit. Before going away he wished once more to beg an answer to the questions he had put. The hermit was outside, on his knees, sowing seeds in the beds that had been dug the day before.
The King approached him, and said:
“For the last time, I pray you to answer my questions, wise man.”
“You have already been answered!” said the hermit still crouching on his thin legs, and looking up at the King, who stood before him.
“How answered? What do you mean?” asked the King.

“Do you not see,” replied the hermit. “If you had not pitied my weakness yesterday, and had not dug those beds for me, but had gone your way, that man would have attacked you, and you would have repented of not having stayed with me. So the most important time was when you were digging the beds; and I was the most important man; and to do me good was your most important business. Afterwards when that man ran to us, the most important time was when you were attending to him, for if you had not bound up his wounds he would have died without having made peace with you. So he was the most important man, and what you did for him was your most important business. Remember then: there is only one time that is important⁠—Now! It is the most important time because it is the only time when we have any power. The most necessary man is he with whom you are, for no man knows whether he will ever have dealings with anyone else: and the most important affair is, to do him good, because for that purpose alone was man sent into this life!”

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
A king decides that he would never fail in anything if he always knew the right time to begin each task, the right people to listen to and avoid, and above all the most important thing to do. He proclaims a reward for anyone who can answer these questions. Learned men come and each says something different. One says to draw up a timetable. Another says you cannot know the right time in advance, so you must pay attention to everything and act when needed. Another says you need a council of wise men, and another says that to know what to do you need priests, or doctors, or soldiers. None of these answers satisfies him, so he decides to consult a hermit who is said to be wise and who receives only simple people.

The king disguises himself, leaves his attendants behind, and walks to the hermit's hut in the woods. The hermit is digging beds in his garden, and he is old and frail. The king asks his questions, but the hermit only nods and keeps digging. Seeing how weak the old man is, the king takes the spade and digs for him. Hours pass, and the king grows impatient and says he will go home without an answer. At that moment a man comes running out of the forest holding his belly, covered in blood, and collapses. The king and the hermit wash and bind the wound, and the king, exhausted, falls asleep.

In the morning the wounded man begs forgiveness. He tells the king that he was his enemy, that the king had executed his brother and taken his property, and that he had been lying in wait to kill him. He was found by the king's bodyguards and wounded, and escaped. Now the king has saved his life. They make peace, and the king promises to send his own doctor and to restore the man's property. Then the king returns to the hermit and asks one more time for his answer. The hermit says he has already been answered, and explains.

The explanation is the heart of the story. If the king had not stopped to dig the beds, the man would have attacked him, so the most important time was when he was digging, the most important man was the hermit, and the most important act was helping him. Later the most important time was when he bandaged the wounded man, because otherwise the man would have died without reconciling. The conclusion is the famous passage. There is only one time that matters, which is now, because it is the only time we have any power. The most necessary person is whoever you are with, and the most important act is to do that person good.

There is a clever layer to this. The king's questions assumed that the answers lay in the future or in special knowledge, in a calendar or a council. The answer turns out to be that the questions are looking in the wrong place. Importance is not in the grand plan but in the person in front of you. Notice too that the king does not learn the lesson by being told it. He learns it by acting, and the explanation only names what he has already done.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
The story has a handsome structure. It begins with a puzzle that sounds as if it needs a philosopher, and resolves it with a day of ordinary labor. The structure is that of a mystery, where the king keeps asking and the hermit keeps not answering, and the answer is hidden in plain view. When the hermit finally says you have already been answered, it is a small shock, because the reader too has been waiting for a speech and missed the lesson in the action.

The use of the wounded man is clever. He is not a random victim but the king's enemy, so that a simple act of kindness turns into a reconciliation that saves the king's life, and the plot gives practical weight to the moral. The details feel right as well. The king's irritation at the long day of digging, his desire to leave, and the quick, practical way he and the hermit tend the wound are all well observed. The hermit's refusal to answer at first makes him a believable teacher, since he understands that the king must see for himself.

But there are real problems. The central claim, that the only important time is now, is a fine idea but it can sound like a greeting card. Tolstoy states it with great force, yet in the story's own terms it rests on a coincidence. The king's kindness happens to save his life, and the structure suggests that doing good is also the safe course. A more honest tale might have shown a good deed that cost the king dearly. Here virtue is conveniently rewarded, so the lesson may be less demanding than it sounds.

There is also an odd gap between the lesson and the king's position. A king, after all, has real responsibilities, to a whole kingdom, which cannot be met by attending to the person in front of him. The story brushes this aside. The idea that the most important person is whoever happens to be with you is moving for a private person, but it is awkward for someone who decides the fates of thousands. The king who executed a man's brother and seized his property was not making the mistake of ignoring the present. He had done something worse, and the story treats that as background. A reader might want to hear more about it.

Finally, the prose is flat in places and the dialogue sounds more like exposition than speech, particularly in the hermit's final explanation. But that is part of the form. Tolstoy was writing a fable, and the plainness is chosen.

One more craft point is the pacing of the middle. Tolstoy lets the day drag, mentioning the sun, the king's tired arms, and his growing impatience, so that when the wounded man bursts from the trees the interruption feels like a real intrusion, as it would in life. That small choice makes the lesson land harder, because we, like the king, have been wishing to be elsewhere.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
By 1903 Tolstoy was the most famous private citizen in Russia and a figure of world interest. His excommunication in 1901 had made him even more visible, and he was getting letters from followers around the world. In that setting this little tale was an attempt to distill his message into something anyone could remember. Of all his late tales it is probably the most directly practical, offering a rule for living rather than a warning.

The story has had a long life outside literature. It has been used for generations in sermons and teaching, and in recent decades it has been taken up in mindfulness, leadership, and self-help writing, where its answer, now, here, this person, is easily turned into advice about attention. The American author and illustrator Jon J Muth published a picture-book version in 2002, based on Tolstoy, which moved the tale into a modern children's story with a boy and his animal friends, and brought it to many young readers who had never heard of the original.

It also connects to Tolstoy's lasting influence on thinkers about service and nonviolence. His idea that goodness lives in small acts toward the people near us is one that Gandhi, who corresponded with him, took seriously, and it remains a strand of the ethics of care. I would not claim that this particular story drove those movements, but it states their spirit in memorable form.

It is also worth noting how little direct reception from its own time is recorded in detail. Tolstoy's name guaranteed that his short pieces were printed, translated, and read, but the critics of the day were more interested in his big religious arguments and his quarrel with the church than in a short fable. The story's real success came later, through repetition, as readers, translators, and teachers passed it along because it was short and clear and seemed to hold a whole philosophy in a few pages. That slow, word-of-mouth life is typical of the late tales.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
What readers love most is how usable the story is. Few works of literature give you something so easy to carry. Three questions, three answers, and a day of labor to prove them. People often say that they remember the central lines for years, and that they return to them in moments when they feel distracted or overwhelmed, thinking about the future when the present needs them.

They love its modesty. It is not a story of dramatic triumph. The king's great deed is digging a garden bed and washing a wound, and the story insists that this is enough. Many readers find that a relief in a culture that tells us importance means scale. It suggests that an ordinary afternoon with an ordinary person can be the most important thing we ever do.

Readers also like the shape of the plot, the way the king's journey seems to fail, and then reveals itself as a success. The sense of a puzzle quietly solved is a pleasure in itself, and it helps the lesson feel earned.

And there is gratitude for its generosity. The hermit does not scold the king. He explains, kindly, and the king leaves better, not humiliated. Many readers see in that gentleness the best side of Tolstoy, a man who could be furious and demanding in his essays, but who in his tales could be patient with human weakness.

There is a particular pleasure in the way the story respects its readers' intelligence. It does not tell us the answers at the start. It sets up the puzzle, lets the wise men fail, and trusts us to feel the pull of the king's anxiety, because we share it. Most of us also want to know the right moment, the right person, and the right task, and the story begins by flattering that wish before it gently corrects it.

Many readers also say that the story changed how they think about ordinary interruptions. The wounded man appears at the worst moment, when the king is tired and wants to leave, and the lesson is that the interruption is the task. People who work in caring jobs, such as nurses, teachers, and parents, often say that this is the part that resonates most. It gives dignity to the unplanned, unglamorous help that makes up so much of a life.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
The usual criticism is that the story is a sermon. Its message is clear from the start and delivered at the end in a speech that tells us exactly what to think. Readers who prefer fiction to leave questions open find the final explanation heavy, and some critics have called these late tales more tract than literature.

A related criticism is that the advice is too simple to be useful. Live in the present and do good to whoever is near you is hard to argue with, but critics point out that real life involves conflicts between the person in front of us and the people far away, between the immediate and the long-term. Planning, saving, and caution, which the story seems to dismiss, are also forms of care. A government that only attended to whoever stood nearest would be a bad one.

There are also political objections. Because the story is set among kings and hermits, it avoids the structural injustices that Tolstoy attacked in his essays. The king is simply a man who made a mistake, and the point of the story is to improve him, not to change the system that made him a king. Some critics have felt that Tolstoy's moral individualism, his focus on personal kindness, was a way of avoiding politics, even though he was a harsh critic of the state.

Finally, a few readers find the coincidence of the wounded man too convenient, and the hermit a little smug. The hermit never really explains why he would not simply answer in the first place, and some feel that his silence is a teaching trick. It works within the fable, but it may strain belief.

There is also an argument from the other direction, that the story is not simple enough. Tolstoy's claim that the important time is now sits oddly beside the story's own plot, which is built on a decision made long ago, the king's execution of his enemy's brother, and on its consequences in the present. The past, in other words, keeps returning in the story, and the lesson about the present does not fully account for it. That tension is easy to miss but may be the most interesting thing about the tale.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
This is a fable, and like all fables its roots are ancient. It belongs with the tales of kings who seek wisdom from a humble sage, which turn up in Eastern and Western traditions alike, and with the Gospel teaching that what we do for the least of people we do for God. Its central idea, that the present moment is the only one in which we can act, echoes Stoic philosophers like Marcus Aurelius, who was himself an emperor, and Buddhist teachings on mindfulness.

Within Tolstoy's work, it belongs with the late tales and with his final religious essays. It is the lightest and clearest statement of an ethic he elaborated at length in works like The Kingdom of God Is Within You and What Then Must We Do? Its descendants are numerous. The picture-book version by Jon Muth is one, and the many self-help books that repeat the formula of now, here, this person are another. The tradition of the wise hermit who answers a seeker with a deed rather than a lecture also appears in later fiction, though it is difficult to draw a straight line.

It is worth reading now because the questions are timeless and the answers are still uncomfortable. We live distracted lives, and the story reminds us how rarely we are fully with the person in front of us. It also reminds us that wisdom may be less a body of knowledge than a habit of attention. At about fifteen hundred words, it takes a few minutes to read, and its last paragraph is among the most quotable in Tolstoy.

A last thing to say is about what kind of reading experience the story offers. It is not a plot-driven thriller or a character study. It is closer to a guided meditation, with a question, a pause, an action, and an answer, and that is perhaps why it has found a home in contemporary writing on attention and presence. Anyone who finds a long book hard to start can read this one in the time it takes to make tea, and may find it harder to forget than most books ten times as long.

stories.title: Alyosha the Pot
stories.author: Leo Tolstoy
stories.epigraph: “I thought you would bring me a man in Simeon’s place,” he said, scanning Alyosha; “and you’ve brought me this! What’s the good of him?”
stories.keyContext: Leo Tolstoy wrote this very short story in 1905, in his late seventies, and it was published after his death. By then he was the most famous writer in the world, but he had spent decades turning away from his own great novels, preferring plain tales about ordinary people that a peasant could understand. Russia in 1905 was shaking with strikes, a failed revolution, and anger at the old order, and Tolstoy was convinced that real change had to begin inside the human heart. Alyosha the Pot is one of his simplest and most quietly devastating pieces. It follows a humble, uncomplaining farm boy sent to work as a servant in a merchant's house. You may find it almost too plain at first, so let the plainness work on you. Pay attention to what Alyosha is asked to do, what he is never asked about, and how he reacts. The story is really asking what a good life looks like when nobody has ever treated you as worth anything.
paragraphs: Alyosha was the younger brother. He was called the Pot, because his mother had once sent him with a pot of milk to the deacon’s wife, and he had stumbled against something and broken it. His mother had beaten him, and the children had teased him. Since then he was nicknamed the Pot. Alyosha was a tiny, thin little fellow, with ears like wings, and a huge nose. “Alyosha has a nose that looks like a dog on a hill!” the children used to call after him. Alyosha went to the village school, but was not good at lessons; besides, there was so little time to learn. His elder brother was in town, working for a merchant, so Alyosha had to help his father from a very early age. When he was no more than six he used to go out with the girls to watch the cows and sheep in the pasture, and a little later he looked after the horses by day and by night. And at twelve years of age he had already begun to plough and to drive the cart. The skill was there though the strength was not. He was always cheerful. Whenever the children made fun of him, he would either laugh or be silent. When his father scolded him he would stand mute and listen attentively, and as soon as the scolding was over would smile and go on with his work. Alyosha was nineteen when his brother was taken as a soldier. So his father placed him with the merchant as a yard-porter. He was given his brother’s old boots, his father’s old coat and cap, and was taken to town. Alyosha was delighted with his clothes, but the merchant was not impressed by his appearance.
“I thought you would bring me a man in Simeon’s place,” he said, scanning Alyosha; “and you’ve brought me this! What’s the good of him?”
“He can do everything; look after horses and drive. He’s a good one to work. He looks rather thin, but he’s tough enough. And he’s very willing.”
“He looks it. All right; we’ll see what we can do with him.”
So Alyosha remained at the merchant’s.

The family was not a large one. It consisted of the merchant’s wife: her old mother: a married son poorly educated who was in his father’s business: another son, a learned one who had finished school and entered the University, but having been expelled, was living at home: and a daughter who still went to school.

They did not take to Alyosha at first. He was uncouth, badly dressed, and had no manner, but they soon got used to him. Alyosha worked even better than his brother had done; he was really very willing. They sent him on all sorts of errands, but he did everything quickly and readily, going from one task to another without stopping. And so here, just as at home, all the work was put upon his shoulders. The more he did, the more he was given to do. His mistress, her old mother, the son, the daughter, the clerk, and the cook⁠—all ordered him about, and sent him from one place to another.

“Alyosha, do this! Alyosha, do that! What! have you forgotten, Alyosha? Mind you don’t forget, Alyosha!” was heard from morning till night. And Alyosha ran here, looked after this and that, forgot nothing, found time for everything, and was always cheerful.

His brother’s old boots were soon worn out, and his master scolded him for going about in tatters with his toes sticking out. He ordered another pair to be bought for him in the market. Alyosha was delighted with his new boots, but was angry with his feet when they ached at the end of the day after so much running about. And then he was afraid that his father would be annoyed when he came to town for his wages, to find that his master had deducted the cost of the boots.

In the winter Alyosha used to get up before daybreak. He would chop the wood, sweep the yard, feed the cows and horses, light the stoves, clean the boots, prepare the samovars and polish them afterwards; or the clerk would get him to bring up the goods; or the cook would set him to knead the bread and clean the saucepans. Then he was sent to town on various errands, to bring the daughter home from school, or to get some olive oil for the old mother. “Why the devil have you been so long?” first one, then another, would say to him. Why should they go? Alyosha can go. “Alyosha! Alyosha!” And Alyosha ran here and there. He breakfasted in snatches while he was working, and rarely managed to get his dinner at the proper hour. The cook used to scold him for being late, but she was sorry for him all the same, and would keep something hot for his dinner and supper.

At holiday times there was more work than ever, but Alyosha liked holidays because everybody gave him a tip. Not much certainly, but it would amount up to about sixty kopecks⁠—his very own money. For Alyosha never set eyes on his wages. His father used to come and take them from the merchant, and only scold Alyosha for wearing out his boots.

When he had saved up two roubles, by the advice of the cook he bought himself a red knitted jacket, and was so happy when he put it on, that he couldn’t close his mouth for joy. Alyosha was not talkative; when he spoke at all, he spoke abruptly, with his head turned away. When told to do anything, or asked if he could do it, he would say yes without the smallest hesitation, and set to work at once.
Alyosha did not know any prayer; and had forgotten what his mother had taught him. But he prayed just the same, every morning and every evening, prayed with his hands, crossing himself.

He lived like this for about a year and a half, and towards the end of the second year a most startling thing happened to him. He discovered one day, to his great surprise, that, in addition to the relation of usefulness existing between people, there was also another, a peculiar relation of quite a different character. Instead of a man being wanted to clean boots, and go on errands and harness horses, he is not wanted to be of any service at all, but another human being wants to serve him and pet him. Suddenly Alyosha felt he was such a man.

He made this discovery through the cook Ustinia. She was young, had no parents, and worked as hard as Alyosha. He felt for the first time in his life that he⁠—not his services, but he himself⁠—was necessary to another human being. When his mother used to be sorry for him, he had taken no notice of her. It had seemed to him quite natural, as though he were feeling sorry for himself. But here was Ustinia, a perfect stranger, and sorry for him. She would save him some hot porridge, and sit watching him, her chin propped on her bare arm, with the sleeve rolled up, while he was eating it. When he looked at her she would begin to laugh, and he would laugh too.

This was such a new, strange thing to him that it frightened Alyosha. He feared that it might interfere with his work. But he was pleased, nevertheless, and when he glanced at the trousers that Ustinia had mended for him, he would shake his head and smile. He would often think of her while at work, or when running on errands. “A fine girl, Ustinia!” he sometimes exclaimed.

Ustinia used to help him whenever she could, and he helped her. She told him all about her life; how she had lost her parents; how her aunt had taken her in and found a place for her in the town; how the merchant’s son had tried to take liberties with her, and how she had rebuffed him. She liked to talk, and Alyosha liked to listen to her. He had heard that peasants who came up to work in the towns frequently got married to servant girls. On one occasion she asked him if his parents intended marrying him soon. He said that he did not know; that he did not want to marry any of the village girls.
“Have you taken a fancy to someone, then?”
“I would marry you, if you’d be willing.”
“Get along with you, Alyosha the Pot; but you’ve found your tongue, haven’t you?” she exclaimed, slapping him on the back with a towel she held in her hand. “Why shouldn’t I?”

At Shrovetide Alyosha’s father came to town for his wages. It had come to the ears of the merchant’s wife that Alyosha wanted to marry Ustinia, and she disapproved of it. “What will be the use of her with a baby?” she thought, and informed her husband.
The merchant gave the old man Alyosha’s wages.
“How is my lad getting on?” he asked. “I told you he was willing.”
“That’s all right, as far as it goes, but he’s taken some sort of nonsense into his head. He wants to marry our cook. Now I don’t approve of married servants. We won’t have them in the house.”
“Well, now, who would have thought the fool would think of such a thing?” the old man exclaimed. “But don’t you worry. I’ll soon settle that.”
He went into the kitchen, and sat down at the table waiting for his son. Alyosha was out on an errand, and came back breathless.
“I thought you had some sense in you; but what’s this you’ve taken into your head?” his father began.
“I? Nothing.”
“How, nothing? They tell me you want to get married. You shall get married when the time comes. I’ll find you a decent wife, not some town hussy.”
His father talked and talked, while Alyosha stood still and sighed. When his father had quite finished, Alyosha smiled.
“All right. I’ll drop it.”
“Now that’s what I call sense.”
When he was left alone with Ustinia he told her what his father had said. (She had listened at the door.)
“It’s no good; it can’t come off. Did you hear? He was angry⁠—won’t have it at any price.”
Ustinia cried into her apron.
Alyosha shook his head.
“What’s to be done? We must do as we’re told.”
“Well, are you going to give up that nonsense, as your father told you?” his mistress asked, as he was putting up the shutters in the evening.
“To be sure we are,” Alyosha replied with a smile, and then burst into tears.

From that day Alyosha went about his work as usual, and no longer talked to Ustinia about their getting married. One day in Lent the clerk told him to clear the snow from the roof. Alyosha climbed on to the roof and swept away all the snow; and, while he was still raking out some frozen lumps from the gutter, his foot slipped and he fell over. Unfortunately he did not fall on the snow, but on a piece of iron over the door. Ustinia came running up, together with the merchant’s daughter.
“Have you hurt yourself, Alyosha?”
“Ah! no, it’s nothing.”
But he could not raise himself when he tried to, and began to smile.
