A final objection is that the story's own best idea, the body swap, is underused. Once the dwarf runs off, we never see him in Guido's body living Guido's life for long. The reader is told about it afterward, which is a missed chance for real horror.

Finally, a few scholars have noted that the story's moral is conventional for its time. The idea that pride is a sin and humility a cure is not new, and a tale that ends with the hero becoming a model citizen can seem to bow to the respectable values of a gift-book audience. Shelley was a radical by upbringing, and some critics wonder whether she toned down her sharper instincts in order to suit the market. Even the narrator's wink about his mirrors cannot entirely remove the sense that the story has been made safe for polite company.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
Where does this story sit in literature? It is a Romantic and Gothic tale, from the tradition that loved passion, wild landscapes, supernatural bargains and the danger of overreaching. Its parents are Goethe's Faust and the old devil-pact stories, in which a man gives up something precious for worldly gain. Its setting in medieval Italy follows a fashion popularized by earlier Gothic writers, and it shares the interest in a doomed noble hero that runs through the Gothic novels Shelley grew up reading.

The Coleridge epigraph is a key to its ancestry. Like the Mariner, Guido is a man who has had a supernatural experience, learned a harsh lesson, and been left with a need to tell it. The story therefore belongs to a kind of tale in which narration itself is a punishment and a cure. It also looks back to Shelley's own Frankenstein, with its theme of an arrogant young man who crosses a line and suffers for it, and with its interest in what makes a person monstrous. In that novel, the creature is called a monster because of how he looks, and here the same cruelty is turned on Guido, who learns what it is like to be judged by the body.

Its descendants are many. Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, The Picture of Dorian Gray and countless doppelganger stories trace similar themes. In the twentieth century, Thomas Mann's The Transposed Heads, which retells an Indian tale of two men whose heads are swapped, turned the idea into a comic philosophical fable. The body-swap film and television comedy, from Freaky Friday to countless others, is a cheerful grandchild.

Why read it now? Because it is a quick, lively example of a major idea, and because it shows that Mary Shelley could write playfully and with moral seriousness at the same time. It also raises a question that has become more relevant, not less: how much of who we are lies in how we look, and how much in what we do? Guido learns the answer the hard way. For a modern reader, the story is a good entrance to the quieter side of the Gothic, where the monster on the shore turns out to be a kind of teacher.

It also rewards a second reading. Once you know that the polite young man at Juliet's side is really the dwarf, the earlier scenes of Guido's courtship and his bullying of Juliet take on a sharper edge, and you notice how often the story is about looking and being looked at. It is a small, odd, absorbing piece, and it is a pleasure to find in it the same restless mind that created Frankenstein.

stories.title: Sredni Vashtar
stories.author: Saki (H. H. Munro)
stories.epigraph: “I thought you liked toast,” she exclaimed, with an injured air, observing that he did not touch it.
stories.keyContext: Sredni Vashtar is one of the most quietly shocking stories in the English language, and it is only a few pages long. It comes from The Chronicles of Clovis, which appeared in 1911. Its author, Hector Hugh Munro, wrote under the name Saki. He was born in Burma in 1870, lost his mother as a small child, and was raised in a gloomy Devon household by strict aunts, an experience he turned into comedy and revenge again and again. He worked as a journalist and satirist in Edwardian London, a world of polite manners that he loved to puncture. In 1914 he enlisted in the army, though he was well over forty, and he was killed in France in 1916. This story is about a lonely, sickly boy and the adult who runs his life. Notice how calmly, even sweetly, it is told, and ask yourself what is being hidden behind the calm.
paragraphs: Conradin was ten years old, and the doctor had pronounced his professional opinion that the boy would not live another five years. The doctor was silky and effete, and counted for little, but his opinion was endorsed by Mrs. de Ropp, who counted for nearly everything. Mrs. de Ropp was Conradin’s cousin and guardian, and in his eyes she represented those three-fifths of the world that are necessary and disagreeable and real; the other two-fifths, in perpetual antagonism to the foregoing, were summed up in himself and his imagination. One of these days Conradin supposed he would succumb to the mastering pressure of wearisome necessary things⁠—such as illnesses and coddling restrictions and drawn-out dullness. Without his imagination, which was rampant under the spur of loneliness, he would have succumbed long ago.

Mrs. de Ropp would never, in her honestest moments, have confessed to herself that she disliked Conradin, though she might have been dimly aware that thwarting him “for his good” was a duty which she did not find particularly irksome. Conradin hated her with a desperate sincerity which he was perfectly able to mask. Such few pleasures as he could contrive for himself gained an added relish from the likelihood that they would be displeasing to his guardian, and from the realm of his imagination she was locked out⁠—an unclean thing, which should find no entrance.

In the dull, cheerless garden, overlooked by so many windows that were ready to open with a message not to do this or that, or a reminder that medicines were due, he found little attraction. The few fruit-trees that it contained were set jealously apart from his plucking, as though they were rare specimens of their kind blooming in an arid waste; it would probably have been difficult to find a market-gardener who would have offered ten shillings for their entire yearly produce. In a forgotten corner, however, almost hidden behind a dismal shrubbery, was a disused tool-shed of respectable proportions, and within its walls Conradin found a haven, something that took on the varying aspects of a playroom and a cathedral. He had peopled it with a legion of familiar phantoms, evoked partly from fragments of history and partly from his own brain, but it also boasted two inmates of flesh and blood. In one corner lived a ragged-plumaged Houdan hen, on which the boy lavished an affection that had scarcely another outlet. Further back in the gloom stood a large hutch, divided into two compartments, one of which was fronted with close iron bars. This was the abode of a large polecat-ferret, which a friendly butcher-boy had once smuggled, cage and all, into its present quarters, in exchange for a long-secreted hoard of small silver. Conradin was dreadfully afraid of the lithe, sharp-fanged beast, but it was his most treasured possession. Its very presence in the tool-shed was a secret and fearful joy, to be kept scrupulously from the knowledge of the Woman, as he privately dubbed his cousin. And one day, out of Heaven knows what material, he spun the beast a wonderful name, and from that moment it grew into a god and a religion. The Woman indulged in religion once a week at a church near by, and took Conradin with her, but to him the church service was an alien rite in the House of Rimmon. Every Thursday, in the dim and musty silence of the tool-shed, he worshipped with mystic and elaborate ceremonial before the wooden hutch where dwelt Sredni Vashtar, the great ferret. Red flowers in their season and scarlet berries in the wintertime were offered at his shrine, for he was a god who laid some special stress on the fierce impatient side of things, as opposed to the Woman’s religion, which, as far as Conradin could observe, went to great lengths in the contrary direction. And on great festivals powdered nutmeg was strewn in front of his hutch, an important feature of the offering being that the nutmeg had to be stolen. These festivals were of irregular occurrence, and were chiefly appointed to celebrate some passing event. On one occasion, when Mrs. de Ropp suffered from acute toothache for three days, Conradin kept up the festival during the entire three days, and almost succeeded in persuading himself that Sredni Vashtar was personally responsible for the toothache. If the malady had lasted for another day the supply of nutmeg would have given out.

The Houdan hen was never drawn into the cult of Sredni Vashtar. Conradin had long ago settled that she was an Anabaptist. He did not pretend to have the remotest knowledge as to what an Anabaptist was, but he privately hoped that it was dashing and not very respectable. Mrs. de Ropp was the ground plan on which he based and detested all respectability.

After a while Conradin’s absorption in the tool-shed began to attract the notice of his guardian. “It is not good for him to be pottering down there in all weathers,” she promptly decided, and at breakfast one morning she announced that the Houdan hen had been sold and taken away overnight. With her shortsighted eyes she peered at Conradin, waiting for an outbreak of rage and sorrow, which she was ready to rebuke with a flow of excellent precepts and reasoning. But Conradin said nothing: there was nothing to be said. Something perhaps in his white set face gave her a momentary qualm, for at tea that afternoon there was toast on the table, a delicacy which she usually banned on the ground that it was bad for him; also because the making of it “gave trouble,” a deadly offence in the middle-class feminine eye.
“I thought you liked toast,” she exclaimed, with an injured air, observing that he did not touch it.
“Sometimes,” said Conradin.
In the shed that evening there was an innovation in the worship of the hutch-god. Conradin had been wont to chant his praises, tonight he asked a boon.
“Do one thing for me, Sredni Vashtar.”
The thing was not specified. As Sredni Vashtar was a god he must be supposed to know. And choking back a sob as he looked at that other empty corner, Conradin went back to the world he so hated.
And every night, in the welcome darkness of his bedroom, and every evening in the dusk of the tool-shed, Conradin’s bitter litany went up: “Do one thing for me, Sredni Vashtar.”
Mrs. de Ropp noticed that the visits to the shed did not cease, and one day she made a further journey of inspection.
“What are you keeping in that locked hutch?” she asked. “I believe it’s guinea-pigs. I’ll have them all cleared away.”

Conradin shut his lips tight, but the Woman ransacked his bedroom till she found the carefully hidden key, and forthwith marched down to the shed to complete her discovery. It was a cold afternoon, and Conradin had been bidden to keep to the house. From the furthest window of the dining-room the door of the shed could just be seen beyond the corner of the shrubbery, and there Conradin stationed himself. He saw the Woman enter, and then he imagined her opening the door of the sacred hutch and peering down with her shortsighted eyes into the thick straw bed where his god lay hidden. Perhaps she would prod at the straw in her clumsy impatience. And Conradin fervently breathed his prayer for the last time. But he knew as he prayed that he did not believe. He knew that the Woman would come out presently with that pursed smile he loathed so well on her face, and that in an hour or two the gardener would carry away his wonderful god, a god no longer, but a simple brown ferret in a hutch. And he knew that the Woman would triumph always as she triumphed now, and that he would grow ever more sickly under her pestering and domineering and superior wisdom, till one day nothing would matter much more with him, and the doctor would be proved right. And in the sting and misery of his defeat, he began to chant loudly and defiantly the hymn of his threatened idol:
Sredni Vashtar went forth, His thoughts were red thoughts and his teeth were white. His enemies called for peace, but he brought them death. Sredni Vashtar the Beautiful.

And then of a sudden he stopped his chanting and drew closer to the windowpane. The door of the shed still stood ajar as it had been left, and the minutes were slipping by. They were long minutes, but they slipped by nevertheless. He watched the starlings running and flying in little parties across the lawn; he counted them over and over again, with one eye always on that swinging door. A sour-faced maid came in to lay the table for tea, and still Conradin stood and waited and watched. Hope had crept by inches into his heart, and now a look of triumph began to blaze in his eyes that had only known the wistful patience of defeat. Under his breath, with a furtive exultation, he began once again the paean of victory and devastation. And presently his eyes were rewarded: out through that doorway came a long, low, yellow-and-brown beast, with eyes a-blink at the waning daylight, and dark wet stains around the fur of jaws and throat. Conradin dropped on his knees. The great polecat-ferret made its way down to a small brook at the foot of the garden, drank for a moment, then crossed a little plank bridge and was lost to sight in the bushes. Such was the passing of Sredni Vashtar.
“Tea is ready,” said the sour-faced maid; “where is the mistress?”
“She went down to the shed some time ago,” said Conradin.

And while the maid went to summon her mistress to tea Conradin fished a toasting-fork out of the sideboard drawer and proceeded to toast himself a piece of bread. And during the toasting of it and the buttering of it with much butter and the slow enjoyment of eating it, Conradin listened to the noises and silences which fell in quick spasms beyond the dining-room door. The loud foolish screaming of the maid, the answering chorus of wondering ejaculations from the kitchen region, the scuttering footsteps and hurried embassies for outside help, and then, after a lull, the scared sobbings and the shuffling tread of those who bore a heavy burden into the house.
“Whoever will break it to the poor child? I couldn’t for the life of me!” exclaimed a shrill voice. And while they debated the matter among themselves Conradin made himself another piece of toast.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
On the surface, this is a simple story about a sick, lonely ten-year-old named Conradin. His doctor has said he will not live another five years, and his cousin and guardian, Mrs. De Ropp, treats him accordingly, with a smothering routine of medicines, rules and forbidden pleasures. He thinks of her as one of the three-fifths of the world that is necessary and disagreeable and real. The other two-fifths belong to himself and his imagination, and his imagination is the only thing that keeps him going.

In a forgotten corner of the garden he has found a disused toolshed, and inside it live two creatures: a ragged Houdan hen, on whom he lavishes the affection he has nowhere else to put, and, in a barred hutch, a large polecat-ferret that a friendly butcher-boy once smuggled in for a hoard of small silver. Conradin is dreadfully afraid of the beast, and it is his most treasured possession. One day he spins it a magnificent name, Sredni Vashtar, and it becomes a god. Every Thursday he holds a ceremony in the shed, offering red flowers and scarlet berries, and on festivals, stolen nutmeg. The Woman, as he privately calls his cousin, takes him to church each week, but to him that is an alien rite. His own religion is wild and fierce, the opposite of hers, and she is shut out of it entirely.

Then she finds out something is happening in the shed. She has the hen sold, to cure him of his hobby, and then goes to inspect the hutch herself, certain that he is hiding a pet. Conradin prays to his god in a new way, no longer chanting praise but asking for one thing: Do one thing for me, Sredni Vashtar. The request is never spelled out. A god, he reasons, must know. On the day she goes into the shed, he stands at the window and watches. After a long wait, the great beast emerges with dark stains on its jaws and throat and slips away into the bushes.

The ending is a masterpiece of restraint. Conradin makes himself a piece of toast, the very treat she had forbidden him, and eats it slowly while the household descends into screams and confusion. The last line has him making another piece. We are never told directly that the ferret killed her, and we are never told that Conradin is glad. We do not need to be.

What the story means depends on how you read it. Some see it as a dark fairy tale in which a child's imagination literally wins against grown-up cruelty. Others see a sharp satire of Edwardian respectability and of those who crush a child's spirit "for his good." And there is a third layer: a disturbing glimpse of what loneliness and repression can produce in a child. The story is funny and appalling at the same time, and that tension is its point.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
As craft, this is nearly flawless, and it is worth saying why. The first strength is compression. In perhaps two thousand words Saki gives us a child, a villain, a religion, a loss, a prayer and a murder, with scarcely a wasted line. Each detail does a job. The Houdan hen, whom Conradin has decided is an Anabaptist, is a case in point. He has no idea what an Anabaptist is, but he privately hopes it is "dashing and not very respectable." That one joke tells us about his hunger for rebellion, about his guardian's rigid idea of propriety and about the narrator's gleeful tone.

The second strength is control of tone. The narrator is cool, ironic and almost clinical, never begging us to feel sorry for Conradin and never apologizing for the violence. Because the story refuses to editorialize, the reader's feelings have room to complicate themselves. We pity the boy. We cheer for him. We are also a little frightened by how easily we cheer. That moral discomfort is exactly what Saki wants, and the toast scene delivers it with extraordinary economy.

Third, the structure is perfect. The details planted early, the doctor's verdict, the forbidden toast, the sold hen, the unspecified prayer, all pay off in the last paragraph. The hymn that Conradin chants, with its red thoughts and white teeth, gives the climax a fierce, ritual beauty. It is a small ceremony with the force of a battle cry.

Yet the story is not beyond criticism. Mrs. De Ropp is a villain drawn in a few strokes, and she is not quite human. Her cruelty is more of a caricature than a character, and a reader looking for a more nuanced portrait of a difficult guardian will not find one. The story also plays its cards close to the chest, and some readers find the final turn too tidy: the monster is slain, the boy is free, and the narrator seems to hold us in a sort of gleeful complicity. There is also a faint cruelty in the way the story uses the sick child's fantasy as a weapon. Its cleverness is sometimes colder than it needs to be. Nonetheless, these are quibbles. The story is built so tightly that even its limitations feel like choices, and few short stories of this length leave such a mark.

One last point of craft deserves mention: the use of absence. We never see Mrs. De Ropp die. We hear it, through a door, as noises and silences that fall in quick spasms, the maid's foolish screaming, the scuttering footsteps, the shuffling tread of those who carry a heavy burden. By keeping the horror offstage and letting a child make toast in the foreground, Saki makes the scene more chilling than any description could. It is a lesson that horror writers still study.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
Saki's story has had a long afterlife, far larger than its modest size would suggest. It has been anthologized for more than a century and is routinely included in collections of the best short stories in English. It is a staple of school and university reading lists, particularly in Britain and the Commonwealth, where teachers use it to introduce irony, point of view and the art of the twist.

It also helped shape a particular style of dark comic short fiction. The cool, polished surface hiding something savage was a technique Saki perfected, and later writers who combined wit with cruelty, such as Roald Dahl, are often said to be his descendants. Dahl's wicked adults, his gleefully vengeful children and his stories that end with a sudden, shocking justice owe a great deal to the Saki tradition, though it would be unwise to claim a precise line of influence. The pattern of a child outwitting or outlasting an oppressive grown-up has since become one of the most popular in children's and young adult fiction.

The story has been read on radio and adapted for the screen in small ways, though it has never needed an adaptation to survive. The name Sredni Vashtar itself has taken on a life of its own. Musicians and writers have borrowed it, and it has become a kind of shorthand for a private god or a secret weapon. Few invented names from a short story have lasted so well, and fewer still have been made up, as this one apparently was, out of nothing at all.

The story also matters for Saki's own legacy. By the time he died, he was known as a clever humorist, but this story and a few others showed a darker and deeper side. His death on the Western Front in 1916 turned his work into a kind of monument to a vanished world, and critics have often read the cold humor of stories like this one as a premonition of the violence that engulfed Europe. That reading is a later one, since the story was written before the war, but it gives the tale an extra shadow that it carries to this day.

It is also worth remembering that Saki's real childhood is part of the story's legend. He and his siblings were brought up by aunts in a strict household in Devon, and readers have long guessed that Mrs. De Ropp owes something to them. That biographical connection, though no one can say how much of the story is memory, has become part of how the story is taught, and it is one of the reasons students often feel that it was written by someone who knew exactly what he was describing.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers love this story first of all for its audacity. It dares to make a murder the happy ending, and it does so in a voice so smooth and so cheerful that we find ourselves going along with it before we realize what we are cheering for. People who read it as children often remember it for life, partly because the toast and the hutch are so vivid, partly because it did not behave like the improving stories they were used to.

Many readers love the way it takes the side of a child. Conradin is not saintly. He is sly, resentful and capable of deep hatred. But the story respects his inner life. It treats his religion as real and his imagination as a living force. Readers who felt misunderstood or controlled in childhood often find in the story an enormous relief, a validation of the idea that a secret inner world can be a source of power.

There is also joy in the language. Saki's sentences are elegant and pointed, full of well-turned phrases, and the story reads aloud beautifully, which matters for anyone listening to it. The hymn to Sredni Vashtar has a barbaric splendor, and the ending, with the distant screams and the slow, deliberate toasting, is a lesson in how to create suspense with almost no action.

Finally, readers admire the economy. A single short story manages to be a comedy, a horror tale and a satire in the span of a few pages. Writers have praised Saki's ability to say a great deal in a few words. He is a favorite of people who love sharp, concentrated prose, and this story is often named as his finest or one of his two or three finest. It rewards rereading, because once you know the ending, you see how much of the humor and menace was planted in the first paragraph.

There is also the thrill of the detail. The idea that a god might be worshipped only on Thursdays, or that a festival could be declared whenever a hated guardian suffers a toothache, is both funny and strangely moving. It tells us everything about a boy who has to find his triumphs where he can. Readers often say they can never forget the line about the nutmeg having to be stolen, a tiny rule of the religion that makes the whole invented faith feel real.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Not everyone has been comfortable with this story. The most obvious objection is moral. It presents the killing of an adult by an animal, at a child's wish, as a triumph. Some readers feel the story takes too much delight in the outcome and ignores the human cost. Mrs. De Ropp may be a bully, but she is a person, and the story's final image of a boy eating toast while she is carried in dead can feel callous.

A related criticism is that the story depends on a caricatured villain. Mrs. De Ropp is not shown acting from any inner life. She does not love, she does not doubt, and she does not seem to understand what she is doing. She is a type, the repressive guardian, and critics have said that her flatness makes the story's revenge too easy. Defenders reply that this is a fable and that fables work with types, and that the narrator makes a sly allowance for her when he says she would never admit to herself that she disliked the boy. Even so, the point stands.

Some critics have pointed to the story's darkness about childhood. The narrator treats the child's hatred and the fantasy of killing as natural and even healthy, which can be unsettling. A psychological reading might see Conradin's worship as a sign of a damaged child, not a triumphant one, and the story's cheerful tone as a refusal to admit this. Others note that the story is a product of Saki's own harsh upbringing and see it as personal score-settling.

There is also the usual charge against Saki: that his wit is cold, that his stories are too neat and that they lean on a cruelty that stands in for depth. Early reviewers of his collections praised his cleverness but sometimes found him heartless, and that reputation has followed him. Others found his world too narrow, a world of drawing rooms, aunts and clever young men, and his politics and attitudes, which now and then include the prejudices of his class and time, can sit awkwardly with modern readers. This particular story is mostly free of those problems, but it shares the tone that provoked them.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
In the big picture, Sredni Vashtar belongs to the Edwardian short story, a period when the form flourished in magazines and collections, and to the tradition of the comic macabre, in which wit and horror share a bed. Saki is often placed beside O. Henry, for his twist endings, and beside Oscar Wilde, for his epigrammatic wit. He shares with Wilde a taste for turning polite society's values upside down.

The story descends from the English fairy-tale and fable, with their small creatures that wreak big vengeance, and from the Victorian tradition of children's stories in which a child suffers under a stern guardian, as in Dickens and Charlotte Bronte's Jane Eyre. But where Dickens usually reforms or rescues his orphans through kindness, Saki rescues his through violence. That is the twist that makes the story modern. It also draws on the fashion for pagan and nature-worship themes in the years around 1900, when writers such as Kenneth Grahame, with his god Pan in The Wind in the Willows, and Arthur Machen were rediscovering older, wilder kinds of belief. Conradin's hutch is a small, comic cousin of those wild gods.

Its descendants include the tradition of dark children's literature that runs through Dahl, Edward Gorey and the stories of Lemony Snicket, and the horror-comedy of writers like Shirley Jackson and Muriel Spark, who share Saki's gift for the smiling menace. It also has relatives in the psychological tales of lonely children, from Henry James's The Turn of the Screw to modern novels of troubled young narrators.

Why read it today? Because it is very short and very good, and because it shows how a perfectly turned story can surprise even a reader who has read a great deal. It also still speaks to anyone who has been told what is good for them by someone who does not listen. Its ending refuses to moralize, and we are left to decide for ourselves whether to cheer or to shudder. Most readers do a little of both, and that mixed response is the best argument that the story is more than a joke.

It is also an easy story to carry around. It takes about ten minutes to read aloud, and it leaves a listener with something to argue about afterward. Anyone who wants to understand why short fiction can hit harder than a long novel could do worse than start here.

stories.title: The Interlopers
stories.author: Saki (H. H. Munro)
stories.epigraph: “A Feud and Its End…”
stories.keyContext: The Interlopers is among the most widely read short stories in the English-speaking world, partly because it is short and partly because its ending is so abrupt that readers remember it for the rest of their lives. It was written by Hector Hugh Munro, who published under the name Saki. Born in Burma in 1870 and raised in Devon by stern aunts, he became a journalist and wit in Edwardian London, known for comic stories that skewered polite society. In 1914 he enlisted in the army, though he was over forty, and in 1916 he was killed by a sniper in France. This story appeared in a collection published after his death, in 1919, which gives its theme an extra weight. It is about two men and a feud inherited from their grandfathers, set in a winter forest. Listen for the irony hidden in the title.
paragraphs: A Feud and Its End

In a forest of mixed growth somewhere on the eastern spurs of the Carpathians, a man stood one winter night watching and listening, as though he waited for some beast of the woods to come within the range of his vision, and, later, of his rifle. But the game for whose presence he kept so keen an outlook was none that figured in the sportsman’s calendar as lawful and proper for the chase; Ulrich von Gradwitz patrolled the dark forest in quest of a human enemy.

The forest lands of Gradwitz were of wide extent and well stocked with game; the narrow strip of precipitous woodland that lay on its outskirt was not remarkable for the game it harboured or the shooting it afforded, but it was the most jealously guarded of all its owner’s territorial possessions. A famous lawsuit, in the days of his grandfather, had wrested it from the illegal possession of a neighbouring family of petty landowners; the dispossessed party had never acquiesced in the judgment of the Courts, and a long series of poaching affrays and similar scandals had embittered the relationships between the families for three generations. The neighbour feud had grown into a personal one since Ulrich had come to be head of his family; if there was a man in the world whom he detested and wished ill to it was Georg Znaeym, the inheritor of the quarrel and the tireless game-snatcher and raider of the disputed border-forest. The feud might, perhaps, have died down or been compromised if the personal ill-will of the two men had not stood in the way; as boys they had thirsted for one another’s blood, as men each prayed that misfortune might fall on the other, and this wind-scourged winter night Ulrich had banded together his foresters to watch the dark forest, not in quest of four-footed quarry, but to keep a lookout for the prowling thieves whom he suspected of being afoot from across the land boundary. The roebuck, which usually kept in the sheltered hollows during a storm-wind, were running like driven things tonight, and there was movement and unrest among the creatures that were wont to sleep through the dark hours. Assuredly there was a disturbing element in the forest, and Ulrich could guess the quarter from whence it came.

He strayed away by himself from the watchers whom he had placed in ambush on the crest of the hill, and wandered far down the steep slopes amid the wild tangle of undergrowth, peering through the tree trunks and listening through the whistling and skirling of the wind and the restless beating of the branches for sight and sound of the marauders. If only on this wild night, in this dark, lone spot, he might come across Georg Znaeym, man to man, with none to witness⁠—that was the wish that was uppermost in his thoughts. And as he stepped round the trunk of a huge beech he came face to face with the man he sought.

The two enemies stood glaring at one another for a long silent moment. Each had a rifle in his hand, each had hate in his heart and murder uppermost in his mind. The chance had come to give full play to the passions of a lifetime. But a man who has been brought up under the code of a restraining civilisation cannot easily nerve himself to shoot down his neighbour in cold blood and without word spoken, except for an offence against his hearth and honour. And before the moment of hesitation had given way to action a deed of Nature’s own violence overwhelmed them both. A fierce shriek of the storm had been answered by a splitting crash over their heads, and ere they could leap aside a mass of falling beech tree had thundered down on them. Ulrich von Gradwitz found himself stretched on the ground, one arm numb beneath him and the other held almost as helplessly in a tight tangle of forked branches, while both legs were pinned beneath the fallen mass. His heavy shooting-boots had saved his feet from being crushed to pieces, but if his fractures were not as serious as they might have been, at least it was evident that he could not move from his present position till someone came to release him. The descending twig had slashed the skin of his face, and he had to wink away some drops of blood from his eyelashes before he could take in a general view of the disaster. At his side, so near that under ordinary circumstances he could almost have touched him, lay Georg Znaeym, alive and struggling, but obviously as helplessly pinioned down as himself. All round them lay a thick-strewn wreckage of splintered branches and broken twigs.

Relief at being alive and exasperation at his captive plight brought a strange medley of pious thank-offerings and sharp curses to Ulrich’s lips. Georg, who was nearly blinded with the blood which trickled across his eyes, stopped his struggling for a moment to listen, and then gave a short, snarling laugh.
“So you’re not killed, as you ought to be, but you’re caught, anyway,” he cried; “caught fast. Ho, what a jest, Ulrich von Gradwitz snared in his stolen forest. There’s real justice for you!”
And he laughed again, mockingly and savagely.

“I’m caught in my own forest-land,” retorted Ulrich. “When my men come to release us you will wish, perhaps, that you were in a better plight than caught poaching on a neighbour’s land, shame on you.”
Georg was silent for a moment; then he answered quietly:

“Are you sure that your men will find much to release? I have men, too, in the forest tonight, close behind me, and they will be here first and do the releasing. When they drag me out from under these damned branches it won’t need much clumsiness on their part to roll this mass of trunk right over on the top of you. Your men will find you dead under a fallen beech tree. For form’s sake I shall send my condolences to your family.”

“It is a useful hint,” said Ulrich fiercely. “My men had orders to follow in ten minutes time, seven of which must have gone by already, and when they get me out⁠—I will remember the hint. Only as you will have met your death poaching on my lands I don’t think I can decently send any message of condolence to your family.”
“Good,” snarled Georg, “good. We fight this quarrel out to the death, you and I and our foresters, with no cursed interlopers to come between us. Death and damnation to you, Ulrich von Gradwitz.”
“The same to you, Georg Znaeym, forest-thief, game-snatcher.”

Both men spoke with the bitterness of possible defeat before them, for each knew that it might be long before his men would seek him out or find him; it was a bare matter of chance which party would arrive first on the scene.

Both had now given up the useless struggle to free themselves from the mass of wood that held them down; Ulrich limited his endeavours to an effort to bring his one partially free arm near enough to his outer coat-pocket to draw out his wine-flask. Even when he had accomplished that operation it was long before he could manage the unscrewing of the stopper or get any of the liquid down his throat. But what a Heaven-sent draught it seemed! It was an open winter, and little snow had fallen as yet, hence the captives suffered less from the cold than might have been the case at that season of the year; nevertheless, the wine was warming and reviving to the wounded man, and he looked across with something like a throb of pity to where his enemy lay, just keeping the groans of pain and weariness from crossing his lips.

“Could you reach this flask if I threw it over to you?” asked Ulrich suddenly; “there is good wine in it, and one may as well be as comfortable as one can. Let us drink, even if tonight one of us dies.”
“No, I can scarcely see anything; there is so much blood caked round my eyes,” said Georg, “and in any case I don’t drink wine with an enemy.”

Ulrich was silent for a few minutes, and lay listening to the weary screeching of the wind. An idea was slowly forming and growing in his brain, an idea that gained strength every time that he looked across at the man who was fighting so grimly against pain and exhaustion. In the pain and languor that Ulrich himself was feeling the old fierce hatred seemed to be dying down.

“Neighbour,” he said presently, “do as you please if your men come first. It was a fair compact. But as for me, I’ve changed my mind. If my men are the first to come you shall be the first to be helped, as though you were my guest. We have quarrelled like devils all our lives over this stupid strip of forest, where the trees can’t even stand upright in a breath of wind. Lying here tonight thinking I’ve come to think we’ve been rather fools; there are better things in life than getting the better of a boundary dispute. Neighbour, if you will help me to bury the old quarrel I⁠—I will ask you to be my friend.”
Georg Znaeym was silent for so long that Ulrich thought, perhaps, he had fainted with the pain of his injuries. Then he spoke slowly and in jerks.

“How the whole region would stare and gabble if we rode into the market-square together. No one living can remember seeing a Znaeym and a von Gradwitz talking to one another in friendship. And what peace there would be among the forester folk if we ended our feud tonight. And if we choose to make peace among our people there is none other to interfere, no interlopers from outside⁠ ⁠… You would come and keep the Sylvester night beneath my roof, and I would come and feast on some high day at your castle⁠ ⁠… I would never fire a shot on your land, save when you invited me as a guest; and you should come and shoot with me down in the marshes where the wildfowl are. In all the countryside there are none that could hinder if we willed to make peace. I never thought to have wanted to do other than hate you all my life, but I think I have changed my mind about things too, this last half-hour. And you offered me your wine-flask⁠ ⁠… Ulrich von Gradwitz, I will be your friend.”

For a space both men were silent, turning over in their minds the wonderful changes that this dramatic reconciliation would bring about. In the cold, gloomy forest, with the wind tearing in fitful gusts through the naked branches and whistling round the tree trunks, they lay and waited for the help that would now bring release and succour to both parties. And each prayed a private prayer that his men might be the first to arrive, so that he might be the first to show honourable attention to the enemy that had become a friend.
Presently, as the wind dropped for a moment, Ulrich broke silence.
“Let’s shout for help,” he said, “in this lull our voices may carry a little way.”
“They won’t carry far through the trees and undergrowth,” said Georg, “but we can try. Together, then.”
The two raised their voices in a prolonged hunting call.
“Together again,” said Ulrich a few minutes later, after listening in vain for an answering halloo.
“I heard nothing but the pestilential wind,” said Georg hoarsely.
There was silence again for some minutes, and then Ulrich gave a joyful cry.
“I can see figures coming through the wood. They are following in the way I came down the hillside.”
Both men raised their voices in as loud a shout as they could muster.
“They hear us! They’ve stopped. Now they see us. They’re running down the hill towards us,” cried Ulrich.
“How many of them are there?” asked Georg.
“I can’t see distinctly,” said Ulrich; “nine or ten.”
“Then they are yours,” said Georg; “I had only seven out with me.”
“They are making all the speed they can, brave lads,” said Ulrich gladly.
“Are they your men?” asked Georg. “Are they your men?” he repeated impatiently as Ulrich did not answer.
“No,” said Ulrich with a laugh, the idiotic chattering laugh of a man unstrung with hideous fear.
“Who are they?” asked Georg quickly, straining his eyes to see what the other would gladly not have seen.
“Wolves.”

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The story opens on a winter night in a forest on the eastern slopes of the Carpathian Mountains. A man named Ulrich von Gradwitz is out hunting, but not for game. He is looking for a human enemy. The prize in question is a narrow strip of steep woodland that is not especially valuable. Its owners have fought over it for three generations, ever since a famous lawsuit in the days of Ulrich's grandfather took it away from a neighboring family of petty landowners. They never accepted the court's decision. Over the years the dispute has produced poaching, brawls and scandals, and now it has become a personal hatred between Ulrich and Georg Znaeym, the heir to the other side of the quarrel.

On this stormy night, the two men meet. Each has a rifle, each has murder on his mind, and each stands in the dark, glaring at the other. But men who have been raised in a civilized society, Saki observes, cannot easily shoot a neighbor without a word. While they hesitate, a gust of wind splits a giant beech tree, and the trunk crashes down on both of them. Ulrich is pinned to the ground, one arm numb, the other tangled in branches, both legs trapped beneath the wood. Georg lies close beside him, half blinded by blood, and when he realizes his enemy is alive and helpless he laughs, savagely, and calls it a fine jest that Ulrich is snared in his stolen forest.

What follows is the real heart of the story. Helpless, they trade insults. Each tells the other that his own men will soon arrive, and that the other will then be sorry to be found in such a plight. But as the cold sets in, something changes. Ulrich manages to get out a flask of wine and offers it to Georg, saying that one may as well be comfortable even if one of them dies. Georg, softened, begins to speak about what it would mean to end the quarrel. He imagines riding into the market square together, as friends, with the whole region staring. He imagines how much peace there would be among the forest people if the feud ended, and says that no outsiders, no interlopers, could stop them from making peace if they chose.

They agree and shout for help. Ulrich sees figures coming through the trees, and the two men start to argue happily about whose men they are. Then Georg asks again, and Ulrich answers with a laugh that Saki calls idiotic and chattering, the laugh of a man unstrung with fear. The single word that ends the story is wolves.

The meaning lies in that last turn. The title refers to the men's belief that the outsiders, the interlopers, were the only ones who could interfere with their peace. The true interlopers are the wolves, representing a nature indifferent to human feuds and human reconciliation. Saki's point is not simply that hatred is foolish. It is that the right moment for reconciliation may not last, and that nature does not care how the story is meant to end.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
The Interlopers is a model of compression, and it is worth admiring on those grounds. In under two thousand words Saki establishes a long feud, a setting, two characters, a crisis, a change of heart and an ending that lands like a blow. The opening paragraphs do their work quickly, laying out the history of the feud in a few sentences and sketching the landscape in a handful of strokes. The reader is never lost and never bored.

The moral turning point is handled with unusual skill. The reconciliation is not sentimental. It grows out of pain, cold and fear, and each man moves a little at a time. Ulrich offers wine, Georg remarks on the kindness, and each admits he has been wrong in small steps. The dialogue is crisp and plausible, and Georg's description of what peace would look like, the stares in the market, the shared feasts, the shooting parties in the marshes, gives the future a warmth that makes its loss sharper.

The ending is the story's great trick, and its reputation depends on it. Saki keeps the reader leaning forward by building hope, then withdraws it in a single word. The last scene works in part because he does not explain it. There is no narrator's comment, no moral. The story simply stops, and silence does the rest. The dramatic irony is cruel, and effective.

Yet there are weaknesses. The whole plot depends on coincidences: the tree falls at the exact moment of confrontation, the two men are pinned within speaking distance and, at the critical moment, the wolves arrive from nowhere. Readers who like their stories to feel inevitable may find the ending too neat, too much a bolt from the blue. A modern audience, used to twist endings, may also see it coming. The characters are little more than types, the proud landowner and the poacher, and the wolves are a somewhat convenient symbol of nature's indifference. The prose, too, is less polished and witty than in Saki's best comic work. Compared with the glitter of stories such as Sredni Vashtar or The Open Window, this one is plainer and more fable-like. That plainness is part of its power, but it also makes it feel slightly mechanical on the page. All the same, it does what it sets out to do, and it does it with admirable economy.

It is also worth asking whether the story earns its irony or merely imposes it. The best defense is that Saki seeds the idea from the beginning: the forest is described as wild and dangerous, the storm is violent, and the men's talk of their own servants is built on an assumption that rescue will come in the shape they expect. The reader, like the characters, is invited to relax, and the final word punishes that relaxation.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
Few short stories have been read by as many young people as this one. The Interlopers is included in school anthologies and examination syllabuses around the world, particularly in Britain, India and other countries with a British educational tradition. For many readers, it is the first short story whose ending they have really had to think about. Teachers use it to explain irony, foreshadowing, symbolism and the idea of the twist ending, and it often appears in discussions of how a short story can work through a single decisive image.

Its influence on later writing is mostly indirect, spread through the many writers who learned the craft of the sudden ending. Stories that end on a sharp, ironic turn, from O. Henry's to those of Roald Dahl and the television tradition of the twist, belong to the family of tales that Saki helped refine. The Interlopers is probably the clearest example of how a single last word can recast everything that came before.

The story also influenced how people talk about feuds. The idea that two sides in a long quarrel might be reconciled only when it is too late has become a common image in discussions of family quarrels, border disputes and political rivalries. It has often been cited in connection with the First World War, in which many men who might have been friends were taught to hate one another and died in the mud.

Whether or not that reading is fair, it has helped keep the story alive in an age that has seen more than enough of such waste. That connection was not in Saki's mind when he wrote the story, as far as we can tell, but it was added to it by history. The story was published after his death at the front, and many readers have found it impossible to read without thinking of the war.

In the end, its main impact has been educational and cultural. It has been reprinted in countless textbooks and read aloud in countless classrooms. It has served as a reference point for writers who wanted to show that a story can be small and still carry a large moral. Its impact lies not in any shift in literary history, but in the number of readers who have met it, felt its sting and remembered it.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers admire The Interlopers for its efficiency. It is the kind of story that can be read in a few minutes and remembered for decades. There is satisfaction in watching a tale about a century-old feud turn on a single wine flask, and in the way each speech nudges the men a step toward friendship.

Many love the emotional shape of the story. It begins with hatred, moves through pain and fear to understanding, and ends in an abrupt reversal. The reconciliation scene is the part readers cite most often, because it feels hard-won and humane. When Georg says that he has changed his mind and offers his friendship, the reader is moved, and the more moved they are, the more the ending hurts.

The setting is another pleasure. The dark winter forest, with the wind tearing through the bare branches, is described in a few strokes and gives the tale its fairy-tale atmosphere. It feels like a legend from the Carpathians, a story told by a fire. The sense of a lonely, wild place where human quarrels seem both enormous and tiny is a large part of its appeal.

Finally, readers value the story's moral clarity and its refusal to preach. It does not tell us what to think. It simply shows two men who waste a lifetime on hatred, learn better in an hour, and are denied the chance to use what they have learned. The result is a parable that feels fresh each time, and that has an emotional force out of proportion to its length. Many people say it taught them to see how silly some of their own quarrels were, and how important it is to make peace while there is still time. That quiet effect on readers' lives is perhaps its greatest tribute.

Readers also enjoy how well the story rewards a second look. Once you know the ending, details leap out: the word interlopers placed in Georg's mouth just before the wolves appear, the hope each man silently holds that his own servants will arrive first, so that he can be the first to show kindness to a former enemy. That detail is especially touching. It shows how fast a lifetime's hatred can turn into eagerness to be generous, and it makes the final reveal feel like a cruel joke played by the universe on two men who have only just grown decent. Many readers say they felt a physical drop in the stomach at the last word, which is perhaps the highest praise a short story can earn. They also appreciate that Saki trusts them to supply the horror that follows. We do not see the wolves reach the men. We do not need to.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Detailed reviews of this story from the time of its first publication are scarce, and the best-documented criticism comes from later readers and teachers. Saki's collections were generally praised for wit and cleverness, though some reviewers thought him a little cold. This story, which is warmer than most of his work, did not provoke much controversy.

The most common objection is that the ending is contrived. Critics argue that Saki manipulates events to deliver his message, bringing in the wolves as a deus ex machina, a sudden outside force that solves or ruins the plot. The coincidence of the falling tree and the arriving wolves, they say, makes the story feel like a lesson rather than a slice of life. Others note that the moral, that hatred is futile and reconciliation is precious, is so simple that it borders on cliche.

Some readers find the story too cynical. If the men are punished for their change of heart, they ask, does the story say that good intentions are pointless? Saki's ironic worldview, they argue, can slide into a shrug. Others argue the opposite, that the story is not cynical at all, since the men's reconciliation is real and moving even if brief. This disagreement about the ending's meaning is one of the reasons the story is so often debated in classrooms.

There are also complaints about thin characters and a dated setting. The two men are almost allegorical figures, and their feud is described in generalities. The aristocratic setting, with its landowners, foresters and game laws, may feel remote to modern readers. Some also feel the story is almost too familiar, having been read so often that its twist has lost its shock. Finally, a few critics have noted that the use of wolves as symbols of nature's cruelty is a conventional device, drawn from a long tradition of fairy tales. These are not damning charges, but they explain why some regard the story as a minor piece compared with Saki's best work, which is wittier and stranger.

A last objection concerns the lack of any real consequence for the men's earlier hatred. We are told that their feud has produced brawls and scandals, but we never see anyone suffer from it, so the loss of the friendship feels less devastating than it might. A more ambitious story might have shown a wife or a child on one side or the other, giving the reconciliation more to heal.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
Where does The Interlopers fit in the larger story of literature? It belongs to the Edwardian short story, the tradition of sharp, concentrated tales in the years before the First World War, and more specifically to the ironic fable, a form that uses a small, simple plot to make a larger point. Its closest relatives are the twist-ending stories of Guy de Maupassant, Ambrose Bierce and O. Henry, in which a sudden reversal changes the meaning of everything.

It also draws on one of the oldest stories in the world: the feud between families that ends in tragedy. Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet tells of two houses whose hatred is healed only after the deaths of their children. Saki's version is smaller and colder, since there are no lovers, but the point is similar: the reconciliation comes too late. Another ancestor is the tradition of nature as an indifferent force, found in Thomas Hardy's novels and in the American naturalists. Jack London's To Build a Fire, in which a man is killed by cold and his own stubbornness, is a cousin in spirit. Saki, however, turns the lens on human pettiness, not on human endurance.

There is a further echo with tales of feud in folk ballads and the family sagas of Iceland, where long cycles of revenge over small plots of land are a major theme.

Its descendants include the many modern stories that use a last-line twist to deliver a moral, and the anti-war fables of the twentieth century. Read after 1914, the tale's picture of men who are taught to hate and who die before they can make peace has often been taken as a miniature of the war itself. Any later story in which two bitter enemies are forced to depend on each other, only to be overtaken by some larger danger, shares its basic logic.

Why read it today? Because it is brief and unforgettable, because it asks a question that never goes away, and because it demonstrates how much can be done in a short space. In a world in which long quarrels still divide families and nations, the story's picture of two men who discover their common humanity too late remains painfully relevant. It is not Saki's cleverest work, but it may be his most humane, and its closing word still lands with a chill.

stories.title: The Lumber Room
stories.author: Saki (H. H. Munro)
stories.epigraph: “How she did howl,” said Nicholas cheerfully, as the party drove off without any of the elation of high spirits that should have characterised it.
stories.keyContext: The Lumber Room is a short comic story about a small boy who outwits a large, self-satisfied aunt, and it is one of the best-loved pieces by the writer known as Saki. His real name was Hector Hugh Munro. He was born in Burma in 1870, lost his mother when he was very young, and was raised in Devon by strict, unimaginative aunts, a background that fuels nearly all of his stories about children. As an adult he became a journalist and a sharp-tongued satirist in Edwardian London. This story appeared in a collection called Beasts and Super-Beasts in 1914, the year the First World War began, and Munro himself was killed in France in 1916. Though it is funny, it is also a story about power: who gets to decide what is forbidden, and what happens when a child understands the rules better than the adult who made them. Listen for how Nicholas wins by being exactly as obedient as he is told to be.
paragraphs: The children were to be driven, as a special treat, to the sands at Jagborough. Nicholas was not to be of the party; he was in disgrace. Only that morning he had refused to eat his wholesome bread-and-milk on the seemingly frivolous ground that there was a frog in it. Older and wiser and better people had told him that there could not possibly be a frog in his bread-and-milk and that he was not to talk nonsense; he continued, nevertheless, to talk what seemed the veriest nonsense, and described with much detail the colouration and markings of the alleged frog. The dramatic part of the incident was that there really was a frog in Nicholas’ basin of bread-and-milk; he had put it there himself, so he felt entitled to know something about it. The sin of taking a frog from the garden and putting it into a bowl of wholesome bread-and-milk was enlarged on at great length, but the fact that stood out clearest in the whole affair, as it presented itself to the mind of Nicholas, was that the older, wiser, and better people had been proved to be profoundly in error in matters about which they had expressed the utmost assurance.

“You said there couldn’t possibly be a frog in my bread-and-milk; there was a frog in my bread-and-milk,” he repeated, with the insistence of a skilled tactician who does not intend to shift from favourable ground.

So his boy-cousin and girl-cousin and his quite uninteresting younger brother were to be taken to Jagborough sands that afternoon and he was to stay at home. His cousins’ aunt, who insisted, by an unwarranted stretch of imagination, in styling herself his aunt also, had hastily invented the Jagborough expedition in order to impress on Nicholas the delights that he had justly forfeited by his disgraceful conduct at the breakfast-table. It was her habit, whenever one of the children fell from grace, to improvise something of a festival nature from which the offender would be rigorously debarred; if all the children sinned collectively they were suddenly informed of a circus in a neighbouring town, a circus of unrivalled merit and uncounted elephants, to which, but for their depravity, they would have been taken that very day.

A few decent tears were looked for on the part of Nicholas when the moment for the departure of the expedition arrived. As a matter of fact, however, all the crying was done by his girl-cousin, who scraped her knee rather painfully against the step of the carriage as she was scrambling in.
“How she did howl,” said Nicholas cheerfully, as the party drove off without any of the elation of high spirits that should have characterised it.
“She’ll soon get over that,” said the soi-disant aunt; “it will be a glorious afternoon for racing about over those beautiful sands. How they will enjoy themselves!”
“Bobby won’t enjoy himself much, and he won’t race much either,” said Nicholas with a grim chuckle; “his boots are hurting him. They’re too tight.”
“Why didn’t he tell me they were hurting?” asked the aunt with some asperity.
“He told you twice, but you weren’t listening. You often don’t listen when we tell you important things.”
“You are not to go into the gooseberry garden,” said the aunt, changing the subject.
“Why not?” demanded Nicholas.
“Because you are in disgrace,” said the aunt loftily.

Nicholas did not admit the flawlessness of the reasoning; he felt perfectly capable of being in disgrace and in a gooseberry garden at the same moment. His face took on an expression of considerable obstinacy. It was clear to his aunt that he was determined to get into the gooseberry garden, “only,” as she remarked to herself, “because I have told him he is not to.”

Now the gooseberry garden had two doors by which it might be entered, and once a small person like Nicholas could slip in there he could effectually disappear from view amid the masking growth of artichokes, raspberry canes, and fruit bushes. The aunt had many other things to do that afternoon, but she spent an hour or two in trivial gardening operations among flower beds and shrubberies, whence she could keep a watchful eye on the two doors that led to the forbidden paradise. She was a woman of few ideas, with immense powers of concentration.

Nicholas made one or two sorties into the front garden, wriggling his way with obvious stealth of purpose towards one or other of the doors, but never able for a moment to evade the aunt’s watchful eye. As a matter of fact, he had no intention of trying to get into the gooseberry garden, but it was extremely convenient for him that his aunt should believe that he had; it was a belief that would keep her on self-imposed sentry-duty for the greater part of the afternoon. Having thoroughly confirmed and fortified her suspicions Nicholas slipped back into the house and rapidly put into execution a plan of action that had long germinated in his brain. By standing on a chair in the library one could reach a shelf on which reposed a fat, important-looking key. The key was as important as it looked; it was the instrument which kept the mysteries of the lumber-room secure from unauthorised intrusion, which opened a way only for aunts and suchlike privileged persons. Nicholas had not had much experience of the art of fitting keys into keyholes and turning locks, but for some days past he had practised with the key of the schoolroom door; he did not believe in trusting too much to luck and accident. The key turned stiffly in the lock, but it turned. The door opened, and Nicholas was in an unknown land, compared with which the gooseberry garden was a stale delight, a mere material pleasure.

Often and often Nicholas had pictured to himself what the lumber-room might be like, that region that was so carefully sealed from youthful eyes and concerning which no questions were ever answered. It came up to his expectations. In the first place it was large and dimly lit, one high window opening on to the forbidden garden being its only source of illumination. In the second place it was a storehouse of unimagined treasures. The aunt-by-assertion was one of those people who think that things spoil by use and consign them to dust and damp by way of preserving them. Such parts of the house as Nicholas knew best were rather bare and cheerless, but here there were wonderful things for the eye to feast on. First and foremost there was a piece of framed tapestry that was evidently meant to be a fire-screen. To Nicholas it was a living, breathing story; he sat down on a roll of Indian hangings, glowing in wonderful colours beneath a layer of dust, and took in all the details of the tapestry picture. A man, dressed in the hunting costume of some remote period, had just transfixed a stag with an arrow; it could not have been a difficult shot because the stag was only one or two paces away from him; in the thickly-growing vegetation that the picture suggested it would not have been difficult to creep up to a feeding stag, and the two spotted dogs that were springing forward to join in the chase had evidently been trained to keep to heel till the arrow was discharged. That part of the picture was simple, if interesting, but did the huntsman see, what Nicholas saw, that four galloping wolves were coming in his direction through the wood? There might be more than four of them hidden behind the trees, and in any case would the man and his dogs be able to cope with the four wolves if they made an attack? The man had only two arrows left in his quiver, and he might miss with one or both of them; all one knew about his skill in shooting was that he could hit a large stag at a ridiculously short range. Nicholas sat for many golden minutes revolving the possibilities of the scene; he was inclined to think that there were more than four wolves and that the man and his dogs were in a tight corner.

But there were other objects of delight and interest claiming his instant attention: there were quaint twisted candlesticks in the shape of snakes, and a teapot fashioned like a china duck, out of whose open beak the tea was supposed to come. How dull and shapeless the nursery teapot seemed in comparison! And there was a carved sandalwood box packed tight with aromatic cotton-wool, and between the layers of cotton-wool were little brass figures, hump-necked bulls, and peacocks and goblins, delightful to see and to handle. Less promising in appearance was a large square book with plain black covers; Nicholas peeped into it, and, behold, it was full of coloured pictures of birds. And such birds! In the garden, and in the lanes when he went for a walk, Nicholas came across a few birds, of which the largest were an occasional magpie or wood pigeon; here were herons and bustards, kites, toucans, tiger-bitterns, brush turkeys, ibises, golden pheasants, a whole portrait gallery of undreamed-of creatures. And as he was admiring the colouring of the mandarin duck and assigning a life-history to it, the voice of his aunt in shrill vociferation of his name came from the gooseberry garden without. She had grown suspicious at his long disappearance, and had leapt to the conclusion that he had climbed over the wall behind the sheltering screen of the lilac bushes; she was now engaged in energetic and rather hopeless search for him among the artichokes and raspberry canes.
“Nicholas, Nicholas!” she screamed, “you are to come out of this at once. It’s no use trying to hide there; I can see you all the time.”
It was probably the first time for twenty years that anyone had smiled in that lumber-room.

Presently the angry repetitions of Nicholas’ name gave way to a shriek, and a cry for somebody to come quickly. Nicholas shut the book, restored it carefully to its place in a corner, and shook some dust from a neighbouring pile of newspapers over it. Then he crept from the room, locked the door, and replaced the key exactly where he had found it. His aunt was still calling his name when he sauntered into the front garden.
“Who’s calling?” he asked.

“Me,” came the answer from the other side of the wall; “didn’t you hear me? I’ve been looking for you in the gooseberry garden, and I’ve slipped into the rainwater tank. Luckily there’s no water in it, but the sides are slippery and I can’t get out. Fetch the little ladder from under the cherry tree⁠—”
“I was told I wasn’t to go into the gooseberry garden,” said Nicholas promptly.
“I told you not to, and now I tell you that you may,” came the voice from the rainwater tank, rather impatiently.

“Your voice doesn’t sound like aunt’s,” objected Nicholas; “you may be the Evil One tempting me to be disobedient. Aunt often tells me that the Evil One tempts me and that I always yield. This time I’m not going to yield.”
“Don’t talk nonsense,” said the prisoner in the tank; “go and fetch the ladder.”
“Will there be strawberry jam for tea?” asked Nicholas innocently.
“Certainly there will be,” said the aunt, privately resolving that Nicholas should have none of it.

“Now I know that you are the Evil One and not aunt,” shouted Nicholas gleefully; “when we asked aunt for strawberry jam yesterday she said there wasn’t any. I know there are four jars of it in the store cupboard, because I looked, and of course you know it’s there, but she doesn’t, because she said there wasn’t any. Oh, Devil, you have sold yourself!”

There was an unusual sense of luxury in being able to talk to an aunt as though one was talking to the Evil One, but Nicholas knew, with childish discernment, that such luxuries were not to be overindulged in. He walked noisily away, and it was a kitchenmaid, in search of parsley, who eventually rescued the aunt from the rainwater tank.

Tea that evening was partaken of in a fearsome silence. The tide had been at its highest when the children had arrived at Jagborough Cove, so there had been no sands to play on⁠—a circumstance that the aunt had overlooked in the haste of organising her punitive expedition. The tightness of Bobby’s boots had had disastrous effect on his temper the whole of the afternoon, and altogether the children could not have been said to have enjoyed themselves. The aunt maintained the frozen muteness of one who has suffered undignified and unmerited detention in a rainwater tank for thirty-five minutes. As for Nicholas, he, too, was silent, in the absorption of one who has much to think about; it was just possible, he considered, that the huntsman would escape with his hounds while the wolves feasted on the stricken stag.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The story begins with a quarrel over a frog. Young Nicholas has refused to eat his bread and milk because, he says, there is a frog in it. Adults who are older, wiser and better, we are told, have assured him that there cannot possibly be a frog in his bread and milk. But there is one. Nicholas put it there himself, which gives him a strong claim to know something about it. When he is proved right, the grown-ups are furious, and as a punishment he is not allowed to go on the treat that has hastily been invented for the other children: a trip to the sands at Jagborough.

The aunt, who calls herself aunt to all the children even though she is only a cousin's aunt, has a habit of inventing a treat whenever one of the children falls from grace, so that the guilty one can be left behind to feel the loss. Nicholas is made to stay at home, and the aunt, aware that he is up to something, settles in to guard the gooseberry garden, which she has forbidden him to enter. He is happy to let her think that is his plan. He makes a few loud, obvious attempts to creep toward the garden, which keep her on sentry duty through the afternoon, and meanwhile slips into the house.

His real goal is the lumber room, a locked storeroom that has been sealed from the children's curiosity, about which no questions are ever answered. He has long dreamed of seeing inside it. The key, he has discovered, sits on a shelf in the library. He climbs on a chair, takes it, and opens the door to find a world of wonders: a tapestry of a hunter, a stag and wolves, snake-shaped candlesticks, a teapot like a china duck, brass figures in a box of cotton-wool and a huge book of colored pictures of birds. To Nicholas it is the greatest treasure house he can imagine, and the aunt, who thinks that things are spoiled by use and prefers to leave them in dust and damp, has no idea of what she has locked away.

Then comes the comic climax. The aunt, seeking him in the gooseberry garden, slips into a rainwater tank and cannot climb out. She calls his name, and he, hearing her, answers politely and refuses to help. He reminds her that she told him never to go into the gooseberry garden. When she tells him he may, he says her voice does not sound like his aunt's and that she must be the Evil One tempting him to disobey. He tests her by asking about strawberry jam, and when she says there is some, he declares that she has proved she is the devil, since the real aunt told him there was none. He strolls away, and it is a kitchenmaid who eventually rescues her.

At its simplest, the story is a delight about a child who beats a grown-up at her own game. But there is a deeper meaning in the way it shows how adult rules can be turned against those who make them. Nicholas never breaks a rule. He obeys the aunt's own words with perfect, merciless literalness. Beneath the comedy is a serious point: the aunt's authority is arbitrary, and her treats, punishments and prohibitions are ways of controlling the children. The lumber room itself is a symbol of the imagination that grown-ups lock away, and Nicholas's afternoon is a small, glorious act of liberation.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
This is a very well-made comic story, and the pleasure of it lies in precision. The first section, with the frog, establishes Nicholas as a master tactician, and the narrator's mock-solemn tone, in which he is described as a skilled tactician who does not intend to shift from favorable ground, sets up the comedy. We learn that the story belongs to him, and that he will win through intelligence.

The second section, in which Nicholas lures the aunt into guarding the wrong place, is a small masterpiece of misdirection. He does not need to be tricky in some elaborate way. He merely lets her assumptions do the work. The long central scene in the lumber room is a surprising change of tone. After the brisk comedy of the beginning, the story slows down and lets itself linger over objects and images. The tapestry, with its huntsman, the stag he has just shot, his two spotted dogs and four galloping wolves, is given a vivid, almost reverent description, and for a moment the story becomes something close to a hymn to the imagination. It is a touch of real beauty in a comic tale.

The final scene, with its beautifully logical refusal, is among the funniest pieces of dialogue Saki wrote. The Evil One gag is perfectly constructed. The strawberry jam detail, which shows the aunt lying to the children about the contents of the larder, gives Nicholas a final blow that is also an act of moral accounting. The coda, with the silent, sullen tea, the boots that pinch and the tide that was high so that there were no sands to play on, completes the portrait of an adult whose cleverness has failed her.

There are weaknesses, though. The aunt is a caricature, a woman made up almost wholly of pomposity and stupidity, and some readers may wish for more complexity in her. The story is also one-sided. We see the world only from Nicholas's point of view, and the other children, Bobby and the cousins, are barely sketched. The ending is sharp, but it does not follow the consequences. We never learn whether Nicholas is punished later, and we may suspect that a real aunt would find a way to get her revenge. The cruelty of leaving a woman in a tank for thirty-five minutes, even if she is a tyrant, is something the story lightly passes over. Yet the comic spirit is strong, and the tale moves so fast that these quibbles seldom trouble us while we read. What lingers is its energy.

One more thing is worth noticing about the craft. The ending of the day, with its tea in a fearsome silence, does not simply repeat the joke. It adds a final image: Nicholas, absorbed in thought, wondering whether the huntsman in the tapestry will escape with his dogs while the wolves feast on the stricken stag. That echo of the picture quietly suggests that Nicholas has been thinking about danger, victory and how things might turn out, and it gives the comedy an odd, lingering shadow. A lesser writer would have stopped at the aunt's humiliation. Saki ends instead on the boy's private world, which is where the story has always belonged.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The Lumber Room has had a long and healthy career as a classroom favorite. It appears in anthologies for young readers and in textbooks in Britain and the Commonwealth, and it is often used to teach irony, characterization and point of view. Because it is short, funny and clear, it is an ideal introduction to Saki.

It also belongs to a long line of stories in which a clever child defeats a stupid or cruel adult. This tradition has been enormously productive in children's literature. Roald Dahl, who wrote Matilda and many other stories in which children triumph over awful grown-ups, is often compared to Saki, and while it is hard to prove direct influence, the family resemblance is plain. Richmal Crompton's William books, which began in the early 1920s, feature a similar mischievous boy, and countless modern comedies about children outsmarting parents and teachers draw on the same pattern.

The story has also helped shape how readers think about Saki as a writer of children. He is one of the few authors of his time who took a child's side without sentimentality. His children are not sweet little angels. They are crafty, ruthless and clever, and they are often right. That unsentimental sympathy was unusual in the age of Edwardian children's fiction, and it helped open the door for later writers who treated childhood as a world with its own logic.

In the broader culture, the story has become a kind of touchstone for the pleasure of seeing a pompous authority figure confounded by her own rules. It is still anthologized more than a century after it was written. Much of this staying power comes from its biographical backdrop. Many readers know that Saki spent his own childhood under the rule of aunts, and they read Nicholas's triumph as a kind of wish-fulfillment, a fantasy of revenge enjoyed by a boy who never got to win.

It is also taught as a lesson in how a writer builds a joke. Students are often asked to trace how each early detail, the frog, the forbidden garden, the key on the shelf, the jam that the aunt says does not exist, comes back later with a new meaning. That tight, interlocking design is part of why the story is so often used in classrooms: it shows plainly, in a few pages, how setup and payoff work. Some teachers also use it to start conversations about fairness, authority and honesty, since the story invites readers to decide for themselves whether Nicholas has been clever, cruel, or both.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers love this story, first of all, because Nicholas wins. There is a deep pleasure in watching a child who has been bossed and scolded and dismissed turn the tables with nothing but wit and logic.
