Many readers remember their own childhood frustrations with adults who invented arbitrary rules, and they enjoy the story as a kind of revenge fantasy.

They also love the language. Saki's sentences are polished and wickedly funny, full of understatement and mock-seriousness. The description of the aunt as one who insisted, by an unwarranted stretch of imagination, on styling herself his aunt also is typical of his deadpan wit. The narrator, who seems to be on the side of the grown-ups but is in fact secretly on Nicholas's side, creates a sly comic tension that gives every page a spark.

Another pleasure is the lumber room itself. After the sharp comedy of the beginning, the story opens into a lovely, dreamy interlude, in which a boy who has been starved of beauty finds himself surrounded by marvels. Readers often cite this scene as the emotional center of the story. The tapestry, in which a huntsman who has just shot a stag does not seem to notice four wolves creeping toward him, becomes a story that Nicholas can live inside, and the birds in the great book are things he has never seen. The passage reminds us that imagination is a form of freedom.

Finally, readers value the story's confidence. It does not apologize for Nicholas. It does not make him learn a lesson or punish him for his cleverness. It simply lets him win, and it lets the adult look foolish. That refusal to moralize is part of its charm, and it is the reason the tale feels fresh and subversive even today. It is a story that trusts children to be smart, and trusts readers to enjoy it.

Readers also delight in how much the story seems to know about being a child. The slow, unfair rhythm of a day in disgrace, the way adults make rules that change with their moods, the strange, charged feeling of being in a place you are forbidden to enter, all ring true. Someone who has stood outside a locked door wondering what was inside will recognize the thrill of Nicholas turning that key. And the story honors that thrill. It does not hurry the scene, and it treats the boy's wonder as something worth the reader's full attention.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Critical reaction to The Lumber Room has been mostly warm, and because it is a minor comic story in a collection of pieces, extensive contemporary reviews are hard to find. Most reviewers of Saki's collections praised his wit while sometimes noting what they saw as a lack of warmth. What follows is therefore mostly a description of the objections that readers have raised over time.

The most common complaint is about the aunt. She is drawn without any depth, and some readers feel she is a straw figure, easy to knock down. A fairer story might have shown her as a person with her own anxieties and limits, instead of a mass of smugness. Others feel that the story is too cozy in its cruelty, that Nicholas's refusal to help a woman who may be injured is more disturbing than funny. The aunt is trapped in a tank for thirty-five minutes, and while the narrator tells us there is no water, a reader who thinks about it may feel a twinge of discomfort.

A second objection is to the story's moral coldness. Saki's humor often depends on cruelty, and critics have noted that his stories tend to side with the clever and the ruthless. Nicholas wins by lying, by manipulating, and by exploiting an adult's weakness. Some readers see this as a weakness, a lack of moral seriousness. Others say that is precisely the point: the children of Saki's stories are driven to cunning by the bullying of adults, and the stories do not pretend that the world is fair.

Finally, some readers have found the story slight. It is a sketch, not a deep exploration of childhood, and it lacks the darker resonance of Sredni Vashtar or the sharp social satire of The Open Window. The Edwardian setting, with its aunts, governesses and seaside treats, is distant from modern life, and a few of the story's period details, such as the aunt's fear of the Evil One, may need a word of explanation. A still more modern objection concerns the story's picture of the child as hero and the adult as fool, which some feel is a simple inversion and not a real insight. Yet most critics agree that the story's lightness is a virtue, not a flaw, and that it achieves what it sets out to do.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
Where does The Lumber Room belong in the larger world of literature? It is a comedy of manners, in the tradition of English satire that mocks the pretensions of polite society, and it also belongs to the long line of stories about children and adults in which the child's point of view subverts adult authority. Its ancestors include Dickens's novels, in which children suffer at the hands of cruel guardians, and Mark Twain's Tom Sawyer, in which a clever boy turns the rules of a puzzled aunt to his own advantage. Saki's Nicholas is closer to Tom than to Oliver Twist, since he does not suffer but triumphs.

It also descends from the Victorian tradition of the unhappy childhood, from Rudyard Kipling's story Baa Baa, Black Sheep, which drew on his own miserable years in a foster home, to the harsh institutions in Charlotte Bronte's Jane Eyre. Saki's twist is to turn that tradition into comedy. He takes the same cold aunts and joyless rules and shows a child who fights back with cunning and wins. The result is lighter in tone than Kipling or Bronte but just as sharp in its criticism of adult tyranny.

Its descendants are many. Dahl's tales of rebellious children, Crompton's William, and in a sense the mischievous protagonists of modern children's comedy owe a debt to this tradition. In the wider world of short fiction, Saki stands beside O. Henry and Oscar Wilde as a master of the polished, ironic tale, and his dry, deadpan manner is often mentioned alongside later comic writers such as P. G. Wodehouse and Roald Dahl, though how much they owed him is a matter of opinion. The idea that a child can be the cleverest person in the room has become a staple of popular culture.

Why read it now? Because it is short, funny, and still true. Anyone who has ever been told to do something for no good reason, or has ever been punished for telling an inconvenient truth, will recognize Nicholas. The story also offers a quiet lesson about imagination: the lumber room is a symbol of everything that adults lock away, and Nicholas's visit is a reminder that wonder is worth stealing a key for. It is a perfect small story, read in minutes, that leaves you smiling.

stories.title: Tobermory
stories.author: Saki (H. H. Munro)
stories.epigraph: “And do you mean to say,” asked Miss Resker, after a slight pause, “that you have taught Tobermory to say and understand easy sentences of one syllable?”
stories.keyContext: Tobermory is a short comic story by the British writer Saki, whose real name was Hector Hugh Munro. It first appeared in a London newspaper in 1909 and is now one of the most famous short stories in English about a talking animal. Saki was born in Burma, raised by strict aunts in Devon, and became a journalist and satirist who loved to poke fun at the polite, wealthy people of Edwardian England. That was the decade just before the First World War, when country-house weekends were a kind of social theater. Saki himself was killed in that war in 1916, at forty-five. The story's idea is simple and wicked. What if a house cat could speak, and what if he had been listening all along? Its meaning is a sly one about manners, gossip, and how much of polite society depends on people not saying what they know. Listen for the deadpan tone, because the humor lives in how calmly everything is said.
paragraphs: It was a chill, rain-washed afternoon of a late August day, that indefinite season when partridges are still in security or cold storage, and there is nothing to hunt⁠—unless one is bounded on the north by the Bristol Channel, in which case one may lawfully gallop after fat red stags. Lady Blemley’s house-party was not bounded on the north by the Bristol Channel, hence there was a full gathering of her guests round the tea-table on this particular afternoon. And, in spite of the blankness of the season and the triteness of the occasion, there was no trace in the company of that fatigued restlessness which means a dread of the pianola and a subdued hankering for auction bridge. The undisguised open-mouthed attention of the entire party was fixed on the homely negative personality of Mr. Cornelius Appin. Of all her guests, he was the one who had come to Lady Blemley with the vaguest reputation. Someone had said he was “clever,” and he had got his invitation in the moderate expectation, on the part of his hostess, that some portion at least of his cleverness would be contributed to the general entertainment. Until teatime that day she had been unable to discover in what direction, if any, his cleverness lay. He was neither a wit nor a croquet champion, a hypnotic force nor a begetter of amateur theatricals. Neither did his exterior suggest the sort of man in whom women are willing to pardon a generous measure of mental deficiency. He had subsided into mere Mr. Appin, and the Cornelius seemed a piece of transparent baptismal bluff. And now he was claiming to have launched on the world a discovery beside which the invention of gunpowder, of the printing-press, and of steam locomotion were inconsiderable trifles. Science had made bewildering strides in many directions during recent decades, but this thing seemed to belong to the domain of miracle rather than to scientific achievement.

“And do you really ask us to believe,” Sir Wilfrid was saying, “that you have discovered a means for instructing animals in the art of human speech, and that dear old Tobermory has proved your first successful pupil?”

“It is a problem at which I have worked for the last seventeen years,” said Mr. Appin, “but only during the last eight or nine months have I been rewarded with glimmerings of success. Of course I have experimented with thousands of animals, but latterly only with cats, those wonderful creatures which have assimilated themselves so marvellously with our civilization while retaining all their highly developed feral instincts. Here and there among cats one comes across an outstanding superior intellect, just as one does among the ruck of human beings, and when I made the acquaintance of Tobermory a week ago I saw at once that I was in contact with a ‘Beyond-cat’ of extraordinary intelligence. I had gone far along the road to success in recent experiments; with Tobermory, as you call him, I have reached the goal.”

Mr. Appin concluded his remarkable statement in a voice which he strove to divest of a triumphant inflection. No one said “Rats,” though Clovis’s lips moved in a monosyllabic contortion which probably invoked those rodents of disbelief.
“And do you mean to say,” asked Miss Resker, after a slight pause, “that you have taught Tobermory to say and understand easy sentences of one syllable?”

“My dear Miss Resker,” said the wonderworker patiently, “one teaches little children and savages and backward adults in that piecemeal fashion; when one has once solved the problem of making a beginning with an animal of highly developed intelligence one has no need for those halting methods. Tobermory can speak our language with perfect correctness.”
This time Clovis very distinctly said “Beyond-rats!” Sir Wilfrid was more polite, but equally sceptical.
“Hadn’t we better have the cat in and judge for ourselves?” suggested Lady Blemley.
Sir Wilfrid went in search of the animal, and the company settled themselves down to the languid expectation of witnessing some more or less adroit drawing-room ventriloquism.
In a minute Sir Wilfrid was back in the room, his face white beneath its tan and his eyes dilated with excitement.
“By Gad, it’s true!”
His agitation was unmistakably genuine, and his hearers started forward in a thrill of awakened interest.

Collapsing into an armchair, he continued breathlessly: “I found him dozing in the smoking-room, and called out to him to come for his tea. He blinked at me in his usual way, and I said, ‘Come on, Toby; don’t keep us waiting;’ and, by Gad! he drawled out in a most horribly natural voice that he’d come when he dashed well pleased! I nearly jumped out of my skin!”

Appin had preached to absolutely incredulous hearers; Sir Wilfrid’s statement carried instant conviction. A Babel-like chorus of startled exclamation arose, amid which the scientist sat mutely enjoying the first fruit of his stupendous discovery.
In the midst of the clamour Tobermory entered the room and made his way with velvet tread and studied unconcern across to the group seated round the tea-table.
A sudden hush of awkwardness and constraint fell on the company. Somehow there seemed an element of embarrassment in addressing on equal terms a domestic cat of acknowledged mental ability.
“Will you have some milk, Tobermory?” asked Lady Blemley in a rather strained voice.

“I don’t mind if I do,” was the response, couched in a tone of even indifference. A shiver of suppressed excitement went through the listeners, and Lady Blemley might be excused for pouring out the saucerful of milk rather unsteadily.
“I’m afraid I’ve spilt a good deal of it,” she said apologetically.
“After all, it’s not my Axminster,” was Tobermory’s rejoinder.

Another silence fell on the group, and then Miss Resker, in her best district-visitor manner, asked if the human language had been difficult to learn. Tobermory looked squarely at her for a moment and then fixed his gaze serenely on the middle distance. It was obvious that boring questions lay outside his scheme of life.
“What do you think of human intelligence?” asked Mavis Pellington lamely.
“Of whose intelligence in particular?” asked Tobermory coldly.
“Oh, well, mine, for instance,” said Mavis, with a feeble laugh.

“You put me in an embarrassing position,” said Tobermory, whose tone and attitude certainly did not suggest a shred of embarrassment. “When your inclusion in this house-party was suggested Sir Wilfrid protested that you were the most brainless woman of his acquaintance, and that there was a wide distinction between hospitality and the care of the feebleminded. Lady Blemley replied that your lack of brainpower was the precise quality which had earned you your invitation, as you were the only person she could think of who might be idiotic enough to buy their old car. You know, the one they call ‘The Envy of Sisyphus,’ because it goes quite nicely uphill if you push it.”

Lady Blemley’s protestations would have had greater effect if she had not casually suggested to Mavis only that morning that the car in question would be just the thing for her down at her Devonshire home.
Major Barfield plunged in heavily to effect a diversion.
“How about your carryings-on with the tortoiseshell puss up at the stables, eh?”
The moment he had said it everyone realized the blunder.

“One does not usually discuss these matters in public,” said Tobermory frigidly. “From a slight observation of your ways since you’ve been in this house I should imagine you’d find it inconvenient if I were to shift the conversation on to your own little affairs.”
The panic which ensued was not confined to the Major.
“Would you like to go and see if cook has got your dinner ready?” suggested Lady Blemley hurriedly, affecting to ignore the fact that it wanted at least two hours to Tobermory’s dinnertime.
“Thanks,” said Tobermory, “not quite so soon after my tea. I don’t want to die of indigestion.”
“Cats have nine lives, you know,” said Sir Wilfrid heartily.
“Possibly,” answered Tobermory; “but only one liver.”
“Adelaide!” said Mrs. Cornett, “do you mean to encourage that cat to go out and gossip about us in the servants’ hall?”

The panic had indeed become general. A narrow ornamental balustrade ran in front of most of the bedroom windows at the Towers, and it was recalled with dismay that this had formed a favourite promenade for Tobermory at all hours, whence he could watch the pigeons⁠—and heaven knew what else besides. If he intended to become reminiscent in his present outspoken strain the effect would be something more than disconcerting. Mrs. Cornett, who spent much time at her toilet table, and whose complexion was reputed to be of a nomadic though punctual disposition, looked as ill at ease as the Major. Miss Scrawen, who wrote fiercely sensuous poetry and led a blameless life, merely displayed irritation; if you are methodical and virtuous in private you don’t necessarily want everyone to know it. Bertie van Tahn, who was so depraved at seventeen that he had long ago given up trying to be any worse, turned a dull shade of gardenia white, but he did not commit the error of dashing out of the room like Odo Finsberry, a young gentleman who was understood to be reading for the Church and who was possibly disturbed at the thought of scandals he might hear concerning other people. Clovis had the presence of mind to maintain a composed exterior; privately he was calculating how long it would take to procure a box of fancy mice through the agency of the Exchange and Mart as a species of hush-money.
Even in a delicate situation like the present, Agnes Resker could not endure to remain too long in the background.
“Why did I ever come down here?” she asked dramatically.
Tobermory immediately accepted the opening.

“Judging by what you said to Mrs. Cornett on the croquet-lawn yesterday, you were out for food. You described the Blemleys as the dullest people to stay with that you knew, but said they were clever enough to employ a first-rate cook; otherwise they’d find it difficult to get anyone to come down a second time.”
“There’s not a word of truth in it! I appeal to Mrs. Cornett⁠—” exclaimed the discomfited Agnes.

“Mrs. Cornett repeated your remark afterwards to Bertie van Tahn,” continued Tobermory, “and said, ‘That woman is a regular Hunger Marcher; she’d go anywhere for four square meals a day,’ and Bertie van Tahn said⁠—”

At this point the chronicle mercifully ceased. Tobermory had caught a glimpse of the big yellow Tom from the Rectory working his way through the shrubbery towards the stable wing. In a flash he had vanished through the open French window.

With the disappearance of his too brilliant pupil Cornelius Appin found himself beset by a hurricane of bitter upbraiding, anxious inquiry, and frightened entreaty. The responsibility for the situation lay with him, and he must prevent matters from becoming worse. Could Tobermory impart his dangerous gift to other cats? was the first question he had to answer. It was possible, he replied, that he might have initiated his intimate friend the stable puss into his new accomplishment, but it was unlikely that his teaching could have taken a wider range as yet.
“Then,” said Mrs. Cornett, “Tobermory may be a valuable cat and a great pet; but I’m sure you’ll agree, Adelaide, that both he and the stable cat must be done away with without delay.”

“You don’t suppose I’ve enjoyed the last quarter of an hour, do you?” said Lady Blemley bitterly. “My husband and I are very fond of Tobermory⁠—at least, we were before this horrible accomplishment was infused into him; but now, of course, the only thing is to have him destroyed as soon as possible.”

“We can put some strychnine in the scraps he always gets at dinnertime,” said Sir Wilfrid, “and I will go and drown the stable cat myself. The coachman will be very sore at losing his pet, but I’ll say a very catching form of mange has broken out in both cats and we’re afraid of it spreading to the kennels.”
“But my great discovery!” expostulated Mr. Appin; “after all my years of research and experiment⁠—”

“You can go and experiment on the shorthorns at the farm, who are under proper control,” said Mrs. Cornett, “or the elephants at the Zoological Gardens. They’re said to be highly intelligent, and they have this recommendation, that they don’t come creeping about our bedrooms and under chairs, and so forth.”

An archangel ecstatically proclaiming the Millennium, and then finding that it clashed unpardonably with Henley and would have to be indefinitely postponed, could hardly have felt more crestfallen than Cornelius Appin at the reception of his wonderful achievement. Public opinion, however, was against him⁠—in fact, had the general voice been consulted on the subject it is probable that a strong minority vote would have been in favour of including him in the strychnine diet.

Defective train arrangements and a nervous desire to see matters brought to a finish prevented an immediate dispersal of the party, but dinner that evening was not a social success. Sir Wilfrid had had rather a trying time with the stable cat and subsequently with the coachman. Agnes Resker ostentatiously limited her repast to a morsel of dry toast, which she bit as though it were a personal enemy; while Mavis Pellington maintained a vindictive silence throughout the meal. Lady Blemley kept up a flow of what she hoped was conversation, but her attention was fixed on the doorway. A plateful of carefully dosed fish scraps was in readiness on the sideboard, but sweets and savoury and dessert went their way, and no Tobermory appeared either in the dining-room or kitchen.

The sepulchral dinner was cheerful compared with the subsequent vigil in the smoking-room. Eating and drinking had at least supplied a distraction and cloak to the prevailing embarrassment. Bridge was out of the question in the general tension of nerves and tempers, and after Odo Finsberry had given a lugubrious rendering of “Melisande in the Wood” to a frigid audience music was tacitly avoided. At eleven the servants went to bed, announcing that the small window in the pantry had been left open as usual for Tobermory’s private use. The guests read steadily through the current batch of magazines, and fell back gradually on the Badminton Library and bound volumes of Punch. Lady Blemley made periodic visits to the pantry, returning each time with an expression of listless depression which forestalled questioning.
At two o’clock Clovis broke the dominating silence.

“He won’t turn up tonight. He’s probably in the local newspaper office at the present moment, dictating the first instalment of his reminiscences. Lady What’s-her-name’s book won’t be in it. It will be the event of the day.”
Having made this contribution to the general cheerfulness, Clovis went to bed. At long intervals the various members of the house-party followed his example.
The servants taking round the early tea made a uniform announcement in reply to a uniform question. Tobermory had not returned.

Breakfast was, if anything, a more unpleasant function than dinner had been, but before its conclusion the situation was relieved. Tobermory’s corpse was brought in from the shrubbery, where a gardener had just discovered it. From the bites on his throat and the yellow fur which coated his claws it was evident that he had fallen in unequal combat with the big Tom from the Rectory.

By midday most of the guests had quitted the Towers, and after lunch Lady Blemley had sufficiently recovered her spirits to write an extremely nasty letter to the Rectory about the loss of her valuable pet.

Tobermory had been Appin’s one successful pupil, and he was destined to have no successor. A few weeks later an elephant in the Dresden Zoological Garden, which had shown no previous signs of irritability, broke loose and killed an Englishman who had apparently been teasing it. The victim’s name was variously reported in the papers as Oppin and Eppelin, but his front name was faithfully rendered Cornelius.
“If he was trying German irregular verbs on the poor beast,” said Clovis, “he deserved all he got.”

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
On the surface, Tobermory is a joke about a cat who learns to talk. A slightly dull guest at a country-house party, Cornelius Appin, announces that after seventeen years of experiments he has taught the household tabby to speak perfect English. Nobody believes him until Sir Wilfrid, the host, goes to fetch the cat and comes back white-faced, saying, "By Gad, it's true!" Then Tobermory strolls in, accepts a saucer of milk, and starts telling the truth.

But the real subject is not the cat. It is the guests. Every person in that drawing room is living a small double life, and the whole social occasion depends on the two halves staying apart. The hostess invited Miss Pellington only because she was stupid enough to buy an old car nobody else wanted. The guests who smile at each other over tea say cruel things behind each other's backs. Tobermory has no malice at all. He simply repeats what he has seen and heard, in the same cool voice a person might use to read out a train timetable. That is what makes it frightening. The cat is not a villain. He is a witness, and a witness who does not understand why anyone would be embarrassed. Notice how the story plays with the difference between lying and politeness. When Lady Blemley spills the milk and apologizes, Tobermory says, "After all, it's not my Axminster." That line is perfectly polite in form and perfectly rude in effect, because he is simply refusing to pretend the carpet matters to him. Cats really do seem to look at us that way, with total indifference to our rules. Saki takes that familiar feeling and makes it speak.

There are layers a first-time reader might miss. The panic spreads beyond what the cat actually says. Major Barfield tries to change the subject by teasing Tobermory about the tortoiseshell cat at the stables, and the cat answers with a calm threat to discuss the Major's own private affairs. From then on, the guests are frightened less of what Tobermory has said than of what he could say. Mrs. Cornett worries about her complexion, which is reputed to be of a nomadic though punctual disposition, a joke that tells you she wears makeup and everyone knows it. Even the guests who are blameless are annoyed, because, as Saki puts it, if you are methodical and virtuous in private you don't necessarily want everyone to know it.

The ending is the cruelest and funniest part. The same people who were charmed by a talking cat an hour earlier now calmly plan to poison him with strychnine in his fish scraps, and Sir Wilfrid will drown the stable cat himself. Nobody asks whether it is right. Their own comfort is all that counts. Tobermory is killed by a rival tomcat from the rectory, and the guests are relieved. Appin dies a few weeks later in Dresden, killed by an elephant he was apparently teasing. Clovis's remark about German irregular verbs is a final deadpan joke that refuses to let the reader feel sad.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
Tobermory is a small masterpiece of comic construction, but it is not flawless, and it is worth being honest about both halves of that. What is masterful first is the control of tone. Saki never winks at the reader. Even the most outrageous events are reported in the grave, slightly bored voice of a society columnist. When the narrator says that Appin had come to Lady Blemley with the vaguest reputation for being clever, the sentence wears its good manners like a suit of armor, and the knife slides out from under it. The dialogue is genuinely quotable, with lines like "Cats have nine lives, you know," followed by "Possibly; but only one liver." That exchange does everything. It is a pun, it is a put-down, and it shows Tobermory's character in six words.

The structure is also very tidy. The story is built like a little machine. A premise is introduced, tested in the drawing room, pushed to a crisis, and then closed off with a symmetrical ending in which both the cat and his teacher die from animal violence. The elephant in the Dresden zoo was even foreshadowed earlier, when Mrs. Cornett suggests Appin experiment on the elephants at the Zoological Gardens instead. A careful reader feels the satisfying click when that suggestion comes true. Saki also knows exactly when to stop. Tobermory's last speech is cut off in the middle of a sentence, "and Bertie van Tahn said," and the narrator mercifully ends the chronicle. Leaving the worst unsaid is better than any amount of scandal spelled out.

Now the weaker side. The story is thin as a human drama. Appin is hardly a character at all, only a device. The guests are nearly all types rather than people, with names that seem chosen mostly for their comic sound. The satire is also aimed at a very narrow target, rich idlers who are easy to mock, and a reader today may feel that the punches are landing on people who were never going to be hurt. There is a class snobbery in the humor as well. The coachman who loves the stable cat is treated as a small inconvenience, and the plan to lie to him about a mange outbreak is told as a trivial detail rather than a cruelty.

The pacing can also feel uneven. The long opening paragraphs and the talk of seventeen years of experiments are written in the elaborate, ornamental style of the period, and the story takes a little while to find its stride. Once Tobermory speaks, it moves beautifully. The final section, the long night in the smoking room, is slightly more labored than the drawing room scene, and the ending is tidy to the point of being slightly mechanical. Overall, though, the strengths are far greater than the flaws. It is short, polished, and completely sure of its effect, and few comic stories in English do so much in so little space.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
It is fair to say that Tobermory made Saki's reputation as a short-story writer, although the full scale of that reputation grew after his death. The story first appeared in the Westminster Gazette in November 1909 and then opened his collection The Chronicles of Clovis in 1911. By then Saki was already known as a journalist and as the author of the Reginald sketches, but Tobermory gave him a calling card that readers could quote. It is the story most often reprinted when anyone wants to introduce him.

His death made him into a kind of legend. He enlisted as a private in the British army in 1914, though he was well over the usual age and could have taken a commission, and he was killed by a sniper in France in November 1916. A famous report claims his last words were a shout telling a comrade to put out a cigarette, though like many such tales it should be held loosely. Whatever the truth, the contrast between his sparkling, mocking prose and his early death made readers feel the loss of a whole kind of Edwardian wit.

The influence spread in several directions. Humorists who combine a perfectly polite style with something cruel underneath, from P. G. Wodehouse's world of idle aristocrats to the dark comedy of Roald Dahl, are often mentioned in Saki's company, though the direct lines of influence vary and are debated. The idea that an animal might speak the truth and expose human hypocrisy has become a staple of comic writing, television, and children's films. Whenever a pet's inner monologue is imagined as dry, sarcastic, and unimpressed with its owners, a little of Tobermory is probably in the room.

The story has also become a schoolroom favorite. It is short enough to read in one sitting, and it is frequently taught as an example of satire, irony, and the deadpan voice. Teachers use it to show how humor can criticize without lecturing. It has been adapted for radio and stage and television in various versions over the years, and anthologies of humorous and animal stories include it again and again. A smaller piece of its impact is simply in the language. The name Tobermory itself sticks in the mind, and the phrase "only one liver" has outlived many longer jokes. The central situation, in which a household discovers that the pet has been listening, has become a general shorthand. People still say it when they imagine what a pet might repeat if it could talk. That is a sign of a story that has entered the shared imagination, not just the shelves.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
What have readers loved about Tobermory? First and most of all, they love how funny it is, and how quickly it gets there. Few stories give you a laugh as early as "After all, it's not my Axminster." Readers often say they still remember the exact moment Tobermory turns to Miss Pellington, asks "Of whose intelligence in particular?" and then calmly reveals what the hosts said about her. The embarrassment is delicious because it is deserved and because it is delivered without anger.

They also love the cat. Anyone who has lived with a cat recognizes the personality at once: aloof, unimpressed, interested only in food and in his own affairs. Tobermory refuses to answer boring questions, makes his entrance with "velvet tread and studied unconcern," and only responds when he feels like it. Saki was clearly an animal lover, and that affection gives the story its warmth. Many readers feel that Tobermory is the most dignified person in the room, and that his death is a real loss, which is exactly why the guests' relief feels so shabby.

Another thing readers admire is how recognizable the human side is. The specific people are from a vanished world, but the situation is universal. Everyone has said something unkind about a friend and then smiled at that friend later. Everyone has dreaded the moment when the thing they said gets repeated. The story lets us laugh at that dread from a safe distance, and the laughter has a slightly guilty edge that makes it more satisfying. Writers have admired the craft. Saki's skill with the epigram, a short, polished, surprising remark, has been envied for more than a century. The description of Mrs. Cornett's complexion, "of a nomadic though punctual disposition," is the sort of line a writer reads twice, partly to enjoy it and partly to wonder how it was done. Lovers of language enjoy that his jokes are built from ordinary words used at an unexpected angle.

Finally, readers like that the story does not preach. It never says that gossip is wrong or that society is hypocritical. It just lets things unfold, and the reader draws the conclusion. There is real respect in that. People who might resist a lecture will happily accept a joke, and then find that it has taught them something anyway. That mixture of fun and sting is probably why the story is still read with such pleasure, over a century later, by people who have never been to a country-house party in their lives.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Even a story this beloved has drawn criticism, and some of it is fair. The most common complaint concerns the thinness of the satire. Some readers have felt that Saki, for all his brilliance, is a humorist of the surface. His targets are rich, idle people, but he does not seem to wish them any real change. He enjoys their embarrassment; he does not ask how they got their money or what harm their manners do. Compared with satirists who attack injustice, he can seem more interested in cleverness than in conscience. Critics have sometimes called his work trivial for that reason, a series of brilliant jokes with no serious argument underneath them.

Another objection is cruelty. The ending, with its calm plan to poison a beloved cat and drown another, is played for laughs, and some readers find it harder to laugh than Saki expects. Saki had a famously dark and mischievous streak, and this was not accidental. But a modern audience, more sensitive to animal suffering, may feel that the joke asks it to enjoy something that is not entirely funny. The final line about the elephant is the same. It invites us to cheer a man's death because he was a bore, and that is a sharp pill to swallow with the tea.

There are also objections about prejudice. Like many writers of his time and class, Saki sometimes leaned on stereotypes, and the world of his stories is one in which servants and outsiders are of little account. In Tobermory this appears mostly as a lack of interest in the people downstairs, such as the coachman, rather than as open insult. His other work, however, contains attitudes that readers today find offensive, and anyone exploring more of his writing should be aware of that.

Some critics have found the story too neat. Its structure is so polished that it can feel like a clever exercise rather than a living piece of writing. Others complain that the premise is not fully worked out. How did Appin teach the cat? Why does Tobermory understand human embarrassment so well, and yet not understand why people mind it? The story waves these questions away in the name of comedy, and a stricter reader might want more. Saki, however, is clearly uninterested in explanations, and most readers forgive that. A joke explained is a joke killed, as the old saying goes. In short, the criticism is mostly about what the story chooses not to be. It is not a deep social novel, and it never claims to be.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
Tobermory belongs to a rich tradition of comedy about manners. Its ancestors include the stage comedies of Oscar Wilde, whose characters also speak in polished, mischievous epigrams while behaving badly, and the long English habit of satirizing high society from the inside. Saki wrote at the very end of the Edwardian era, the decade of country-house weekends, motoring, and apparent calm before the First World War. Reading him now, one feels the ice that was about to break. Many readers see his brittle elegance as the last bright flash of that world.

On the animal side, the story belongs to the old tradition of talking beasts, from the fables of Aesop to Puss in Boots. It is closer to German writer E. T. A. Hoffmann's Life and Opinions of the Tomcat Murr, from the early nineteenth century, in which a cat writes his own memoirs and mocks his human owners. H. G. Wells, in The Island of Doctor Moreau, had earlier imagined animals made human by surgery, but with horror. Saki turns the same idea into comedy. Where Wells asks what it would mean to make an animal human, Saki asks what would happen if an animal simply told us what it saw.

Looking forward, the story is a distant ancestor of everything from sitcom pets with sarcastic voices to modern satires about technology that listens. Today's smart speakers and surveillance gadgets give Tobermory a fresh edge. A device that hears everything we say in our own homes is a version of the same problem, and readers sometimes find the story uncomfortably timely. Many comic writers of the twentieth century, including some who never admitted any debt, work in the same tradition of the polite sentence with a hidden sting.

Within Saki's own work, Tobermory sits beside stories like Sredni Vashtar, in which a lonely boy worships a ferret, and The Open Window, with its famous teenage liar. Together they show his range, from comedy to something nearer to cruelty and revenge. Many of his stories treat children and animals as the wise ones, and adults as pompous fools who deserve a comeuppance. That outlook was shaped by his own childhood under the rule of strict aunts, and it gives the stories an emotional undertone that the jokes alone do not explain. Why read it today? Partly for sheer pleasure, because few stories are so funny in so few pages. Partly because the central idea has not aged. We all still live in a world of polite fictions, of things said in the kitchen and not in the drawing room. And partly because it reminds us that the sharpest satire can come in the form of a cat saying, in a perfectly calm voice, exactly what he thinks.

stories.title: The Ransom of Red Chief
stories.author: O. Henry
stories.epigraph: “Hey, little boy!” says Bill, “would you like to have a bag of candy and a nice ride?”
stories.keyContext: The Ransom of Red Chief is a comic crime story by O. Henry, the pen name of an American writer named William Sydney Porter. It appeared in 1907 and has been a classroom and campfire favorite ever since. Porter's own life was stranger than most of his plots. He worked as a bank teller in Texas, was accused of embezzling, fled the country, came home, and served time in prison, where he began writing the stories that made him famous. After his release he moved to New York and turned out short stories for newspapers and magazines, with a warm, jokey voice and a twist at the end. This one is told by a small-time crook who kidnaps a rich man's son for ransom. The joke, which you will see coming and enjoy anyway, is that the plan goes wrong because the boy is far worse than his captors. Underneath the fun is a gentle idea about how a clever scheme can be defeated by plain human nature.
paragraphs: It looked like a good thing: but wait till I tell you. We were down South, in Alabama⁠—Bill Driscoll and myself⁠—when this kidnapping idea struck us. It was, as Bill afterward expressed it, “during a moment of temporary mental apparition”; but we didn’t find that out till later.

There was a town down there, as flat as a flannel-cake, and called Summit, of course. It contained inhabitants of as undeleterious and self-satisfied a class of peasantry as ever clustered around a Maypole.

Bill and me had a joint capital of about six hundred dollars, and we needed just two thousand dollars more to pull off a fraudulent town-lot scheme in Western Illinois with. We talked it over on the front steps of the hotel. Philoprogenitiveness, says we, is strong in semi-rural communities; therefore and for other reasons, a kidnapping project ought to do better there than in the radius of newspapers that send reporters out in plain clothes to stir up talk about such things. We knew that Summit couldn’t get after us with anything stronger than constables and maybe some lackadaisical bloodhounds and a diatribe or two in the Weekly Farmers’ Budget. So, it looked good.

We selected for our victim the only child of a prominent citizen named Ebenezer Dorset. The father was respectable and tight, a mortgage fancier and a stern, upright collection-plate passer and forecloser. The kid was a boy of ten, with bas-relief freckles, and hair the colour of the cover of the magazine you buy at the newsstand when you want to catch a train. Bill and me figured that Ebenezer would melt down for a ransom of two thousand dollars to a cent. But wait till I tell you.

About two miles from Summit was a little mountain, covered with a dense cedar brake. On the rear elevation of this mountain was a cave. There we stored provisions. One evening after sundown, we drove in a buggy past old Dorset’s house. The kid was in the street, throwing rocks at a kitten on the opposite fence.
“Hey, little boy!” says Bill, “would you like to have a bag of candy and a nice ride?”
The boy catches Bill neatly in the eye with a piece of brick.
“That will cost the old man an extra five hundred dollars,” says Bill, climbing over the wheel.

That boy put up a fight like a welterweight cinnamon bear; but, at last, we got him down in the bottom of the buggy and drove away. We took him up to the cave and I hitched the horse in the cedar brake. After dark I drove the buggy to the little village, three miles away, where we had hired it, and walked back to the mountain.

Bill was pasting court-plaster over the scratches and bruises on his features. There was a fire burning behind the big rock at the entrance of the cave, and the boy was watching a pot of boiling coffee, with two buzzard tail-feathers stuck in his red hair. He points a stick at me when I come up, and says:
“Ha! cursed paleface, do you dare to enter the camp of Red Chief, the terror of the plains?”

“He’s all right now,” says Bill, rolling up his trousers and examining some bruises on his shins. “We’re playing Indian. We’re making Buffalo Bill’s show look like magic-lantern views of Palestine in the town hall. I’m Old Hank, the Trapper, Red Chief’s captive, and I’m to be scalped at daybreak. By Geronimo! that kid can kick hard.”

Yes, sir, that boy seemed to be having the time of his life. The fun of camping out in a cave had made him forget that he was a captive himself. He immediately christened me Snake-eye, the Spy, and announced that, when his braves returned from the warpath, I was to be broiled at the stake at the rising of the sun.
Then we had supper; and he filled his mouth full of bacon and bread and gravy, and began to talk. He made a during-dinner speech something like this:

“I like this fine. I never camped out before; but I had a pet possum once, and I was nine last birthday. I hate to go to school. Rats ate up sixteen of Jimmy Talbot’s aunt’s speckled hen’s eggs. Are there any real Indians in these woods? I want some more gravy. Does the trees moving make the wind blow? We had five puppies. What makes your nose so red, Hank? My father has lots of money. Are the stars hot? I whipped Ed Walker twice, Saturday. I don’t like girls. You dassent catch toads unless with a string. Do oxen make any noise? Why are oranges round? Have you got beds to sleep on in this cave? Amos Murray has got six toes. A parrot can talk, but a monkey or a fish can’t. How many does it take to make twelve?”

Every few minutes he would remember that he was a pesky redskin, and pick up his stick rifle and tiptoe to the mouth of the cave to rubber for the scouts of the hated paleface. Now and then he would let out a war-whoop that made Old Hank the Trapper shiver. That boy had Bill terrorized from the start.
“Red Chief,” says I to the kid, “would you like to go home?”
“Aw, what for?” says he. “I don’t have any fun at home. I hate to go to school. I like to camp out. You won’t take me back home again, Snake-eye, will you?”
“Not right away,” says I. “We’ll stay here in the cave a while.”
“All right!” says he. “That’ll be fine. I never had such fun in all my life.”

We went to bed about eleven o’clock. We spread down some wide blankets and quilts and put Red Chief between us. We weren’t afraid he’d run away. He kept us awake for three hours, jumping up and reaching for his rifle and screeching: “Hist! pard,” in mine and Bill’s ears, as the fancied crackle of a twig or the rustle of a leaf revealed to his young imagination the stealthy approach of the outlaw band. At last, I fell into a troubled sleep, and dreamed that I had been kidnapped and chained to a tree by a ferocious pirate with red hair.

Just at daybreak, I was awakened by a series of awful screams from Bill. They weren’t yells, or howls, or shouts, or whoops, or yawps, such as you’d expect from a manly set of vocal organs⁠—they were simply indecent, terrifying, humiliating screams, such as women emit when they see ghosts or caterpillars. It’s an awful thing to hear a strong, desperate, fat man scream incontinently in a cave at daybreak.

I jumped up to see what the matter was. Red Chief was sitting on Bill’s chest, with one hand twined in Bill’s hair. In the other he had the sharp case-knife we used for slicing bacon; and he was industriously and realistically trying to take Bill’s scalp, according to the sentence that had been pronounced upon him the evening before.

I got the knife away from the kid and made him lie down again. But, from that moment, Bill’s spirit was broken. He laid down on his side of the bed, but he never closed an eye again in sleep as long as that boy was with us. I dozed off for a while, but along toward sunup I remembered that Red Chief had said I was to be burned at the stake at the rising of the sun. I wasn’t nervous or afraid; but I sat up and lit my pipe and leaned against a rock.
“What you getting up so soon for, Sam?” asked Bill.
“Me?” says I. “Oh, I got a kind of a pain in my shoulder. I thought sitting up would rest it.”

“You’re a liar!” says Bill. “You’re afraid. You was to be burned at sunrise, and you was afraid he’d do it. And he would, too, if he could find a match. Ain’t it awful, Sam? Do you think anybody will pay out money to get a little imp like that back home?”
“Sure,” said I. “A rowdy kid like that is just the kind that parents dote on. Now, you and the Chief get up and cook breakfast, while I go up on the top of this mountain and reconnoitre.”

I went up on the peak of the little mountain and ran my eye over the contiguous vicinity. Over toward Summit I expected to see the sturdy yeomanry of the village armed with scythes and pitchforks beating the countryside for the dastardly kidnappers. But what I saw was a peaceful landscape dotted with one man ploughing with a dun mule. Nobody was dragging the creek; no couriers dashed hither and yon, bringing tidings of no news to the distracted parents. There was a sylvan attitude of somnolent sleepiness pervading that section of the external outward surface of Alabama that lay exposed to my view. “Perhaps,” says I to myself, “it has not yet been discovered that the wolves have borne away the tender lambkin from the fold. Heaven help the wolves!” says I, and I went down the mountain to breakfast.
When I got to the cave I found Bill backed up against the side of it, breathing hard, and the boy threatening to smash him with a rock half as big as a coconut.
“He put a red-hot boiled potato down my back,” explained Bill, “and then mashed it with his foot; and I boxed his ears. Have you got a gun about you, Sam?”
I took the rock away from the boy and kind of patched up the argument. “I’ll fix you,” says the kid to Bill. “No man ever yet struck the Red Chief but what he got paid for it. You better beware!”
After breakfast the kid takes a piece of leather with strings wrapped around it out of his pocket and goes outside the cave unwinding it.
“What’s he up to now?” says Bill, anxiously. “You don’t think he’ll run away, do you, Sam?”

“No fear of it,” says I. “He don’t seem to be much of a home body. But we’ve got to fix up some plan about the ransom. There don’t seem to be much excitement around Summit on account of his disappearance; but maybe they haven’t realized yet that he’s gone. His folks may think he’s spending the night with Aunt Jane or one of the neighbours. Anyhow, he’ll be missed today. Tonight we must get a message to his father demanding the two thousand dollars for his return.”

Just then we heard a kind of war-whoop, such as David might have emitted when he knocked out the champion Goliath. It was a sling that Red Chief had pulled out of his pocket, and he was whirling it around his head.

I dodged, and heard a heavy thud and a kind of a sigh from Bill, like a horse gives out when you take his saddle off. A niggerhead rock the size of an egg had caught Bill just behind his left ear. He loosened himself all over and fell in the fire across the frying pan of hot water for washing the dishes. I dragged him out and poured cold water on his head for half an hour.
By and by, Bill sits up and feels behind his ear and says: “Sam, do you know who my favourite Biblical character is?”
“Take it easy,” says I. “You’ll come to your senses presently.”
“King Herod,” says he. “You won’t go away and leave me here alone, will you, Sam?”
I went out and caught that boy and shook him until his freckles rattled.
“If you don’t behave,” says I, “I’ll take you straight home. Now, are you going to be good, or not?”

“I was only funning,” says he sullenly. “I didn’t mean to hurt Old Hank. But what did he hit me for? I’ll behave, Snake-eye, if you won’t send me home, and if you’ll let me play the Black Scout today.”

“I don’t know the game,” says I. “That’s for you and Mr. Bill to decide. He’s your playmate for the day. I’m going away for a while, on business. Now, you come in and make friends with him and say you are sorry for hurting him, or home you go, at once.”

I made him and Bill shake hands, and then I took Bill aside and told him I was going to Poplar Cove, a little village three miles from the cave, and find out what I could about how the kidnapping had been regarded in Summit. Also, I thought it best to send a peremptory letter to old man Dorset that day, demanding the ransom and dictating how it should be paid.

“You know, Sam,” says Bill, “I’ve stood by you without batting an eye in earthquakes, fire and flood⁠—in poker games, dynamite outrages, police raids, train robberies and cyclones. I never lost my nerve yet till we kidnapped that two-legged skyrocket of a kid. He’s got me going. You won’t leave me long with him, will you, Sam?”
“I’ll be back some time this afternoon,” says I. “You must keep the boy amused and quiet till I return. And now we’ll write the letter to old Dorset.”

Bill and I got paper and pencil and worked on the letter while Red Chief, with a blanket wrapped around him, strutted up and down, guarding the mouth of the cave. Bill begged me tearfully to make the ransom fifteen hundred dollars instead of two thousand. “I ain’t attempting,” says he, “to decry the celebrated moral aspect of parental affection, but we’re dealing with humans, and it ain’t human for anybody to give up two thousand dollars for that forty-pound chunk of freckled wildcat. I’m willing to take a chance at fifteen hundred dollars. You can charge the difference up to me.”
So, to relieve Bill, I acceded, and we collaborated a letter that ran this way:
Ebenezer Dorset, Esq.:

We have your boy concealed in a place far from Summit. It is useless for you or the most skilful detectives to attempt to find him. Absolutely, the only terms on which you can have him restored to you are these: We demand fifteen hundred dollars in large bills for his return; the money to be left at midnight tonight at the same spot and in the same box as your reply⁠—as hereinafter described. If you agree to these terms, send your answer in writing by a solitary messenger tonight at half-past eight o’clock. After crossing Owl Creek, on the road to Poplar Cove, there are three large trees about a hundred yards apart, close to the fence of the wheat field on the right-hand side. At the bottom of the fence-post, opposite the third tree, will be found a small pasteboard box.
The messenger will place the answer in this box and return immediately to Summit.
If you attempt any treachery or fail to comply with our demand as stated, you will never see your boy again.
If you pay the money as demanded, he will be returned to you safe and well within three hours. These terms are final, and if you do not accede to them no further communication will be attempted.
Two Desperate Men.
I addressed this letter to Dorset, and put it in my pocket. As I was about to start, the kid comes up to me and says:
“Aw, Snake-eye, you said I could play the Black Scout while you was gone.”
“Play it, of course,” says I. “Mr. Bill will play with you. What kind of a game is it?”
“I’m the Black Scout,” says Red Chief, “and I have to ride to the stockade to warn the settlers that the Indians are coming. I’m tired of playing Indian myself. I want to be the Black Scout.”
“All right,” says I. “It sounds harmless to me. I guess Mr. Bill will help you foil the pesky savages.”
“What am I to do?” asks Bill, looking at the kid suspiciously.
“You are the hoss,” says Black Scout. “Get down on your hands and knees. How can I ride to the stockade without a hoss?”
“You’d better keep him interested,” said I, “till we get the scheme going. Loosen up.”
Bill gets down on his all fours, and a look comes in his eye like a rabbit’s when you catch it in a trap.
“How far is it to the stockade, kid?” he asks, in a husky manner of voice.
“Ninety miles,” says the Black Scout. “And you have to hump yourself to get there on time. Whoa, now!”
The Black Scout jumps on Bill’s back and digs his heels in his side.
“For Heaven’s sake,” says Bill, “hurry back, Sam, as soon as you can. I wish we hadn’t made the ransom more than a thousand. Say, you quit kicking me or I’ll get up and warm you good.”

I walked over to Poplar Cove and sat around the post-office and store, talking with the chawbacons that came in to trade. One whiskerando says that he hears Summit is all upset on account of Elder Ebenezer Dorset’s boy having been lost or stolen. That was all I wanted to know. I bought some smoking tobacco, referred casually to the price of black-eyed peas, posted my letter surreptitiously and came away. The postmaster said the mail-carrier would come by in an hour to take the mail on to Summit.
When I got back to the cave Bill and the boy were not to be found. I explored the vicinity of the cave, and risked a yodel or two, but there was no response.
So I lighted my pipe and sat down on a mossy bank to await developments.

In about half an hour I heard the bushes rustle, and Bill wabbled out into the little glade in front of the cave. Behind him was the kid, stepping softly like a scout, with a broad grin on his face. Bill stopped, took off his hat and wiped his face with a red handkerchief. The kid stopped about eight feet behind him.

“Sam,” says Bill, “I suppose you’ll think I’m a renegade, but I couldn’t help it. I’m a grown person with masculine proclivities and habits of self-defense, but there is a time when all systems of egotism and predominance fail. The boy is gone. I have sent him home. All is off. There was martyrs in old times,” goes on Bill, “that suffered death rather than give up the particular graft they enjoyed. None of ’em ever was subjugated to such supernatural tortures as I have been. I tried to be faithful to our articles of depredation; but there came a limit.”
“What’s the trouble, Bill?” I asks him.

“I was rode,” says Bill, “the ninety miles to the stockade, not barring an inch. Then, when the settlers was rescued, I was given oats. Sand ain’t a palatable substitute. And then, for an hour I had to try to explain to him why there was nothin’ in holes, how a road can run both ways and what makes the grass green. I tell you, Sam, a human can only stand so much. I takes him by the neck of his clothes and drags him down the mountain. On the way he kicks my legs black-and-blue from the knees down; and I’ve got to have two or three bites on my thumb and hand cauterized.

“But he’s gone”⁠—continues Bill⁠—“gone home. I showed him the road to Summit and kicked him about eight feet nearer there at one kick. I’m sorry we lose the ransom; but it was either that or Bill Driscoll to the madhouse.”
Bill is puffing and blowing, but there is a look of ineffable peace and growing content on his rose-pink features.
“Bill,” says I, “there isn’t any heart disease in your family, is there?”
“No,” says Bill, “nothing chronic except malaria and accidents. Why?”
“Then you might turn around,” says I, “and have a took behind you.”

Bill turns and sees the boy, and loses his complexion and sits down plump on the round and begins to pluck aimlessly at grass and little sticks. For an hour I was afraid for his mind. And then I told him that my scheme was to put the whole job through immediately and that we would get the ransom and be off with it by midnight if old Dorset fell in with our proposition. So Bill braced up enough to give the kid a weak sort of a smile and a promise to play the Russian in a Japanese war with him as soon as he felt a little better.

I had a scheme for collecting that ransom without danger of being caught by counterplots that ought to commend itself to professional kidnappers. The tree under which the answer was to be left⁠—and the money later on⁠—was close to the road fence with big, bare fields on all sides. If a gang of constables should be watching for anyone to come for the note they could see him a long way off crossing the fields or in the road. But no, sirree! At half-past eight I was up in that tree as well hidden as a tree toad, waiting for the messenger to arrive.

Exactly on time, a half-grown boy rides up the road on a bicycle, locates the pasteboard box at the foot of the fence-post, slips a folded piece of paper into it and pedals away again back toward Summit.

I waited an hour and then concluded the thing was square. I slid down the tree, got the note, slipped along the fence till I struck the woods, and was back at the cave in another half an hour. I opened the note, got near the lantern and read it to Bill. It was written with a pen in a crabbed hand, and the sum and substance of it was this:
Two Desperate Men.

Gentlemen: I received your letter today by post, in regard to the ransom you ask for the return of my son. I think you are a little high in your demands, and I hereby make you a counter-proposition, which I am inclined to believe you will accept. You bring Johnny home and pay me two hundred and fifty dollars in cash, and I agree to take him off your hands. You had better come at night, for the neighbours believe he is lost, and I couldn’t be responsible for what they would do to anybody they saw bringing him back. Very respectfully,
Ebenezer Dorset.
“Great pirates of Penzance!” says I; “of all the impudent⁠—”
But I glanced at Bill, and hesitated. He had the most appealing look in his eyes I ever saw on the face of a dumb or a talking brute.

“Sam,” says he, “what’s two hundred and fifty dollars, after all? We’ve got the money. One more night of this kid will send me to a bed in Bedlam. Besides being a thorough gentleman, I think Mr. Dorset is a spendthrift for making us such a liberal offer. You ain’t going to let the chance go, are you?”
“Tell you the truth, Bill,” says I, “this little he ewe lamb has somewhat got on my nerves too. We’ll take him home, pay the ransom and make our getaway.”
We took him home that night. We got him to go by telling him that his father had bought a silver-mounted rifle and a pair of moccasins for him, and we were going to hunt bears the next day.

It was just twelve o’clock when we knocked at Ebenezer’s front door. Just at the moment when I should have been abstracting the fifteen hundred dollars from the box under the tree, according to the original proposition, Bill was counting out two hundred and fifty dollars into Dorset’s hand.

When the kid found out we were going to leave him at home he started up a howl like a calliope and fastened himself as tight as a leech to Bill’s leg. His father peeled him away gradually, like a porous plaster.
“How long can you hold him?” asks Bill.
“I’m not as strong as I used to be,” says old Dorset, “but I think I can promise you ten minutes.”
“Enough,” says Bill. “In ten minutes I shall cross the Central, Southern and Middle Western States, and be legging it trippingly for the Canadian border.”
And, as dark as it was, and as fat as Bill was, and as good a runner as I am, he was a good mile and a half out of Summit before I could catch up with him.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The Ransom of Red Chief is a story in which the supposed victim becomes the aggressor. Two small-time crooks, Sam, who narrates, and Bill Driscoll, need two thousand dollars to fund a fraudulent land scheme. They decide that kidnapping is easy money in a sleepy Alabama town called Summit, where there are no big-city reporters to stir up trouble. They choose the only son of a stern, tight-fisted local banker, Ebenezer Dorset, and expect his father to pay up at once.

The plan fails because the boy, who is ten and calls himself Red Chief, is delighted to be kidnapped. He thinks camping in a cave is the best thing that has ever happened to him. From the first moment he is the one in charge. When Bill offers him candy and a ride, the boy throws a piece of brick and hits him in the eye. In the cave he declares, "Ha! cursed paleface, do you dare to enter the camp of Red Chief, the terror of the plains?" and puts Bill in the role of Old Hank the Trapper, who is to be scalped at daybreak. Soon the scalping becomes real enough that Bill screams, and Sam is told he will be burned at the stake at sunrise. The two grown men, who think of themselves as dangerous criminals, are reduced to servants of a child's imagination.

What the story is really about is reversal. The reader expects crime to be frightening and the victim to be helpless. Henry turns every expectation upside down, so that the criminals are the ones in terror and the father is the one with all the power. The big joke arrives at the end, when Dorset sends a counter-offer. He will take his son back if the kidnappers pay him two hundred and fifty dollars. Bill, who has been ridden like a horse and hit with rocks and boiled potatoes, begs Sam to accept. They pay the ransom themselves, and when the boy realizes he is being left at home, he clings to Bill's leg, until his father peels him away "gradually, like a porous plaster."

There is a layer of social comedy as well. Henry invites us to notice how the two men talk. Sam's voice is an odd mixture of country slang and enormous, mock-important words. He calls the kidnapping a project of "philoprogenitiveness," a very grand word that means love of children, and Bill supposedly said they were acting "during a moment of temporary mental apparition," which is a misused phrase that tells you they are not as clever as they think. The language reveals the gap between how these men see themselves and what they are. Finally, the story is a quiet joke about parents. Everyone has met a child who exhausts adults. Dorset's refusal to pay is shocking at first, but it is also the most honest line in the story. He knows his son. The humor works because it touches something true about family life.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
As a piece of comic engineering, The Ransom of Red Chief is almost perfect, and as literature it has real limits. Both are worth saying. The strengths first. The central idea is simple and strong enough to carry the whole story without strain. A single reversal, the kidnapped child as tormentor, generates scene after scene of slapstick, and each escalation is a little funnier than the last. The boy's speeches are a delight. His long, rambling chatter at supper, jumping from possums to Jimmy Talbot's aunt's hens to whether oranges are round, captures exactly how a ten-year-old thinks, with no logic except enthusiasm. Henry also knows how much a reader can bear, and the story ends before the joke wears thin.

The narration is the second great strength. Sam is a delightful voice, boastful, pompous, and a little foolish. His comparisons are inventive, and often absurd. The boy "put up a fight like a welterweight cinnamon bear," and Bill's screams are "such as women emit when they see ghosts or caterpillars." Henry loves overblown vocabulary, and he uses it to puncture dignity rather than to display his own learning. The deliberately pompous phrases make a comic contrast with the childish chaos, and they fit a narrator who is trying to talk himself into believing he is a professional.

The pacing is also expert. The opening promises that the plan "looked like a good thing: but wait till I tell you." That sentence, a promise of a story told over a fence, sets the tone at once, and the story keeps the promise. The last scene, in which the kidnappers flee while the father holds the boy for ten minutes, ends on a perfectly timed image, Bill running a mile and a half before Sam catches up. Now the weaknesses. The story has very little interior life. The characters are cartoons, which is fine for comedy, but it means there is no depth to return to. Once you know the twist, there is not much to discover on a second reading, apart from enjoying the sentences. The long middle section, in which the boy tortures Bill, repeats a single joke in slightly different forms, and some readers feel the invention runs out.

There is also the matter of dated material. The Indian play-acting, with its "paleface" and "redskin" language, was a standard children's game in 1907, but it relies on stereotypes that we now recognize as crude. And the boy's cruelty, the hot potato and the case-knife at Bill's head, is played as harmless fun, which is a convention of slapstick, though a reader may notice how strange it is. Even so, the story's good humor and its tidy mechanism have kept it alive for over a century.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
O. Henry was already well known when The Ransom of Red Chief appeared in 1907. It came after The Gift of the Magi and the stories of The Four Million, and it was collected later in his book Whirligigs. His career had taken off quickly after he arrived in New York around 1902, and by his death in 1910 he was among the most widely read American short-story writers. This story, more than most, became a permanent part of his fame. Its impact is partly in its sheer circulation. For generations it has appeared in school textbooks and anthologies of humor, often as a first example of how a short story can build a joke from a reversal. It is also one of the stories people most easily retell from memory, because the premise can be summed up in a sentence. The kidnappers who pay the father to take the child back have become a familiar piece of popular culture.

The idea has been borrowed many times. The 1952 anthology film O. Henry's Full House, which brought several of his stories to the screen, included a version of Red Chief. Later comedies about incompetent kidnappers whose victim turns out to be unwanted, or impossible, owe an obvious debt, and the 1986 film Ruthless People is often mentioned as a story with a similar spirit, in which a husband would rather not have his wife returned. Whether that film borrowed directly or arrived at the idea on its own, the situation is clearly part of the same comic tradition. Television comedy has used the "kidnap the wrong person" plot over and over.

The story also helped define a style. Henry's approach, with a chatty narrator, wordplay, a surprise at the end, became a model for magazine fiction throughout the early twentieth century. Many writers of popular short stories imitated him, and the phrase "an O. Henry ending" entered the language for a sudden ironic reversal. The annual O. Henry Prize for short stories, begun in 1919, keeps his name alive in a more serious setting, though the prize is for a more literary kind of fiction than his own.

In the classroom, Red Chief remains useful because it is easy to see how it works. Teachers use it to explain irony, point of view, and exaggeration. Students who struggle with older texts often find this one accessible, because the humor is physical and the language, though old-fashioned, is lively. It is also frequently used to teach unreliable narrators, since Sam describes himself as a fearsome outlaw while behaving like a nervous employee. The effect on Henry's own legacy is large. When many people think of him, they think first of Magi, and then of this story. Together they show the two poles of his art, tender irony and broad comedy.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
What have people loved about The Ransom of Red Chief? Mostly, they love the fun of it. Readers of all ages have laughed at the picture of two grown crooks being outmatched by a ten-year-old with feathers in his red hair. The story is cheerfully on the side of the child, and it invites the reader to enjoy the chaos without worrying about who gets hurt. In a world of serious stories, a laugh this simple is a treasure.

Readers have also loved the voice. Sam's narration is a pleasure to hear, especially read aloud. His long, comic sentences, his exaggerations, and his solemn nonsense words give the story a rhythm that many readers say they remember long after the plot has faded. People quote phrases like "the minutest coin and himself were strangers" or "a sylvan attitude of somnolent sleepiness" for the same reason one quotes a good joke. It is verbal comedy of a kind that has become rare, a love of the sound of language for its own sake.

There is also a deep satisfaction in the idea that the clever are undone by the simple. Readers enjoy seeing criminals who think they are professionals brought low by a child. It resembles the pleasure of a fairy tale in which the giant is tricked by the small boy. And there is a little justice in it, since the kidnappers are punished by their own plan, not by the law. Nobody is really hurt, and the boy goes home, so the reader can laugh without guilt.

Many readers, especially young ones, love the boy himself. He is not a villain, only a child with an enormous imagination and no fear. His speeches are exactly what real children say, a mixture of questions and boasts that never stops. Parents and teachers often say they recognize him. A child who has been told that he is a nuisance can enjoy the fantasy of being so much of a nuisance that adults give up. Finally, the story is admired for its economy. In just a few pages, it sets up a plan, shows it going disastrously wrong, and ends with a perfect punchline. Many writers of humor have said they admire the way every detail serves the joke, from the hired buggy to the half-grown boy on a bicycle who delivers the father's reply. Readers sense that a skilled craftsman is at work, and trust him to carry them to the end.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
The Ransom of Red Chief has never been a critics' darling in the way that more serious fiction has, and the criticisms are worth understanding. The most common objection to O. Henry in general, and to this story in particular, is that it is mechanical. Critics of the next generation, who preferred the quiet, ambiguous endings of Chekhov or the realism of later American writers, often found Henry's neat twists artificial. His stories, they said, are built backward from the final surprise, and the characters are made to fit the plot. Red Chief shows this clearly. The characters exist to produce the joke, and little else about them is explored. By the middle of the twentieth century, many literary critics regarded him as a skilled entertainer and not a writer of first rank.

A related complaint is that his style is too showy. The big words, the puns, the elaborate similes can feel like a performance that never stops. Some readers find that the humor becomes tiresome when every sentence is trying to be clever. The story's habit of stopping to comment on itself, as when the narrator says "But wait till I tell you," can be seen as charming or as a little forced.

There is also a modern discomfort with certain details. The boy's pretend Indian identity relies on old stereotypes, and words like "redskin" are jarring now. Some teachers choose to discuss this with students directly, rather than skip the story. The violence in the story is another issue. The boy attacks Bill with a rock, a knife, and a hot potato, and the story presents all this as slapstick. In an age more alert to child safety and to the real horror of kidnapping, some readers find the premise uncomfortable. The story makes light of a crime that, in life, is among the most terrifying.

Others have criticized the comfortable social view behind the story. The only real authority is the rich man, who simply refuses to be pressured, and the poor crooks end up poorer. There is no sense that wealth might be questioned. Some readers see this as unadventurous, though others would reply that the story is a comedy, not a sermon. It is fair to say that most of the criticism concerns what the story is not, and very little is aimed at its comic effect, which has seldom been disputed.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
The Ransom of Red Chief belongs to the great American tradition of the tall tale and the humorous sketch. Its ancestors include Mark Twain, whose Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn feature boys who are far smarter and more mischievous than the adults around them, and who also play at pirates and Indians. The story's comic voice, that of a rough speaker who exaggerates and digresses, also draws on the frontier humorists of the nineteenth century, who told stories in dialect and relied on absurd comparisons. Henry took that spoken style and combined it with the polished surprise endings that magazine readers wanted.

There is also a link to the French writer Guy de Maupassant, whose short stories often end with an ironic twist. Henry was sometimes called the American Maupassant, though his tone is much lighter. Where Maupassant tends toward bitterness, Henry prefers kindness, and even his crooks are rather lovable. In this he is closer to Dickens, another writer who gave comic names and warm feelings to rogues. In the real world of 1907, the story had a topical edge. Kidnapping for ransom had been in the headlines in America, and a widely reported case in Omaha in 1900 is often mentioned as part of the atmosphere in which Henry wrote. Making a joke of the crime reflected a public curiosity about it, but it also suggests how sharply the story departs from reality.

Looking forward, the story is a forerunner of comedies about criminals who are not up to the job. From silent film slapstick to modern movies about bumbling thieves, the idea that crime is harder than it looks has been a reliable source of laughs. It also belongs to a long tradition of comedies about terrible children, from the Little Rascals to the mischievous boys of modern sitcoms. The story anticipates the later comic belief that children are the true force of nature in a household.

Among O. Henry's works, it sits beside the sentimental stories like The Gift of the Magi and The Last Leaf, and the sly urban tales like The Cop and the Anthem. It is among the broadest and least sentimental, a story that wins by cheerful nonsense. That range is part of why he remains a figure worth knowing. Why read it now? For one thing, it is still funny, and not many century-old comedies can say that. It is a model of how to tell a joke at story length. And its central point, that people who try to exploit others may find the tables turned, has a timeless appeal. It takes ten minutes to read, and most people finish it smiling.

stories.title: The Last Leaf
stories.author: O. Henry
stories.epigraph: “One morning the busy doctor invited Sue into the hallway with a shaggy, gray eyebrow.”
stories.keyContext: The Last Leaf is one of the best-loved short stories by O. Henry, the pen name of William Sydney Porter. It was published in 1907 and gathered in his collection The Trimmed Lamp. Porter lived a rough, restless life. He worked in Texas, spent time in prison, and then settled in New York, where he wrote stories about ordinary city people, clerks, shop girls, struggling artists, and drifters, with sympathy and a gift for the surprise ending. This story is set among poor young painters in Greenwich Village, at a time when pneumonia was a dreaded killer and doctors had few cures. A sick young woman decides she will die when the last leaf falls from the ivy outside her window. What happens next is quiet, moving, and a little miraculous. It is a story about hope, and about the idea that the greatest work of art may not be hanging in a gallery at all.
paragraphs: In a little district west of Washington Square the streets have run crazy and broken themselves into small strips called “places.” These “places” make strange angles and curves. One street crosses itself a time or two. An artist once discovered a valuable possibility in this street. Suppose a collector with a bill for paints, paper and canvas should, in traversing this route, suddenly meet himself coming back, without a cent having been paid on account!
