So, to quaint old Greenwich Village the art people soon came prowling, hunting for north windows and eighteenth-century gables and Dutch attics and low rents. Then they imported some pewter mugs and a chafing dish or two from Sixth Avenue, and became a “colony.”

At the top of a squatty, three-story brick Sue and Johnsy had their studio. “Johnsy” was familiar for Joanna. One was from Maine; the other from California. They had met at the table d’hôte of an Eighth Street “Delmonico’s,” and found their tastes in art, chicory salad and bishop sleeves so congenial that the joint studio resulted.

That was in May. In November a cold, unseen stranger, whom the doctors called Pneumonia, stalked about the colony, touching one here and there with his icy fingers. Over on the east side this ravager strode boldly, smiting his victims by scores, but his feet trod slowly through the maze of the narrow and moss-grown “places.”

Mr. Pneumonia was not what you would call a chivalric old gentleman. A mite of a little woman with blood thinned by California zephyrs was hardly fair game for the red-fisted, short-breathed old duffer. But Johnsy he smote; and she lay, scarcely moving, on her painted iron bedstead, looking through the small Dutch windowpanes at the blank side of the next brick house.
One morning the busy doctor invited Sue into the hallway with a shaggy, gray eyebrow.

“She has one chance in⁠—let us say, ten,” he said, as he shook down the mercury in his clinical thermometer. “And that chance is for her to want to live. This way people have of lining-up on the side of the undertaker makes the entire pharmacopeia look silly. Your little lady has made up her mind that she’s not going to get well. Has she anything on her mind?”
“She⁠—she wanted to paint the Bay of Naples some day,” said Sue.
“Paint?⁠—bosh! Has she anything on her mind worth thinking about twice⁠—a man, for instance?”
“A man?” said Sue, with a jew’sharp twang in her voice. “Is a man worth⁠—but, no, doctor; there is nothing of the kind.”

“Well, it is the weakness, then,” said the doctor. “I will do all that science, so far as it may filter through my efforts, can accomplish. But whenever my patient begins to count the carriages in her funeral procession I subtract 50 percent from the curative power of medicines. If you will get her to ask one question about the new winter styles in cloak sleeves I will promise you a one-in-five chance for her, instead of one in ten.”
After the doctor had gone Sue went into the workroom and cried a Japanese napkin to a pulp. Then she swaggered into Johnsy’s room with her drawing board, whistling ragtime.
Johnsy lay, scarcely making a ripple under the bedclothes, with her face toward the window. Sue stopped whistling, thinking she was asleep.

She arranged her board and began a pen-and-ink drawing to illustrate a magazine story. Young artists must pave their way to Art by drawing pictures for magazine stories that young authors write to pave their way to Literature.

As Sue was sketching a pair of elegant horseshow riding trousers and a monocle on the figure of the hero, an Idaho cowboy, she heard a low sound, several times repeated. She went quickly to the bedside.
Johnsy’s eyes were open wide. She was looking out the window and counting⁠—counting backward.
“Twelve,” she said, and a little later “eleven;” and then “ten,” and “nine;” and then “eight” and “seven,” almost together.

Sue looked solicitously out the window. What was there to count? There was only a bare, dreary yard to be seen, and the blank side of the brick house twenty feet away. An old, old ivy vine, gnarled and decayed at the roots, climbed halfway up the brick wall. The cold breath of autumn had stricken its leaves from the vine until its skeleton branches clung, almost bare, to the crumbling bricks.
“What is it, dear?” asked Sue.

“Six,” said Johnsy, in almost a whisper. “They’re falling faster now. Three days ago there were almost a hundred. It made my head ache to count them. But now it’s easy. There goes another one. There are only five left now.”
“Five what, dear. Tell your Sudie.”
“Leaves. On the ivy vine. When the last one falls I must go, too. I’ve known that for three days. Didn’t the doctor tell you?”

“Oh, I never heard of such nonsense,” complained Sue, with magnificent scorn. “What have old ivy leaves to do with your getting well? And you used to love that vine so, you naughty girl. Don’t be a goosey. Why, the doctor told me this morning that your chances for getting well real soon were⁠—let’s see exactly what he said⁠—he said the chances were ten to one! Why, that’s almost as good a chance as we have in New York when we ride on the street cars or walk past a new building. Try to take some broth now, and let Sudie go back to her drawing, so she can sell the editor man with it, and buy port wine for her sick child, and pork chops for her greedy self.”

“You needn’t get any more wine,” said Johnsy, keeping her eyes fixed out the window. “There goes another. No, I don’t want any broth. That leaves just four. I want to see the last one fall before it gets dark. Then I’ll go, too.”

“Johnsy, dear,” said Sue, bending over her, “will you promise me to keep your eyes closed, and not look out the window until I am done working? I must hand those drawings in by tomorrow. I need the light, or I would draw the shade down.”
“Couldn’t you draw in the other room?” asked Johnsy, coldly.
“I’d rather be here by you,” said Sue. “Besides I don’t want you to keep looking at those silly ivy leaves.”

“Tell me as soon as you have finished,” said Johnsy, closing her eyes, and lying white and still as a fallen statue, “because I want to see the last one fall. I’m tired of waiting. I’m tired of thinking. I want to turn loose my hold on everything, and go sailing down, down, just like one of those poor, tired leaves.”
“Try to sleep,” said Sue. “I must call Behrman up to be my model for the old hermit miner. I’ll not be gone a minute. Don’t try to move ’till I come back.”

Old Behrman was a painter who lived on the ground floor beneath them. He was past sixty and had a Michelangelo’s Moses beard curling down from the head of a satyr along the body of an imp. Behrman was a failure in art. Forty years he had wielded the brush without getting near enough to touch the hem of his Mistress’s robe. He had been always about to paint a masterpiece, but had never yet begun it. For several years he had painted nothing except now and then a daub in the line of commerce or advertising. He earned a little by serving as a model to those young artists in the colony who could not pay the price of a professional. He drank gin to excess, and still talked of his coming masterpiece. For the rest he was a fierce little old man, who scoffed terribly at softness in anyone, and who regarded himself as especial mastiff-in-waiting to protect the two young artists in the studio above.

Sue found Behrman smelling strongly of juniper berries in his dimly lighted den below. In one corner was a blank canvas on an easel that had been waiting there for twenty-five years to receive the first line of the masterpiece. She told him of Johnsy’s fancy, and how she feared she would, indeed, light and fragile as a leaf herself, float away when her slight hold upon the world grew weaker.
Old Behrman, with his red eyes, plainly streaming, shouted his contempt and derision for such idiotic imaginings.

“Vass!” he cried. “Is dere people in de world mit der foolishness to die because leafs dey drop off from a confounded vine? I haf not heard of such a thing. No, I will not bose as a model for your fool hermit-dunderhead. Vy do you allow dot silly pusiness to come in der prain of her? Ach, dot poor lettle Miss Johnsy.”

“She is very ill and weak,” said Sue, “and the fever has left her mind morbid and full of strange fancies. Very well, Mr. Behrman, if you do not care to pose for me, you needn’t. But I think you are a horrid old⁠—old flibbertigibbet.”

“You are just like a woman!” yelled Behrman. “Who said I will not bose? Go on. I come mit you. For half an hour I haf peen trying to say dot I am ready to bose. Gott! dis is not any blace in which one so goot as Miss Yohnsy shall lie sick. Some day I vill baint a masterpiece, and ve shall all go away. Gott! yes.”

Johnsy was sleeping when they went upstairs. Sue pulled the shade down to the windowsill, and motioned Behrman into the other room. In there they peered out the window fearfully at the ivy vine. Then they looked at each other for a moment without speaking. A persistent, cold rain was falling, mingled with snow. Behrman, in his old blue shirt, took his seat as the hermit-miner on an upturned kettle for a rock.
When Sue awoke from an hour’s sleep the next morning she found Johnsy with dull, wide-open eyes staring at the drawn green shade.
“Pull it up; I want to see,” she ordered, in a whisper.
Wearily Sue obeyed.

But, lo! after the beating rain and fierce gusts of wind that had endured through the livelong night, there yet stood out against the brick wall one ivy leaf. It was the last on the vine. Still dark green near its stem, but with its serrated edges tinted with the yellow of dissolution and decay, it hung bravely from a branch some twenty feet above the ground.
“It is the last one,” said Johnsy. “I thought it would surely fall during the night. I heard the wind. It will fall today, and I shall die at the same time.”
“Dear, dear!” said Sue, leaning her worn face down to the pillow, “think of me, if you won’t think of yourself. What would I do?”

But Johnsy did not answer. The lonesomest thing in all the world is a soul when it is making ready to go on its mysterious, far journey. The fancy seemed to possess her more strongly as one by one the ties that bound her to friendship and to earth were loosed.

The day wore away, and even through the twilight they could see the lone ivy leaf clinging to its stem against the wall. And then, with the coming of the night the north wind was again loosed, while the rain still beat against the windows and pattered down from the low Dutch eaves.
When it was light enough Johnsy, the merciless, commanded that the shade be raised.
The ivy leaf was still there.
Johnsy lay for a long time looking at it. And then she called to Sue, who was stirring her chicken broth over the gas stove.

“I’ve been a bad girl, Sudie,” said Johnsy. “Something has made that last leaf stay there to show me how wicked I was. It is a sin to want to die. You may bring me a little broth now, and some milk with a little port in it, and⁠—no; bring me a hand-mirror first, and then pack some pillows about me, and I will sit up and watch you cook.”
An hour later she said.
“Sudie, some day I hope to paint the Bay of Naples.”
The doctor came in the afternoon, and Sue had an excuse to go into the hallway as he left.

“Even chances,” said the doctor, taking Sue’s thin, shaking hand in his. “With good nursing you’ll win. And now I must see another case I have downstairs. Behrman, his name is⁠—some kind of an artist, I believe. Pneumonia, too. He is an old, weak man, and the attack is acute. There is no hope for him; but he goes to the hospital today to be made more comfortable.”
The next day the doctor said to Sue: “She’s out of danger. You’ve won. Nutrition and care now⁠—that’s all.”
And that afternoon Sue came to the bed where Johnsy lay, contentedly knitting a very blue and very useless woolen shoulder scarf, and put one arm around her, pillows and all.

“I have something to tell you, white mouse,” she said. “Mr. Behrman died of pneumonia today in the hospital. He was ill only two days. The janitor found him on the morning of the first day in his room downstairs helpless with pain. His shoes and clothing were wet through and icy cold. They couldn’t imagine where he had been on such a dreadful night. And then they found a lantern, still lighted, and a ladder that had been dragged from its place, and some scattered brushes, and a palette with green and yellow colors mixed on it, and⁠—look out the window, dear, at the last ivy leaf on the wall. Didn’t you wonder why it never fluttered or moved when the wind blew? Ah, darling, it’s Behrman’s masterpiece⁠—he painted it there the night that the last leaf fell.”

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The Last Leaf looks like a simple tale about a sick girl and a vine, but it is really about what keeps a person alive, and what a work of art can truly be for. The setting is a cramped corner of Greenwich Village, in the early twentieth century, where young painters rent cheap rooms. Two women, Sue and Johnsy, share a studio at the top of a brick building. In November, pneumonia moves through the neighborhood. Johnsy catches it, and the doctor tells Sue that her friend has a one-in-ten chance, and that the chance depends on whether she wants to live. Johnsy has given up. From her bed she counts the leaves falling from an old ivy vine on the wall opposite, and tells Sue, "When the last one falls I must go, too."

This is a familiar idea, and Henry knows it. People in the nineteenth century were fond of stories in which a sickly heroine's fate was tied to nature, as if her life were a flower or a leaf. Johnsy has absorbed that romantic picture and now believes it. Sue, who is practical and warm, tries to argue her out of it, and cannot.

The turning point comes through a third character, the old painter Behrman who lives downstairs. He is a failure. For forty years he has been about to paint a masterpiece, and the blank canvas in his room has been waiting twenty-five years for its first line. He drinks gin, grumbles in a thick German accent, and calls himself the protector of the two young women. When Sue tells him about Johnsy's fancy, he shouts that it is foolishness. But he is the one who takes it seriously. During a night of freezing rain and wind, the last leaf somehow does not fall. Johnsy, shamed by its stubborn courage, says "It is a sin to want to die," and begins to recover.

Then comes the reveal. Behrman has died of pneumonia, and the janitor found a lantern, a ladder, scattered brushes, and a palette with green and yellow paint. Sue tells Johnsy, "it's Behrman's masterpiece—he painted it there the night that the last leaf fell." The leaf on the wall was a painting, so true to life that it fooled a sick woman for two days, and its painter gave his own life for it. The deepest layer is the meaning of "masterpiece." Behrman spent his life talking about one, and when he finally makes it, it is not on canvas and no one will hang it in a museum. It is a single painted leaf, and it saves a life. The story suggests that art matters most when it does something, and that love can be a kind of craft.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
Is The Last Leaf as good as its reputation? In large part, yes, but with some honest reservations. The strongest thing about it is its emotional design. The story begins with comedy and a touch of mockery, with its description of crazy Greenwich Village streets and the cold figure of "Mr. Pneumonia" as a rough old gentleman who is not very chivalrous. Then it narrows to a bedroom, a window, a vine, and a dying girl, and the humor drains away just as the tension rises. The counting of the leaves, "Twelve," then "eleven," then "ten," is a simple device that creates real suspense. We are being told a clock is running down, and we know that something must change.

Behrman is the story's most vivid creation. In a few strokes Henry gives him a Michelangelo beard on an imp's body, a smell of juniper berries, and a comic accent, "Vass! Is dere people in de world mit der foolishness to die because leafs dey drop off from a confounded vine?" The roughness hides tenderness, and when he agrees to pose, he shouts, "Gott! dis is not any blace in which one so goot as Miss Yohnsy shall lie sick." We laugh at him, and then we are asked to honor him, which is a difficult trick.

The structure is clever, too. Henry keeps the secret from us and gives a fair set of clues, the cold night, the wind, the unmoving leaf, and then the doctor's remark that an old man downstairs named Behrman has acute pneumonia. The twist does not cheat, which is what a good twist should do. It explains everything that came before. But the story also has weaknesses. The plot depends on some convenient assumptions. Would a painted leaf, from a window twenty feet away, fool a sick woman for two full days, in daylight, as she stared at it? Henry hurries past the problem, and most readers accept it as part of the fairy-tale spell, but a skeptical reader may notice. The idea that a person's will to live can decide the outcome of pneumonia is the doctor's, and it sits uneasily with medical fact.

Some of the narration is also overwritten. Henry's decorative style, with phrases like the "red-fisted, short-breathed old duffer," can feel like a performance. The portrayal of Johnsy is rather thin. She is a passive figure who must be rescued by others, and we learn almost nothing about her except that she wants to paint the Bay of Naples. And the sacrifice of the old man to save the young woman is, frankly, sentimental. Still, the sentiment is earned by how little the story insists on it.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The Last Leaf appeared in The Trimmed Lamp in 1907, at the height of O. Henry's popularity. Within a few years he was dead, from cirrhosis, in 1910, but by then the story had begun its long life as one of his signature works. Along with The Gift of the Magi, it is the piece that readers most often name when they think of him. Its influence can be seen first in education. For more than a century, it has been a regular in school reading, partly because it is short and partly because it teaches so much so clearly: symbolism in the leaf, foreshadowing in the cold night, irony in the ending. Teachers use it to show how an object can carry a theme, and how a surprise can be prepared in advance. Many students encounter it as their first example of a twist ending that feels earned.

It has also been adapted many times. The 1952 anthology film O. Henry's Full House included a version of the story, with the cast including Anne Baxter and Jean Peters, among others, and it has appeared in television dramas, radio programs, and in stage and animated versions in many countries. The basic image has become so familiar that it has been borrowed, sometimes without credit, in all sorts of fiction about patients, hospitals, and magic tricks of hope. A story about a patient who believes in a sign, and a friend who quietly arranges for the sign to hold, has become a recognizable shape in popular storytelling.

The leaf itself has become a piece of general cultural shorthand. People speak of "the last leaf" as a symbol of a final hope, a last thread, or someone who hangs on when others have fallen. It is also associated with the idea that a small, loving deception can heal. Doctors and nurses sometimes cite it when talking about the power of hope in recovery, though that is a matter of folk wisdom more than science.

In Henry's own career, the story shows that he could do more than amuse. Much of his fame rests on his twist endings, but here the twist serves tenderness rather than a joke. It gave critics and readers a reason to take him seriously as a humane writer, one who understood poverty and failure from inside. Because he had himself known disgrace and hardship, the portrait of Behrman, a man whose life has not gone as planned but who still finds a way to be great, carries a personal weight.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers have loved The Last Leaf mainly because it moves them. Many people remember the first time they read it, usually in school, and the moment they realized what the last leaf really was. The ending is one of the most celebrated in short fiction because it makes the reader feel two things at once, relief that Johnsy lives and grief that Behrman does not. It is hard to get both so quickly in so few words.

They also love Behrman. Readers are drawn to the old failure who turns out to be a hero. He has the dignity of someone who has never been recognized, and the story gives him recognition at the cost of his life. The idea that a failed artist could, in one cold night, paint what he had been promising for forty years has an almost religious force. For anyone who has doubted their own talent, or watched a parent or teacher go unappreciated, it offers a deep consolation. A life is not wasted if it ends in one great act of love.

The friendship between Sue and Johnsy is another source of affection. Sue's loyalty, shown in her tears over the Japanese napkin and then her noisy whistling of ragtime as she walks into the sickroom, is a model of what it means to care for someone while pretending to be cheerful. Readers who have nursed a sick friend recognize that mixture of fear and false brightness at once. There is also a pleasure in the setting. Henry's Greenwich Village, with its crooked streets and struggling painters, is a charming little world, and the details, the chicory salad, the pewter mugs, the "squatty, three-story brick," make it vivid. Many readers say they would like to have visited that place.

Then there is the language of the ending. Its calm and simplicity affect readers deeply. Sue's last speech is not grand. She just says what happened, in plain words, and invites Johnsy to look out the window. Many writers have praised this restraint, because Henry could easily have ended with a flourish. Instead he lets the quiet fact do the work. Lastly, readers love that the story believes in hope. In a world in which pneumonia killed many, the idea that a person might be saved by seeing something brave is comforting, and that is part of why the story has been retold for so long.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
The Last Leaf has plenty of admirers, but it has also met reservations over the years, and they deserve a fair hearing. The most frequent criticism is sentimentality. Critics who prefer restraint have found the story too eager to bring tears. The dying heroine, the noble old drunk, the heroic sacrifice, and the miraculous recovery all follow patterns that were well worn by 1907. Some readers feel that Henry is manipulating them, arranging events so that the emotional payoff is guaranteed. A more demanding kind of fiction, they say, would have left Johnsy's recovery uncertain, or would have let death be less tidy and less meaningful. In a real hospital, a painted leaf does not save a life, and the story's comfort comes at the price of truth.

Related to that is the objection to the mechanism of the plot. As with much of Henry's work, the story is built around a surprise, and some critics say that the surprise matters more than the people. The idea that a woman could be fooled for two days by a painted leaf is difficult to believe, and the medical idea that a patient's despair decides the outcome of pneumonia is at best exaggerated. Henry rushes past these problems because he knows the reader wants the ending to work.

There are also some uncomfortable details of characterization. Behrman is a comic German immigrant, with a thick accent that Henry spells out phonetically, and the accent was a stock comic device of the time that can read as mockery. His drinking, his bluster, and his failure are all handled in a familiar way. And the story gives its female characters little to do beyond suffering and nursing, while the one man performs the great act. A modern reader may notice that the women are objects of rescue and that the man's sacrifice is what the story honors most.

Some readers have also pointed out a moral ambiguity that the story does not look at. Behrman is a man past sixty with, presumably, a weak constitution, and he climbs a ladder in a freezing storm to paint a leaf. The story praises him, but it does not ask whether he had other choices, such as getting Sue to help, or telling Johnsy the truth. It treats his death as noble and necessary, which is a romantic choice. Finally, there is the stylistic criticism that Henry's heavy ornament, the jokes in the narration and the literary asides, sometimes gets in the way of the emotion. Critics who prefer plainness find some of the early pages too busy. None of these objections have damaged the story's reputation, but they explain why it is admired more by general readers than by academic critics.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
The Last Leaf belongs to the tradition of local-color and urban sketches that flourished in American magazines around 1900, when writers discovered that ordinary city life, with its small tragedies and comedies, made good fiction. Henry's New York stories, collected in books like The Four Million, The Trimmed Lamp, and The Voice of the City, were the most popular of the kind. They gave voice to the shop clerks and out-of-work artists who filled the city but not, until then, its literature.

At a deeper level, the story descends from the Victorian tradition of the dying young person, which includes figures like Little Nell in Dickens's The Old Curiosity Shop, and the whole era's fascination with consumption and fading. Nature, in such stories, mirrors the heroine's fate. Henry takes that pattern and turns it upside down in a characteristic way. Instead of letting the heroine fade with the leaves, he lets a human hand intervene, which is both a rejection of fatalism and a tribute to the power of kindness. In this he is closer to the Dickens of A Christmas Carol than to the Dickens of Nell.

It also fits a larger theme in literature about the relationship between art and life. A painter who has failed all his life makes one image that is more alive than any he has ever made. There is an echo of the old legend of Pygmalion, the sculptor whose statue comes to life, and of countless stories about artists whose best work is a sacrifice. In this version, the work does not become alive. It makes someone else alive, which is a gentler twist on the idea.

Compared with other works about illness, such as Katherine Anne Porter's Pale Horse, Pale Rider, which treats the influenza epidemic with a far darker and more ambiguous eye, The Last Leaf is a story of consolation. It offers the hope that Porter withholds. Readers who want both kinds of truth will find that they complement each other. Among Henry's own stories, it pairs naturally with The Gift of the Magi, which also turns on sacrifice and a small object, and with The Cop and the Anthem, which has the same gentle eye for the poor of New York. All three show his belief that dignity can be found in unlikely places. Why read it now? Because its central question remains alive: what gives a person the will to go on? The story answers, with great simplicity, that sometimes it is a sign of courage from someone who loves you, and that such a gesture can matter more than a masterpiece in a museum. It takes only a few minutes to read, and it tends to stay with people for years.

stories.title: The Cop and the Anthem
stories.author: O. Henry
stories.epigraph: “On his bench in Madison Square Soapy moved uneasily.”
stories.keyContext: The Cop and the Anthem is a short story by O. Henry, the pen name of William Sydney Porter, first published in 1904 and later collected in The Four Million. That title was a playful answer to a snobbish phrase of the day that said only four hundred people in New York really mattered. Henry insisted the other millions mattered too. Porter had known hard times himself. He had worked in Texas, served a prison sentence for embezzlement, and then become the most popular storyteller in New York, writing about the poor, the odd, and the overlooked. This story follows a homeless man named Soapy as winter approaches. Oddly, all he wants is to get arrested, so he can spend the cold months in jail. It is funny and sharp, with an ending that is both ironic and surprisingly sad. Underneath the jokes is a question about how a society treats those at the bottom.
paragraphs: On his bench in Madison Square Soapy moved uneasily. When wild geese honk high of nights, and when women without sealskin coats grow kind to their husbands, and when Soapy moves uneasily on his bench in the park, you may know that winter is near at hand.

A dead leaf fell in Soapy’s lap. That was Jack Frost’s card. Jack is kind to the regular denizens of Madison Square, and gives fair warning of his annual call. At the corners of four streets he hands his pasteboard to the North Wind, footman of the mansion of All Outdoors, so that the inhabitants thereof may make ready.

Soapy’s mind became cognisant of the fact that the time had come for him to resolve himself into a singular Committee of Ways and Means to provide against the coming rigour. And therefore he moved uneasily on his bench.

The hibernatorial ambitions of Soapy were not of the highest. In them there were no considerations of Mediterranean cruises, of soporific Southern skies drifting in the Vesuvian Bay. Three months on the Island was what his soul craved. Three months of assured board and bed and congenial company, safe from Boreas and bluecoats, seemed to Soapy the essence of things desirable.

For years the hospitable Blackwell’s had been his winter quarters. Just as his more fortunate fellow New Yorkers had bought their tickets to Palm Beach and the Riviera each winter, so Soapy had made his humble arrangements for his annual hegira to the Island. And now the time was come. On the previous night three Sabbath newspapers, distributed beneath his coat, about his ankles and over his lap, had failed to repulse the cold as he slept on his bench near the spurting fountain in the ancient square. So the Island loomed big and timely in Soapy’s mind. He scorned the provisions made in the name of charity for the city’s dependents. In Soapy’s opinion the Law was more benign than Philanthropy. There was an endless round of institutions, municipal and eleemosynary, on which he might set out and receive lodging and food accordant with the simple life. But to one of Soapy’s proud spirit the gifts of charity are encumbered. If not in coin you must pay in humiliation of spirit for every benefit received at the hands of philanthropy. As Caesar had his Brutus, every bed of charity must have its toll of a bath, every loaf of bread its compensation of a private and personal inquisition. Wherefore it is better to be a guest of the law, which though conducted by rules, does not meddle unduly with a gentleman’s private affairs.

Soapy, having decided to go to the Island, at once set about accomplishing his desire. There were many easy ways of doing this. The pleasantest was to dine luxuriously at some expensive restaurant; and then, after declaring insolvency, be handed over quietly and without uproar to a policeman. An accommodating magistrate would do the rest.

Soapy left his bench and strolled out of the square and across the level sea of asphalt, where Broadway and Fifth Avenue flow together. Up Broadway he turned, and halted at a glittering café, where are gathered together nightly the choicest products of the grape, the silkworm and the protoplasm.

Soapy had confidence in himself from the lowest button of his vest upward. He was shaven, and his coat was decent and his neat black, ready-tied four-in-hand had been presented to him by a lady missionary on Thanksgiving Day. If he could reach a table in the restaurant unsuspected success would be his. The portion of him that would show above the table would raise no doubt in the waiter’s mind. A roasted mallard duck, thought Soapy, would be about the thing⁠—with a bottle of Chablis, and then Camembert, a demitasse and a cigar. One dollar for the cigar would be enough. The total would not be so high as to call forth any supreme manifestation of revenge from the café management; and yet the meat would leave him filled and happy for the journey to his winter refuge.

But as Soapy set foot inside the restaurant door the head waiter’s eye fell upon his frayed trousers and decadent shoes. Strong and ready hands turned him about and conveyed him in silence and haste to the sidewalk and averted the ignoble fate of the menaced mallard.
Soapy turned off Broadway. It seemed that his route to the coveted island was not to be an epicurean one. Some other way of entering limbo must be thought of.

At a corner of Sixth Avenue electric lights and cunningly displayed wares behind plate-glass made a shop window conspicuous. Soapy took a cobblestone and dashed it through the glass. People came running around the corner, a policeman in the lead. Soapy stood still, with his hands in his pockets, and smiled at the sight of brass buttons.
“Where’s the man that done that?” inquired the officer excitedly.
“Don’t you figure out that I might have had something to do with it?” said Soapy, not without sarcasm, but friendly, as one greets good fortune.

The policeman’s mind refused to accept Soapy even as a clue. Men who smash windows do not remain to parley with the law’s minions. They take to their heels. The policeman saw a man halfway down the block running to catch a car. With drawn club he joined in the pursuit. Soapy, with disgust in his heart, loafed along, twice unsuccessful.

On the opposite side of the street was a restaurant of no great pretensions. It catered to large appetites and modest purses. Its crockery and atmosphere were thick; its soup and napery thin. Into this place Soapy took his accusive shoes and telltale trousers without challenge. At a table he sat and consumed beefsteak, flapjacks, doughnuts and pie. And then to the waiter be betrayed the fact that the minutest coin and himself were strangers.
“Now, get busy and call a cop,” said Soapy. “And don’t keep a gentleman waiting.”
“No cop for youse,” said the waiter, with a voice like butter cakes and an eye like the cherry in a Manhattan cocktail. “Hey, Con!”

Neatly upon his left ear on the callous pavement two waiters pitched Soapy. He arose, joint by joint, as a carpenter’s rule opens, and beat the dust from his clothes. Arrest seemed but a rosy dream. The Island seemed very far away. A policeman who stood before a drug store two doors away laughed and walked down the street.

Five blocks Soapy travelled before his courage permitted him to woo capture again. This time the opportunity presented what he fatuously termed to himself a “cinch.” A young woman of a modest and pleasing guise was standing before a show window gazing with sprightly interest at its display of shaving mugs and inkstands, and two yards from the window a large policeman of severe demeanour leaned against a water plug.

It was Soapy’s design to assume the role of the despicable and execrated “masher.” The refined and elegant appearance of his victim and the contiguity of the conscientious cop encouraged him to believe that he would soon feel the pleasant official clutch upon his arm that would insure his winter quarters on the right little, tight little isle.

Soapy straightened the lady missionary’s ready-made tie, dragged his shrinking cuffs into the open, set his hat at a killing cant and sidled toward the young woman. He made eyes at her, was taken with sudden coughs and “hems,” smiled, smirked and went brazenly through the impudent and contemptible litany of the “masher.” With half an eye Soapy saw that the policeman was watching him fixedly. The young woman moved away a few steps, and again bestowed her absorbed attention upon the shaving mugs. Soapy followed, boldly stepping to her side, raised his hat and said:
“Ah there, Bedelia! Don’t you want to come and play in my yard?”

The policeman was still looking. The persecuted young woman had but to beckon a finger and Soapy would be practically en route for his insular haven. Already he imagined he could feel the cozy warmth of the station-house. The young woman faced him and, stretching out a hand, caught Soapy’s coat sleeve.
“Sure, Mike,” she said joyfully, “if you’ll blow me to a pail of suds. I’d have spoke to you sooner, but the cop was watching.”
With the young woman playing the clinging ivy to his oak Soapy walked past the policeman overcome with gloom. He seemed doomed to liberty.

At the next corner he shook off his companion and ran. He halted in the district where by night are found the lightest streets, hearts, vows and librettos. Women in furs and men in greatcoats moved gaily in the wintry air. A sudden fear seized Soapy that some dreadful enchantment had rendered him immune to arrest. The thought brought a little of panic upon it, and when he came upon another policeman lounging grandly in front of a transplendent theatre he caught at the immediate straw of “disorderly conduct.”
On the sidewalk Soapy began to yell drunken gibberish at the top of his harsh voice. He danced, howled, raved and otherwise disturbed the welkin.
The policeman twirled his club, turned his back to Soapy and remarked to a citizen.
“ ’Tis one of them Yale lads celebratin’ the goose egg they give to the Hartford College. Noisy; but no harm. We’ve instructions to lave them be.”

Disconsolate, Soapy ceased his unavailing racket. Would never a policeman lay hands on him? In his fancy the Island seemed an unattainable Arcadia. He buttoned his thin coat against the chilling wind.

In a cigar store he saw a well-dressed man lighting a cigar at a swinging light. His silk umbrella he had set by the door on entering. Soapy stepped inside, secured the umbrella and sauntered off with it slowly. The man at the cigar light followed hastily.
“My umbrella,” he said, sternly.
“Oh, is it?” sneered Soapy, adding insult to petit larceny. “Well, why don’t you call a policeman? I took it. Your umbrella! Why don’t you call a cop? There stands one on the corner.”
The umbrella owner slowed his steps. Soapy did likewise, with a presentiment that luck would again run against him. The policeman looked at the two curiously.

“Of course,” said the umbrella man⁠—“that is⁠—well, you know how these mistakes occur⁠—I⁠—if it’s your umbrella I hope you’ll excuse me⁠—I picked it up this morning in a restaurant⁠—If you recognise it as yours, why⁠—I hope you’ll⁠—”
“Of course it’s mine,” said Soapy, viciously.
The ex-umbrella man retreated. The policeman hurried to assist a tall blonde in an opera cloak across the street in front of a street car that was approaching two blocks away.

Soapy walked eastward through a street damaged by improvements. He hurled the umbrella wrathfully into an excavation. He muttered against the men who wear helmets and carry clubs. Because he wanted to fall into their clutches, they seemed to regard him as a king who could do no wrong.

At length Soapy reached one of the avenues to the east where the glitter and turmoil was but faint. He set his face down this toward Madison Square, for the homing instinct survives even when the home is a park bench.

But on an unusually quiet corner Soapy came to a standstill. Here was an old church, quaint and rambling and gabled. Through one violet-stained window a soft light glowed, where, no doubt, the organist loitered over the keys, making sure of his mastery of the coming Sabbath anthem. For there drifted out to Soapy’s ears sweet music that caught and held him transfixed against the convolutions of the iron fence.

The moon was above, lustrous and serene; vehicles and pedestrians were few; sparrows twittered sleepily in the eaves⁠—for a little while the scene might have been a country churchyard. And the anthem that the organist played cemented Soapy to the iron fence, for he had known it well in the days when his life contained such things as mothers and roses and ambitions and friends and immaculate thoughts and collars.

The conjunction of Soapy’s receptive state of mind and the influences about the old church wrought a sudden and wonderful change in his soul. He viewed with swift horror the pit into which he had tumbled, the degraded days, unworthy desires, dead hopes, wrecked faculties and base motives that made up his existence.

And also in a moment his heart responded thrillingly to this novel mood. An instantaneous and strong impulse moved him to battle with his desperate fate. He would pull himself out of the mire; he would make a man of himself again; he would conquer the evil that had taken possession of him. There was time; he was comparatively young yet; he would resurrect his old eager ambitions and pursue them without faltering. Those solemn but sweet organ notes had set up a revolution in him. Tomorrow he would go into the roaring downtown district and find work. A fur importer had once offered him a place as driver. He would find him tomorrow and ask for the position. He would be somebody in the world. He would⁠—
Soapy felt a hand laid on his arm. He looked quickly around into the broad face of a policeman.
“What are you doin’ here?” asked the officer.
“Nothin’,” said Soapy.
“Then come along,” said the policeman.
“Three months on the Island,” said the Magistrate in the Police Court the next morning.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
On the surface, The Cop and the Anthem is a comic story about a man who cannot get himself arrested. Underneath, it is a story about dignity, about how hard it is to climb out of poverty, and about a cruel irony in how the world works. Soapy is a homeless man who spends his days on a bench in Madison Square. When a dead leaf falls in his lap, which the narrator jokes is "Jack Frost's card," he knows winter is coming. Where wealthier New Yorkers buy tickets to Palm Beach or the Riviera, Soapy has a simpler plan. He wants "three months on the Island," meaning the jail on Blackwell's Island, with its guaranteed bed, meals, and company. The story's first joke is that jail is a kind of vacation, and the narrator treats it with a perfectly straight face.

Soapy refuses the charity that is on offer, and the reason is worth noticing. He says that "the gifts of charity are encumbered," and that if you do not pay in coin you must "pay in humiliation of spirit for every benefit received at the hands of philanthropy." The beds of charity come with a mandatory bath, and the loaf of bread with "a private and personal inquisition." He would rather be a guest of the law, which "does not meddle unduly with a gentleman's private affairs." This is both a joke and a real social observation. Help that comes with strings can feel worse than punishment, and a man with nothing may still cling to pride.

Then the comedy of failure begins. Soapy tries to be arrested over and over. He attempts to eat a fine meal he cannot pay for, but the head waiter throws him out before he sits down. He smashes a shop window, and the policeman simply assumes that no one who stayed behind could be the culprit. He eats a cheap dinner and cannot pay, and the waiters throw him onto the pavement. He pesters a young woman, and she cheerfully invites him to buy her a drink. He yells like a drunk, and the officer decides he is a harmless college boy. He steals an umbrella, and the owner apologizes. The world refuses to punish him exactly when he wants it.

Then comes the turn. Outside an old church, he hears an organ playing an anthem he once knew, "in the days when his life contained such things as mothers and roses and ambitions and friends and immaculate thoughts and collars." A sudden wave of shame and hope comes over him. He decides to find work the next day and make something of himself. And at that very moment a policeman puts a hand on his arm. "What are you doin' here?" "Nothin'." "Then come along." The next morning, the magistrate gives him three months on the Island. The meaning is the cruelty of timing. The law that ignored his crimes arrests him for doing nothing, at the instant he decides to be good.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
As craft, The Cop and the Anthem is among the most skilled of O. Henry's stories, though it is not without flaws. The best thing about it is the structure. The story is built on a pattern of repetition and variation, in which Soapy tries one method after another and fails in a different way each time. This is a classic comic form, and Henry handles it well. Each failure is shorter than the last, and each has its own small surprise, such as the young woman's "Sure, Mike, if you'll blow me to a pail of suds," or the policeman's remark that Soapy must be one of "them Yale lads celebratin'" after a game. The accumulation makes us laugh, and also makes us feel an odd pity, because we sense that Soapy is being refused not just jail but recognition. The world does not see him at all.

That is where the story gets its power. The final reversal works because everything before it has trained us to expect the opposite. We have watched a man try and fail to be arrested. When his heart changes and the policeman at last seizes him, the effect is of a joke that suddenly turns bitter. Henry gives us the hint with the single word "Tomorrow," and then the hand on the arm cuts it off in midsentence, with Soapy's thoughts left unfinished: "He would be somebody in the world. He would——" It is a beautiful touch, a sentence broken off, in the same way his hope is.

The voice is also a strength. Henry's narrator mixes high and low language in a way that mocks the pompous and cheers the humble. Describing a cheap restaurant whose "crockery and atmosphere were thick" while its "soup and napery thin," or calling the police "the law's minions," makes a little theater of every scene. The ornamental phrases keep a story about homelessness from becoming grim, yet the sadness is never completely forgotten.

There are weaknesses, however. The conversion in the church scene is a little too convenient. A man who has been joking and scheming for pages suddenly experiences a moral awakening because of a hymn, and the narrator describes it in a rush of conventional language, "the pit into which he had tumbled, the degraded days, unworthy desires, dead hopes." This is the most sentimental passage, and it can feel like a stage effect more than a real change of heart. Also, Henry's habit of coincidence is on full display. The timing of the arrest is so neat that it seems arranged by the author rather than by life. Still, the neatness is partly the point. The cruelty of the ending seems to be arranged by a cold universe, and the cold universe is the real target. The balance of jokes and sorrow is difficult, and Henry brings it off in a very short space.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The Cop and the Anthem first appeared in 1904, and was gathered in The Four Million in 1906, the book that made O. Henry a national figure. The book's title was a deliberate answer to a society phrase of the time, the "Four Hundred," which referred to the elite of New York. Henry argued that the real city was the millions of ordinary people, and this story is a clear example of what he meant. Its first impact was on Henry's own career. The story helped establish the type of tale for which he became known, the New York sketch that mixes comedy, social observation, and an ironic final twist. Its success contributed to his reputation as a chronicler of the city's poor. He went on to publish several books and write for newspapers until his death in 1910, and this story remained one of his most reprinted.

It has had a long afterlife in schools. Because it is short, funny, and rich in irony, it is a standard for teaching how a story can turn on a twist. Teachers also use it to discuss social class, poverty, and the justice system, since the story raises serious questions beneath its humor. Students often respond to Soapy's predicament with surprising feeling, and many remember the broken sentence at the end.

The story has also been adapted. The 1952 film O. Henry's Full House included a version, with the great actor Charles Laughton as Soapy and a young Marilyn Monroe in a small part, and it has been performed on radio and stage and in other languages. Laughton's performance, in particular, is often remembered by classic film fans. The story's plot has also been borrowed in sitcom episodes and cartoons, wherever a character tries desperately to be arrested or evicted and the world refuses to cooperate.

Beyond adaptations, the story has become part of the way people talk about irony. The notion of a man being punished at the moment he turns good is a recognizable image, and writers on law and social policy sometimes mention it when discussing how institutions treat the poor. Also, the question the story raises, about whether charity humiliates and whether jail is better, has not disappeared. In a world where homelessness remains a serious problem, a story that treats a homeless man as a person, not a statistic, has not lost its relevance. In short, the story's impact is partly literary and partly moral. It helped fix a style, and it kept alive a point of view, that of the ordinary person, that popular fiction sometimes forgets.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers have loved The Cop and the Anthem for several connected reasons. The first is plain enjoyment. The story is funny, and it stays funny. The parade of failed attempts at arrest is a delight, and many readers recall particular moments, the waiter with "an eye like the cherry in a Manhattan cocktail," the policeman who waves off the shouting as college high spirits, the woman who answers Soapy's pickup line by cheerfully accepting. The jokes are gentle, and they never make fun of Soapy himself in a cruel way. We laugh with a kind of fondness, as we would at a friend.

Readers also love the humanity of the main character. Soapy is a bum, a petty thief, and a bit of a faker, and yet he has a certain pride and wit. His philosophy of charity, that it costs a man his self-respect, strikes many readers as quietly true. His gloomy comedy gives him a style of his own. When the hymn reaches him, readers feel the force of his shame and hope, because Henry has taken the trouble to make him real. Many say that they suddenly stop laughing at the church scene, which is a sign of how well the story shifts its mood.

Another thing people admire is the economy and surprise of the ending. Many readers say that the ending hit them like a small shock, and they remember it for years. The broken sentence, "He would——," seems to many readers like one of the best uses of an interrupted thought in short fiction. It leaves a feeling of loss, and also a sense of the world's indifference.

There is also admiration for how the story treats poverty. Henry was writing at a time when many popular stories treated the poor as comic types or moral warnings. Here the poor man is the center, with his own reasons and his own dreams, and the powerful are shown as blind, not wicked. Readers who care about social justice find this surprisingly modern. Finally, readers love the music. The anthem, never named, is a clever choice, since it lets each reader imagine the tune that would stop them in their tracks. The scene's images, the moon, the sleepy sparrows, the iron fence, create a short, quiet pause in a noisy story. It is a moment of grace, even though the story cannot give it a happy outcome.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Even a favorite story draws objections, and The Cop and the Anthem has attracted some. The most common is the charge of sentimentality, which is made against Henry in general. The church scene in particular has been criticized as too sudden and too conventional. Soapy's conversion, brought about by an organ hymn, relies on a Victorian belief that a good memory or a good melody can awaken the soul. Critics who prefer the realism that came after Henry's day find this old-fashioned. They say it is more a stage device than a believable change.

Another criticism is that the story is more about its twist than about its people. Like much of Henry's work, it is built to arrive at one ironic moment, and some readers feel the characters are made to fit it. Soapy is vivid, but we learn nothing about how he came to be homeless, what he did before, or why he cannot find work. The story is not curious about causes, and a more serious social writer might have been. It is a comedy of surfaces, and some readers say that its sympathy for the poor is real but shallow.

There is also a point about politics. The story's picture of the poor is warm, but it does not call for change. The law is presented as an indifferent machine, charity as an insult, and the only escape is private will. Critics on the left have sometimes argued that this is a comfortable kind of compassion, one that invites pity but not action. Readers who are sensitive about such matters may notice that the story's irony holds its audience at a safe distance from the problem. Other complaints are about coincidence. It is rather convenient that the policeman should appear at the exact moment of Soapy's conversion. A skeptical reader might say that Henry has arranged life so that his joke can land. Defenders reply that this is the nature of ironic fiction, and that the coincidence is the story's point.

Finally, a few readers have noticed unattractive details in the way minor figures are drawn, such as the broad ethnic accent in the policeman's voice, or the story's casual use of the idea of a "masher," a man who bothers women on the street. These reflect the manners of 1904, and they can jar. Some also find that Soapy's treatment of the young woman, whom he pesters in the hope of being arrested, is not much examined by the narrator. None of this has hurt the story's standing, but it shows where the story is open to challenge.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
The Cop and the Anthem belongs to the tradition of the urban sketch, a form that grew in the late nineteenth century alongside the newspapers and magazines of big American cities. Writers like Stephen Crane, in Maggie, and Jacob Riis, in How the Other Half Lives, had shown the world of the poor in New York, one with stark realism and the other with documentary photographs. Henry's approach was softer, a mixture of humor and sympathy. He did not argue, but invited the reader to like the people he described.

Its other ancestors are the picaresque tradition, which goes back centuries and follows a lovable rogue through a series of scrapes, and the comic literature of poverty, including Dickens, who often placed warmth and wit among the destitute. Soapy is a distant cousin of Dickens's Mr. Micawber, a man who gets by on language and hope. There is also a link to the French tradition of the short story with a final twist, perfected by Guy de Maupassant, though Henry's version is warmer.

Looking forward, the story is part of a long line of tales about the cruelty of timing and the irony of institutions. One can see its kinship with stories in which a man tries to do wrong and is thwarted, or does right and is punished, from Kafka's absurd trials to modern comedies of bureaucracy. In a gentler way, it anticipates the point of many later social comedies, that the system does not respond to people on the basis of their needs. It should also be read alongside Henry's own life. He knew prison from the inside, and he knew how a man's past could follow him. The idea of a man who wants to be in jail, then is jailed for the wrong reason, carries the shadow of a writer who had learned that the law is blind to a person's inner life. That personal weight, never stated, gives the story a depth that its jokes might suggest it lacks.

Among Henry's own work, it sits close to The Gift of the Magi and The Last Leaf, with the same tenderness for the poor, and close to The Ransom of Red Chief, with its comic exaggeration. It mixes both modes, and may be the best single example of his range. Why read it today? Because homelessness, charity, and the ways society handles its poorest members are still pressing questions. The story's central insight, that dignity matters as much as shelter, is one that policymakers and ordinary people still struggle to learn. And because, in a few pages, it makes the reader laugh, and then leaves a small silence behind, which is a rare and valuable thing.

stories.title: After Twenty Years
stories.author: O. Henry
stories.epigraph: “Until five years ago,” said the policeman. “It was torn down then.”
stories.keyContext: After Twenty Years is a very short story by O. Henry, the pen name of William Sydney Porter, published in 1906 and later collected in a book of city stories called The Voice of the City. Porter knew his subject. He had lived in Texas, fled the country when he was accused of embezzling from a bank, returned home, and served time in prison, so the questions of law, loyalty, and second chances were not abstract to him. He then became one of the most popular storytellers in America, famous for tales with a surprise at the end. This one takes place on a single chilly night on a New York street, where a man waits in a doorway for an old friend he promised to meet twenty years ago. It runs only a few minutes, and what it says about friendship and duty is more complicated than it first appears.
paragraphs: The policeman on the beat moved up the avenue impressively. The impressiveness was habitual and not for show, for spectators were few. The time was barely 10 o’clock at night, but chilly gusts of wind with a taste of rain in them had well nigh de-peopled the streets.

Trying doors as he went, twirling his club with many intricate and artful movements, turning now and then to cast his watchful eye adown the pacific thoroughfare, the officer, with his stalwart form and slight swagger, made a fine picture of a guardian of the peace. The vicinity was one that kept early hours. Now and then you might see the lights of a cigar store or of an all-night lunch counter; but the majority of the doors belonged to business places that had long since been closed.

When about midway of a certain block the policeman suddenly slowed his walk. In the doorway of a darkened hardware store a man leaned, with an unlighted cigar in his mouth. As the policeman walked up to him the man spoke up quickly.

“It’s all right, officer,” he said, reassuringly. “I’m just waiting for a friend. It’s an appointment made twenty years ago. Sounds a little funny to you, doesn’t it? Well, I’ll explain if you’d like to make certain it’s all straight. About that long ago there used to be a restaurant where this store stands⁠—‘Big Joe’ Brady’s restaurant.”
“Until five years ago,” said the policeman. “It was torn down then.”

The man in the doorway struck a match and lit his cigar. The light showed a pale, square-jawed face with keen eyes, and a little white scar near his right eyebrow. His scarfpin was a large diamond, oddly set.

“Twenty years ago tonight,” said the man, “I dined here at ‘Big Joe’ Brady’s with Jimmy Wells, my best chum, and the finest chap in the world. He and I were raised here in New York, just like two brothers, together. I was eighteen and Jimmy was twenty. The next morning I was to start for the West to make my fortune. You couldn’t have dragged Jimmy out of New York; he thought it was the only place on earth. Well, we agreed that night that we would meet here again exactly twenty years from that date and time, no matter what our conditions might be or from what distance we might have to come. We figured that in twenty years each of us ought to have our destiny worked out and our fortunes made, whatever they were going to be.”
“It sounds pretty interesting,” said the policeman. “Rather a long time between meets, though, it seems to me. Haven’t you heard from your friend since you left?”

“Well, yes, for a time we corresponded,” said the other. “But after a year or two we lost track of each other. You see, the West is a pretty big proposition, and I kept hustling around over it pretty lively. But I know Jimmy will meet me here if he’s alive, for he always was the truest, stanchest old chap in the world. He’ll never forget. I came a thousand miles to stand in this door tonight, and it’s worth it if my old partner turns up.”
The waiting man pulled out a handsome watch, the lids of it set with small diamonds.
“Three minutes to ten,” he announced. “It was exactly ten o’clock when we parted here at the restaurant door.”
“Did pretty well out West, didn’t you?” asked the policeman.

“You bet! I hope Jimmy has done half as well. He was a kind of plodder, though, good fellow as he was. I’ve had to compete with some of the sharpest wits going to get my pile. A man gets in a groove in New York. It takes the West to put a razor-edge on him.”
The policeman twirled his club and took a step or two.
“I’ll be on my way. Hope your friend comes around all right. Going to call time on him sharp?”
“I should say not!” said the other. “I’ll give him half an hour at least. If Jimmy is alive on earth he’ll be here by that time. So long, officer.”
“Good night, sir,” said the policeman, passing on along his beat, trying doors as he went.

There was now a fine, cold drizzle falling, and the wind had risen from its uncertain puffs into a steady blow. The few foot passengers astir in that quarter hurried dismally and silently along with coat collars turned high and pocketed hands. And in the door of the hardware store the man who had come a thousand miles to fill an appointment, uncertain almost to absurdity, with the friend of his youth, smoked his cigar and waited.
About twenty minutes he waited, and then a tall man in a long overcoat, with collar turned up to his ears, hurried across from the opposite side of the street. He went directly to the waiting man.
“Is that you, Bob?” he asked, doubtfully.
“Is that you, Jimmy Wells?” cried the man in the door.

“Bless my heart!” exclaimed the new arrival, grasping both the other’s hands with his own. “It’s Bob, sure as fate. I was certain I’d find you here if you were still in existence. Well, well, well!⁠—twenty years is a long time. The old restaurant’s gone, Bob; I wish it had lasted, so we could have had another dinner there. How has the West treated you, old man?”
“Bully; it has given me everything I asked it for. You’ve changed lots, Jimmy. I never thought you were so tall by two or three inches.”
“Oh, I grew a bit after I was twenty.”
“Doing well in New York, Jimmy?”
“Moderately. I have a position in one of the city departments. Come on, Bob; we’ll go around to a place I know of, and have a good long talk about old times.”

The two men started up the street, arm in arm. The man from the West, his egotism enlarged by success, was beginning to outline the history of his career. The other, submerged in his overcoat, listened with interest.
At the corner stood a drug store, brilliant with electric lights. When they came into this glare each of them turned simultaneously to gaze upon the other’s face.
The man from the West stopped suddenly and released his arm.
“You’re not Jimmy Wells,” he snapped. “Twenty years is a long time, but not long enough to change a man’s nose from a Roman to a pug.”

“It sometimes changes a good man into a bad one,” said the tall man. “You’ve been under arrest for ten minutes, ‘Silky’ Bob. Chicago thinks you may have dropped over our way and wires us she wants to have a chat with you. Going quietly, are you? That’s sensible. Now, before we go on to the station here’s a note I was asked to hand you. You may read it here at the window. It’s from Patrolman Wells.”
The man from the West unfolded the little piece of paper handed him. His hand was steady when he began to read, but it trembled a little by the time he had finished. The note was rather short.

Bob: I was at the appointed place on time. When you struck the match to light your cigar I saw it was the face of the man wanted in Chicago. Somehow I couldn’t do it myself, so I went around and got a plainclothes man to do the job.
Jimmy.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
After Twenty Years is a story built on one night and one conversation, and its meaning rests on a question it asks quietly: what do you owe a friend when you also owe something to the law?

The story begins with a patrolman walking his beat in the cold, trying doors and twirling his club. In the doorway of a darkened hardware store, he finds a man waiting with an unlit cigar. The man explains that twenty years ago, a restaurant stood here, and that he and his best friend, Jimmy Wells, promised to meet at this spot, at ten o'clock, exactly twenty years later, "no matter what our conditions might be or from what distance we might have to come." He has come a thousand miles. He is prosperous, with a diamond in his scarf pin and a watch with diamonds on its lid, and he speaks with the loud confidence of a man who has made his pile out West. Jimmy, he admits, was always "a kind of plodder," a good fellow who would never have the sharp wits needed to succeed.

The patrolman listens, chats, and moves on. A little later, a tall man in a long overcoat arrives, greets the waiting man warmly, takes his arm, and starts to walk him toward a place where they can talk. Then, under the bright electric light of a drugstore, the man from the West stops. "You're not Jimmy Wells," he snaps. The tall man replies that he is a plainclothes officer, that the man is under arrest, and that Chicago wants a word with him. He hands over a note. It reads, "I was at the appointed place on time. When you struck the match to light your cigar I saw it was the face of the man wanted in Chicago. Somehow I couldn't do it myself, so I went around and got a plainclothes man to do the job. Jimmy."

The reader, in a moment, realizes the truth. The patrolman at the start was Jimmy Wells himself. He had stood and talked with his old friend, listened to him brag, and said nothing. The story's emotional core is in that one silent encounter, and in the sentence "Somehow I couldn't do it myself." The layers beneath this are what give the story its power. Bob, who thought Jimmy a plodder, is outdone by him in both honesty and character. Jimmy kept the promise, and he also did his duty, and he did it with a conscience. He does not hide behind the law, but he does not betray it either. The line "It sometimes changes a good man into a bad one," spoken by the plainclothes man in answer to Bob's complaint about his nose, is a sharp bit of irony, for it speaks of what twenty years did to Bob, and only by implication of what it did not do to Jimmy.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
Judged purely as a piece of craft, After Twenty Years is admirably compact, and it is also a little too neat. It is worth looking at both sides.

The strengths are plain. The story does a great deal in very little space, around twelve hundred words, and every detail is useful. The opening description of the patrolman, with his "slight swagger" and his twirling club, seems at first to be scene-setting, and only on a second reading do we realize that Henry is introducing a character in disguise. The little clues, such as the policeman's remark that the restaurant was torn down "five years ago," or his question, "Did pretty well out West, didn't you?" are fair signs for an attentive reader. Bob himself gives away every detail needed to identify him, the scar near his right eyebrow, the odd diamond, the cigar and match, and he does it out of pure vanity. The final twist does not cheat. It is built from what we have already been given.

The writing has a pleasing plainness. Unlike some of Henry's more ornamental stories, this one keeps its language cleaner, and the cold, windy atmosphere, the rising wind and "fine, cold drizzle," supports the tone of waiting. The ending, with the note, is economical and moving. Jimmy never explains himself. He says only that he could not do it. That restraint is what makes it work. Yet the story has weaknesses. It is, in the end, a sketch more than a story. The two men are seen almost entirely from outside, and Bob is a rather one-dimensional braggart. We never learn what crime he committed, only that Chicago wants him. We know little about Jimmy except through one note. The moral conflict is stated rather than explored, and a reader who wishes to feel what it cost Jimmy to act may feel short-changed.

There are also plausibility problems. Would a man wanted by the police wait for twenty years in the hope of seeing a friend, and at a fixed place where the law could easily find him? Would Jimmy, who recognized him, not have simply made the arrest on the spot, or at least warned him, rather than hurrying off to find a plainclothes officer, which allows twenty minutes for the fugitive to flee? And is it believable that Bob chats face to face with a patrolman and never suspects it might be the boyhood friend he came a thousand miles to see? Henry is counting on the reader to accept these things for the sake of the story's emotional design. These are small matters beside the story's real accomplishment, which is to leave a reader with a silence and a feeling.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
After Twenty Years was published in 1906, when O. Henry was at the height of his popularity and writing steadily for New York newspapers and magazines, and it was later collected in The Voice of the City, a book of New York tales. The story did not become as famous as The Gift of the Magi, but it grew steadily as a favorite of schools and anthologies, and it is now among the most frequently reprinted short stories in English.

Its biggest impact has been in the classroom. Teachers choose it because it is short enough to read in a single period, and because it demonstrates several important ideas at once. It is a textbook example of dramatic irony, in which the reader understands something the character does not. It shows how a surprise ending can be prepared by fair clues. It presents a moral dilemma that students can debate, whether loyalty to a friend or duty to the law should come first. Many English teachers use it to teach inference, asking students to go back through the story and find the signs that the first policeman was Jimmy.

It has also been adapted. The story has been dramatized on radio, in television anthology series, and in short films and student productions in several countries. Its basic situation, in which one friend discovers that the other is on the wrong side of the law, has been repeated in countless crime stories and films, from police dramas in which an officer must arrest a childhood friend to novels about old companions who find themselves on opposite sides. The detail of an appointment kept after many years is a familiar romantic device, and Henry's version, with its dark twist, may have helped make that device a staple of fiction.

In terms of Henry's reputation, the story shows a harder, more severe side of his work. Much of his fame came from sentimental tales of sacrifice and from comic romps. This one is crisp, short, and morally serious, and it suggests that he could write with discipline when he wished. It also reflects the experience of a man who had himself been on the wrong side of the law, and who understood what it meant to be pursued and to be judged. The phrase "O. Henry ending" is associated with stories like this one, and it has become a common way to describe any narrative that closes with a sharp reversal. Even people who have never read him use it. After Twenty Years is one of the pieces that put the phrase into circulation, along with a general expectation that a short story should end with a surprise. That expectation, good or bad, has shaped generations of short fiction.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
What have readers loved about After Twenty Years? First, they love the ending. Many people recall the moment when "You're not Jimmy Wells" is spoken, and the gradual unfolding of the truth. The reveal works because it makes the reader reinterpret the whole story. The patrolman, who seemed a mere background figure, becomes the center. Few endings in short fiction manage to reverse the meaning of what came before so completely and so fairly, and readers often say that they went back and read the story again at once, in order to see how it was done.

They also love the emotional complexity. Readers admire Jimmy because he does not do the easy thing. He could have turned a blind eye, or he could have made the arrest himself without feeling anything. Instead he does his duty in a way that shows his love. The idea that mercy and justice can coexist, that a man can be loyal and honest at the same time, has a moving simplicity. Many readers have said that the note, with its brief confession, is among the most affecting passages in Henry's work, precisely because it explains so little.

Another source of pleasure is the atmosphere. The night, the drizzle, the empty street, the policeman's slow walk, all create a mood of loneliness and anticipation. Readers who enjoy a story that has a strong sense of place often cite this one. It has the feel of an old black-and-white film, and it is easy to picture.

People also respond to the theme of time. Twenty years is long enough for a boy to become a stranger, and the story plays on the shock of meeting someone you thought you knew. Readers in middle age sometimes say that the story struck them differently than it did in school, because they now know how much a person can change, and how impossible it is to keep a youthful promise exactly as it was made. The pleasure, then, is partly one of recognition. Finally, many appreciate how short it is. It tells its whole story in the time it takes to drink a cup of coffee. Readers often praise Henry's economy and say that the story demonstrates what the short form can do. For many people, it is the first story that made them realize how much can be said in a few pages.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Despite its popularity, After Twenty Years has been criticized on several grounds. The commonest complaint is that it is too contrived. Critics have pointed out that the story depends on a long series of coincidences and conveniences. The two friends happen to choose a spot that later becomes a policeman's beat. The policeman happens to be the very friend. The friend happens to recognize the fugitive from his description. And the fugitive, a man wanted by the police, happens to walk into a trap through his own sentiment. Those who prefer fiction that grows from character rather than design say that Henry is working too hard to produce his surprise, and that the result feels more like a clever puzzle than a human event.

A second line of criticism concerns characterization. Bob is a thin figure, a boastful man defined by his diamonds and his pride, and some readers feel that Henry has made it too easy for us to accept his arrest. We are not told what Bob did, and we are given little reason to care about him except as a foil. Jimmy, for his part, barely speaks as a character. The moral weight of the story rests on a single note, and a demanding reader might wish for more of the struggle behind it.

There is also a moral objection. Some readers dislike Jimmy's decision, finding it either cold or cowardly. By sending someone else to do the arrest, he avoids the difficult confrontation, and one might argue that he deceives his friend twice, first by standing silently beside him and then by letting a stranger take his place. The note presents this as an act of feeling, but it can also be read as an evasion. Others argue the opposite, that he should have let Bob go, and that loyalty to a friend ought to outweigh the law. Henry does not settle the debate, which some find admirable and others find evasive.

Finally, a few readers have found the story slight, a trick without much substance. In comparison with Henry's more complex pieces, it can seem small. The prose, though clear, has little of the humor and richness that characterize his best work. And some have noted that the portrait of the West as a place where sharp wits get rich, while the East breeds plodders, is a stock idea of the period that does not stand up to much thought. Even so, these complaints rarely lessen the story's effect. They tend to come from readers who admire it but wish it were something else.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
After Twenty Years belongs to the tradition of the short story with a twist, which was brought to its highest polish in the late nineteenth century by the French writer Guy de Maupassant, whose stories often turn on a sudden reversal, and by American magazine writers who adapted the method for a mass audience. Henry was the supreme American master of the form. His surprises were seldom cruel, and often tender, and the best of them, like this one, made the reader feel as well as gasp. The story is also part of the literature of the city. In the early 1900s, American writers began to explore urban life with fresh attention, and Henry's New York stories, with their policemen, clerks, and drifters, were among the most popular examples. The man on the beat is a familiar figure of that world, and Henry treats him with dignity, as someone who sees much and says little. In this respect the story fits with The Cop and the Anthem, which makes gentler fun of the same kind of officer.

Its central subject, the clash between friendship and duty, is as old as literature. Greek tragedy is full of characters who must choose between personal loyalty and public law, and the question has returned in countless forms, from stories of soldiers who must judge their comrades to modern crime fiction in which detectives face the criminals they once knew. Henry's treatment is modest and compact, but it touches the same nerve. In particular, it resembles later police stories in which the hardest moment is not the chase but the quiet decision about what to do with someone you love.

The promised reunion is another ancient device. Stories about pledges kept across years, from old ballads to the novels of Dumas, depend on the idea that a promise can bind across time. Henry's twist is that the promise is kept by both friends, but in ways that destroy it. Bob keeps the promise out of sentiment, and Jimmy keeps it out of conscience, and each is rewarded as he deserves. Compared with Henry's other famous stories, this one is leaner and darker. The Gift of the Magi and The Last Leaf end in tender sacrifice, and The Ransom of Red Chief ends in comedy. After Twenty Years ends in an arrest, with a note that carries a shadow of grief. It shows another side of his range.

Why read it now? Because it asks an old question in a fresh and brief form, and because it still works. A reader in the twenty-first century, who may never have heard of Big Joe Brady's restaurant, will recognize the feeling of seeing an old friend after many years and wondering who each of you has become. The story takes five minutes to read, and its question, what would you do in Jimmy's place, can last much longer.

koreaStories.title: The Secret Laboratory of King Sejong & the Invention of Hangul (1443)
